To address this threat, we propose a diagnostic-first methodology that localizes trigger-relevant features through constrained perturbation analysis and detects poisoning-induced behavioral drift by comparison with a distilled baseline model. The proposed methodology further enables targeted mitigation via automated data sanitization or neuron pruning. Our findings expose the operational risks of near-undetectable backdoors and provide a scalable approach to analyzing, quantifying, and mitigating backdoor exposure in AI-based IDS.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 6 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Cyber Security and Resilience

Cryptography and Security.title: No Way To Steal My Face: Proactive Defense Against Identity-Preserving Personalized Generation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Recent advances in diffusion models have enabled high-fidelity, identity-preserving image generation for personalized applications such as digital avatars and virtual try-on systems. However, their reliance on sensitive facial reference images raises growing privacy concerns. Existing defense mechanisms are primarily designed for training-based personalization and struggle to generalize to emerging training-free approaches, due to fundamental differences in their identity integration paradigms. To bridge this gap, we propose IDGuardian-the first generalizable and model-agnostic identity protection framework capable of defending against both training-based and training-free personalization methods. IDGuardian abstracts the personalization process into two critical stages: identity extraction and identity injection. It then introduces crafted adversarial perturbations to simultaneously disrupt both stages. Specifically, it degrades the identity features extracted by external encoders and establishes an adversarial conceptual bridge that misdirects the generative trajectory away from the target identity. Extensive experiments show that IDGuardian effectively protects identity across various personalization pipelines and model architectures, while remaining robust to post-processing, adaptive attacks, and cross-dataset generalization. Our code is available at https://github.com/OpenAscent-L/IDGuardian.git.

Cryptography and Security.title: Towards Secure Agent Skills: Architecture, Threat Taxonomy, and Security Analysis
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agent Skills is an emerging open standard that defines a modular, filesystem-based packaging format enabling LLM-based agents to acquire domain-specific expertise on demand. Despite rapid adoption across multiple agentic platforms and the emergence of large community marketplaces, the security properties of Agent Skills have not been systematically studied. This paper presents a systematization of the security of the Agent Skills framework. We define a threat model for the framework and decompose the full lifecycle of an Agent Skill across four phases---Creation, Distribution, Deployment, and Execution---identifying the structural attack surface each phase introduces. Building on this lifecycle analysis, we construct a threat taxonomy comprising seven categories and nineteen scenarios organized across three attack layers, grounded in both architectural analysis and real-world evidence. Each scenario is annotated with whether the exposure follows from the specification or from the latitude the specification leaves to individual runtimes, with the strength of the public evidence supporting it, and with the feasibility of its mitigation. We map seven documented security incidents onto the taxonomy. Based on these findings, we discuss defense directions for each threat category, identify open research challenges, and provide actionable recommendations for stakeholders. The most severe threats arise from structural properties of the framework itself: the absence of a data-instruction boundary, a single-approval persistent trust model, and a capability declaration mechanism to which the specification attaches no enforcement semantics. None of these is addressable through incremental mitigations alone.

Cryptography and Security.title: X.js: A Live Benchmark for Node.js Taint-Style Vulnerabilities
Cryptography and Security.summary: JavaScript vulnerabilities in npm packages pose a significant risk to the Node$.$js ecosystem, and a growing body of work aims to detect, exploit, and mitigate them. Studying and evaluating this work requires up-to-date collections of real vulnerabilities, yet the most commonly used datasets stop recording vulnerabilities in 2022. We present X$.$js, a live benchmark of real-world Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities covering code and command injection, prototype pollution, and path traversal. Built from 1,738 advisories collected through mid-2026, primarily from the GitHub Advisory Database, X$.$js pairs each vulnerability with precise source and sink locations, a validated executable exploit and its execution trace, and, when available, a patched version of the package. X$.$js supports long-term reproducibility and growth: dependencies are mirrored in a self-hosted registry to guard against package removal from the ecosystem, and dedicated infrastructure generates and validates exploits for newly reported vulnerabilities. The current release contains 1,159 validated exploits for 965 packages. Using X$.$js, we characterize how the frequency, structure, and complexity of Node$.$js taint-style vulnerabilities have evolved over time. We find that these vulnerabilities are increasingly reported in large packages: the median vulnerable package grew from roughly 250 LoC in 2021--2022 to 6,100 LoC in 2026.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, 12 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: EthCluster: An Unsupervised Static Analysis Method for Ethereum Smart Contract
Cryptography and Security.summary: Poorly designed smart contracts are particularly vulnerable, as they may allow attackers to exploit weaknesses and steal the virtual currency they manage. In this study, we train a model using unsupervised learning to identify vulnerabilities in the Solidity source code of Ethereum smart contracts. To address the challenges associated with real-world smart contracts, our training data is derived from actual vulnerability samples obtained from datasets such as SmartBugs Curated and the SolidiFI Benchmark. These datasets enable us to develop a robust unsupervised static analysis method for detecting five specific vulnerabilities: Reentrancy, Access Control, Timestamp Dependency, tx.origin, and Unchecked Low-Level Calls. We employ clustering algorithms to identify outliers, which are subsequently classified as vulnerable smart contracts.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 9 pages, 7 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: AWARE-RG: Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs for Cyber Physical Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Understanding the security posture of cyber physical systems (CPS) requires reasoning across both information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT). However, a security analyst often holds an incomplete, role-specific view of the underlying system which has most likely resulted from their knowledge limited by a need-to-know framework. Such an incomplete view can potentially lead them to incorrectly assess if a cyber attack produces an untoward physical consequence resulting in making uninformed decisions about system resilience. In this work, we present AWARE-RG (Abstraction Aware Explanation of Resiliency Graphs), a semi-automated, human-in-the-loop framework that provides an analyst with a role-bounded, need-to-know explanations of resiliency paths in a CPS. The AWARE-RG abstraction structure is derived using Formal Concept Analysis over MITRE ATT&CK for ICS tactics, ordered by the ICS Cyber Kill Chain. For valid attack-fault queries, plan repair and backward means-end analysis identify the missing dependencies, explain why the physical hazard is reachable, and suggest defensive strategies. For invalid attack-fault queries, AWARE-RG localizes the first abstraction level at which the path fails, and reports confirmed blocking conditions as hardening pointers.

Cryptography and Security.title: Doctor Trigger: A Framework for Release-Bound Face Verification
Cryptography and Security.summary: Face swapping and generative editing enable realistic facial manipulation, while online redistribution complicates publisher oversight of circulating face images. Existing approaches establish provenance, detect manipulation, recover embedded watermarks, verify image integrity, or disrupt unauthorized face manipulation. These capabilities do not necessarily establish consistency with a specific publisher-enrolled release, limiting the evidence available for verification and human review. To address this gap, we introduce Doctor Trigger, a framework for verifying circulating faces against private publisher-held release records. Before publication, the publisher embeds a weak keyed Fourier-phase signal in each face while preserving visual fidelity and stores its spectral reference. Afterward, verification compares the circulating face with that reference and uses key projection to measure retention of the release-specific signal. Therefore, relation and key evidence jointly help publishers identify suspicious copies for review, potentially reducing the circulation of manipulated images. Experimental results across FF++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF show that spectral agreement separates tested face swaps and generative manipulations from enrolled releases, while the keyed signal distinguishes published versions from their unreleased originals under the evaluated key-preserving benign transformations. Doctor Trigger complements provenance metadata with release-specific face verification and record-linked evidence for further assessment.
Cryptography and Security.comment: View our project page: https://ming053l.github.io/Doctor-Trigger/

Cryptography and Security.title: A Graph-Based Analysis of Comparability, Scale, and Attribution in Private Transformer Inference
Cryptography and Security.summary: Rising privacy concerns around large language models have accelerated research in private Transformer inference (PTI). Synthesizing the empirical claims in this line of research, however, is hindered by multi-dimensional cryptographic progress and inconsistent evaluation contracts. In this work, we systematize the field by constructing an empirical graph of 62 PTI systems, mapping system attributes to node features and evaluation compatibility to edges. A three-tiered analysis of this graph illuminates the state of private inference. Node-level attribution shows that cryptographic progress drives performance gains across most systems, yet always co-occurs with other factors (model fidelity, hardware, cost accounting). Edge-level auditing shows that only 1 of 1891 candidate system pairs is directly comparable under shared assumptions. Finally, graph-level analysis shows that the scaling frontier of private inference has plateaued at 13B parameters and projects the cost of deploying current PTI techniques on production-scale Transformers. Overall, this graph-based framework equips the community to evaluate PTI claims transparently and channel technical speedups into deployment-scale private inference.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Penetration Testing for System Security: Methods and Practical Approaches
Cryptography and Security.summary: Penetration testing refers to the process of simulating hacker attacks to evaluate the security of information systems . This study aims not only to clarify the theoretical foundations of penetration testing but also to explain and demonstrate the complete testing process, including how network system administrators may simulate attacks using various penetration testing methods. Methodologically, the paper outlines the five basic stages of a typical penetration test: intelligence gathering, vulnerability scanning, vulnerability exploitation, privilege escalation, and post-exploitation activities. In each phase, specific tools and techniques are examined in detail, along with practical guidance on their use. To enhance the practical relevance of the study, the paper also presents a real-life case study, illustrating how a complete penetration test is conducted in a real-world environment. Through this case, readers can gain insights into the detailed procedures and applied techniques, thereby deepening their understanding of the practical value of penetration testing. Finally, the paper summarizes the importance and necessity of penetration testing in securing information systems and maintaining network integrity, and it explores future trends and development directions for the field. Overall, the findings of this paper offer valuable references for both researchers and practitioners, contributing meaningfully to the improvement of penetration testing practices and the advancement of cybersecurity as a whole.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 17 pages,4 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: SecReason: Vulnerability Detection and In-Stream Self-Repair for LLM Code Generation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language models (LLMs) may introduce security vulnerabilities into generated code, which can persist into production when verification focuses on functional correctness. Existing defenses act before, during, or after generation, but none inspects the code during generation. Security prompts and retrieved security knowledge act before any code exists, constrained decoding limits token choices but cannot guide repair, and post-hoc repair must regenerate the full response. Reasoning LLMs draft code early in their streamed chain of thought, and in this pre-delivery window the code exists only inside the reasoning stream. We present SecReason, an in-stream defense that monitors this window. Dual-track incremental scanning applies security rules, checking each statement as it is emitted and tracing dataflows across the accumulated code. When a security rule fires, SecReason interrupts generation, inserts an in-stream warning, and resumes decoding, so the model repairs the draft within the same reasoning trace without regenerating the full response. On tasks where unassisted generation introduces vulnerabilities, \system raises the share of runs delivering secure and functionally correct code from below 15\% to 72.8\%--98.1\% on \tool{CWEval} and \tool{SecCodeBench}. \system consumes fewer tokens than post-hoc repair, and when security rules misfire on secure code, it limits the functional regressions from false warnings.

Cryptography and Security.title: SkillScreen: High-Recall Screening of Malicious Agent Skills with Decision Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agent skills turn natural-language instructions into actions, creating a security challenge: legitimate automation and malicious behaviour can look deceptively similar. A practical screen must catch nearly every attack while keeping the review load manageable. We present SkillScreen, a compact decision model trained to score skill maliciousness directly from SKILL$.$md in a single forward pass. On MaliciousSkillBench, SkillScreen flags 20-25% of benign skills at 99% recall on unseen attack families, substantially fewer than the word-level classifier and prompted LLM judges tested. Under the same training protocol, it also generalizes better than a fully fine-tuned encoder to unseen sources. Yet unfamiliar benign sources sharply increase false positives, showing that recognizing new attacks does not ensure reliable screening of new skill collections. Our results demonstrate the value of task-trained decision models for high-recall skill screening. Project page: https://jerroldh.github.io/SkillScreen-webpage/
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, including references and appendices

Cryptography and Security.title: Mission (Im)Possible: Towards Autonomous Discovery of Autopilot Logic Flaws in Open-Source Drone Frameworks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Autonomous drones are increasingly deployed in safety-critical tasks, yet their autopilot software can still contain subtle logic flaws that lead to unsafe behaviors. These flaws are difficult to discover with existing techniques because they often depend on semantic relationships across modules, commands, and runtime state, and rarely manifest as crashes or detectable failures. With recent advances in LLMs, we observe that, when equipped with essential domain knowledge and carefully crafted context, LLMs demonstrate strong capabilities in understanding the high-level semantics of autopilot systems, making them suitable for logic flaw discovery. However, LLMs are limited by their context and can be biased to the vulnerabilities frequently occurs in training dataset, while logic flaws often require higher-level semantic bug oracles to identify their existence. To bridge the gap, we present Impossible Mission Finder (IMF), a multi-agent system combining static analysis, dynamic execution and log analysis, that supports fully automated identify, test, and validate logic flaws in autonomous vehicles. IMF primarily contains three LLM agents, it first uses the auditor agent to propose logic flaw hypothesis based on carefully-crafted program slicing, then it launches tester agents to write and execute test cases for each candidate, and finally it spawns the log analyzer agent to validate the execution log against the flaw hypothesis. This enables IMF dynamically validate bug oracles in a case-by-case manner, making it suitable for discovering logic flaws that do not have a unified pattern. We evaluated IMF on two widely used open-source autopilot systems, PX4 and Ardupilot, leading to 105 previously unknown logic flaws, that can cause unsafe behaviors including mission interruption failures, invalid actions, entering into restricted fly zones etc.

Cryptography and Security.title: Characterizing Statistical Separability in TP-CRIV for Probabilistic AI Models
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Third-party challenge-response identity verification (TP-CRIV) enables an independent verifier to assess whether a claimant possesses a model identical to a remotely deployed model without directly accessing the reference model. However, for probabilistic AI models, repeated executions of the same query may produce different outputs and therefore different verification observations. This raises the question of how such stochastic evidence should be accumulated and how much evidence is required for reliable verification.
  In this work, we characterize statistical separability in TP-CRIV of probabilistic AI models. Specifically, we relate challenge-wise behavior of matching and non-matching provers to verification-level separability. The characterization explicitly describes how the numbers of independent challenges and repeated responses affect detection performance and enables the verification budget required for a target AUC to be estimated. We instantiate the proposed characterization for LLMs using open-ended challenges. The experiments demonstrate matching-non-matching separation, close agreement between theoretical and empirical AUCs, and consistent estimates of the minimum verification budgets. These results provide a statistical basis for relating probabilistic model behavior to verification-level separability and the evidence required for third-party verification.

Cryptography and Security.title: Few-Shot Truly Benign DPO Attack for Jailbreaking LLMs
Cryptography and Security.summary: Fine-tuning APIs make frontier LLMs easy to customize, but they can also weaken safety alignment during fine-tuning. While prior work shows that benign supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can reduce refusal behavior, deployed fine-tuning pipelines increasingly support preference-based objectives, whose safety risks remain less understood. We show that Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) introduces a stronger and harder-to-audit failure mode. We propose a truly benign DPO attack using only 10 harmless preference pairs, the minimum data scale accepted by OpenAI's fine-tuning service. Each pair contains a benign prompt, a normal helpful answer as the preferred response, and a refusal as the dispreferred response. Unlike prior benign fine-tuning attacks, our data exhibits no suspicious behavior: it is practically indistinguishable from the fine-tuning request of a legitimate user seeking to reduce over-refusal, making harmful intent almost impossible to infer from the request alone. Nevertheless, because DPO directly optimizes the model to prefer helpful answers over refusals, this seemingly benign objective broadly suppresses refusal behavior and transfers to harmful prompts outside the fine-tuning data. Across OpenAI models supporting DPO fine-tuning, our attack achieves attack success rates of 59.13% on GPT-4o, 70.20% on GPT-4.1, 54.80% on GPT-4.1-mini, and 81.73% on GPT-4.1-nano, at costs of only \$1.7, \$1.7, \$0.3, and \$0.1. Moreover, on open-weight models that do not impose minimum data requirements, we find that this effect can emerge from even a single benign preference pair.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: What You Sign Is Not What You Run: The Verifiability Gap in Quantized LLM Supply Chains
Cryptography and Security.summary: Model signing authenticates the full-precision weights W an LLM is released with, yet users run a quantized artifact Q whose producing transformation is not uniquely determined under current disclosure. We separate the non-environment inputs from the execution environment E and measure a quantity that, to our knowledge, has not been measured before: the Independent Verifiability Rate (IVR), the fraction of a popularity-sampled GGUF ecosystem that a third party can re-derive bit-for-bit. Across the 200 most-downloaded Hugging Face GGUF repositories (198 in scope), no artifact or model card records the build environment, so under a recorded-inputs protocol the IVR is 0/198. Yet the artifacts are not irreproducible. On four in-sample repositories that disclose their inputs, the card's information alone reproduces no Q4_K_M file, but two coordinates the card omits - the build's floating-point-contraction setting and, for hybrid models, the per-tensor quantization recipe - re-derive 7/8 target-quant files bit-for-bit on x86 (5/8 on arm64); the fp16 re-derives from the provider's checkpoint, but the calibration imatrix must be shipped and hash-bound, since recomputing it did not match. An older release additionally pins the instruction set and did not re-derive. Reproducing the divergence reported with llama.cpp PR #25353, we show that E is a necessary coordinate and that one compiler setting yields a unique output across the tested platforms at negligible quality cost (+0.06% perplexity). As a security characterization, benign floating-point non-determinism separates from uniformly placed nibble-flip tampering above a detection floor that grows with the environments a verifier must allow, but a targeted embedding edit evades the statistic, so the proposed protocol rests on exact re-derivation; adversarial-fp16 attacks lie outside it. We release the audit data and a re-runnable harness.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 15 pages, 3 figures, 4 tables. Artifact: https://github.com/Rlonglong/gguf-verifiability-artifact

Cryptography and Security.title: Quantum-Resilient Secure Protocol for Decentralized Edge-IoT Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: The rise of quantum computing presents substantial challenges to the security of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) energy trading systems. This paper introduces an innovative mutual authenticated session key agreement protocol aimed at protecting edge-IoT P2P energy trading communications in the quantum era. Each peer is an IoT-enabled smart metering device that is registered by an edge registration authority and acts as both producer and consumer. The proposed protocol incorporates CRYSTALS-Kyber's quantum-resistant cryptographic suite to guarantee the authenticity and confidentiality of negotiated session keys in the presence of quantum threats. Furthermore, it leverages the Hedera Hashgraph public blockchain, which is recognized for its quantum-resilient design, to ensure transparency and support efficient revocation mechanisms. Extensive comparative analyses have been conducted to demonstrate the protocol's superiority over existing alternatives, including both traditional schemes based on classical cryptography and emerging early-stage post-quantum approaches, in terms of performance and security features. By combining robust security and high efficiency, the proposed protocol fosters the development of resilient decentralized energy markets, paving the way for secure and sustainable energy distribution in the future.

Cryptography and Security.title: NOMOS: Compiling Written Policies into Statically Verified Tool-Call Gates for LLM Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Tool-using LLM agents violate the policies they are deployed to enforce, often silently. Prior defenses hand-write rules, query an LLM verifier per action, or compile policies through heavyweight formal machinery. Naive compilation fails: extracted rules block the tool satisfying their own precondition, or read arguments their tool lacks. NOMOS, a four-pass compiler, turns a natural-language policy into a deterministic tool-call gate; static verification with tool-schema-level checks alone (no prover, solver, or LLM) repairs or rejects 37% (airline) and 13% (retail) of candidates, without which most shipped rules are inoperable. Replaying compiled rules over undefended transcripts flags bindings that refuse legitimate work (a development binding refused 95.9% of task-passing calls); no evaluation binding is flagged. On $τ^2$-bench the gate cuts violations of reference-encoded clauses among state-changing calls from 66.3% to 2.6% (airline) and 30.8% to 6.9% (retail), raising airline task success significantly for $2 \le k \le 4$; a 26B on-premise compilation is not significantly worse than hand-written or frontier-compiled rules. Unlike AgentDojo's shipped defenses, it reaches a zero attack success rate (ASR) on banking, where nine attack families collapse onto three structural rules. On the other three suites its ASR is at most 3.6%, from goals with no tool call to govern and one write admitted by a binding weaker than its clause; a second agent model, Llama-3.3-70B, reproduces the effect on both benchmarks. Decisions take microseconds without an LLM call, at a domain-dependent benign-utility cost; compilation runs on-premise on open-weight gemma-4-26B.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 28 pages, 5 figures, 19 tables. Submitted to IEEE Access

Cryptography and Security.title: MMA-SafetyBench: A Benchmark for Multimodal Agent Safety Evaluation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Multimodal agents increasingly rely on visual interfaces to perceive state and select actions, creating an attack surface not captured by text-only safety evaluations. We study Visual Semantic Hijacking, in which deceptive but semantically meaningful interface elements, such as forged system alerts, cause an agent to depart from its authorized task. We propose a trajectory-guided procedure that identifies candidate injection points and inserts reproducible visual payloads into the observation stream. Using this procedure, we construct MMA-SafetyBench, which contains 1,083 adversarial trajectories across web automation, desktop GUI control, mobile navigation, document understanding, and video processing. Across nine evaluated models, Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaches 87.96%, while Semantic Compromise Rate (SCR) reaches 98.09%. A 1--3--5 scoring scheme distinguishes target-matching outputs, semantic disruption without a target match, and successful preservation of the benign task. Controls covering all nine models and five domains show that attacks persist under neutral prompts. A safety-priority prompt lowers ASR without eliminating the failure mode.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 19 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations and Datasets Track (Poster)

Cryptography and Security.title: SecJev: Bringing Security Expertise to System One Decision Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Security workflows need models that turn complex observations and explicit policies into decisions. System One models introduced by Jev return typed predictions and probabilities; security specialization supplies the domain expertise behind those predictions. We introduce SecJev, to our knowledge the first family of Jev-style decision models specialized for security, spanning 0.8B to 9B parameters. Built on Kev's single-pass candidate scorer, SecJev learns Boolean, choice, and ordered decisions from text, telemetry, and observation histories. We develop SecJev-Corpus to unify source-label prediction and explicit-policy evaluation across 14 tasks and eight sources. It covers tool outputs, traffic, federated updates, consensus, authentication, and vehicle messages. Scene-weighted training adapts the models across these domains while preserving a shared typed decision interface. Security specialization improves every model in the family; SecJev-0.8B outperforms general Kev-9B by 20.51 percentage points in task-macro accuracy. At 0.8B and 4B, SecJev achieves accuracy and latency close to answer-only generative fine-tuning with lower peak allocated GPU memory. SecJev-4B improves on Kev-4B and security-trained generation in prompt-injection and traffic transfer tests. We release adapters, decision heads, SecJev-Corpus, and training and inference code.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 16 pages, 1 figure; updated experiments and analysis, revised presentation, and streamlined appendix

Cryptography and Security.title: Differentially Private Learning of Markov Chains: Near-Optimal Sample Complexity for Item and User Level Privacy
Cryptography and Security.summary: Sequential data such as documents, conversations, and trajectories are naturally partitioned across users, motivating privacy guarantees that protect each user's entire trajectory. We initiate the study of privately estimating the transition matrix of a discrete ergodic Markov chain from N independent trajectories of length T, with arbitrary initial distributions, under maximum row-wise ell 1 error. Besides N, T, and the number of states, our bounds depend on the minimum stationary probability and the pseudo-spectral gap, which govern state coverage and mixing. Under item-level privacy, we give upper and lower bounds that separate the costs of sampling, state occupancy and mixing, and privacy. Under user-level privacy, we reduce the problem for sufficiently long trajectories to private product distribution estimation. Along the way, we establish optimal user-level private bounds for estimating products of discrete distributions, which may be of independent interest. In the user level setting, our bounds are nearly tight in the large T regime, whereas in the item-level setting, our bounds as tight up-to a non-private term.

Cryptography and Security.title: AutoPoly-HE: Autonomous Design of Polynomial Activations for Privacy-Preserving Encrypted Inference
Cryptography and Security.summary: Privacy-preserving machine learning has become critical for deploying artificial intelligence in sensitive domains such as healthcare, finance, and infrastructure monitoring. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure inference on encrypted data. Despite its advantages, HE is not compatible with nonlinear activation functions found in machine learning models. Existing methods mitigate this problem by manually designing polynomial approximations for these activation functions. However, these functions do not account for the differences in dataset characteristics or model architecture. Furthermore, these functions are also limited to the accuracies of convolutional neural network (CNN) models. In this work, we propose an autonomous framework that selects polynomial activation functions tailored to each dataset and model. Using this framework, we analyze the interdependence between polynomial activation design and model architecture by evaluating several CNN ResNet and Vision Transformer models across multiple datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework generalizes across multiple architectures, including ResNet-18, ResNet-34, ResNet-50, ViT-S/16, ViT-B/16, and ViT-L/16. Across all datasets, transformer-based models maintain higher accuracy under polynomial approximation, while convolutional models exhibit increased degradation as task complexity grows. In addition, latency analysis reveals that the proposed CLS token based inference pipeline significantly reduces computational overhead by eliminating depth-dependent operations, shifting the primary cost to encryption and decryption. These findings demonstrate that the proposed method not only adapts polynomial activations across architectures, but also enables efficientencrypted inference through both activation design and pipeline optimization.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at IEEE GLOBECOM 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Limitations on Autoregressive Token Generation via Sequential Sampling
Cryptography and Security.summary: We study autoregressive token generation through the notion of sequential samplers: A circuit that samples the next symbol only given the previous ones and possibly a small amount of state. We show that (1) a sequential sampler with $k$ bits of state can be simulated by a stateless one at a roughly $O(2^{k})$ size overhead; (2) efficient insertional sampling (Stern, Chan, Kiros, Uszkoreit, ICML 2019) is more powerful than efficient sequential sampling in any fixed order; (3) sequential samplers with small state cannot establish certain forms of covert cryptographic channels. Result (1), together with the pseudoentropy vs. sequential sampleability duality of Vadhan and Zheng (STOC 2012), characterizes efficient sequential sampleability with small state. Result (3) provides a potential safety mechanism against subliminal coordination among malicious LLM agents.
Cryptography and Security.comment: In submission to ICLR 2027

Cryptography and Security.title: Practical wavelength selection for quantum-augmented networks over shared optical fiber
Cryptography and Security.summary: In a quantum augmented network, sharing optical fiber with classical traffic requires quantum wavelength selection to balance logical fidelity, block acceptance, and classical data reception. Here we develop a wavelength-selection framework for an error-corrected three-stage quantum communication protocol. Under a thermal-background model with independent errors, an ideal one-photon receiver, and ideal recovery, we derive an accepted qubit channel and a key-independent lower bound on logical entanglement fidelity. Combining this bound with block acceptance gives an entanglement-fidelity yield bound, which we maximize over evaluated wavelengths subject to fidelity and classical link-budget requirements. For the Steane [[7,1,3]] code at 5 km per traversal and -10 dBm per classical channel, the largest fidelity certificate occurs near 1537 nm, whereas the largest yield bound occurs near 1551 nm. Along the 1.25 Gb/s classical link budget with 0.2% base error, the optimized yield bound falls below 10^-6 near 10 km per traversal, while fidelity remains certified at 0.99 or higher at longer spans. These results distinguish fidelity and yield constraints and identify certified operating regions for quantum-augmented networks sharing optical fiber.

Cryptography and Security.title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
Cryptography and Security.summary: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

Cryptography and Security.title: Does Client Diversity Protect the Lightning Network? Evidence from the 2026 Core Lightning Shutdown
Cryptography and Security.summary: Client diversity is often cited as the Lightning Network's defence against a bug in any one implementation, yet LND runs 84% of public nodes and holds 84% of public channel capacity, a share that has barely moved since 2023. We test what diversity buys with a natural experiment. On 26 August 2026, amid security fixes in every implementation, Core Lightning (CLN) maintainers told operators who could not upgrade to disconnect their nodes. Using 805 daily gossip snapshots, 132,360 on-chain channel closes and a client classifier validated against self-identifying aliases and against the wallet that builds each node's funding transactions, we find that 22% of CLN nodes went dark overnight, ten times the usual rate, mostly Tor-reachable ones; a third were still dark five weeks later. The rest of the network barely noticed. Reachability among all node pairs fell by 7.8 percentage points, a loss exceeded in 4 of 94 ordinary two-day windows and half that of a Tor denial-of-service wave in July, while among CLN pairs it fell by 24.5 points, more than in any ordinary window. Calibrated failure scenarios explain the containment: the blast radius depends on whether a failure reaches the hubs, not on how many nodes run the failing software. Losing ACINQ's Eclair node alone costs the surviving network four times the reachability lost with all 619 routable CLN nodes, and minority clients' reliance on LND for connectivity is what their size implies; CLN nodes in fact peer with each other more than chance. Diversity statistics that count nodes mislead; the quantity to track is which software the hubs run.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 11 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables. Code and aggregate data: https://github.com/bitcoindatalabs/ln-client-diversity

Cryptography and Security.title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
Cryptography and Security.summary: We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors. An LLM attacker edits a transcript so that the agent causes a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent. The edited actions are never executed, so we use an LLM verifier to reject attacks that are inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar. The attacker revises the edit until the monitor no longer flags it. We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff, optimizing against our own monitors. Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors. Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer. We therefore demonstrate that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures of the developer's monitor. We expect to find more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure, with frontier attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. Developers can use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators can use them as counterexamples to safety claims about the monitor.

Cryptography and Security.title: From Detection to Decision: Calibration and Deferral for Prompt-Injection Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Prompt-injection defenses are commonly evaluated as binary detectors, although deployed LLM applications must make operational decisions about whether to allow, block, or escalate potentially malicious inputs. Recent probabilistic decision models aim to support such decisions through calibrated confidence estimates, but their reliability under distribution shift remains uncertain. We evaluate a native probabilistic decision model (Jev), two Llama Prompt Guard 2 classifiers (22M and 86M), and an LLM-based judge on 47,611 held-out examples spanning direct and indirect prompt injections, hard-benign inputs, obfuscation, and distribution shift. Using separate development and calibration splits, we assess detection performance, probability calibration, and allow-block-defer policies under a frozen evaluation protocol. The LLM judge achieves the highest overall discrimination (AUROC 0.897), followed by Jev (0.871), Prompt Guard 2 86M (0.757), and Prompt Guard 2 22M (0.714). However, Jev's native probabilities do not consistently outperform post-hoc calibrated classifier scores, and temperature scaling improves calibration without improving discrimination. At an empirical false-negative-rate target of 1%, all evaluated gate-reviewer systems require more than 91.8% escalation and incur substantial false-positive rates. These findings demonstrate that probabilistic outputs alone do not establish reliable security decisions under distribution shift. Effective LLM security systems must jointly evaluate detection, calibration, reviewer behavior, and operational decision policies.

Cryptography and Security.title: Thinking in Graphs: Neo4j-Backed Exploit-Chain Reasoning for LLM Penetration-Testing Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex can drive penetration-testing tools, but they reason about an engagement as a flat list of findings in a context window. Attackers think in graphs: isolated low-severity exposures turn catastrophic once chained through credential capture, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. This gap feeds a common belief that AI agents cannot truly chain exploitation; we argue this describes the flat context window, not the model. We present ChainGraph, a pattern that externalizes exploit-chain reasoning into a Neo4j property graph wired to an off-the-shelf agent via the Model Context Protocol, no bespoke harness. Findings, attack steps, credentials, assets, and tamper-evident evidence receipts are typed nodes with pre/post-condition edges; JSON/Markdown holds documentary memory while Neo4j holds reasoning memory. We formalize five operator questions (next-step inference, entry-to-crown-jewel pathing, combined-severity promotion, evidence provenance, and chokepoint identification) as reusable Cypher and Graph Data Science queries, plus a chain-severity score distinct from per-finding local severity. On a synthetic multi-forest Active Directory engagement modeled on GOAD, in live Neo4j with GDS, three findings rated Medium in isolation become Critical once their path to the forest root is materialized, and betweenness centrality names the best chain break-points. Scoping each decision to a graph result rather than re-reading the engagement cut the reasoning payload by about 98% on a token proxy. We give a reproducible setup for Claude Code and Codex. Results are illustrative single-run measurements, not a benchmark.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 16 pages, 7 figures, 9 tables, 18 code listings

Cryptography and Security.title: Declared but Unaccountable: Measuring the Seller-Identity Gap in Advertising Supply-Chain Transparency
Cryptography and Security.summary: Public advertising transparency relies on a minimum accountability condition: an account authorized by a publisher in ads$.$txt or app-ads$.$txt should appear in the applicable sellers$.$json registry. When an available registry omits the declared seller ID, the authorization remains visible and machine-readable, but its public verification path breaks. We call this failure the seller-identity gap. We measure the gap using 233.4 million normalized advertising-transparency records and an absent-only, coverage-aware evidence rule. A declaration enters the numerator only when the applicable registry is available and omits its seller ID; unavailable, malformed, confidential, and other non-evaluable states remain separate. The resulting row-level floor is 24.25% in a high-popularity, low-removal reference population and 30.71% among publishers associated with at least 100 copyright-removal requests, a 6.45 percentage-point increase. The gap then remains near one third at stricter cumulative thresholds. Standardizing the populations to common weights over 1,469 shared ad systems reduces the primary contrast to 4.65 points: about 72% remains within systems, while 28% forms a composition-associated residual. We connect these population estimates to recurring seller-account coordinates, byte-identical declaration configurations, and provenance-bearing case packets. We frame this declaration-centered investigative use of public advertising records as Ad Transparency Intelligence: it reconstructs declared supply-chain relationships, identifies where public verification stops, and prioritizes evidence for corroboration without equating correlation with attribution. Advertising transparency supports accountability and investigation only when visible authorizations remain publicly verifiable.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables. Preprint

Cryptography and Security.title: GhostLock: Learning-Assisted Blind GPS Signal Nullification Without Victim-Side Information
Cryptography and Security.summary: The Global Positioning System (GPS) provides critical positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services for numerous safety- and mission-critical applications, making it an attractive target for physical-layer attacks. While GPS spoofing and jamming have been extensively studied, GPS Signal Nullification (GSN)-a physical-layer attack that suppresses authentic satellite signals through destructive interference prior to acquisition-remains largely unexplored. Existing wireless signal nullification techniques target conventional communication systems and typically require victim-side information, such as channel estimates or synchronization parameters, making them impractical for GPS. Furthermore, many GPS spoofing defenses assume authentic satellite signals remain available as trusted references, an assumption invalidated by GSN. To address this gap, we present GhostLock, a learning-assisted blind GSN framework requiring only an approximate target location estimate. GhostLock integrates a Blind Adaptive Filter (BAF) with a deep learning-based synchronization module to generate and align an anti-signal using only the attacker's locally received GPS signal, eliminating the need for victim-side observations. We implement GhostLock on a real-time software-defined radio (SDR) platform using GPS-SDR-SIM and GNU Radio. Experimental results demonstrate successful suppression of GPS signal acquisition, establishing the feasibility of blind GSN and motivating new detection and mitigation techniques for this emerging GPS threat model.

Cryptography and Security.title: Performance Characterization of Pulsar's Software-defined Watermark Verifier
Cryptography and Security.summary: Pulsar provides the world's most secure PNT service by incorporating a Combinatorial Watermark into its ranging service. Under conservative signal conditions, Pulsar's Combinatorial Watermark, where 21 ranging code chips are inverted among the 1023, provides 32-bit authentication security each second. In this work, we present our software-defined radio (SDR) implementation of the Pulsar watermark processor. We discuss various threat models, multiple receiver architectures, implications to the receiver, and results from using Pulsar's SDR processing watermarked signals daily from the Pulsar-0 mission. Our results demonstrate the feasible implementation of Pulsar's watermark verification process in commercial GNSS receivers. This is an important milestone in making Xona's Pulsar service available to customers later this year after deployment of our first four production satellites.

Cryptography and Security.title: Privacy-Preserving Text Inference for Health-Misinformation Classification and Semantic Retrieval
Cryptography and Security.summary: Health-misinformation analysis presents a dual challenge: misleading claims can affect public well-being, while systems designed to detect them may expose sensitive user-submitted text. This motivates privacy-preserving inference for public-health applications in which user queries may contain confidential medical information and trained models and reference databases are maintained on organizational servers. We design a privacy-preserving text inference framework based on CKKS homomorphic encryption for health-misinformation classification and semantic retrieval. The classification pipeline fuses BioBERT embeddings, PCA-reduced MPNet embeddings, and SVD-reduced TF-IDF features, while the retrieval pipeline combines MPNet embeddings with ISCC-SCT semantic fingerprints through late fusion. We evaluate predictive performance and benchmark plaintext versus ciphertext-based execution. The hybrid classifier achieved an accuracy of 0.971 and a macro-F1 score of 0.950, with identical reported metrics under plaintext and ciphertext-based inference. The hybrid late-fusion similarity model achieved a Pearson correlation of 0.8691 with human sentence-pair similarity scores on STS-B. For ciphertext-based retrieval, we evaluated naive and optimized implementations. The optimized implementation uses CKKS single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) packing to compute and return multiple similarity scores together, reducing single-query latency over 7,128 indexed items from 222.028 to 5.168 seconds and communication overhead from 6.11 GB to 2.13 MB. These findings demonstrate the technical feasibility of privacy-preserving text inference for health-misinformation applications and characterize its predictive utility and efficiency trade-offs.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Published as a conference paper at SMASH 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Privacy Foundations for Multi-Institutional Scientific Artificial Intelligence
Cryptography and Security.summary: Scientific artificial intelligence (AI), spanning foundation models (FMs) to federated data-analysis pipelines, is becoming shared infrastructure across national laboratories, universities, hospitals, and industrial partners. This collaboration creates privacy risks whose natural unit is often an institution's participation, research strategy, or technical capability rather than a single record. Differential privacy (DP), federated learning (FL), secure computation, trusted execution, and provenance each protect parts of the stack, but their guarantees rarely compose across mixed-trust institutions, access tiers, and autonomous agents. This perspective recasts privacy for scientific AI as an assurance problem defined by six elements: protected asset, observer, channel, permitted disclosure, guarantee, and evidence. We demonstrate the framing through a claim register for a composite cross-institutional scenario and use it to assess the model lifecycle. Two of the resulting gaps are specific to leadership-class facilities: scheduler, allocation, and telemetry metadata expose an institution's resource posture, and instrument-attached control loops leak research strategy through timing and contention on shared accelerators. We identify six research priorities: institution-level guarantees, agent-communication privacy, cross-tier information flow, privacy-compatible reproducibility, leadership-scale accounting, and instrument side channels. The contribution is a common form for stating, comparing, and auditing claims whose guarantees otherwise remain fragmented across the scientific AI stack.

Cryptography and Security.title: INFUSE: A Unified Surface Benchmark for Indirect Prompt Injection in Agentic Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM-based agents increasingly execute long-horizon, end-to-end workflows involving shell commands, code modification, dependency installation, and interaction with remote services. This growing autonomy expands their exposure to indirect prompt injection (IPI), where adversarial instructions embedded in external content are interpreted as legitimate task directives. Existing evaluations, however, often focus on isolated malicious strings, single-step tool calls, or narrowly scoped agent configurations. We introduce INFUSE, an end-to-end benchmark for evaluating IPI throughout the lifecycle of long-horizon agent workflows. INFUSE comprises 40 realistic tasks and a structured taxonomy of 56 attack scenarios spanning five threat categories. Attacks are injected through realistic interaction surfaces encountered during task execution, extending evaluation beyond attacks placed only in initial prompts or isolated tool interactions. We evaluate 19 LLMs from the GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, Gemma, and Qwen families, producing 41,824 adversarial trajectories (26,220 without defenses) and 720 benign reference runs. Across the benchmark, mean attack success reaches 19.6% under LLM-based evaluation and 15.4% under heuristic verification, with per-model ASR-L ranging from 3.2% to 41.9%. Existing guard models provide limited protection, while prompt-level instructional hardening reduces mean attack success from 58.2% to 14.3%, revealing substantial but model-dependent security-utility trade-offs. Our code is available at https://github.com/judydnguyen/infuse.

Cryptography and Security.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences.
  A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Author's manuscript. Final publication is available at Springer via https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-95-8617-2_4

Cryptography and Security.title: Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields: Evidence-Grounded Selective Safety for Vision-Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Representation-based safety defenses for vision-language models (VLMs) often learn to separate harmful from benign inputs, but separation alone does not establish what a risk score means or when it should be trusted. We introduce Counterfactual Neighborhood Risk Fields (CNRF), an evidence-grounded framework for selective VLM safety. CNRF constructs context-matched benign-harmful counterfactual pairs, uses their representation differences as capability-related risk directions, and estimates neighborhood support separately from risk. This separation prevents unfamiliarity from being conflated with harmfulness and enables selective intervention rather than blanket rejection. A victim-adaptive interface accommodates different safety observations across VLM architectures and routes selected requests for same-victim response review, which either releases acceptable candidates or produces constrained alternatives with reduced harmful capability. Across three VLMs and five multimodal jailbreak families, CNRF achieves 86.06-89.30% macro defense success rate while retaining substantial benign-task utility. Controlled experiments further show that query-matched references and preserved context-direction correspondence materially improve risk ranking in the low-false-positive regime. CNRF thus reframes representation-based VLM safety from learning harmfulness boundaries to constructing applicable evidence for selective risk decisions.

Cryptography and Security.title: CascadeLedger: Counterfactual Auditing of Information and Resource Integrity in LLM Cascades
Cryptography and Security.summary: We introduce CascadeLedger, a counterfactual execution-audit framework for budgeted language-model cascades. The protocol enforces call-before-read semantics, binds successful reads to service and cache identities, records availability and component-wise budget transitions, and freezes the event trace before any target or task scorer is joined. The central object is aggregate-equivalent trace validity: two executions can share a final answer, declared resource projection, and service histogram while differing in whether their routing decisions used only legitimately observable information. We complement single-trace invariants with counterfactual prefix non-interference (CPNI), which couples a visible prefix and policy randomness while changing only a declared hidden family. The counterfactual influence frontier (CIF) localizes the earliest violating prefix and a minimal hidden witness; projection-preserving adversarial mutation (PPAM) searches for invalid traces that remain acceptable to a non-counterfactual checker. Across frozen-cache, independently generated, and serving evaluations, the two-layer audit reports a clean false-positive rate of 0.0000, detects 0.9983 of serialized faults and 0.9982 of unlogged hidden-read faults, and changes 0.3403 of corrupted quality-resource conclusions after deterministic recomputation. The online recorder and offline CPNI audit have separate overhead measurements. Learned routing and semantic verification provide downstream compatibility studies under the same execution contract.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 38 pages, 6 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network for Interpretable Big Data Analytics and Secure Cloud Decision-Making Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Big data analytics supports modern intelligent systems, but model complexity and limited transparency can undermine interpretability, trust, and security in decision-making. This paper presents the Hybrid DeepXAI Fusion Network, a deep learning framework that integrates temporal, relational, and contextual features with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) mechanisms. The architecture combines one-dimensional convolutional neural networks (1D-CNNs) for temporal feature extraction, Transformer encoders for contextual modeling, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for inter-feature dependency analysis. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates these representations. Class Activation Mapping (CAM) and an explanation loss are incorporated to improve interpretability and explanation consistency. The framework is designed for deployment in a federated cloud architecture, using homomorphic encryption and blockchain-based auditing to support data privacy and accountability. Experimental evaluations across healthcare, finance, and energy datasets report 98.42% accuracy, 97.9% precision, 98.1% recall, and a 98.0% F1-score, outperforming the evaluated CNN-LSTM, Transformer-only, and XGBoost baselines. Under projected gradient descent (PGD) adversarial perturbations, the model reportedly retains accuracy above 91.5%. Scalability experiments report throughput of 80,000 messages per second with latency below 200 milliseconds. These results suggest that the proposed framework has potential for interpretable and secure cloud-based decision-support systems.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Six authors. Corresponding author: B. Nancharaiah

Cryptography and Security.title: Empirical Evaluation of Machine Learning for Cloud Cryptojacking Detection: Effects of Preprocessing and Evaluation Protocols
Cryptography and Security.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has been widely applied to cloud cryptojacking detection. Classical machine learning models remain among the most widely used approaches for cloud cryptojacking detection. This paper presents an empirical evaluation of six widely used classical machine learning models for AI-based cloud cryptojacking detection under different preprocessing and evaluation settings. Because no public cloud-native cryptojacking dataset is currently available, experiments were conducted using two publicly available proxy datasets, DS2OS and NSL-KDD. The evaluated models include Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, Gradient Boosting, Decision Tree, and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Experimental results show that preprocessing choices and evaluation protocols have a measurable impact on model performance. On DS2OS, removing identifier-related features reduced the accuracy of most models to approximately 96%, while KNN achieved higher accuracy with lower attack recall. On NSL-KDD, models obtained 77 to 80\% accuracy on the official test set containing unseen attack types, compared with above 99.5% under a random train-test split. Attack-class precision, recall, and Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) further provide complementary insights into classifier performance beyond overall accuracy. The results provide an empirical comparison of commonly used classical machine learning models under consistent experimental settings and offer insights into how preprocessing, dataset selection, and evaluation methodology influence reported performance.

Cryptography and Security.title: Beyond Boundaries: A Comprehensive Survey of Transferable Attacks on AI Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Transferable attacks allow adversarial manipulations or learned attack mechanisms constructed in one setting to compromise other AI systems, potentially reducing attack costs and amplifying security and privacy risks. Yet fragmented terminology and evaluation practices hinder understanding of what transfers, why it transfers, and where transfer fails. This survey synthesizes representative research and develops a unified taxonomy spanning six complementary axes: cross-instance, cross-domain, cross-modality, cross-model, cross-task, and cross-deployment. By separating source-target configuration changes from attacker access and adaptation budgets, the taxonomy provides a common framework for comparing transfer across evasion, poisoning, backdoors, privacy inference, model stealing, and prompt-based attacks. We connect transfer mechanisms, including gradient alignment, shared representations, training persistence, and deployment invariances, to enhancement methods based on augmentation, disentanglement, and optimization. Our synthesis identifies inconsistent transfer, incompatible metrics, and gaps between simulated and physical evaluations, and establishes a research agenda for compositional transfer, configuration differences, temporal persistence, and reproducible benchmarking. Together, this work supports systematic investigation of shared vulnerabilities and guides transfer-aware security assessment and defense.

Programming Languages.title: Explorable Proofs: Making Written Proofs Explorable by Grounding Them in Formal Representations
Programming Languages.summary: LLM-generated explanations can make technical content more accessible, but there is a ceiling on what they can support interactively. Because LLM outputs are static text, they cannot be executed or stepped through. We argue that grounding explanations in a formalized representation enables interactive affordances beyond what static text supports. We instantiate this idea for mathematical proof comprehension with explorable theorems, a system that uses LLMs to translate a theorem and its written proof into Lean, a programming language for machine-checked proofs, and links the written proof with the Lean code. Readers can work through the proof at a step-level granularity, test custom examples or counterexamples, and trace the logical dependencies bridging each step. Each worked-out step is produced by executing the Lean proof on that example and extracting its intermediate state. A user study ($n = 16$) shows potential advantages of this approach: in a proof-reading task, participants who had access to the provided explorability features gave better, more correct, and more detailed answers to comprehension questions, demonstrating a stronger overall understanding of the underlying mathematics.

Programming Languages.title: Open-Source AI-Powered Optimization in Scalene: Advancing Python Performance Profiling with DeepSeek-R1 and LLaMA 3.2
Programming Languages.summary: Python's flexibility and ease of use come at the cost of performance inefficiencies, requiring developers to rely on profilers to optimize execution. SCALENE, a high-performance CPU, GPU, and memory profiler, provides fine-grained insights into Python applications while running significantly faster than traditional profilers. Originally, SCALENE integrated OpenAI's API to generate AI-powered optimization suggestions, but its reliance on a proprietary API limited accessibility. This study explores the feasibility of using opensource large language models (LLMs), such as DeepSeek-R1 and Llama 3.2, to generate optimization recommendations within SCALENE. Our evaluation reveals that DeepSeek-R1 provides effective code optimizations comparable to proprietary models. We integrate DeepSeek-R1 into SCALENE to automatically analyze performance bottlenecks and suggest improvements, enhancing SCALENE's utility while maintaining its open-source nature. This study demonstrates that open-source LLMs can be viable alternatives for AI-driven code optimization, paving the way for more accessible and cost-effective performance analysis tools.

Programming Languages.title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
Programming Languages.summary: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

Programming Languages.title: Cover Semantics for Intuitionistic Modalities
Programming Languages.summary: Intuitionistic modal logic (IML) has inspired several developments in programming languages including modal type systems for staging, computational effects and language-based security. IMLs are typically studied using Kripke-style relational semantics, which simplifies proofs of meta-theoretic properties, such as completeness and consistency, by making it easy to construct models. Kripke-style relational semantics, however, relies upon classical reasoning principles, which makes it unappealing from a computational perspective and unsuitable for formalization in a constructive type theory. Goldblatt provides an alternative semantics for IMLs by extending Beth-Kripke-Joyal-style "cover" semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic with relations to support modalities. Goldblatt's "relational cover" semantics overcomes classical reasoning but introduces a new limitation: it relies upon a "modal localization" condition that restricts the class of models and complicates model construction. Goldblatt bypasses this restriction by using intricate order-theoretic completion arguments to prove completeness. In this article, we present a conservative extension of relational cover semantics that alleviates this restriction and is amenable to simpler and standard model construction techniques. We formalize our semantics in Agda and prove completeness constructively in the style of Normalization by Evaluation for a variety of IMLs featuring independent box and diamond modalities.
Programming Languages.comment: Revised after MFPS 2026

Programming Languages.title: Typechecking without Minimum Types: Finite Bases and Backward Checking for $F_{<:}^{\top}$
Programming Languages.summary:
System $F_{<:}^{\top}$ has decidable subtyping but lacks minimum types. We prove that typechecking is decidable for arbitrary explicitly annotated terms with unrestricted subsumption. The difficulty is that type abstraction uses a variable's declared bound to type its body, while quantified subtyping forgets that bound. We construct finite covers that preserve all required subtype comparisons across this change of context. These covers yield a compositional finite typing basis and a decision procedure.
  We then derive a backward checker that propagates acceptable targets without constructing the complete typing basis. Rectangularity of typing families gives a uniform elimination domain while retaining every result type, even when the canonical type is not least. Finite inverse families transport targets through type substitution. The same inverse specification recovers bound forgetting and yields finite type-avoidance families. Both typechecking procedures are total Rocq functions proved equivalent to the original typing judgment. For a separate symbolic word-RAM realization, we prove a quartic worst-case work bound. We measure family representation sizes and comparison storage in independent OCaml prototypes on synthetic checking judgments.
Programming Languages.comment: 44 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables. Includes appendices

Programming Languages.title: sGLP: Simulating People with Stochastic Agents
Programming Languages.summary:
Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that are run by the participants. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed.
  Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour.
  We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate.
  We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.

Programming Languages.title: Formalizing Flag Algebras in Lean
Programming Languages.summary:
Razborov's flag algebra method is one of the most successful tools for proving asymptotic density inequalities in extremal graph theory. It reduces an inequality about all large graphs avoiding a forbidden pattern to finitely many algebraic conditions, and a certificate satisfying them can be found by semidefinite programming. We formalize the method for finite simple graphs in Lean 4, building on Mathlib. The formalization covers flags and their densities, the flag algebra as a quotient vector space, positive homomorphisms as limits of graph sequences, Razborov's random extensions, and the downward operator that averages out labels. On top of this theory, we build verified computation of flag densities and a tactic that turns certificates found by semidefinite programming into Lean proofs. The certificate serves only as candidate data; Lean checks every fact the proof uses.
  With this development we verify seven Turán-type upper bounds. Adding lower-bound constructions proved in Lean yields the asymptotic form of Mantel's theorem and the asymptotic Erdős pentagon theorem $π(C_5;K_3)=24/625$; to our knowledge, the latter has not previously been formalized in a proof assistant. We also prove two inequalities of Goodman. All density theorems reported here depend only on the standard axioms of Lean's logic.
  Formalization also led us to treat forbidden subgraphs with a different semantics. Instead of building a separate flag algebra for each forbidden family, we keep a single algebra of all graphs and impose the constraint only when interpreting an inequality, through randomly labeled limits of graphs satisfying it. We prove that this ensemble semantics yields the intended density bounds, and that a condition we call root-plantability characterizes when it agrees with the standard semantics.
Programming Languages.comment: 47 pages, 1 figure. Lean development: https://github.com/taeyool/lean-flag-algebras-release (release v1.0)

Programming Languages.title: Verifying deployed bytecode against executable EVM semantics, with exact gas and no added axioms
Programming Languages.summary: Much of Ethereum's most consequential code is immutable bytecode: old output of unverified compilers, and protocol logic run as contract code. We show that such bytecode can be verified as it is, without trusting what produced it, without simplifying the machine it runs on, and with no axioms beyond Lean's own. Blanc, a Lean 4 verification stack, reads fixed runtime bytes via kernel-checked certificates and states every theorem against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing that passes all 34,205 blockchain-test cases of Ethereum's fixture release v20.0.2 that involve only forks that have governed mainnet since May 2025. Eight artifacts, deployed from 2017 to 2026, come from seven compiler versions and an assembler. For the EIP-7002 contract, we prove that the end-of-block call to it, whose failure would invalidate the block, succeeds whatever its storage holds, and that each block's withdrawal requests are exactly the oldest pending submissions; mainnet met these theorems' starting premises when Prague began. For a Uniswap V2 pair, we prove that after any valid history whose hashed slots stay apart, from any checkpoint representing its Solidity model's state, the storage represents that model replayed over exactly the committed calls, a balanced liquidity ledger stays balanced, and, under a premise on token answers, geometric-mean reserves per share fall only through the protocol fee. Exact gas makes liveness provable: a tracked WETH9 holder without code can withdraw by a transaction whose gas has a closed form, matching all 3,748 comparable mainnet receipts of its shape in 30,000 blocks. On Curve pool bytes compiled with the lock bug exploited in 2023, Jaune executes such a reentrancy from deployment; for bytes from a fixed compiler, we prove the lock excludes it. AI agents wrote the proofs in fifteen days under one author's direction, atop an existing stack.
Programming Languages.comment: 37 pages, 5 tables, 4 figures. Verification package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23351349

Programming Languages.title: Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities
Programming Languages.summary: We introduce FormCraft, a framework for representing acquired operations as first-class capabilities that can be recursively composed, directly invoked, and selectively retained in a persistent library through domain-specific verification. The framework separates capability well-formedness and public callability from later admission to persistent storage while preserving formation provenance and operational identity. We formalize recursive compositional closure over a uniform capability space and show that formed composites can be reused through the same public interface without re-forming their historical derivation.
