We instantiate this paradigm in SealCall, a framework combining learned audit representations, CKKS-based encrypted similarity computation, and execution control bound to audited tool calls. Evaluated on 1,252 public binary candidates, SealCall achieves a mean F1 score of 0.840 under grouped nested evaluation, while preserving plaintext audit decisions in all measured cases. A representative configuration completes each encrypted scoring operation in 0.176 s.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: BlindStep: A Secure One-Step Kernel for Privacy-Preserving Collaborative Reasoning
Cryptography and Security.summary:
A recurring step in two-party collaborative workflows combines a private candidate frontier with a partner's compatible evidence, scores the resulting candidates, and retains only a small frontier. Direct execution can expose intermediate candidates, local scores, or unauthorized evidence provenance. Existing MPC platforms and PSI protocols provide useful building blocks, but they do not define a unified post-alignment boundary for bounded-slot aggregation, fail-closed overflow handling, retained-frontier selection, and downstream disclosure. We present BlindStep, a fixed-shape MPC-online kernel for one such post-alignment step between two semi-honest parties. Given a frontend realizing the bounded-slot contract and an application enforcing the reveal policy $ρ$, BlindStep provides a per-invocation simulation-based guarantee in the $F_{\mathrm{align}}$-hybrid model: the kernel leaks only public setup parameters, fixed execution-shape metadata, a global overflow bit, and $ρ$-authorized Layer-2 disclosures. The guarantee excludes malicious security and multi-invocation composition, and treats frontend leakage and offline preprocessing separately.
  Within this kernel boundary, we implement six semi2k realizations in MP-SPDZ, crossing two sharing styles and three top-K strategies: H-variants compare over arithmetic shares, while B-variants convert packed ranking values to Boolean shares before selection. Under LAN, B-Queue is 6-7 times faster and uses about 40 times less communication than H-Queue at N = 256 and 2048. Against H-Sort on the same backend, B-Queue achieves speedups of 21 and 30 times and communication reductions of 204 and 290 times at N = 2048 and 8192, respectively. Under the evaluated N = 256, 100 ms RTT WAN profile, H-Sort becomes fastest, showing that round complexity can dominate backend choice for the measured MPC-online kernel.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted by The Annual Computer Security Applications Conference 2026 (ACSAC, 2026)

Cryptography and Security.title: Efficient cross-domain multi-factor authentication
Cryptography and Security.summary: Secure cross-domain authentication is crucial for protecting information exchange across terminals in different security domains. However, existing cross-domain authentication models suffer from inflexibility, high storage and computational consumption. In response to these problems, a cross-domain multi-factor authentication protocol with improved efficiency (CDAuth) is proposed. CDAuth employs a universally applicable multi-factor authentication approach, integrating pseudo-identity, attribute concealment, and biometric hiding. The authentication information sets can be freely added or modified to accommodate various access scenarios. This boosts privacy, flexibility, and applicability compared to traditional methods. Furthermore, multi-edge servers as Certification Authorities (CAs) store only the union of terminal attributes and a verification token per user in their subdomains, instead of each user's attribute and biometric sets as in traditional schemes, significantly reducing storage consumption. Additionally, replacing the bilinear pairing operations with the native group operations, while maintaining security, significantly reduces computational consumption. Our analysis shows that CDAuth can resist common security attacks and is more efficient than the previous schemes.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 13 pages, 5 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: OrionLink: Single Sign-On with Oblivious Identity Brokers
Cryptography and Security.summary: Single Sign-On (SSO) is a federated authentication mechanism that improves user experience by enabling access to multiple services, or Relying Parties (RPs), through a single authentication at an Identity Provider (IdP). To reduce integration complexity, many RPs rely on third-party Identity Brokers (Brokers) that aggregate numerous IdPs into a unified interface, thereby simplifying protocol management and interoperability. However, while brokers ease development, they introduce a fundamental security and privacy risk: sensitive authentication credentials and user behavioral data are exposed to the broker, creating a high-value single point of failure. Existing SSO solutions provide limited protection against these risks. With the goal of achieving broker obliviousness, we address these challenges at their root and present OrionLink, a comprehensive privacy-enhancing SSO pipeline that is compatible with existing brokered SSO architectures and systematically mitigates broker-induced risks without sacrificing usability. OrionLink incorporates two core components: (a) an anonymous pseudonym derivation scheme that generates unlinkable, per-RP identifiers to prevent cross-service user tracking; (b) an anonymous key exchange protocol that establishes end-to-end encrypted channels to protect user data from broker visibility. We further instantiate OrionLink with two new features, preserving broker functionality and deployability. We implemented a prototype of OrionLink within a brokered SSO environment, and experimental evaluation shows that the framework achieves substantial security and privacy improvements with acceptable performance overhead.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 25 pages, 11 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Erase the Injected Region: Multimodal Prompt-Injection Defense with On-Policy Self-Distillation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Multimodal indirect prompt injection embeds malicious instructions in external media that also contains information needed for the user's task. Existing defenses can block the attack yet impair the model's use of that information, leaving a gap between attack defense and task preservation. We propose ERASE, an on-policy self-distillation method that constructs its reference by erasing the injected region in place. Modality-appropriate blank content replaces the injection while the surrounding media is preserved. A student reading attacked media learns from a frozen base model reading the erased view through full-distribution token-level feedback on its own rollouts. Across image, audio, and video on two model sizes, ERASE records near-zero observed attack success on the evaluated benchmark while retaining task utility close to the undefended clean-input level. On 3B audio, ERASE reaches 60.1% attacked-input accuracy compared with ARGUS's 33.1%, within 0.5 points of the undefended clean-input level. Experiments show that ERASE reduces injection dependence from 6.26 to 0.0095 on 3B audio while staying close to the base model on the erased input. Out-of-domain accuracy also stays near the base level. Our code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.

Cryptography and Security.title: Janus Vehicles: Entity-Centric Threat Modelling of Protocol-Conformant Vehicles under a Malicious-Manufacturer Assumption
Cryptography and Security.summary: Automotive cybersecurity commonly assumes benign end-product manufacturers and design authorities, focusing on supply-chain threats, external attacks, and compromised network participants observable through misbehaviour. This assumption overlooks malicious-by-design vehicles that remain authentic and protocol-conformant while performing undeclared sensing, communication, or context-triggered actuation. We formulate an Entity-Centric Threat Model spanning three subcomponents. The first, Malign Entity Archetypes, describes four types of malign entity: peer-benign, purpose-malicious vehicles; compromised vehicles; reappropriated genuine components; and imitated vehicles or components. The model exposes two assurance gaps: authenticity does not establish declared-purpose conformance, while malicious functionality can evade detection based on behavioural history or peer-visible evidence. Reappropriated components can remain genuine and retain usable identities or capabilities outside authorised contexts, reducing the effectiveness of signal fingerprinting and certificate-based authentication. To structure this threat space, we introduce a Behaviour-Locus Matrix that maps covert, overt, and concealment actions across hardware, software, and network loci. For peer-benign, purpose-malicious vehicles, we further present a Behavioural Interaction Model that represents how hidden capabilities are contextually activated, realised through actions, manifested within the vehicle and its environment, and potentially observed or concealed.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, This is a preprint of a paper accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 31st IEEE Pacific Rim International Symposium on Dependable Computing (PRDC 2026) - which will be held in 2~4 December 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: ANGLER: Verifier-Grounded Benchmarking with an Adaptive Attacker for Web Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Web agents are increasingly deployed to complete tasks autonomously on real websites, where adversarially injected content can induce them to perform unauthorized actions. Existing evaluations primarily use fixed attacks or focus on a single attack type, and evaluate attacks at the text level rather than through real state changes, thus underestimating how vulnerable agents are to diverse attacks. To address the gap, we introduce REEF, a benchmark of red-teaming executable environments with faithful verification for measuring the security vulnerabilities of web agents. REEF covers 9 verifier-grounded websites spanning travel, commerce, productivity, media, and communication, and pairs every authentic benign task with a malicious objective delivered through 5 attack types at both the user and the environment level. REEF's state-based verifiers provide the execution feedback that drives ANGLER, an adaptive near-miss-guided lure evolution framework for red-teaming. Rather than evaluating a fixed attack set, ANGLER uses outcomes from prior rollouts to guide LLM-based attack mutation and candidate selection, prioritizing near-miss seeds during refinement. Across 8 VLM-based web agents, ANGLER achieves an end-to-end attack success rate (ASR) of 20.36%, compared with 15.24% for the non-adaptive setting. Compared with attack-free execution on the same benign tasks, attacks generated by ANGLER reduce benign task success rate (BSR) from 61.9% to 44.4%.

Cryptography and Security.title: Watermark Robustness and Radioactivity May Be at Odds in Federated Learning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Federated learning (FL) enables fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) across distributed data sources. As these sources increasingly include LLM-generated text, provenance tracking becomes essential for accountability and transparency. We adapt LLM watermarking for FL data provenance, where a subset of clients computes local updates on watermarked data, and the server averages all updates into the global LLM. We find that several evaluated LLM watermarks remain radioactive in this setup: the watermark signal stays detectable after fine-tuning, with a $p-$value reaching $10^{-24}$ even when only 6.6% of data is watermarked. However, the server can act as an active adversary, aiming to preserve model utility while evading provenance tracking. We observe that updates from watermarked synthetic data appear as outliers relative to clean updates. Our adversary thus applies strong robust aggregation to filter out these outliers along with the watermark signal. All evaluated radioactive watermarks are not robust against such an adversarial server. Our work suggests fundamental trade-offs between radioactivity, robustness, and utility.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 7 pages, 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: 3rd Workshop on Attributing Model Behavior at Scale: Data Attribution and Provenance

Cryptography and Security.title: Expected Harm: Rethinking Safety Evaluation of (Mis)Aligned LLMs
Cryptography and Security.summary: Current evaluations of LLM safety predominantly rely on severity-based taxonomies to assess the harmfulness of models' responses to malicious queries. We argue that this formulation requires re-examination as it implicitly equates model output with realized harm while neglecting Execution Likelihood-the conditional probability of a threat being realized by a real-world actor given a model's response. In this work, we introduce Expected Harm, a metric that weights the severity of a jailbreak by its execution likelihood, modeled as a function of execution cost. Through empirical analysis of state-of-the-art models, we reveal a systematic Inverse Risk Calibration: models disproportionately exhibit stronger refusal behaviors for low-likelihood (high-cost) threats while remaining vulnerable to high-likelihood (low-cost) queries. Mechanistically, we first provide an analysis using linear probing, revealing that while refusal mechanisms linearly separate queries by severity, they do not use execution likelihood as an indicator for refusal. Then, we use Olmo-3's open-source staged checkpoints to trace the root cause of miscalibration to the Supervised Fine Tuning (SFT) training data distribution (82.8% of safety examples at cost levels 0-1) and show that cost representations are weak from the SFT stage onward. Finally, we demonstrate that this miscalibration creates a vulnerability: by exploiting this property, we increase the attack success rate of existing jailbreaks by up to $2\times$.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Dataset Track (spotlight paper)

Cryptography and Security.title: When AI Investigators Cannot Trust Their Tools: Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification for Cyber Threat Investigation
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM agents increasingly triage security alerts by combining the outputs of several detection tools, implicitly treating those tools as trustworthy. Unlike prior work on conflicts between a model's knowledge and its context, we study conflicts among the tools themselves: what happens when this machine-generated evidence is conflicting or wrong. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 dataset, four heterogeneous detectors emit labels and confidences that we corrupt under a threat model varying the number of corrupted tools, the persistence of the corruption, and the confidence attached to wrong outputs. Across open-weight LLMs from 3B to 14B parameters, unverified investigators are fragile: one corrupted detector out of four lowers naive accuracy to .50-.72, three lower every unverified investigator to .13 or less, and honest disagreement alone makes them abstain on up to 63% of flows. We propose Conflict-Aware Evidence Verification (CAV), built from established components: an equal-weight vote that ignores reported confidences, an evidence-conflict gate, and an independent nearest-neighbour trust check that tests the leading candidates. With its prompt frozen before testing, CAV-LLM improves on the naive investigator in every corrupted condition ($p < 0.001$), reaching .84-.88 with three corrupted detectors against at most .08, while calling the LLM on 0.4% of clean traffic. A fixed verification rule is as accurate or better unless most tools are corrupted. When we make the independent channel itself noisy, CAV inherits its errors: it stays ahead when two or more tools are corrupted, but adding the channel as an extra voter is better when at most one is. Verification thus moves trust from the tools to the check, which must be measured and protected in turn.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at WAITI 2026 (3rd Workshop on AI for Cyber Threat Intelligence), co-located with ACSAC 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: AgentShield: Fortifying Web Applications Against AI Agents and Agentic Browsers
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM-powered browser agents are transforming web automation by autonomously interacting with websites and executing complex workflows. However, the effectiveness of existing anti-bot defenses against these systems remains unclear. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of modern agentic browsers against widely deployed anti-bot mechanisms, characterizing their capabilities, limitations, and behavioral differences from humans. Our results show that many defenses designed for traditional automation struggle to reliably detect autonomous AI-driven agents. Accordingly, we introduce AgentShield, a behavioral fingerprinting framework that targets the Perception-Reasoning-Action (PRA) loop underlying agentic user clients. By leveraging dynamic web forms that progressively reveal content and capture fine-grained interaction telemetry, AgentShield exposes behavioral artifacts that enable differentiation between human users and autonomous agents. We further demonstrate Extinction-induced Policy Drift (EPD), a novel attack in which repeated obstruction of task completion causes agents to relax their safeguards and engage in unsafe behaviors. Finally, we present defensive prompt injection techniques that exploit agent-specific weaknesses to mitigate emerging forms of autonomous web abuse that rely on content extraction. Our results highlight both the shortcomings of current web defenses against agentic user clients and the feasibility of practical detection mechanisms tailored to this new generation of web automation.
Cryptography and Security.comment: To appear in Proceedings of IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy Oakland (IEEE S&P 2027)

Cryptography and Security.title: PP-Mark: Provable and Publicly Verifiable Watermarking for Generative AI
Cryptography and Security.summary: Generative AI models now produce images indistinguishable from real data, making publicly verifiable provenance essential; however, existing watermarking methods become vulnerable to forgeries and adversarial optimization attacks once their detectors are made public. We propose PP-Mark, a provenance framework that anchors lightweight statistical detection to a zero-knowledge proof of the embedding process, ensuring that forged content cannot pass full verification by construction. We establish formal unforgeability under standard cryptographic assumptions and validate PP-Mark against representative baselines across two latent-diffusion models (SD2.1 and SDXL), demonstrating resistance to black-box imprint forgery, white-box optimization, and regeneration attacks while remaining practical for decentralized verification. Code is available at https://github.com/hko920920/PP-Mark_NeurIPS2026
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 35 pages, 12 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Can Agentic Code Review Catch Vulnerabilities Before They Are Merged?
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. In this paper, we present SecPRBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic security review on validated real-world code changes. More specifically, we have built an automated agentic pipeline to autonomously harvest, build, and validate massive real-world bug-introducing commits for popular software systems. To ensure precise evaluation, we also adopt LLM-as-a-judge to credit the findings matching ground-truth vulnerabilities. To date, we have collected 265 tasks from nine critical systems, including Firefox, V8, and OpenSSL with millions of lines of code. Across eight frontier models, recall ranges from 32.5% to 78.1%, with Grok 4.6 and GPT-6 sol ranking at the top. Our study also shows that most misses are not simply oversights: in 68% of them, the agent reports on a file that holds the flaw but argues for a different mechanism. Security-focused harnesses also behave differently: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers recall by 8.3 points, mostly by abstaining, while Anthropic's Defending Code harness raises it by 7.7 points, at a higher cost.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Benchmark: https://github.com/secprbench/secprbench Results website: https://secprbench.github.io

Cryptography and Security.title: Who Swept My ETH? Uncovering EIP-7702-Based Ether Redirection Attacks on Ethereum
Cryptography and Security.summary: EIP-7702 introduces a new transaction type that allows Externally Owned Accounts (EOAs) on major EVM-compatible chains to delegate execution to arbitrary contract codes temporarily. While enhancing functionality, this mechanism facilitates a novel threat: the \underline{E}IP-7702-Based \underline{E}ther \underline{R}edirection \underline{A}ttack (EERA). In such an attack, a victim is delegated to a malicious sweeper contract, which automatically redirects incoming ETH transfers to an address controlled by the attacker. As a nascent attack paradigm arising from protocol evolution, the underlying mechanisms and security implications of EERA remain systematically unexplored. To bridge this gap, we provide the first formal analysis of the EERA attack model and propose SweeperHunter, a framework that detects these attacks through transaction analysis. By evaluating transactions from the first ten months following the introduction of EIP-7702 on Ethereum mainnet, we have identified 4,668,209 malicious delegations, 20,443 attack transactions and 508 ETH sweeper contracts, forming the first EERA dataset. Finally, we analyze this attack from both attacker and victim perspectives, derive key insights, and propose corresponding mitigation strategies. We reveal the prevalence of EERA, as approximately 70\% of the observed delegations point toward ETH sweeper contracts. Furthermore, we observe a notable lack of effective responses from victims; specifically, over 600,000 accounts failed to revoke or update their malicious delegations promptly, thereby remaining in a state of vulnerability. Our research is expected to facilitate understanding and mitigation of this emerging threat posed by EIP-7702.

Cryptography and Security.title: Multimodal User Authentication via Keystroke-Triggered Fusion of Glove-Based Finger Pressure and Hand Kinematics
Cryptography and Security.summary: Keystroke dynamics constitute a cost-effective behavioral biometric, but their timing features degrade under environmental and hardware variation. We replace these features with 19 dimensions of finger pressure and hand kinematics, sampled around each keystroke by a custom data glove - ten piezoresistive pressure sensors and a nine-axis inertial measurement unit (IMU). The two modalities are encoded by separate convolutional neural network-long short-term memory (CNN-LSTM) branches and joined only at the embedding. We collected typing data from ten participants, one enrolled as the genuine user. Training uses a desktop keyboard and evaluation a laptop keyboard recorded on a later day; the held-out impostor is excluded from training, and each of the nine takes that role in turn (Leave-One-Impostor-Out). Under this condition the method attains a mean Equal Error Rate (EER) of $0.53 \pm 0.42$% after three consecutive keystrokes, about 0.77 s of typing at the measured median pace, and $0.18 \pm 0.22$% after five. Results depend strongly on which impostor is held out. A per-modality ablation finds the fused model significantly better than both single-modality models at every smoothing window. The pressure-level channels carry that advantage and have to be scale-matched to deliver it, by separate encoders or by standardization indifferently.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 13 pages, 11 figures, 6 tables. Published in IEEE Access, vol. 14, pp. 163209-163221, 2026. v2: final published version (updated title, Leave-One-Impostor-Out evaluation, and results). Code: https://github.com/Issei-hyakuda/multimodal-keystroke-glove-authentication

Cryptography and Security.title: Efficient Scalable Oversight via Rewinding
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Scalable oversight asks how a weak verifier can check the outputs of computations performed by more powerful AI systems. One proposed approach uses relativizing interactive proofs, in which a weak verifier checks the output of a complex oracle-aided computation by interacting with one or more powerful provers. A prominent example is debate, which is highly efficient but assumes that one of two powerful AI models, or provers, is truthful. For certain classes of oracle-aided computations, this assumption can be removed, but at substantially greater computational cost.
  In this work, we introduce \emph{rewindable interactive proofs} (RIPs), a new model of relativizing interactive proofs for scalable oversight. In an RIP, the verifier may rewind the prover to an earlier state of the interaction and continue from there. This is possible when the prover is an AI model, since the verifier can save a snapshot of the model's state and later restore it. We construct a relativizing RIP for computations whose outputs are robust to changing a small fraction of oracle answers. Our construction is more efficient than prior relativizing proofs that do not assume a truthful prover, and it uses no cryptography.
  In our construction the honest prover runs in time linear in that of the original computation, and the verifier, after a one-time preprocessing step, runs in time nearly linear in the input length (which can be much smaller than the computation itself). We implement our protocol, report a preliminary MNIST experiment, and show that an RIP can be faster than a state-of-the-art deployed proof system.
  RIPs may be of independent interest. Rewinding is possible whenever the verifier controls the prover's machine, for example when the prover runs on trusted hardware or in a virtual machine whose state can be checkpointed.

Cryptography and Security.title: Blockchain-Based Privacy-Preserving Data Management
Cryptography and Security.summary: Privacy-preservation policies are guidelines formulated to protect data providers private data. Previous privacy-preservation methodologies have addressed privacy in which data are permanently stored in repositories and disconnected from changing data provider privacy preferences. This occurrence becomes evident as data moves to another data repository. Hence, the need for data providers to control and flexibly update their existing privacy preferences due to changing data usage continues to remain a problem. This paper proposes a blockchain-based methodology for preserving data provider's private and sensitive data. The research proposes to tightly couple data provider's private attribute data element to privacy preferences and data accessor data element into a privacy tuple. The implementation presents a framework of tightly-coupled relational database and blockchains. This delivers secure, tamper-resistant, and query-efficient platform for data management and query processing. The evaluation analysis from the implementation validates efficient query processing of privacy-aware queries on the privacy infrastructure. Moreover, a comparative analysis to other methodology approaches indicates that our approach offers efficient and better technique for data provider's private data protection and identity preservation.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 25 pages, 14 figures, 2 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Spoofing the Latent State: Imperceptible Goal-Image Attacks Derail Planning in LeWorldModel
Cryptography and Security.summary: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as general-purpose visual world models for control. A prominent example is LeWorldModel (LeWM), which trains end-to-end from pixels using an isotropic Gaussian anti-collapse regularizer (SIGReg) and plans by minimizing the squared Euclidean distance between predicted and goal embeddings. In this work, we investigate the test-time robustness of this latent planning interface. Analyzing the learned metric on Push-T, we first find that task-relevant object state heavily dominates latent distance: shifting the block by a single pixel displaces the embedding $3\times$ further than an equivalent agent shift, and swapping the block pose alone accounts for $99\%$ of the distance between scene pairs. However, because this pose information is distributed across a curved, high-dimensional manifold rather than a fixed linear subspace, the encoder cannot be trivially edited post-hoc to isolate or redirect it. We next demonstrate that this geometry is highly vulnerable at test time. A white-box $\ell_\infty$ perturbation of just $ε{=}4/255$ applied to a single input frame causes the encoder to register the block at an arbitrary, attacker-chosen pose in $73$--$95\%$ of scenes without disturbing the encoded agent state. Perturbing either the goal image or the live camera observation drops Push-T planning success from $87\%$ to $32\%$, whereas uniform random noise at twice the magnitude has negligible impact. This vulnerability persists across all four standard LeWM benchmarks (Push-T, Two-Room, Reacher, and OGBench-Cube). At $ε{=}8/255$, the attack bridges $82$--$97\%$ of the squared latent distance to the target embedding in every environment, inducing planning degradation proportional to each task's reliance on the spoofed entity.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 13 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: AuthRank: Scoring Source Credibility to Counter Poisoning in CTI LLM Pipelines
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) pipelines have become essential for processing Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) to quickly extract updated threat information from open source feeds and reports for real time processing. However, these pipelines are susceptible to poisoning attacks, and previously proposed defenses can fail for CTI contexts as cyber threat information is often completely novel, and attackers can easily mimic the stylistic conventions. We propose that the robustness of LLM pipelines can be improved by applying source credibility algorithms on document corpora, using PageRank as an example. We introduce AuthRank, a credibility score computed from citation networks built using explicit citations, LLM-inferred citations, and claim-level entailment, enhanced with time decay and author credibility. Our experiments on the standardized MS MARCO dataset demonstrate improved accuracy under poisoning, and we show proof-of-concept performance on CTI documents and feeds.
Cryptography and Security.comment: In Proceedings of IEEE ACSAC Workshop on AI for Cyber Threat Intelligence (WAITI) 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee
Cryptography and Security.summary: Transactions differ in how their value changes with execution time and relative position. Ethereum's EIP-1559 lets them compete through fee fields, but a fee bid gives no enforceable claim to an earlier position in the block, and no way to express willingness to accept a later one. Its base fee is a hard admission floor. We introduce temporal liquidity markets (TLM), a framework for crossing complementary temporal requirements: transactions seeking early-region execution (consumers) can fund transactions that opt into exclusion from that region (providers). Selected consumers complete within the early region and are ordered among themselves by authorization density, both validator-checked. In our block-local EIP-1559 extension, providers may be admitted below the base-fee floor. Under TLM regulation, funding-conditioned and capacity-capped provider gas is excluded from the ordinary EIP-1559 controller input. Counting it there instead raises the base fee and displaces ordinary demand at a positive base-fee fixed point. Exclusion lets the controller regulate ordinary demand at its original target and preserves the no-TLM ordinary allocation by construction; in synthetic experiments it raises total utilization with funded gas. Selected consumers pay their signed authorizations, which fund provider shortfalls; the surplus is burned. We state an adversary model with strategic senders and builders and prove eight properties under it, among them validator-checked rule validity, full burn of the base fee, and no subsidy. An inserted consumer bid cannot raise any other consumer's charge. With a provider fee-cap floor, a small, capped inclusion fee and a consumer allowance tied to funded provider gas by a large enough link ratio, no finite set of consumer bids or providers that the builder inserts raises its direct fee payoff.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 28 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: When appearance and motion disagree: evaluating class--motion consistency against disguised uncrewed surface vessels
Cryptography and Security.summary: Defense systems for maritime assets must distinguish approaching benign craft from uncrewed surface vessels (USVs) with sufficient warning to act. Shore cameras using computer vision can separate hostile vessels from benign traffic, but these systems may be attacked using an adversarial hull patch or physical disguise. We evaluate adversarial hull patches and find they suppress detection in up to 29% of attempts but never cause misclassification as benign. Physical disguise, however, can bypass both a camera check and a radar presence check. To evaluate defenses, we develop a hybrid replay protocol from automatic identification system (AIS) tracks that combines recorded benign motion with direct or off-axis attack run-ins. We find that for recreational-labeled vessels attacking via direct run-in within 4 nautical miles, an asset-relative closing-rate check flags 94-95% at 15-20 knots, compared with 12% for a track-only speed check. The checks are complementary on off-axis approaches, constraining the attacker to remain below both thresholds and extending the time required to reach the asset. Flagging on either check has a 4.9% held-out false-alarm rate overall and 12.3% on recreational traffic. The replay-based evaluation protocol supports comparative test and evaluation of defense methods.

Cryptography and Security.title: Explainability-Aware Evaluation of Transfer Learning Models for IoT DDoS Detection Under Resource Constraints
Cryptography and Security.summary: Distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks threaten the availability of Internet of Things (IoT) infrastructures, especially in resource-constrained deployments. Although transfer learning models have shown promising detection accuracy, their reliability, computational feasibility, and interpretability in operational environments remain insufficiently explored. This study presents an explainability-aware empirical evaluation of seven pre-trained convolutional neural network architectures for multi-class IoT DDoS detection using the CICDDoS2019 dataset and an image-based traffic representation. The analysis integrates classification performance metrics, complementary statistical indicators (MCC, Cohen's kappa, and Youden Index), training and inference cost assessment, and interpretability evaluation using Grad-CAM and SHAP. Results indicate that DenseNet and MobileNet-based architectures achieve strong detection performance while demonstrating superior reliability and compact, class-consistent attribution patterns. MobileNet achieves the highest reported classification accuracy and several of the strongest reliability statistics, whereas DenseNet169 exhibits the most favorable qualitative interpretability characteristics based on Grad-CAM and SHAP. MobileNetV3 offers a potential trade-off between inference latency, classification performance, and qualitative interpretability for resource-constrained deployment. The findings emphasize the importance of combining performance, reliability, and explainability criteria when selecting deep learning models for IoT DDoS detection.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Updated version with several corrections, contains more clarification, and corrected typos in the text and references

Cryptography and Security.title: Humanized but Still True? Auditing Facts and Detection in AI-Text Humanizers
Cryptography and Security.summary: AI "humanizers" rewrite machine-generated text so that detectors classify it as human-written. Public leaderboards score evasion and embedding similarity, but not whether checkable details survive. We check whether numbers, dates, person and organization names, and quoted spans survive each rewrite, using a rule-based checker validated by two AI annotators (precision 0.84-1.00, recall 0.93-0.95; no human annotation). In the October 2026 cycle of a public humanizer leaderboard, all 11 commercial tools changed or dropped at least one of these units in 35-65% of the documents that contained one. Most changes were to quoted spans; counting numbers and names alone, 10 of the 11 tools still altered at least one in 20% or more of the documents. The September 2026 cycle was similar (19-50%). An open 12B humanizer kept at least 97% of numbers and names in fact-dense U.S. federal agency text, but reworded 67-78% of the quoted spans, against its own prompt. Unit retention and detector evasion were not clearly related across tools (Spearman rho = -0.46, 95% CI -0.65 to 0.08), and the open model's four released files (two of them quantization-aware low-bit files) did not show the pre-registered monotone trade-off. On federal texts with matched human, AI-styled and humanized versions, a general-purpose decision model, Jev, asked a single zero-shot question, separated human originals from humanized rewrites with AUROC 0.864 (0.827-0.902), 0.18-0.22 higher than Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT and the adversarially trained RADAR, while calling 24% of the human originals AI at a 0.5 threshold. On the AI-styled rewrites by 2026 models, both perplexity-based detectors scored below chance (AUROC 0.37 and 0.39), also with line breaks removed. Hypotheses, data rules and analyses were frozen before the main runs; two earlier data contacts are disclosed. We release the checker and the per-item results.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/zwang-devv/humanizer-fact-audit

Cryptography and Security.title: Dataset and Experimental Testbed for Deep Learning-Based Bluetooth Device Fingerprinting
Cryptography and Security.summary: AI-enabled wireless networks have emerged as vital components of future-generation wireless communication systems. Among various wireless architectures, Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) networks have attracted significant research interest due to their widespread adoption and low cost. In these networks, deep learning (DL) models can be integrated directly into the physical-layer infrastructure to perform diverse tasks, including environment sensing, localization, radio frequency fingerprinting (RFFP), and signal denoising. While highly effective under their original training configurations, these DL models often fail significantly when deployed in unseen environments---such as different rooms, varying temperature conditions, or altered carrier frequencies. Addressing this limitation requires rigorous benchmarking of models and algorithms against unseen configurations to evaluate their generalization and robustness. To bridge this gap, this paper makes two key contributions: i) we introduce a comprehensive, large-scale wireless BLE dataset consisting of raw IQ transmissions from 31 distinct commercial devices captured across diverse days, locations, environments, temperatures, receiver hardware, and frequency channels; ii) we present a case study evaluating state-of-the-art techniques for domain-robust RFFP to advance real-world AI reliability.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 6-page paper; accepted and presented at the Experimental Research on Networking (ERN 2026) workshop, part of 17th International Conference on Network of the Future (NoF 2026)

Cryptography and Security.title: Removing Speech, Keeping Activities: Speech Removal for Privacy-Preserving Acoustic Sensing in Assisted Living
Cryptography and Security.summary: Acoustic sensing can monitor the daily activities of older adults without cameras or wearables, yet the possibility of capturing private conversations remains a barrier to its deployment. The engineering application addressed in this paper is privacy-preserving acoustic monitoring of daily activities in assisted living. Our contribution in artificial intelligence is a speech-removal front end: a U-Net that masks the short-time Fourier transform of ambient audio and returns a waveform in which speech is suppressed and the sounds needed for activity recognition are kept. The model is trained only on synthetic mixtures of public sounds and speech, so no speech has to be recorded in the target homes. We evaluate it with group-disjoint cross-validation on environmental and domestic sound datasets mixed with reverberant speech, on speech from unseen corpora and on real home recordings, and measure privacy with three voice activity detectors, Whisper speech recognition and a speaker-verification attack. With speech 5 dB above the background, the macro-averaged F1 score of activity recognition is 0.574 and 0.661 after removal on the two datasets, compared with 0.233 and 0.178 without processing, and higher than that of speech enhancement, speech separation and detector-gated muting at every speech level. Whisper recovers 5.2% of the spoken words, compared with 89.0% without processing and a chance floor of 2.2%. On the real recordings, the speech proportion estimated by a voice activity detector falls from 8.5% to 2.7%. The method reduces, but does not eliminate, spoken content and speaker identity.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 44 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence

Cryptography and Security.title: Randomized Caches in Hardware: Challenges and Trade-offs
Cryptography and Security.summary: Randomized caches protect against side-channel attacks by obfuscating the mapping of memory addresses to cache locations. Existing proposals typically describe architectural behavior, leaving practical hardware implementation challenges largely unexplored. We implement four prominent designs, CEASER-S, ScatterCache, SassCache, and MIRAGE, and integrate them as the last-level cache (LLC) of a multi-core out-of-order RISC-V system-on-chip (SoC). We identify common and design-specific implementation challenges and develop practical solutions. We evaluate complete FPGA implementations by running SPEC CPU 2017 rate and GAPBS workloads to completion, providing, to our knowledge, the first comparative evaluation of these designs on a common full-system hardware platform. Pipelining the index derivation function (IDF) alone is insufficient: in three of the four variants, other components become the frequency bottleneck, reducing frequency by up to 35% relative to the baseline set-associative cache. Redesigning the critical paths while preserving mappings, rekeying, and victim-selection policies brings the three affected variants to no more than 10% below the baseline frequency, at the cost of added latency or reduced concurrency. Increased LLC access latency, rather than additional misses, dominates IPC degradation, reducing instructions per cycle by up to 5% for SPEC and 11% for GAPBS. Hardware overhead depends on the design and implementation technology: FPGA lookup-table usage increases by 10-35%, while ASIC area increases by 1-14%.

Cryptography and Security.title: Cheap Reverse Engineering and What It Will Do
Cryptography and Security.summary: Generative AI is putting the law of reverse engineering (RE) under severe strain. Existing IP and technology laws assume that RE is expensive and time-consuming, and that it requires specialized expertise. They generally allow it, but they rely on its difficulty as a filter to separate (permissible) RE from (impermissible) copying and theft. Generative AI is changing this equation by making \RE much faster, cheaper, and easier. AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract. In this article, we describe the ways in which AI is changing \RE, map these new practices onto existing laws, and sketch ways that the legal system could respond and their associated trade-offs.

Programming Languages.title: On the Expressiveness of Asynchronous Processes with Nested Session Types (Extended Version)
Programming Languages.summary: Session types are a type-based approach to correct message-passing programs, where types specify protocols for channels and type checking guarantees communication correctness. Traditional session types express regular protocols only, which leaves out many protocols found in practice. Aiming at overcoming this limitation, Nested Session Types (NSTs) can specify nested recursive protocols. NSTs are known to be characterised by one-counter machines and deterministic context-free languages. In this paper, we study the expressiveness of ASP (Asynchronous Session Processes), the process model associated with NSTs as introduced by Das et al. We prove that AST is Turing complete by giving a correct encoding of two-counter machines into typed processes. Our encoding uses a non-trivial state-aware representation of counters and instructions that is neatly governed by NSTs.
Programming Languages.comment: Extended version of a paper submitted to EXPRESS/SOS 2026

Programming Languages.title: M$^\star$: Every Task Deserves Its Own Memory Harness
Programming Languages.summary: Large language model agents rely on a memory harness to write, organize, retrieve, and use past experience. A harness that works for one task often fails on another, because conversations, embodied planning, and expert reasoning require different storage and retrieval behavior. To address this limitation, we introduce Mstar, a method that automatically discovers task-optimized memory programs through reflective code evolution. Specifically, Mstar operationalizes a memory harness as an executable Python memory program that defines the Schema, Logic, and Instruction, and optimizes these components jointly. We evaluate Mstar on four tasks covering conversation, embodied planning, and specialized reasoning. Our results demonstrate that Mstar improves performance over existing baselines across all evaluated tasks. Furthermore, the evolved memory programs exhibit structurally distinct processing mechanisms for each evaluated domain. These findings suggest that every task benefits from its own memory harness, and that memory-program search provides a concrete way to discover it.
Programming Languages.comment: NeurIPS 2026 (poster). Code: https://github.com/wbopan/mstar ; Live demo: https://mstar.wenbo.io

Programming Languages.title: TIRx: A Unified Tile Primitive ML Compiler Across Heterogeneous Backends
Programming Languages.summary: Modern ML kernels evolve rapidly with new optimizations and hardware features. ML compiler abstractions must accommodate richer memory hierarchies, more forms of thread cooperation, and increasingly heterogeneous backends while retaining the control required for peak performance. We present TIRx, an ML compiler for GPUs and AI accelerators that exposes these ingredients through explicit interfaces. TIRx introduces an explicit execution-scope abstraction that captures participating hardware teams at multiple granularities. It also uses tensor layouts to map logical tensors to heterogeneous hardware spaces through named axes and shard/replica/offset semantics. Finally, it introduces tile-primitive dispatch, which lowers high-level operations to efficient implementations according to scope, layout, and backend. This design preserves native-level control while automating recurring address calculation, operand preparation, and instruction-loop generation. Our evaluation shows vendor-level performance across the latest GPUs and AI accelerators, while native-code case studies show substantial reductions in low-level implementation code.
Programming Languages.comment: Accepted to ASPLOS 2027

Programming Languages.title: Iris on Indirection Theory: Lightweight Higher-order Ghost State
Programming Languages.summary: Today, semantic models of languages with concurrency and higher-order state are constructed using step-indexed predicates over resources and higher-order ghost state. There are two main lines of work for constructing such models. On the one hand, Iris provides these in full generality, at the cost of a large body of mechanised domain theory that is difficult to learn and port to new proof assistants. On the other hand, Indirection Theory is much simpler through the use of ordinary dependent types, but its foundation in separation algebra limits the expressiveness of its resource model compared to Iris-style higher-order ghost state. We resolve this conundrum by showing that Indirection Theory can be as expressive as Iris. To that end, we give a lightweight mechanisation of Indirection Theory in Lean, generalised so knots contain resources from an Iris-style resource algebra functor. We then reconstruct the Iris base logic on top of it. The advantage of this approach is in the elementary metatheory: a user can follow the whole construction without domain theory. We conduct two case studies to show that the base logic is expressive and faithful to Iris: a biorthogonal logical relation for higher-order state, and an Iris-style program logic with invariants and user-definable ghost state, complete enough to verify concurrent and higher-order programs.

Programming Languages.title: Can Agentic Code Review Catch Vulnerabilities Before They Are Merged?
Programming Languages.summary: LLM agents have been increasingly adopted for security-focused code review, but existing benchmarks mostly derive the reviewed changes from their later fixes instead of the real-world bug-introducing commits. In this paper, we present SecPRBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating agentic security review on validated real-world code changes. More specifically, we have built an automated agentic pipeline to autonomously harvest, build, and validate massive real-world bug-introducing commits for popular software systems. To ensure precise evaluation, we also adopt LLM-as-a-judge to credit the findings matching ground-truth vulnerabilities. To date, we have collected 265 tasks from nine critical systems, including Firefox, V8, and OpenSSL with millions of lines of code. Across eight frontier models, recall ranges from 32.5% to 78.1%, with Grok 4.6 and GPT-6 sol ranking at the top. Our study also shows that most misses are not simply oversights: in 68% of them, the agent reports on a file that holds the flaw but argues for a different mechanism. Security-focused harnesses also behave differently: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers recall by 8.3 points, mostly by abstaining, while Anthropic's Defending Code harness raises it by 7.7 points, at a higher cost.
Programming Languages.comment: 20 pages, 2 figures, 10 tables. Benchmark: https://github.com/secprbench/secprbench Results website: https://secprbench.github.io

Programming Languages.title: Isomorphism Is Not Enough: An Agentic Audit of Verified Code Generation in Lean
Programming Languages.summary: Agentic systems have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for automated theorem proving in formal mathematics. To assess how far these capabilities extend to program verification and how reliably existing benchmarks can measure them, we audit CLEVER, a Lean 4 benchmark for verifiable code generation, using three independent agentic stacks based on Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.4, and Kimi K2.5. Our audit finds arguably erroneous reference specifications in 80 of 161 entries, each accepted by the benchmark's authors, distills a taxonomy of benchmark errors, and exposes structural limitations of isomorphism-based scoring, whose signal breaks down when generated and reference specifications formalize different yet defensible readings. In the process, the stacks generate arguably valid specifications for up to 98.8% of entries, certify implementations against sound reference specifications for up to 92.3%, and reach up to 96.2% end-to-end success over entries with sound premises, suggesting that CLEVER no longer stresses modern agentic provers as much as its design intended. Looking ahead, we translate our findings into recommendations for future work, with our error analysis doubling as a repair list for CLEVER and a heuristic checklist for the next generation of benchmarks.

Programming Languages.title: Trellis: Bringing Compiler-Guided Repair into Agentic Code Generation
Programming Languages.summary: Coding agents regularly generate programs that do not compile and require substantial tokens to repair. Yet most repairs are small and local to the edit that caused them. We present Trellis, a system that integrates incremental compiler feedback into code generation to improve code correctness while controlling repair costs. Trellis uses rollback-based search for targeted repair and asynchronous checking and checkpointing for efficient execution. We adapt Clang and tsc to Trellis's checker interface and integrate Trellis transparently into OpenCode. On C/C++ and TypeScript software engineering tasks, Trellis improves compilation rate by up to 13% and test pass rate by up to 11% with comparable token consumption to baseline OpenCode.

Programming Languages.title: ScenicProver: A Framework for Compositional Probabilistic Verification of Learning-Enabled Systems
Programming Languages.summary: Full verification of learning-enabled cyber-physical systems (CPS) has long been intractable due to challenges including black-box components and complex real-world environments. Existing tools either provide formal guarantees for limited types of systems or test the system as a monolith, but no general framework exists for compositional analysis of learning-enabled CPS using varied verification techniques over complex real-world environments. This paper introduces a tool, ScenicProver, that aims to fill this gap by enabling the construction of sound, formally-checked assurance cases for CPS. ScenicProver is backed by a formal theory, which we lay out in this paper. ScenicProver supports: (1) environment modeling using the Scenic probabilistic programming language; (2) compositional system modeling with clear component interfaces, ranging from interpretable code to black boxes; (3) assume-guarantee contracts over those components using an extension of Linear Temporal Logic containing arbitrary Scenic expressions; (4) evidence generation through testing, formal proofs in Lean 4, and external assumptions; (5) sound combination of generated evidence using contract operators with Pacti; and (6) automatic generation of assurance cases tracking the provenance of system-level guarantees. We demonstrate its effectiveness through two case studies: one on an automatic emergency braking system with sensor fusion and one on drone safety. By leveraging manufacturer guarantees for sensors and focusing testing effort on uncertain conditions, our approach enables stronger probabilistic guarantees than monolithic testing with the same computational budget.
Programming Languages.comment: 36 pages, 8 figures. Full version (including appendices) of a paper submitted to TACAS 2027

Programming Languages.title: VerusWeave: A Benchmark for Proof Repair in Concurrent Verus Programs
Programming Languages.summary:
Concurrent software underpins critical infrastructure, including operating systems and databases, yet thread interactions can have bugs that bypass conventional testing. Verus extends Rust with formal verification capabilities, enabling developers to specify, implement and prove the correctness of concurrent code in the same language. Although coding agents have been explored for automated proof construction, existing Verus benchmarks offer limited coverage of concurrency-specific examples that connect atomic operations to abstract protocols.
  To address this gap, we introduce VerusWeave, the first benchmark dedicated to concurrent proof repair, derived from four open-source projects. It comprises 75 focused tasks and 17 full-module variants that exercise features used to verify low-level concurrent code. Tasks remove selected proof annotations and require agents to fill gaps, while preserving executable code and specifications. The evaluation harness validates repairs using Verus and a change checker, recording solutions, execution traces, and resource usage. An initial evaluation of four general-purpose coding-agent harnesses achieved 75-85% success on focused tasks and 29-47% on full-module variants, highlighting the challenge of autonomous module-wide repairs. VerusWeave provides a reusable foundation for evaluating automated proof construction for concurrent software.
Programming Languages.comment: 4 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables

Programming Languages.title: Blazing-Fast SMT-LIB Parsing for Rust and Lean
Programming Languages.summary: SMT-LIB is a standard input format for Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) solvers. However, parsing the format is non-trivial and can become a bottleneck, e.g. when retrieving benchmark metadata or normalising the input for solvers. We introduce blazing-smtlib, a Rust parsing library for SMT-LIB, and BSmtLib, its port to Lean. We outline the library API we designed for composability and extensibility (including non-standard SMT-LIB commands), and discuss our implementation decisions for fast lexing and parsing. We proved that our lexing and parsing with Lean-specific optimisations match our formalised reading of the SMT-LIB syntax. We measured performance on a representative sample from the 2025 SMT-LIB corpus and found that blazing-smtlib is more than 6 times faster on the geometric mean than previous parsing libraries and BSmtLib is faster or comparable to them.
Programming Languages.comment: 18 pages, 5 pages appendix, 11 figures

Programming Languages.title: Grassmann: The Coordinate-Independent Linear Algebra Programming Language
Programming Languages.summary: Scientists, engineers, and mathematicians often formulate algorithms using coordinate-independent linear algebra because its tools are composable and harder to misuse. For numerical processing, however, users must translate these ideas into coordinate-dependent array code. Most practitioners do so prematurely because tools such as NumPy lack coordinate-independent representations, while existing languages with such constructs do not model enough linear algebra for the situations where they matter. We propose Grassmann, a small language bridging coordinate-independent linear algebra and coordinate-dependent implementations. It uses dependent types, linear types, and partially (pseudo-)invertible computation to model situations arising in exterior algebra and differential geometry. It targets the linear algebra at a point on a manifold, a prerequisite for many specifications in scientific computing and computer graphics. A language for coordinates lets users move between these representations. We give a denotational semantics assigning meaning without coordinates and an operational semantics translating Grassmann to array code under a choice of coordinates. Our main metatheoretic result shows that operational evaluations agree with the denotational semantics under an arbitrary choice of coordinates. This models how practitioners translate linear algebra for computers and suggests an approach to algorithmic optimization at a high level of abstraction. Our optimized implementation generates code for exterior algebra operations with overheads no more than 10%.
Programming Languages.comment: 147 pages, including references and appendices

Programming Languages.title: Coinduction in Grounded Arithmetic
Programming Languages.summary: A grounded arithmetic counts a sentence as true only when a terminating process establishes it; a sentence no such process settles has no value. Such a logic can state that an event happens, but not that it never happens under unbounded choice. This paper extends such a logic so that it can. The base is Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) with Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA)'s least-fixed-point reading and ground induction. It adds a separate greatest-fixed-point former $ν$ with Park's coinduction rule, proves that one former cannot carry both ground induction and coinduction, and adds a dichotomy rule: the classical disjunction between a least-fixed-point atom and the greatest-fixed-point atom of its dual, under a derivable premise that the body's leaves are decided. The systems are sound for an explicit model reading every $ν$-body at its greatest fixed point, hence consistent; they agree with the least model wherever it has a value and prove sentences it leaves without one. The dichotomy replaces the underivable hypothesis that an order is well-founded by the derivable one that its steps are decided; the change of model pays for the move. With ground induction the dichotomy derives the omniscience rule of the sibling arithmetic OGA, so the system has no semantics whose certificates for universals are its own proofs. The systems prove, as single sentences, that every decided tree is well-founded or has an infinite branch given by a term, total in the new model; that random assignment terminates while its divergent twin runs forever; that a fair loop terminates and the alternating-bit protocol delivers every message; that open games are determined; that the termination gap in Nakata and Uustalu's trace semantics closes; and that Cinderella wins the bucket game at capacity three. Isabelle/HOL checks every result.
Programming Languages.comment: 75 pages

Programming Languages.title: Excel: A Financial Modelling System
Programming Languages.summary: Since the calculation engine of Excel was the subject of a major upgrade to accommodate Dynamic Arrays in 2018, there has been a series of seismic changes to the art of financial modelling. This paper will show the traditional financial modelling techniques for spreadsheets can be replaced by radically different approaches that have significant gains in readability, performance and flexibility. With so much power added to the Excel engine in recent years, it is the responsibility of financial modellers to ensure that they are building in the simplest and most auditable way possible going forward.

Software Engineering.title: Dittany: Contribution-Guided Repair Framework for MAS Applications
Software Engineering.summary: LLM-based multi-agent system (MAS) applications can produce useful intermediate results while leaving task requirements unsatisfied. Repairing such executions requires identifying the work still needed and the completed results that can support it. We present \tool, a contribution-guided runtime repair framework for MAS applications. \tool derives expected contributions and acceptance conditions from task requirements and method specifications, and connects their dependencies in a contribution graph. Runtime checks locate unmet conditions and establish which results remain usable. These results guide action-level correction when available inputs suffice, or graph-level recovery when prerequisites or unfinished work need revision. Both repair scopes retain validated contributions and check repaired outputs before subsequent work uses them. We evaluate \tool on 30 applications across six MAS frameworks and 9,000 tasks. It detects runtime failures with 88.28\% precision and 79.18\% recall, and achieves 84.76\% task accuracy, improving over Native execution by 26.74 percentage points and the strongest of four recovery baselines by 21.28 points. Estimated deployment token consumption is 17.92\% above Native, but 24.19\% below Reflexion and 13.05\% below Iterative Rollback. Ablation results show that combining the two repair scopes achieves higher accuracy and lower token consumption than graph-level repair alone.

Software Engineering.title: Instruction-Tuning Open-Weight Language Models for BPMN Model Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Domain models are central to software engineering, as they enable a shared understanding, guide implementation, and support automated analyses and model-driven development. Yet, despite these benefits, practitioners often skip modeling because it is time-consuming and demands scarce expertise. We address this barrier by investigating whether open-weight large language models, adapted via instruction tuning, can generate high-quality BPMN process models directly from natural language descriptions in a cost-effective and privacy-preserving way. We introduce InstruBPM, a reproducible approach that prepares paired text-diagram data and instruction tunes an open source large language model with parameter-efficient fine-tuning and quantization for on-prem deployment. We evaluate the tuned model through complementary perspectives: (i) text/code similarity using BLEU, ROUGE-L, and METEOR, (ii) structural fidelity using Relative Graph Edit Distance, (iii) guidelines conformance using external tool checks, and (iv) a small expert review. Using a curated subset of a multi-domain BPMN dataset, we compare the tuned model with untuned open-weight baselines and strong proprietary models under consistent prompting regimes. Our compact tuned model outperforms all baselines across sequence and structural metrics while requiring substantially fewer resources; guideline analysis and expert feedback further indicate that the generated diagrams largely follow BPMN best practices and are useful starting points that reduce modeling effort. Overall, instruction tuning improves structural accuracy and robustness compared to untuned baselines and reduces reliance on heavy prompt scaffolding. We publicly share the trained models and scripts to support reproducibility and further research.
Software Engineering.comment: Preprint. Under preparation for journal submission

Software Engineering.title: No More Import Errors: Constrained Decoding for Guaranteed Valid Imports in LLM-Generated Tests
Software Engineering.summary:
One of the most common failure reasons of LLM-based test generation pipelines is import errors. Grammar constrained decoding can modify the probabilities of the LLM's final layer during token generation to guarantee valid imports. However, we find that it can lead to degenerate solutions, i.e., repetitive valid imports (import streaks) that exhaust the token budget before a test is generated. We propose Constrained Beam Decoding with Lookup (CBDL), a novel method that guarantees import validity while addressing import streaks by avoiding premature commitment to tokens that lead to repetitive imports. Because it operates at the decoding stage, CBDL can be integrated into existing LLM-based test generation pipelines.
  We implement CBDL for Python and Java and evaluate it on two test generation tasks, showing that generated tests have 100% valid imports, outperforming both static (RAG and LIBRO) and dynamic (Agentic Repair) import-validity approaches that leave 45%, 10%, and 43% of import errors unresolved. CBDL converts on average 14% of initial import errors into functionally correct tests, increasing overall test correctness by 1-4 percentage points over unconstrained generation.
  Even when import validity does not directly lead to a correct test, it allows agentic repair pipelines to allocate the repair budget to remaining errors, increasing correct tests by 2-7 percentage points for Python and 1-6 for Java. Finally, we show that a hybrid pipeline, where a small local model equipped with CBDL generates imports while the frontier GPT-5.2 model generates the test body, outperforms generating both with GPT-5.2 alone by 1-3 percentage points.
  Overall, CBDL removes a major bottleneck in LLM-based test generation: by guaranteeing import validity with a small overhead (16-21 seconds per test), it improves test correctness and enables cost-effective hybrid generation.

Software Engineering.title: Stuck on Red? Understanding GitHub Actions Failing Streaks
Software Engineering.summary: GitHub Actions is the de facto CI/CD service for GitHub repositories. Its workflows should not fail when they are not expected to, nor keep on failing too long. We empirically study failing streaks, i.e., uninterrupted series of failing runs of a workflow, in 30.9M+ runs of 154K+ workflows of 43K+ GitHub repositories over 238 days. We study how failing streaks begin and end, and what happens during them, based on the trigger and the commit of each run. We also classify all workflows by their purposes, such as building, testing or deploying, and we inspect the logs of a small sample of failing streaks. Failing runs mostly come in streaks: three quarters of them follow another failing run, and half of the workflows with at least three runs have at least one failing streak. Workflows serving multiple purposes have failing streaks more often, even at the same size. Most failing streaks end within hours, but the one in five that last more than a day account for the lion's share of the time that workflows spend failing. A third of the failing streaks start, and two in five end, without any change to the repository. In a sample of 100 failing streaks, those that end this way most often fail because of network issues or an external service. These findings suggest that maintainers should not assume that a failure comes from the last commit. GitHub and tool builders could flag failures that occur without any change to the repository, and alert the active maintainers when a workflow stays failing for more than a day.

Software Engineering.title: Reparo: Synthesizing and Validating Access Control Policies
Software Engineering.summary: Writing correct access control policies for software applications is difficult because it requires expertise in the authorization language and a thorough understanding of the application's authorization requirements. Existing synthesis and mining approaches assume explicit authorization inputs and a trusted reference policy. However, authorization logic is often distributed across code, comments, and documentation rather than captured in a single artifact, and developer-defined policies in real-world application repositories are often incomplete, outdated, or incorrect. We present Reparo, an LLM-aided pipeline for access control policy synthesis, repair, and validation. Reparo collects repository evidence for authorization intent and uses it to guide an LLM in generating an initial policy. It then uses official policy-language validation tools to identify and automatically repair errors. For semantic validation, a different LLM derives a behavioral oracle from the same repository evidence, consisting of concrete authorization requests with expected allow or deny decisions, which Reparo executes against the generated policy. We manually assess the oracle on a statistically sized sample of 390 test cases. We evaluate Reparo on 228 real-world GitHub repositories that use Cedar, OpenFGA, or Rego. In these repositories, 40.6-55.7% of the repository policies fail their language's validation tool, whereas Reparo produces 99.0-100% valid policies after repair. Agreement with the oracle is 98.2-99.6% for OpenFGA, 82.0-86.5% for Cedar, and 76.3-80.2% for Rego. Manual review confirms 91.5-96.9% of the sampled test cases as correct. Synthesizing and validating the policy for one repository takes about five minutes and costs $0.55-$1.57. These results show that repository evidence can support both access policy synthesis and independent validation, even when no reliable reference policy exists.

Software Engineering.title: Human-AI Synergy in Agentic Code Review
Software Engineering.summary: Code review is a critical software engineering practice where developers review code changes before integration to ensure code quality, detect defects, and improve maintainability. In recent years, AI agents that can understand code context, plan review actions, and interact with development environments have been increasingly integrated into the code review process. However, there is limited empirical evidence to compare the effectiveness of AI agents and human reviewers in collaborative workflows. To address this gap, we conduct a large-scale empirical analysis of 278,790 code review conversations across 300 open-source GitHub projects. In our study, we aim to compare the feedback differences provided by human reviewers and AI agents. We investigate human-AI collaboration patterns in review conversations to understand how interaction shapes review outcomes. Moreover, we analyze the adoption of code suggestions provided by human reviewers and AI agents into the codebase and how adopted suggestions change code quality. We find that human reviewers provide additional feedback than AI agents, including understanding, testing, and knowledge transfer. Human reviewers exchange 11.8% more rounds when reviewing AI-generated code than human-written code. Moreover, code suggestions made by AI agents are adopted into the codebase at a significantly lower rate than suggestions proposed by human reviewers. Over half of unadopted suggestions from AI agents are either incorrect or addressed through alternative fixes by developers. When adopted, suggestions provided by AI agents produce significantly larger increases in code complexity and code size than suggestions provided by human reviewers. Our findings suggest that while AI agents can scale defect screening, human oversight remains critical for ensuring suggestion quality and providing contextual feedback that AI agents lack.

Software Engineering.title: A Failure Mode Taxonomy and Severity Model for Ethereum Smart Contracts
Software Engineering.summary: Smart contracts are a core component of blockchain systems, but their immutability makes failures in deployed code catastrophic and irreversible. Existing work classifies vulnerabilities, defects, and attacks, yet the observable failures of smart contracts, the deviations from intended behavior or the expected ledger state seen once a contract is deployed, have been largely disregarded. In this paper, we design and validate a failure mode taxonomy for Ethereum smart contracts, together with a severity model that ranks failures by their observable impact. Using a literature review as input, we follow the taxonomy development method of Nickerson et al. to derive the failure modes and their dimensions, and we subject the resulting taxonomy to a saturation exercise over a systematic literature review, the OpenSCV vulnerability catalog, and smart contract incidents reported after the search cutoff. Each failure mode is characterized along five dimensions, namely root cause, violated security property, impact (recorded as primary, secondary, and other), affected component, and nature, and is given a standardized name targeting the observable malfunction rather than the underlying vulnerability. From the taxonomy, we derive CIPER, a five-level severity model that groups failure modes by their observable impact. The saturation exercise produced no new failure modes or dimensions. The taxonomy offers a shared vocabulary for describing what smart contracts do wrong when they fail, and CIPER links that vocabulary to the severity of each observable outcome.

Software Engineering.title: What Carries Architectural Signal? A Code-to-Architecture Mapping Study
Software Engineering.summary:
Code-to-architecture mapping assigns source files to modules of a reference architecture. Representations of implementation artifacts can capture code text, dependencies, and directory organization, but predictive gains alone do not establish the contribution of additional graph processing. Dependencies may already be encoded in these representations, while directories may closely match the reference decomposition. We investigate how artifact representations and graph context affect mapping on ten Java, C, and C++ systems with a limited labeling budget. We compare lexical, structural, and contextual file representations and assess each predictor with and without dependency neighbors. Using a Heterogeneous Graph Transformer (HGT), we compare file-level graphs extended with member nodes summarizing each file's program elements, folder nodes, or both, alongside a variant encoding folder paths directly in file representations. We compare folder-aware predictions with a directory rule using the same labeled files.
  Representations encoding dependency information outperform lexical representations on most systems. Additional neighbor aggregation can improve mapping, depending on the predictor and aggregation direction. Folder-aware variants yield the largest and most consistent gains across the evaluated HGT configurations. However, the directory rule achieves per-system median accuracy of 89-100%, and adding folder information does not consistently improve predictions for files the rule misclassifies. Member nodes provide no consistent improvement over file-level graphs. These findings support assessing what file representations and directory organization already provide before attributing improvements to graph neural networks.

Software Engineering.title: Prompt Less, Infer More: Static Analysis-Guided LLM Type Annotation for Python
Software Engineering.summary: Type annotations improve the maintainability and reliability of Python programs, but many real-world projects remain under-annotated because manual annotation is time-consuming and error-prone. Recent neural and LLM-based type inference systems can recover missing annotations, yet they often trade accuracy for efficiency. Existing approaches often fail to exploit project-wide type evidence, or do so inefficiently through unnecessary model calls and noisy prompts. We present SALT, an LLM-based type inference system guided by static analysis. SALT integrates static analysis with LLM inference to resolve types statically, prioritize LLM queries, and construct concise type-aware context. To demonstrate the effectiveness of SALT, we evaluated it on 12 real-world Python projects. SALT achieves the best accuracy among the evaluated systems and reduces estimated LLM cost by up to 78.5% compared with a strong coding-assistant baseline. It also shows similar cost savings with the frontier model GPT-5.5, demonstrating that SALT remains effective with strong LLMs.

Software Engineering.title: SCRBench: Beyond Equivalence Checking for Semantic Change Reasoning in Code
