Cryptography and Security.summary: In recent years, the growing adoption of Edge AI systems has been accompanied by a surge in security threats. Edge AI deployments face an rapidly evolving spectrum of security threats, from side-channel information leakage to ad- versarial model manipulation and physical device tampering. Conventional security mechanisms such as malware scanners and resource-intensive firewall solutions are unsuitable due to edge AIs typically limited computational resources, strict energy budgets and thermal constraints especially in battery-powered and field-deployed environments. This paper proposes a stacked, hardware-based security mechanism that enables low-overhead, continuous detection of anomalous execution patterns. Anomaly detection utilizing hard- ware performance counters and physical sensors outperforms software-based alternatives by providing key capabilities such as tamper-resistant root-of-trust isolation, negligible runtime overhead, and resilience against compromised operating systems. Experimental analysis shows that adversarial or malicious ap- plications produce observable deviations in sensor and thermal readings on Edge AI systems and hardware-based anomaly detection provides effective and low-overhead anomaly detection.
Cryptography and Security.comment: IEEE 3DIC Conference

Cryptography and Security.title: Side-Channel Attack Prevention for Post Quantum Cryptography Algorithms: A 3D-Shield Approach
Cryptography and Security.summary: Despite their theoretical quantum attack resistance, practical implementations of post-quantum cryptography (PQC) algorithms remain susceptible to side-channel attacks. This includes all standard algorithms selected the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) such as Kyber/ML-KEM, Dilithium/ML-DSA, Falcon/FN-DSA and SPHINCS+/SLH-DSA. This paper proposes an alternative defense for side-channel resilience based on 3D integration that uses 3D hardware to shield the underlying cryptographic activity by introducing decoy keys and physical shielding through stacking. The proposed approach can complement other security measures (such as masking and shuffling) on protecting Number Theoretic Transform (NTT) that move computation to dedicated NTT chips. We outline the construction of our approach and validate the effectiveness on a generic attack targeting intermediate computation inside an NTT butterfly.
Cryptography and Security.comment: IEEE 3DIC Conference 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: What Must Be Done Here? Using a Bounded Application-Security Ontology at the Point of Change
Cryptography and Security.summary: The security guidance that bears on code is real but scattered. It lives across secure-development frameworks, verification standards, controls catalogues, threat taxonomies, and, increasingly, normative regimes such as the EU's NIS2 -- and most of it is written for readers other than the engineer, or the AI assistant, at a point of change. Existing cybersecurity ontologies largely model attacks, indicators, and risk for detection and analysis, not the engineering-practice substance one must act on. This paper presents a use case for an existing bounded application-security ontology, AppSec Core, whose construction and validation are reported separately. We show how it is used. It makes the engineering-actionable fraction of those authorities addressable as a typed working set: the control objectives that apply, the practices that realize them, the mechanisms that implement them, and the evidence artifacts they expect, each traceable to the sources that justify it. We reach that working set from two entry points that recur in practice. Forward, from a code change: a change to authentication middleware scopes to its governing domain slice and returns the obligations the change must satisfy. Inverse, from a normative obligation: "make this NIS2-compliant" resolves a generic legal duty into the concrete engineering obligations it implies across slices, surfacing precisely the fraction of a mostly-governance regulation that lands in code. The same working set is what a human engineer reads and what an LLM-grounded assistant is handed as grounding. The use turns "read every applicable authority" into "satisfy this typed working set", for a code change or a compliance duty alike. The contribution is the demonstrated use; the artefact, its validation, and its governance are companion work.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at Semantic Shields 3: the 3rd International Workshop on Modeling for Cybersecurity, co-located with JOWO 2026 / FOIS 2026, Vitória, Brazil, September 2026. To appear in the JOWO 2026 proceedings (CEUR-WS)

Cryptography and Security.title: The Blind Spots of Detection: Adversarial Perturbation Attacks against Watchdogs in Distributed LLM Inference
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Decentralizing large language model (LLM) inference across untrusted Web nodes requires robust verification to ensure computational integrity. Existing activation-based verification and detection mechanisms validate intermediate outputs against reference values, permitting bounded numerical deviations to accommodate benign cross-hardware discrepancies. However, a critical security question remains: what can a malicious worker achieve while operating within these tolerance bounds?
  In this work, we introduce Hush-Up, a stealthy availability attack against distributed LLM inference, where a single malicious worker halts generation while evading attribution. The attacker first profiles its local execution to model an empirical bound of benign hardware errors. Using this error bound as a feasibility constraint, the attacker optimizes an adversarial perturbation on its output activations to maximize the final-layer probability of the end-of-sequence (EOS) token, i.e., to hush up the model. Across diverse models and benchmarks, Hush-Up effectively forces premature generation termination and collapses model capabilities. Furthermore, the attack hushes up the watchdogs themselves: existing defenses often fail to detect the sabotage entirely or falsely attribute the amplified downstream anomalies to honest workers. Our findings expose a fundamental gap between local numerical verification and end-to-end accountability: perturbations too small to indict a worker locally can nevertheless be powerful enough to break distributed inference globally.

Cryptography and Security.title: Pop Goes the Verifier: Phoneme-Targeted Data Poisoning of Voice Liveness Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Many Automated Speaker Verification Systems (ASVs) commonly employ liveliness detection techniques, such as VoicePop, which identify genuine speech by analyzing low- frequency pop bursts from plosive phonemes using Gammatone Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (GFCC) and an SVM classifier. While effective against traditional replay attacks, such systems are vulnerable to data poisoning techniques. Prior work shows that broadly applied SyntheticPop attacks can collapse model to accuracy to as low as 14.01% using only 20% poisoned samples, but the resulting artifacts are easily detectable when visualizing the waveform energies. This paper introduces Pop Goes the Verifier, a stealthier phoneme injection poisoning attack. By leveraging FastSpeech 2 (FS2) with a modified HiFi-GAN vocoder, we inject localized pop bursts at plosive phoneme locations and overlay subtle Gaussian noise to reduce the visibility of injected artifacts in waveform and spectrogram analysis. Using the ASVSpoof 2019 as the dataset, we observe that the approach achieves a moderate poisoning attack while providing greater resistance to signal-level inspection than the original SyntheticPop attack.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at IEEE International Joint Conference on Biometrics (IJCB) 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: VeilFL: Two-Stage Accountability for Anonymous Federated Learning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Anonymous credentials can hide which registered client participates in federated learning, but their unlinkability also makes repeated misconduct difficult to associate. We present VeilFL, a two-aggregator protocol that adds staged accountability to PINE (USENIX Security '24). Each submission binds two private PINE messages, a round-specific pseudonym, and a tracing pair to the same hidden credential secret. This design enables detection of duplicate submissions within a round without introducing a persistent identifier for normal participation. VeilFL implements accountability in two stages. After a confirmed duplicate or joint PINE rejection, a threshold tracing committee reveals a stable handle that links faults associated with the same credential. The client's registered identity is recoverable only after the public log records the requisite number of linked faults and a separate threshold committee authorizes identification. Accepted and unopened submissions remain unlinkable under the stated assumptions. This work establishes submission binding and duplicate detection, anonymity, fault non-frameability, controlled two-stage opening, and preservation of PINE's privacy and validity guarantees. In the prototype implementation, creating a submission requires a median of 2.11 ms, while verification requires 3.01 ms. Batch verification reduces the cost to 1.86 ms per submission for a batch of 1,000. The public part of each submission is 608 bytes, with 1,248 bytes of additional VeilFL protocol data across the two aggregator submissions. Each opening stage completes within 4.3 ms for the different committee configurations.

Cryptography and Security.title: Trouble With Time: Compile Timestamps and First-Seen Date Regression in EMBER2024
Cryptography and Security.summary: Reliable first-seen dates are important for constructing temporal malware evaluation splits, but this information often comes from external services that are not equally accessible to all researchers. We investigate whether machine learning can instead estimate an executable's first-seen date or determine when its PE/COFF compilation timestamp is unreliable. Using EMBER2024, we evaluate feature-based and raw-byte models across classification, regression, ranking, and latent-reliability formulations. Direct first-seen regression produces errors comparable to a substantial portion of the dataset's collection window, and none of the evaluated scores provides a useful chronological ordering of files. Current models therefore cannot replace externally sourced first-seen metadata. In contrast, classifiers can identify timestamps that fall within specified tolerances of first seen and can detect clearly implausible timestamps with high discrimination. We also find substantial timestamp disagreement among both benign and malicious executables, indicating that unreliable timestamps are not exclusively a product of malicious manipulation. These results establish baselines and identify timestamp reliability as a distinct direction for future security-ML research.
Cryptography and Security.comment: To appear in the Conference on Applied Machine Learning for Information Security (CAMLIS) 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: E-UDE: A Scientific Machine Learning Model for Malware Propagation Dynamics
Cryptography and Security.summary: Understanding the malware propagation dynamics over the Internet is crucial for effectively controlling its spread. Existing mechanistic and data-driven models in the context of malware propagation dynamics, have some issues with either interpretability or predictive accuracy. This study presents an Enhanced Universal Differential Equation (E-UDE) framework that explicitly incorporates more detailed key factors that influence malware propagation. Evaluation on real-world malware propagation data shows that the E-UDE achieves the best overall performance, attaining an overall RMSE of 783.70 and MAE of 421.65. Compared with the Classical ODE and the UDE models, the proposed approach reduces RMSE by approximately 66 percent and 39 percent, respectively. Its robustness to predictive capability is further evaluated. In this experiment, the E-UDE achieves a Test RMSE of 634.6, a Test MAE of 419.3, and a Test Correlation of 0.964. The E-UDE maintains relatively stable prediction performance as the noise level increases, showing limited degradation compared with the baseline models. Furthermore, this E-UDE model enables us to perform several scenario analyses under different cybersecurity scenarios, providing a useful framework for better understanding the effective control factors. To study the wide applicability of the E-UDE framework, the model performance is assessed by two different datasets, namely, Code Red dataset and Witty Worm dataset.

Cryptography and Security.title: Trustworthy Blockchain-based Federated Learning for Electronic Health Records: Identity-Gated Participation against Sybil Attacks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Federated learning allows hospitals to train a shared clinical model without exchanging patient records, but its aggregation assumes that each participant is a distinct institution. In an open federation, an adversary can register many fake identities (a Sybil attack) and outweigh honest hospitals. Byzantine-robust aggregation mitigates such attacks only while the adversary is a minority. We ask whether binding participation to accountable institutional identity closes that gap, and at what cost. We present TBFL, a framework in which an accountable authority issues Verifiable Credentials to the Decentralized Identifiers of hospitals, and a smart-contract registry on a peer-to-peer ledger admits model updates only from credentialed senders. We evaluated a prototype on in-hospital mortality prediction with MIMIC-IV records split across simulated hospitals, comparing the identity gate with federated averaging, three robust aggregators, norm clipping, and a similarity-based defense. Robust aggregators held against a Sybil minority, and norm clipping only against random vectors; all failed when half the participants were Sybils trained on real records with flipped labels. The similarity-based defense stopped mutually similar Sybils but yielded to perturbed ones. The gate rejected all unauthorized submissions and maintained attack-free performance for every strategy up to 60% Sybils. It did not stop credentialed hospitals that flipped their own labels, whereas the gate followed by the coordinate-wise median withstood both. On a local node, on-chain checks added about 1% to training time; fees made training impractical on a public mainnet but affordable on a rollup. Identity gating complements robust aggregation rather than replacing it.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 28 pages, 10 figures, 14 tables. v2: substantially revised. Fixes credential replay after revocation in the registry contract, adds testnet deployments (Ethereum Sepolia, Arbitrum Sepolia), credentialed-insider and label-flipping experiments, and replaces the illustrative results of v1 with multi-seed results. Code and run logs: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23836753

Cryptography and Security.title: Illusion: Safeguarding Topology Confidentiality in LLM Multi-Agent Systems via Behavior-Preserving Obfuscation
Cryptography and Security.summary: The communication topology of Large Language Model Multi-Agent Systems (LLM-MASs) governs how information propagates among agents and encodes critical domain knowledge and expert workflow design. It is valuable intellectual property and plays a decisive role in system utility and safety, yet remains vulnerable to inference attacks that stealthily reconstruct it from agent outputs. Existing defenses detect or mitigate such attacks but do not proactively conceal the topology itself. We propose \textit{Illusion}, a proactive topology obfuscation defense for LLM-MAS. \textit{Illusion} injects fake edges and fake messages to present attackers with a deceptive topology, while selecting low-impact candidates that preserve output-distribution equivalence and task-accuracy non-inferiority. The resulting fake edges are designed to be indistinguishable from genuine messages under black-box observation. Extensive experiments show that \textit{Illusion} reduces edge-level F1 from over 0.87 to 0.62 and graph similarity from over 0.94 to 0.71. It also largely preserves output distributions and task performance, and its fake edges resist both similarity-based and LLM-judge filtering, even under adaptive pruning.

Cryptography and Security.title: Intent-Bound Authorization for Cryptocurrency Withdrawals Under Backend Compromise
Cryptography and Security.summary: Binance's preliminary account of its October 2026 attack raises a custody question that key protection alone cannot answer: how can a provider prevent unauthorized withdrawals when an attacker controls a service permitted to request signatures? We propose the Intent-Bound Withdrawal Authorization Protocol (IWAP). Before signing, independent enforcement checks customer intent, exact transaction effects, fresh workload evidence, and a committed single-use spending reservation. Administrative actions use a separate authorization path. We specify the protocol's trust assumptions and give conditional arguments for intent preservation, replay resistance, and a fixed-epoch exposure bound. A Python reference monitor authenticates synthetic records with Ed25519 and serializes reservations with SQLite. It rejects 1,200 negative requests, accepts 3,000 valid synthetic requests, and preserves a 100-unit budget under 64 concurrent attempts in each of 20 trials. When the intent authority is deliberately compromised, malicious requests pass, but the independent budget still limits admitted exposure. The study evaluates a normalized policy model, not Binance's infrastructure or a deployed custody platform. Its contribution is an explicit authorization boundary and reproducible tests of that boundary.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 1 table

Cryptography and Security.title: Cross-Evidence Authorization State Learning for Runtime Detection of Broken Object-Level Authorization in Black-Box Web Applications
Cryptography and Security.summary: Broken object-level authorization (BOLA) remains difficult to detect in black-box Web applications because external runtime monitors generally lack access to source code, authorization policies, and object-ownership records. This paper proposes a cross-evidence authorization-state learning method that reconstructs subject--resource--object--action relations from request--response transactions. The method represents authorization relations with confidence-aware states, aggregates positive and negative evidence while accounting for provenance independence, and applies contamination-gated promotion, evidence quarantine and rollback, expiration, and revocation. A Python prototype is evaluated using a deterministic synthetic benchmark comprising 64,400 requests across five independent random seeds. In this benchmark, the proposed method achieves 100.00% recall, an F1-score of 56.63%, and a false-positive rate of 33.65%, while the measured unauthorized-relation pollution rate is 0.00%. Ablation experiments show that removing provenance independence or evidence quarantine increases the pollution rate to 100.00%. The experiments provide an initial evaluation under controlled synthetic conditions.

Cryptography and Security.title: AgentCap: Capability-Based Runtime Authorization for Secure LLM Agent Execution
Cryptography and Security.summary: Language-model agents commonly collapse two decisions that security systems separate: selecting an action and determining whether that action is authorized. When a model exercises standing authority, indirect prompt injection can convert influence over its reasoning into unauthorized effects. We present AgentCap, a runtime authorization layer that externalizes this decision from the model and mediates every tool invocation through an MCP wrapper. Each request declares an intent, and AgentCap evaluates policy constraints over trust, workflow prerequisites, mutually exclusive authority, and the provenance of security-sensitive arguments. Authorized requests receive short-lived, budget-bounded capability tokens that are validated at the tool boundary. Delegation is restricted to session-bound parent-child chains that preserve action and resource while budget and lifetime can only be attenuated, preventing authority from being expanded or reused across unrelated agent sessions. A declarative policy language provides a common representation for runtime enforcement and predeployment analysis. Across AgentDojo and InjecAgent, AgentCap reduces attack success in every evaluated model-benchmark setting, including zero attack success with GPT-5.4 on both benchmarks. Controlled adversarial scenarios further show that AgentCap blocks every attempted unauthorized execution (ASR 0%) while preserving all legitimate operations exercised. These results demonstrate that agent security requires authorization of model-proposed effects at the tool boundary, independently of the model's reasoning.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted at the Third Workshop on Agents in the Wild, NeurIPS 2026 (non-archival)

Cryptography and Security.title: Constructing Budgeted KGW Evasion through Token-Event Evidence Replacement
Cryptography and Security.summary: KGW watermarks bias sampling to accumulate keyed detection evidence. We construct budgeted evasion through token-event evidence replacement using ordinary phrase rewrites. Our construction jointly selects compositions of LLM-proposed alternatives from an independent model and measures global token-edit distance on complete outputs. At the largest attainable cost within the budget, exact coverage search maximizes removal of original scored token pairs. It uses a known tokenizer without the key, detector feedback or queries to the watermarked model. Exact accounting separates source evidence removed, evidence created and length effects, with initial strength setting the required reduction. Separate signed-event analysis found that mean suppression arose mainly from removing watermark-enriched source events. In controlled, occurrence-counted, one-token-context KGW tests on short passages, 39 of 82 qualified, initially detected sources yielded rewrites with terminal detector score Z < 4 that passed blinded source-relative model review, at a mean actual token-edit cost of 16.0% under a 20% allowance. To examine whether this initial requirement can be inferred, a separate historical 95-passage study estimated initial detector score Z0 from generation traces with correlation 0.793 and an in-sample association beyond length. This aggregate information did not establish improved allocation, and the separate no-trace stopping test did not reliably exploit cheaper reviewed crossings in the candidate bank. Comparisons did not establish an advantage over simpler selection and ordinary constrained rewriting. The construction makes budgeted evidence replacement executable while exposing limits in signed reduction and recognition of sufficient editing.

Cryptography and Security.title: The Long Con on the Web: Earn-then-Exploit Fraud Attacks against Coding Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Coding agents increasingly operate with web access and high privileges, creating a new attack surface where web fraud can directly target autonomous agents. Existing studies mainly focus on malicious links, prompt injection, and interface deception, while content-level web fraud against agents and the amplification of attacks through agent trust remain underexplored. In this paper, we present EtE (Earn-then-Exploit), a web fraud attack framework against coding agents, in which a malicious website first provides multiple rounds of genuinely verifiable assistance to establish trust and then introduces task-related instructions that cross intended operational boundaries. To systematically evaluate its effectiveness, we construct 56 organizational environments (8 task contexts x 7 attack consequences) and evaluate three representative coding agents. EtE achieves an average scene-level attack success rate of 71.4%, including 85.7% on Codex-GPT-5.5, 67.9% on ZCode-GLM-5.3-Flash, and 60.7% on QwenCode-Qwen3.7-Plus, significantly outperforming all injection-based baselines. More importantly, our experiments reveal that coding agents exhibit trust-like behavioral reliance on previously helpful Web sources, and that such accumulated credibility significantly increases their susceptibility to subsequent malicious instructions. Based on this finding, we propose action-authorization separation (AAS), which prevents web content from directly authorizing privileged actions and reduces the attack success rate to 0% while preserving 100% task completion, outperforming all evaluated defense baselines.

Cryptography and Security.title: Adversarial Robustness Is Not Zero-Day Generalization: A Controlled Evaluation of Flow-Based Intrusion Detectors on Corrected CIC-IDS2017
Cryptography and Security.summary: Synthetic variants of known attacks, including feature-space adversarial perturbations, are sometimes used as stand-ins for unseen ("zero-day") attacks when evaluating machine-learning network intrusion detection systems (NIDS). We test whether this proxy holds. On the corrected CIC-IDS2017 release we train Random Forest, XGBoost, a 1D-CNN and an FT-Transformer and compare, at a fixed 1% false-positive rate over five seeds, detection under constrained perturbations of known attacks (gradient-based and black-box attacks on 42 attacker-controllable features) with leave-one-attack-family-out (LOAO) detection, where an entire family is absent from training. Detection under the strongest perturbation we tested, with budgets of at most 0.2, stays between 90.9% and 99.7%, yet mean detection of held-out families falls to 76.2% (RF), 40.2% (XGBoost), 25.8% (1D-CNN) and 22.8% (FT-Transformer). Robustness exceeds LOAO detection for every model (gaps of 24 to 72 percentage points, 23 to 66 when robustness is also averaged over families; Holm-adjusted p $\le$ 0.00096), and the two measures agree at most on a coarse ranking of the models. An exact mixed-integer evasion search confirms the tree ensembles' scores. Benign-only anomaly detectors and a simple multi-class open-set baseline do not close the gap. A temporal split on 5 seeds (3 of the 4 models) leaves the gap in place. On CSE-CIC-IDS2018 the gap recurs for every model (16 to 68 points). On these benchmarks and under this threat model, a robustness score should not be read as a zero-day score, and the two should be reported separately. Code and per-seed results are publicly available.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 10 pages, 10 tables. Code and per-seed results: https://github.com/abdulhamid-zaro/robustness-vs-zeroday-nids

Cryptography and Security.title: CISAF: A Framework for Risk Assessment of Academic and Research Cyberinfrastructure
Cryptography and Security.summary: Academic and research cyberinfrastructures (AR-CIs) present unique risk and security challenges due to their collaborative nature and heterogeneous components. However, the industry-well-accepted risk assessment approaches have limited compatibility and specificity for complex systems like cyberinfrastructures (CIs). We propose CyberInfrastructure Security Analysis Framework (CISAF) -- a simple, systematic, mission-centric, and integrable approach to file for CI risk assessment. CISAF serves as a plug-in to traditional risk assessment/management frameworks, a convenient tool to extrapolate the cybersecurity risks for complex cybersystems. It guides AR-CI administrators through a top-down process: (1) defining unacceptable losses, (2) identifying associated system hazards and critical assets, (3) analyzing possible attack paths targeting these critical assets, (4) cross-referencing security mechanisms deployed along these attack paths, and (5) integrating results into established risk assessment/management frameworks. By combining information about CI architecture, missions, attack graphs, and security mechanisms, CISAF provides actionable guidelines, structured views of high-priority security risks, and streamlined translation into established frameworks.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Total of 19 pages: formal text 8 pages, LLM usage + citation for 2 pages, an appendix of the LLM prompt for 9 pages. 2 figures. Pending next revision for submission

Cryptography and Security.title: Compressed Oracle Duality: A simple framework for knowing what quantum adversaries know
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The Compressed Oracle method of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) is one method that records the queries that the adversary makes; this recording serves as a representation of the information that is learned. However, a significant limitation of the Compressed Oracle method is that it may continue to store information that the adversary has "forgotten." This issue is especially pertinent in the space-bounded setting, where the adversary may uncompute information to free up space, while the information may still reside in the compressed oracle.
  In this work, we present a simple and interpretable framework called "Compressed Oracle Duality," which extends the Compressed Oracle method for space-bounded algorithms. By applying an isometry to the memory of a quantum adversary, we obtain a pair of compressed oracles with identical marginal distributions and classical correlations which correspond to the knowledge the adversary retains. In fact, we show that the outcome of measuring the new compressed oracle database corresponds exactly to applying the pretty-good measurement on the adversary's memory.
  As an application of our framework for collision search, we give a simplified proof of the recent $T^2S = Ω(N\log N)$ quantum time-space tradeoff for label-symmetric algorithms due to Magniez-Zur (arXiv:2609.10808); we also prove a stronger classical tradeoff of $TS=Ω(N\log N)$ assuming label symmetry. The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 34 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: Beyond Sensitive APIs: Detecting Access Control Flaws at Sensitive Callsites in Android Firmware
Cryptography and Security.summary: Existing studies of vulnerable pre-installed Android apps identify dangerous behavior by checking whether an app invokes an API from a predefined set of security-sensitive APIs. These sets usually exclude generic APIs to avoid false positives; unfortunately, this misses a class of vulnerabilities in which a generic API, such as a database read, appears benign in general but becomes security-sensitive when operating on protected data, yet is left without sufficient access control. While this class of vulnerabilities appears addressable via access control analysis, existing studies focus only on the presence of checks, not on whether those checks enforce sufficient protection for the operation at a given callsite. In this work, we propose Callix, which first assesses callsite sensitivity by jointly analyzing the invoked API functionality and the data involved in the operation, then recovers each security check on the execution path as an explicit security property, and finally introduces the notion of restriction context to decide whether these checks are sufficient for the identified sensitive operation. We evaluated Callix on 1,750 distinct pre-installed apps from the 10 top-tier Android vendors as of 2025. In total, Callix discovered 819 vulnerable paths across these vendors, 42.1% of which allow reading or modifying private user data through generic database operations. Manual validation of a random 60% sample shows a precision of 95.1%. Many of our findings have been confirmed and rewarded through vendor bug bounty programs.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted to NDSS 2027. 17 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: Price is Only the Symptom: Understanding and Analyzing Economic-State Manipulation Vulnerabilities in DeFi
Cryptography and Security.summary: Economic-state manipulation has emerged as a significant security threat to decentralized finance (DeFi), causing substantial financial losses. Existing studies predominantly characterize these attacks as price manipulation, focusing on observable price distortions while overlooking underlying violations of economic-state integrity. We conduct a comprehensive empirical study of Economic-State Manipulation (ESM) vulnerabilities in DeFi. We first curate a diverse dataset comprising 276 real-world attacks and 91 Code4rena audit findings. Based on these cases, we develop a cause-oriented taxonomy comprising four primary categories and eleven subcategories. Our analysis reveals that ESM vulnerabilities extend beyond conventional price manipulation, frequently involving violations of protocol-internal accounting, AMM state consistency, and execution-time constraints. We further investigate the evaluation datasets of six existing studies and find that, although they cover 6-10 vulnerability subcategories, their distributions remain dominated by limited manipulation mechanisms. Furthermore, we systematically evaluate seven representative detection approaches on our dataset. Our results reveal limited coverage, with the best-performing approach identifying only 50.4% of real-world attacks. Through an analysis of false negatives and false positives, we identify fundamental limitations arising from reliance on predefined attack patterns, insufficient reasoning about economic-state semantics, and incomplete exploitability validation. These findings provide empirical insights for developing more generalizable ESM vulnerability detection techniques.

Cryptography and Security.title: DERED: Enhancing Third-Party Library Detection in Binaries via Deceptive Reuse Mitigation
Cryptography and Security.summary: This paper introduces the concept of deceptive reuse a misleading reuse relationship between recipient software that share common TPL code and proposes a novel approach, DERED, to enhance TPL detection by distinguishing between real reuse and deceptive reuse.

Cryptography and Security.title: Clawdrain: Exploiting Tool-Calling Chains for Stealthy Token Exhaustion in OpenClaw Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary: Tool-calling LLM agents rely on third-party skills to extend their capabilities, but this openness exposes a supply-chain attack surface in which malicious skill instructions can manipulate agent execution across multiple turns. In this work, we present Clawdrain, a Trojanized OpenClaw skill that induces resource exhaustion through a Segmented Verification Process (SVP). SVP combines stateful progression, repair-driven repetition, and termination to create costly tool-calling chains while preserving a legitimate final payload. We evaluate Clawdrain in a production-like OpenClaw deployment with real API billing across Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek V4 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Clawdrain achieves 2-16 times token amplification with plain SVP, while the three models exhibit distinct behaviors, including autoregressive compliance, proactive scripting, and extended trial-and-error reasoning. Our findings reveal that agent resource exhaustion arises not only from output generation, but also from repeated context re-ingestion, tool coordination, reasoning, and recovery, motivating system-level controls over cumulative skill behavior.

Cryptography and Security.title: Practical Preimages for 19- and 20-Step SHA-256 with Standard Padding
Cryptography and Security.summary: We present practical preimage attacks on 19- and 20-step SHA-256 that respect the standard IV, Davies-Meyer feed-forward, and full FIPS 180-4 padding, for arbitrary prescribed 256-bit targets. Building on Basra's algebraic selector saturation and backward padding absorption, we introduce three techniques: an exact $O(1)$ inversion of the low padding byte $(W_{13} \bmod 256) = \mathtt{0x80}$ that leaves $(a_5, a_6)$ free for exact context shaping; a causal bit-slice equivalence theorem that prunes $99.74\%$ of right-hand candidate nodes across seven stages; and a closed-form $\mathbf{F}_2$ upper-half inverse paired with compact $Q_0^{-1}$ lookup tables. One CPU core solves arbitrary 19-step padded targets in $1.2$--$86.4$ s (median $19.5$ s) after an $18$ s table build. A 20-step padded preimage costs $2^{46.6}$ CPU-reference evaluations: $191$ node-hours on one 10-core Apple M4 CPU node (16 threads), or $9.0$--$22.2$ GPU-hours on one NVIDIA L4. A companion Zero-$a_3$ bridge inverts the unpadded 20-step compression function in $2^{38.1}$ evaluations. We provide 46 self-verifying witnesses, including 55-byte preimages of SHA-256("abc") and $0^{256}$. These attacks cover 19--20 of 64 steps and do not threaten full SHA-256.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 25 pages, 7 tables, 2 algorithms. Source code and 46 self-verifying witnesses: https://github.com/srw/sha256-19-and-20-step-preimages-with-padding

Cryptography and Security.title: Proximity Gaps for Gabidulin Codes and Applications
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Proximity gaps are central to the soundness of interactive oracle proofs of proximity (IOPPs) and polynomial commitment schemes (PCSs). An $[n,k,d]$ linear code $C\subseteq\mathbb F^n$ has a $δ$-proximity gap with error $ε$ if, for every $u_0,u_1\in\mathbb F^n$, either all points on $\ell_{u_0,u_1}=\{u_0+αu_1:α\in\mathbb F\}$ are $δ$-close to $C$, or at most an $ε$ fraction are. Although proximity gaps for Hamming-metric codes are well understood, their rank-metric counterparts remain largely unexplored despite their applications in coding theory and cryptography. In this work, we study proximity gaps for linear rank-metric codes and their cryptographic applications.
  First, we show that every $[n,k,d]$ linear rank-metric code $C$ over $\mathbb F_{q^m}$ admits a proximity gap for every $δ\le(d-1)/(3n)$, with error at most $q^{e+1}/q^m$, where $e=\lfloorδn\rfloor$. For Gabidulin codes, we improve the gap to $(d-1)/(2n)$ with error $10q^{n-1}/q^m$. These two proximity gaps match those for general linear Hamming-metric codes and Reed--Solomon (RS) codes, respectively. We prove the $(d-1)/(2n)$ bound is tight by constructing an infinite family of constant-rate Gabidulin codes and affine lines $\ell_{u_0,u_1}$ on which a $1-o(1)$ fraction of points are $d/(2n)$-close to the code, while $u_1$ is at least $3d/(4n)$-far from it. At $δ=(d-1)/(2n)$, a further counterexample gives a lower bound of order $q^{n-1}/q^m$ on $\varepsilon$, matching our upper bound up to a constant factor.
  As applications, we construct an IOPP for interleaved Gabidulin codes by adapting the Ligero IOPP for interleaved RS codes. We then adapt the Ligero-based PCS for ordinary polynomials to obtain a $q$-linearized polynomial commitment scheme. To our knowledge, this is the first PCS framework based on rank-metric error-correcting codes.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 40 pages

Cryptography and Security.title: Threat Modeling Intimate Partner Abuse in Agentic Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Agentic systems are AI-powered technologies capable of autonomous action within digital environments, such as sending emails or making reservations. They are deeply connected to external tools as well as users' data and resources, making them vulnerable to attacks which exploit their access and capabilities. In this work, we apply the technology-facilitated abuse threat model, in the context of intimate partner violence and surveillance, to these systems, revealing threats that require deliberate investigation and mitigation. We categorize attacks based on system ownership: (1) Abuser-as-owner attacks demonstrate how agentic systems make existing forms of technology-facilitated abuse far easier and more scalable. (2) Victim-survivor-as-owner attacks show how agentic systems create a new attack surface which abusers can exploit. In light of these risks, we outline research and development directions for effective mitigation strategies.

Programming Languages.title: WFDB-x: Conformance-Tested Implementations of the WFDB Software Package in Seven Programming Languages
Programming Languages.summary: The WFDB format is widely used to store and exchange physiological waveforms and annotations. However, existing software implementations are limited to C, Python, and MATLAB/Octave, can produce different results in corner cases and checksum calculations, and have defaults such as sampling frequency and gain, that can lead to silent misinterpretation of recordings. We developed WFDB-x, a cross-language, performance-optimized reimplementation of WFDB in seven programming languages, with extensive unit tests, to provide consistent WFDB processing across programming languages. We reimplemented the WFDB Software Package 10.7.0 natively in Python, C++, Rust, Julia, R, MATLAB/Octave, and Kotlin, using AI-assistance under human direction and review. Each implementation has library functions, a high-level interface, and command-line tools. We compared their outputs with those of the original C programs using 1098 conformance cases, 877 legacy-mode cases, unit tests, and differential fuzzing. Deliberate changes remove implicit waveform parameters, restrict file and network access, and prevent annotation loss. A legacy mode retains the original behavior. All seven implementations passed every conformance and legacy-mode case on the tested Linux platform, with matching outputs. The unit tests contain 9353 assertions. C++, Rust, and Julia read records 1.5-6.9 times faster than the original C library, while the Python implementation wrote records 9.2 times faster than the existing wfdb-python library in the benchmark. WFDB-x provides a tested, open-source basis for reading and writing physiological recordings consistently across seven languages, supporting reproducible research and software development without requiring a shared programming environment. We also share details of the AI-assisted development process and token utilization, which may be useful for other applications.

Programming Languages.title: Specifying Hardware Communication as Programs
Programming Languages.summary: To test and debug hardware modules, it is common to write two programs. A driver maps high-level transactions to cycle-level I/O behavior, and a monitor looks at the low-level I/O trace and recovers transactions. Both programs bridge the same abstraction gap between RTL and functional models. Writing them separately risks inconsistency. ProtoLang is a DSL for specifying hardware protocols. The same ProtoLang program can both drive and monitor transactions. Users specify RTL communication protocols as succinct imperative programs. We present a novel reconstructor algorithm that, given a ProtoLang specification and a waveform, automatically infers a transaction-level trace consistent with the waveform. We demonstrate ProtoLang's utility via case studies focusing on the Wishbone and AXI-Stream interconnects, showing that ProtoLang can model complex protocol features such as burst mode. We highlight how our tools can identify protocol violation bugs in real-world implementations.
Programming Languages.comment: Significantly rewritten version of paper, with a new evaluation section

Programming Languages.title: Stochastic Summaries: Characterizing Structured Datasets Using Probabilistic Programs
Programming Languages.summary: What does my data look like? We study the problem of representing and learning summaries of datasets that account for both their structural and statistical properties. This problem is widely useful across many application domains that involve large datasets and analysis/modeling of data, and is of particular interest to Programming Languages. In particular, in this work we focus on the problem of learning these "stochastic summaries" for tree-like data composed of inductive datatypes and argue that probabilistic programs over inductive datatypes can effectively represent the desired summaries. We present Tali, a Probabilistic Programming Language over inductive datatypes, and study the problem of learning such programs from data samples. We identify a semantic property, called Observation-Bounded Compilability, which identifies a set of recursive probabilistic programs which admit exact inference, and can represent many useful and complex probabilistic structures. We then propose an algorithm for learning Tali programs satisfying the OBC property from observations using a combination of program synthesis (stochastic search) and maximum likelihood inference. We implement our learning framework, evaluate it on a diverse benchmark suite, and record our observations on the merits of our approach. We demonstrate the utility of learning stochastic summaries as symbolically-represented priors for downstream learning tasks. We also showcase another utility by using our technique to learn operational profiles of real-world datasets.

Programming Languages.title: Cartesian closedness of lax comma categories
Programming Languages.summary: For a finitely complete category X, we prove that the lax comma category Cat//X is cartesian closed if and only if its free coproduct completion Fam(X) is cartesian closed. The proof uses a change-of-base theorem: postcomposition with a functor induces a left adjoint between lax comma categories precisely when that functor is a left multiadjoint. We describe the exponentials and derive examples from known results on family categories.
Programming Languages.comment: 7 pages

Programming Languages.title: XLA from the Trenches: Correctness on TPU Workloads at Scale
Programming Languages.summary: Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.

Programming Languages.title: te-comp: A Complete MLIR Compiler Generating Self-Contained C Inference Engines for MCUs
Programming Languages.summary:
Deploying deep learning on microcontrollers (MCUs) requires fitting both the model weights and runtime activations within tens to hundreds of kilobytes of SRAM and Flash. Existing approaches either use an interpreter with a pre-written kernel library or combine a Python code generator with hand-written C kernels. This incurs dispatch overhead and requires framework dependencies. None produces self-contained, dependency-free C code specialized to a given model.
  In this paper, we present te-comp, the first complete MLIR-based compiler that takes a standard model in .tflite or .safetensors format and emits all C source files needed for deployment: the inference engine (kernels, weight arrays, memory layout) and the RTOS integration layer with zero runtime dependencies.
  On 10 MCUNet CNN benchmarks, te-comp outperforms MCUNet TinyEngine by using 38% less SRAM (up to 5.9$\times$) and 15% less Flash, while generating complete C code rather than linking a pre-written kernel library. To demonstrate, we use te-comp to compile an 8.3M-parameter GPT-Neo transformer (TinyStories-v2) and deploy it on a single-core Cortex-M7 at 160MHz. The full firmware uses 249KB of 512KB SRAM and 3.62MB of 4MB Flash and achieves approximately 1 token/s interactive text generation via Q4_0 weight quantization, a stateful int4 KV cache, and vocabulary pruning -- a capability no existing MCU inference framework supports.

Software Engineering.title: WFDB-x: Conformance-Tested Implementations of the WFDB Software Package in Seven Programming Languages
Software Engineering.summary: The WFDB format is widely used to store and exchange physiological waveforms and annotations. However, existing software implementations are limited to C, Python, and MATLAB/Octave, can produce different results in corner cases and checksum calculations, and have defaults such as sampling frequency and gain, that can lead to silent misinterpretation of recordings. We developed WFDB-x, a cross-language, performance-optimized reimplementation of WFDB in seven programming languages, with extensive unit tests, to provide consistent WFDB processing across programming languages. We reimplemented the WFDB Software Package 10.7.0 natively in Python, C++, Rust, Julia, R, MATLAB/Octave, and Kotlin, using AI-assistance under human direction and review. Each implementation has library functions, a high-level interface, and command-line tools. We compared their outputs with those of the original C programs using 1098 conformance cases, 877 legacy-mode cases, unit tests, and differential fuzzing. Deliberate changes remove implicit waveform parameters, restrict file and network access, and prevent annotation loss. A legacy mode retains the original behavior. All seven implementations passed every conformance and legacy-mode case on the tested Linux platform, with matching outputs. The unit tests contain 9353 assertions. C++, Rust, and Julia read records 1.5-6.9 times faster than the original C library, while the Python implementation wrote records 9.2 times faster than the existing wfdb-python library in the benchmark. WFDB-x provides a tested, open-source basis for reading and writing physiological recordings consistently across seven languages, supporting reproducible research and software development without requiring a shared programming environment. We also share details of the AI-assisted development process and token utilization, which may be useful for other applications.

Software Engineering.title: ProofPatch: Reviewing Lean Statements and Keeping the Reviews Valid as Formalizations Evolve
Software Engineering.summary: The kernel of the Lean proof assistant checks that a proof establishes its statement. Whether the statement says what was intended is left to human reviewers. This is the old problem of validating a specification, and it grows more pressing as language models write formal statements in bulk and agents edit formal developments continuously. We present ProofPatch, a tool that helps reviewers judge Lean statements and keeps their judgments valid while the development changes. A reviewer can ask the kernel targeted questions about a statement, such as whether a hypothesis is needed or whether a counterexample exists. Each decision is stored with fingerprints of the statement as Lean elaborated it and of the definitions it depends on, and any declaration can be pinned so that a patch changing it is blocked, whether a person or an agent built on a large language model (LLM) wrote the patch. Working on elaborated terms rather than source text is the central design choice: notation and formatting changes leave a decision intact, and a changed definition reaches every theorem that uses it. On 229 pairs of consecutive revisions of Mathlib, Lean's mathematics library, ProofPatch sends 118 of 12,898 synthetic decisions back for review. Every text-based alternative misses at least 38 of these or sends back at least 13 times as many. On 1,527 labeled statements, kernel evidence flags unfaithful ones with precision 0.88 to 0.96, and in 344 runs of an LLM agent no change to a pinned statement got through.

Software Engineering.title: Causality-Based Fault Localization
Software Engineering.summary: We introduce Causality-Based Fault Localization (CBFL), a novel approach to fault localization grounded in the theory of actual causality. We use the notion of causal responsibility to formalize and define the contribution of a given location in the source code under the context of a failing test. We also utilize a distance metric to prioritize minimal fixes and penalize broken tests, leading to more interpretable and fixable fault localization. We implemented CBFL in a tool, SoftReX, and our evaluation results demonstrate that SoftReX outperforms state-of-the-art Mutation-Based Fault Localization (MBFL) tools based on Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) and Top-1 by 16% on both metrics, when using the same set of mutants. We also propose a sophisticated mutation generation strategy based on the structure and representation of the program to improve the accuracy of our ranked list, which outperforms state-of-the-art methods by 2.6x in terms of required mutants evaluated while remaining competitive in performance.

Software Engineering.title: Toward Bounding Coding-Agent Autonomy in Software Maintenance: A Pilot Study of Boundary Contracts
Software Engineering.summary:
As coding agents gain greater autonomy to modify software repositories, relevant context alone does not define their operational authority. An artifact may be relevant to a maintenance task while being inappropriate to edit; conversely, another artifact may be required even when it is not explicitly mentioned in the request. We explore Boundary Contracts, a machine-readable abstraction that makes task-specific artifact roles (editable, inspect-only, required, and protected) explicit before repository modification begins.
  We conduct a pilot study on 40 maintenance tasks from a real enterprise repository, comparing the same Codex-based coding agent with and without Boundary Contract information. The boundary-informed condition improves macro edit-selection F1 from 0.440 to 0.682, required-behavior coverage from 0.429 to 0.673, and the number of strictly acceptable patches from 9 of 40 to 18 of 40. To probe whether these gains are explained only by improved file localization, we additionally analyze 21 tasks in which both conditions modify at least one identical file. Differences remain in edit selectivity and patch outcomes, providing initial evidence that explicit artifact roles may influence maintenance behavior beyond localization alone.
  This pilot does not establish the general effectiveness of Boundary Contracts. Rather, it provides initial evidence for a broader research question: how should the operational boundaries of coding agents be generated, validated, revised, and ultimately enforced as repository-level maintenance becomes increasingly autonomous?
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at the 2nd Joint Workshop on AI for Software Engineering (JAWS 2), co-located with ASE 2026, Munich, Germany

Software Engineering.title: AdapBench: Adaptive Early-Stopping and Prioritization for Efficient Microbenchmarking in Cloud-based CI/CD
Software Engineering.summary: Cloud-based software systems frequently release new versions, a fact further accelerated through agentic coding. Each new release, however, brings the risk of performance regressions which can irritate end users, increase infrastructure costs, and increase carbon footprints. Therefore, developers strive to catch such regressions in testing stages, usually through so-called continuous benchmarking. The standard way of doing this is using microbenchmark suites which, however, take notoriously long to execute. Optimizing the execution of microbenchmark suites is, hence, an active field of research. In this paper, we propose AdapBench, an online scheduling system for reducing the execution duration of microbenchmark suites. AdapBench is the first approach which dynamically makes at-runtime decisions for prioritizing the most informative benchmarks and early-stopping each one once enough evidence has accumulated to accept or reject a performance change hypothesis. We evaluate our prototype on eight popular Java projects, commonly used by microbenchmark research, and four additional Go projects. At matched 90% change detections and false-positive rate compared to an optimistic uniform run, AdapBench saves 42% of the aggregate execution duration on the Java projects, with negligible scheduling overhead (below 0.001% of the total runtime). On the Go projects, AdapBench finds every performance change with zero false positives while saving 85% of the full run.
Software Engineering.comment: 11 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at the 19th IEEE/ACM International Conference on Utility and Cloud Computing (UCC 2026). Code and data: https://github.com/s3bastiankoch/adapbench

Software Engineering.title: A Domain Driven Design Based Reference Architecture for IoT Systems Engineering
Software Engineering.summary: The Internet of Things (IoT) paradigm continues to gain significant traction across diverse do-mains, primarily driven by its transformative and socio-economic benefits. However, engineering robust IoT systems remains a formidable challenge, largely due to the inherent dynamism, volatility, and uncertainty of their operational environments. To mitigate this architectural complexity, microservices have emerged as a viable alternative to traditional, rigid monolithic frameworks, offering a scalable mechanism to fulfill critical quality attributes. To maximize the efficacy of a microservices architecture, its technical boundaries must align precisely with domain-specific business requirements. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) addresses this need by strategically decomposing complex domains into modular, highly manageable subdomains that map directly to individual microservices. Furthermore, to minimize architectural coupling, enhance system integrability, and optimize device energy efficiency, Event-Driven Architecture (EDA) serves as a critical operational enabler. This paper proposes a comprehensive reference architecture for IoT systems engineering, systematically leveraging DDD and EDA principles to harmonize business logic with decoupled, event-driven microservices.

Software Engineering.title: Do Coding Agents Catch Their Own Bugs? (They Don't.)
Software Engineering.summary: In software development, engineers need to foresee and fix potential problems with their code that are not explicitly specified in requirements---such as pre-emptively considering vulnerabilities or other bugs from a code change. But current benchmarks often do not measure these future-looking consequences. We introduce $\textbf{Foresight-SWE}$, a benchmark for measuring whether coding agents can anticipate and address unstated problems during software engineering tasks. Foresight-SWE consists of 212 samples spanning 4 languages and 35 popular open-source repositories. Each sample contains two pull requests (PRs), the second of which resolves defects the first one introduced. To measure whether agents exhibit foresight, we define the $\textbf{foresight resolve rate (FRR)}$ as the fraction of instances where an agent fully resolves the original task while also avoiding the defect identified by a later PR. We evaluate eleven large language models and find that FRR ranges from only 6.13% to 24.53%, indicating that models largely fail to address problems introduced by the first PR change. This raises important questions about how models are trained and aligned in coding contexts, as well as how code review tools should be improved for more fail-safe coding. Foresight-SWE shifts evaluations in this direction.

Software Engineering.title: From Stories to Bugs: Story-Based Semantic Fuzzing of Interactive Systems
Software Engineering.summary: Complex interactive systems hide business-logic failures along two complementary axes: deep state-dependent behaviors that require long valid prefixes and concurrency-sensitive failures that depend on the ordering of otherwise legal operations. We present story-based semantic fuzzing, a methodology that treats semantically constrained compositions of behavioral stories as primary search objects. Implemented through Behavioral Programming, semantic binding and state constraints preserve legal prefixes, while event eligibility, schedule selection, and replay expose failure-relevant interleavings. We evaluate the methodology on Magento and four stateful REST APIs. On Magento, overlap-aware ranking increased reproduction of a sporadic Shipping Fee race from 3.6% to 41.2%; a controlled ordering intervention reduced a second failure signature from 100/100 initial executions to 0/200 constrained executions. For the REST study, a versioned end-to-end pipeline took each frozen public OpenAPI contract as its sole benchmark-specific model-generation input and automatically generated the Basic and Complex stories, dependency structure, and interface bindings. Under a shared black-box task and sequence-local evaluation contract, Basic and Complex confirmed 0/11 and 11/11 semantic fault classes, while RESTler and EvoMaster confirmed 2/11 and 0/11. A paired binding ablation produced 250/250 valid dependent operations with binding and 0/250 without it, while supplementary prefix controls localized the difference to preservation of legal relational state. Together, the studies show that searching admissible semantic compositions provides a unified and effective representation for reaching deep states and exposing concurrency-sensitive business-logic failures.

Software Engineering.title: Annealing chains that communicate: low-energy cluster structures across engines with one configuration
Software Engineering.summary: The global minimum of a cluster decides which structure a simulation predicts. We present anneal, a global optimizer of communicating chains. Each chain draws its move by Thompson sampling from a Normal-Gamma posterior on quench depth. A stalled chain completes the orbits of a symmetric core. A chain retires on a Good-Turing estimate of its unseen mass, a rule with a Lean derivation. The chains share minima through an annealed-flow bank, and a ledger charges each force call to the chain that spent it. On 64 shared starts of LJ$_{38}$ and LJ$_{75}$ the hop matches the hit rate of GMIN, 64 of 64, at a lower median cost a paired test does not separate. On the Cambridge Morse table it reaches 145 of 244 targets and GMIN 131.
Software Engineering.comment: v2: rewritten with new global-optimization benchmarks against GMIN and ABCluster. 34 pages, 3 figures, 12 tables, Supporting Information included

Software Engineering.title: What Must Be Done Here? Using a Bounded Application-Security Ontology at the Point of Change
Software Engineering.summary: The security guidance that bears on code is real but scattered. It lives across secure-development frameworks, verification standards, controls catalogues, threat taxonomies, and, increasingly, normative regimes such as the EU's NIS2 -- and most of it is written for readers other than the engineer, or the AI assistant, at a point of change. Existing cybersecurity ontologies largely model attacks, indicators, and risk for detection and analysis, not the engineering-practice substance one must act on. This paper presents a use case for an existing bounded application-security ontology, AppSec Core, whose construction and validation are reported separately. We show how it is used. It makes the engineering-actionable fraction of those authorities addressable as a typed working set: the control objectives that apply, the practices that realize them, the mechanisms that implement them, and the evidence artifacts they expect, each traceable to the sources that justify it. We reach that working set from two entry points that recur in practice. Forward, from a code change: a change to authentication middleware scopes to its governing domain slice and returns the obligations the change must satisfy. Inverse, from a normative obligation: "make this NIS2-compliant" resolves a generic legal duty into the concrete engineering obligations it implies across slices, surfacing precisely the fraction of a mostly-governance regulation that lands in code. The same working set is what a human engineer reads and what an LLM-grounded assistant is handed as grounding. The use turns "read every applicable authority" into "satisfy this typed working set", for a code change or a compliance duty alike. The contribution is the demonstrated use; the artefact, its validation, and its governance are companion work.
Software Engineering.comment: 8 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at Semantic Shields 3: the 3rd International Workshop on Modeling for Cybersecurity, co-located with JOWO 2026 / FOIS 2026, Vitória, Brazil, September 2026. To appear in the JOWO 2026 proceedings (CEUR-WS)

Software Engineering.title: Refusing the Impossible: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Code Hallucination in Large Language Models
Software Engineering.summary: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) for code generation can recognize a programming request that cannot be satisfied. Coding assistants are widely deployed, yet they are evaluated almost exclusively on solvable tasks where a test suite can score the output. A request may instead name a package that does not exist or ask for an algorithm that is mathematically impossible, and the appropriate response is to refuse. Models nevertheless respond with plausible code, and such fabrications are also a security concern because attackers can register the package names that models invent. We define code hallucination as ungrounded code generation, distinguish it from ordinary programming errors, and introduce a taxonomy of these failures together with a benchmark of 270 adversarial requests and 91 matched solvable controls across six languages and 24 subcategories. We evaluate 17 open-weight models with 6.7B to 671B parameters, collecting 6,137 responses. Models hallucinate on 54% of the adversarial requests and correctly refuse 31%. Larger models do better on algorithmic impossibilities and conflicting requirements, where hallucination falls from 84% for models at or below 7B parameters to 32% for those at or above 80B. For plausible but nonexistent dependencies and features, the rates are 88% and 61%, and even the largest model hallucinates on all 22 requests for nonexistent JavaScript and Rust packages. Two-thirds of hallucinations are confident fabrications without caveats, and some reasoning models fail to return an answer on solvable tasks. Scale teaches models to recognize what is impossible but not what does not exist, so grounding code generation in the real software ecosystem, for example by checking package names against registries, remains necessary regardless of model size.

Software Engineering.title: Counterfactual Rollout Replay: Forkable Environments as Free Process Rewards for Software Engineering Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Outcome-only reinforcement learning gives software engineering (SWE) agents a terminal success signal but little direct guidance about intermediate decisions. We introduce Counterfactual Rollout Replay (CRR), a training-time procedure that uses forkable executable environments to obtain step-level return contrasts. CRR selects a small set of decision points, restores each state, samples an alternative action, and rolls the branch forward under the policy. It retains the realized training trajectory and replaces the advantage at selected steps with the difference between its terminal return and the sampled counterfactual return. The method needs no human process labels or learned process reward model; free refers to those supervision costs, not replay compute. With a 14B policy, CRR improves pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live, and SWE-rebench, and combines with process-reward and trajectory-search methods. On SWE-bench Verified, an equal-wall-clock comparison on the same hardware yields 41.7% versus 36.7% for extended vanilla (outcome-only) GRPO, a 5.0-point gain with fork overhead included. These results apply to environments with affordable, reliable state restoration; stochastic continuations and expensive or imperfect replay remain limitations.

Software Engineering.title: Dependable Agents Need Hard and Fuzzy Rules
Software Engineering.summary: Language models let software read requests in ordinary language, but they keep rules as people do: usually, and less so under pressure. Conventional code keeps rules exactly, but it cannot read a request. We argue that dependable agents need both, because the two kinds of rule cover overlapping and unequal regions of what an agent might do. Code holds the limits that can be stated exactly. Learned fuzzy rules cover the judgment that cannot. We test the hard layer in three domains, purchasing, delegation of authority and data access, on 1,340 episodes written by authors outside our team. Models left to decide for themselves executed unauthorized actions in up to 151 of 340 purchasing episodes and 269 of 470 delegation episodes, and the strongest model breached in every condition. A hard guard between proposal and action executed none, and an exhaustive search of 183,204 proposals agreed. In a further test, where an outsider wrote the owner's rules and a program mapped them to the guard, two episodes breached at a boundary we had written down in advance. We then test the pair. Concept Programming instills a named rule in a model and measures its errors on wording it never saw. A small model taught four judgment rules this way flagged 95 of 96 rule-breaking purchases that no exact rule can see, and 4 of 108 legitimate requests. Placed in front of the guard, it left 1 of 192 rule-breaking requests unstopped, where the guard alone left 77 and 70, and the guard still held every exact limit. A prompted frontier model did about as well, so the claim is that a small taught rule can do the job, not that it does it better.

Software Engineering.title: SWE-Opt: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLMs on Performance-Oriented Repository-Level Optimization
Software Engineering.summary: Software performance optimization is a notoriously complex and manual task. Despite the growing use of Large Language Models (LLMs) for code refinement, we still lack benchmarks that capture how optimization actually happens in real-world codebases. Existing frameworks often oversimplify the problem by focusing on isolated functions or a single performance metric, missing the critical trade-offs between execution time and memory footprint, the inherent noise of the measurement environment, and the variability introduced by different input data and execution conditions. We address this by introducing SWE-Opt, a repository-level benchmark derived from 102 expert-written optimizations from open-source projects. Unlike previous benchmarks, SWE-Opt pairs each task with parameterized tests to evaluate runtime, peak memory, and Time-Weighted Memory Usage (TWMU) across varying input data and execution conditions under noise-aware measurement conditions. Our evaluation shows that current LLMs struggle significantly: runtime gains are sparse and inconsistent, and memory optimizations are nearly non-existent. An agentic setting with iterative repository exploration improves patch correctness substantially but does not translate into performance gains. This stands in sharp contrast to expert implementations, which achieve an aggregate speedup of 15.5x and peak memory reduction of 171.3x over benchmark tasks. Expert-written improvements are observed in 93.1% of tasks for runtime and 70.6% for peak memory. Our findings expose a substantial gap between current LLM capabilities and the demands of expert-level engineering.

Software Engineering.title: SNAPPerf: Software-Aware Tabular Foundation Model for Retraining-Free Performance Prediction of Configurable Systems
Software Engineering.summary:
Modern software systems expose hundreds of configuration options whose combinations can substantially affect execution time, memory and energy usage. Measuring software performance resulting from a configuration set requires running a realistic workload. Since the configuration space grows exponentially, exhaustive benchmarking is infeasible. Prior work therefore trains models on a small set of measured configurations to predict the performance of the rest. Yet these models are specific to a particular software version, hardware platform, and workload, so changes require new measurements and retraining, and such changes are becoming more frequent with coding agents.
  We challenge this per-system training assumption with SNAPPERF (Software-aware, No-retraining, Adaptive Prediction), a sample-efficient tabular foundation model specialized for configurable software. SNAPPERF is pretrained once on synthetic data. Each new update only requires a few measured configurations as context to predict the rest without any per-system training or hyperparameter tuning. Across 39,866 configurations from 12 real-world systems, spanning 6 domains and 4 performance metrics, SNAPPERF reduces prediction error by 38% over the prior state of the art at the same measurement budget, and by 25% over the best general-purpose tabular foundation model. It matches the state of the art's accuracy with 54% fewer measurements on average. These results suggest that knowledge about software can be encoded in pretraining data rather than in per-system models, opening a new research direction in software-aware pretraining.

Software Engineering.title: SWE-Manager: Selecting and Synthesizing Golden Proposals Before Coding
Software Engineering.summary:
Large language model (LLM) research in software engineering has largely focused on tasks such as code generation and bug repair. In practice, teams often draft multiple candidate proposals for fixing an issue and then deliberate on one golden proposal for implementation. This selection requires not only assessing the issue's scope, impact, and urgency, but also a clear understanding of each proposal's strengths and weaknesses. A good selection could make issue resolution more reliable while reducing regression and operational risk, whereas a poor choice can increase risk and even cause unpredictable failures.
  We first conduct a manual study of real-world issues to characterize the rationales maintainers use when selecting among competing proposals. Motivated by these findings, we introduce SWE-Manager, a joint selection and synthesis approach that selects the best proposal and synthesizes a golden proposal. SWE-Manager is an 8B model trained via reinforcement learning (RL) to compare proposals, justify its choice, and synthesize a golden proposal for implementation. We view proposal selection as a reasoning task, mirroring how technical managers review competing proposals by weighing issue context and each proposal's solution without executing code or running tests. On the SWE-Lancer Manager benchmark, SWE-Manager achieves 53.21 selection accuracy and 57.75 earn rate, earning 152,750 dollars and outperforming strong baselines including GPT-5. To further evaluate the effectiveness of SWE-Manager in real-world issue resolution, we design the P2A framework, which simulates a real-world workflow where multiple proposals are drafted, reviewed, and a golden proposal is selected for implementation ...

Software Engineering.title: Trans-Domain Digital Twin: Conceptual Foundations, Architecture, and Research Outlook
Software Engineering.summary: Complex systems comprise heterogeneous domains whose states, uncertainties, risks, and control consequences can cross domain boundaries. Existing cross-domain digital twin approaches broadly focus on comparison, reuse, semantic mapping, standardization, and interoperability, but do not inherently require operational connections among domain states, errors, objectives, constraints, decisions, and controls. This article proposes the trans-domain digital twin as an operational formulation along the continuum of Composite/Federated Digital Twin Systems. This approach connects heterogeneous domain twins through an aligned shared state, explicit coupling of data, models, states, errors, objectives, and controls, heterogeneous temporal coordination, joint decision-making, and feedback-based adaptation. The proposed framework presents a seven-layer conceptual architecture, a trans-domain orchestration core, minimum compliance conditions, a general operational formalism, progressive fast-meso-slow loops, and a single-episode offline training mechanism linked to bounded online adaptation. It also describes conceptual validation and evaluation criteria, a maturity model, a reference deployment architecture, and requirements for runtime safety, provenance, versioning, and model lifecycle management. The framework is conceptually mappable to standards for digital twins, model exchange, distributed simulation, and smart transducers; however, its formal compliance and operational effectiveness must be examined through independent benchmarks, uncertainty quantification, ablation testing, and field validation.

Software Engineering.title: MediaWiki Code2Code Search: Neural Retrieval for the Semantic Discovery of Open-Source Software Entities
Software Engineering.summary: Code search in large-scale ecosystems is often hindered by the lexical gap between user queries and implementation details, alongside the trade-off between the low latency of traditional Information Retrieval (IR) and the precision of Deep Learning (DL). We present MediaWiki Code2Code Search, a neural retrieval system for semantic code-to-code discovery. By indexing 1.29 million structural entities (functions, types, and templates) across 2,500+ MediaWiki repositories, our system enables retrieval based on computational intent rather than surface tokens. We employ a split-build architecture, decoupling GPU-intensive offline indexing from a CPU-only serving layer; our FAISS IVF-PQ index occupies 168.6 MiB: a 96.6\% reduction compared to a flat float32 baseline, and achieves a median query latency of 1.85 seconds on commodity hardware, satisfying the 6 GiB RAM constraint of Wikimedia Toolforge. In a blinded evaluation graded by a three-model LLM jury (inter-judge Krippendorff's $α= 0.74$), our system improves ranking quality over a BM25 baseline across a 27-query benchmark, raising the jury-mean nDCG@10 (to 0.81 from 0.63), a positive and consistent gain across all judges. Gains are most pronounced in name-obfuscated and cross-language tasks where lexical methods fail. The system is available at https://code2codesearch.toolforge.org under the Apache 2.0 licence and provides an open RESTful API.
Software Engineering.comment: Published in SoftwareX. 24 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables
