Operating Systems.title: MARS: Towards High Goodput and Low KV Thrashing in Agent Serving under GPU Memory Constraints
Operating Systems.summary:
Self-hosted LLM agents offer greater control over sensitive data and model customization while avoiding per-request API fees. However, serving concurrent, multi-turn workflows within limited GPU memory makes it difficult to achieve high workflow-level goodput. In particular, as workflows accumulate context, their reusable key-value (KV) caches can easily outgrow GPU capacity, triggering repeated eviction and recovery, known as KV cache thrashing. This process consumes resources and delays workflow completion. Although existing approaches propose various methods, our motivation study shows that the evaluated baselines still incur substantial thrashing overhead or fail to address the workflow-level goodput issue.
  We present MARS, an agent serving system that coordinates workflow admission and in-engine scheduling to achieve high workflow-level goodput on memory-constrained devices while avoiding KV cache thrashing. Specifically, outside the engine, an admission controller selects root workflows using initial prefix footprint estimates and live KV availability, adapting admissions to memory pressure. Inside, an agent-centric scheduler prioritizes turn completion and coordinates prefill allocation with KV reclamation to reduce disruptive evictions. Across two models and three GPU configurations, MARS achieves 1.59x-7.56x mean end-to-end latency speedups over the fastest baseline. Integrated as the serving backend for OpenCode, Codex, and OpenHands, MARS further improves mean workflow completion time by 1.17x-1.87x.
  Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/Afterglow231/MARS_preview .
Operating Systems.comment: 13 pages, 11 figures. Major revision with updated title, system design, and expanded evaluation. Preprint

Performance.title: Measuring Tabular Data Formats Cold: A Replicated Cold-Cache Benchmark of Serialization, Scan, and Index Performance on Real Datasets
Performance.summary: Choosing a file format for tabular data is a routine engineering decision, yet published comparisons often time reads served from the operating-system page cache, use one session, or rely on a single synthetic dataset. This article benchmarks fifteen format and access-path configurations (CSV, JSON Lines, Pickle, Feather, Parquet, ORC, DuckDB, and SQLite, with several access paths) on two real public datasets, New York City taxi trips and United States airline on-time records, at 50,000 to 3 million rows. Every measurement uses an explicitly cold cache, randomized execution order, and three independent sessions (with restarts on the laptop), and is analyzed with bootstrap intervals and Holm-adjusted permutation tests. Parquet answered a filtered aggregation 2.6 to 11 times faster than CSV, while JSON Lines was 10 to 27 times slower. A secondary index made SQLite queries 2.6 to 4.8 times slower on randomly ordered data and helped only on data sorted by the filtered column, at low selectivity. A row filter inside the Parquet reader was significantly faster than a projected scan on flight data from one million rows and on both datasets at three million, and row-group skipping needs several row groups, which the default writer produced only at 3 million rows. A 4 GB Linux host ran out of memory on configurations that a 24 GB laptop completed and reversed some orderings, such as Pickle versus Parquet. Code, derived data, and raw timings are released.
Performance.comment: Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Computer Society

Performance.title: Performance Portability Explained: Insights from accelerating ICON microphysics
Performance.summary:
Scientific computing is under increasing pressure to adapt to HPC hardware that is shaped by AI workloads. In these modern ecosystems, extracting reasonable performance without investing major engineering effort is a central issue for domain scientists. Correctness constraints and intricate reference implementations represent further impediments to development. Instead of using a double-precision implementation as a reference, considering the underlying scientific problem directly opens more opportunities for performance improvements when updating and rewriting applications.
  We take seven different portability frameworks---covering pragma-based, DSL, and data-centric approaches---and evaluate them on a microphysics kernel of the ICON climate model. Our performance benchmarks show that each different HPC system benefits from a different combination of optimizations, so we develop the measure of framework expressivity to gauge how easily each framework can customize portable implementations in this way.

Performance.title: WINIC: An Automatic Cycle-Accurate Multi-Platform Microbenchmarking Tool for Instruction Performance Metrics
Performance.summary: Performance models allow developers to gain important insights into the interaction of their code with the hardware that executes it, and enable them to apply target-specific optimizations. To create in-core performance models for out-of-order processors, architecture-specific performance metrics like latency, throughput, and port binding of individual instructions are indispensable. For x86 microarchitectures, there already exist tools to automatically obtain those values; however, the extension of performance modeling tools like the Open Source Architecture Code Analyzer (OSACA) to support further architectures like RISC-V emphasizes the need for a multi-platform microbenchmarking tool. We present WINIC (What I Need Is Cycles), an automatic cross-platform microbenchmarking tool. Unlike previous tools, it can obtain throughput and operand-based latency metrics for most supported instructions of any 64-bit x86, AArch64, and RISC-V microarchitecture without the need for root permissions or extended system control levels. We cover the methodology of microbenchmarking and the approach of WINIC to collect cycle-accurate performance data for assembly instructions. We show that WINIC can be used to automatically obtain a vast number of accurate results and demonstrate for four target microarchitectures that our results match between 71% and 99% of the performance data of instructions obtained by similar tools and documentation. Furthermore, we investigate how operand-based metrics measured by WINIC can be used to improve the in-core performance predictions on selected micro-kernels, exemplarily for the Neoverse V2 microarchitecture.
Performance.comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 3 tables, 10 listings

Performance.title: Scaling Shapley Energy Attribution to Large LLM Batches
Performance.summary:
LLM services have become essential infrastructure for applications such as chat assistants and coding agents. Service providers need to attribute resource consumption to individual requests for purposes such as billing. Among these resources, energy is a key metric for assessing the cost of serving each request. However, serving engines batch requests together, and GPUs report only aggregate energy consumption. Providers typically estimate each request's share in proportion to its token consumption, but this approach can produce substantially unfair estimates. The Shapley value provides a principled solution to fair energy allocation, but computing it directly requires $2^N-1$ GPU runs for $N$ requests, which is infeasible for large batches.
  To address this problem, we propose StepSplit. Across GPU generations, we observe that the energy consumed by each inference step, a forward pass over a batch, consists of a shared energy, largely due to reading model weights, and a request-specific energy. We derive a closed-form Shapley value: each request is charged its own energy plus an equal part of the shared energy of every step in which it participates. A microbenchmark of 2.5-17.8 minutes calibrates both parts of the step energy once per model and GPU configuration. Under static batching, StepSplit uses this closed form in a single pass over the scheduler log. Under continuous batching, removing a request can change how the remaining requests are batched, so StepSplit adds a correction to the closed form, computed by replaying the scheduler on a CPU. We evaluate StepSplit against Shapley values measured using 529,513 GPU runs. Under static batching with batch sizes of 8-256, StepSplit achieves an $L_1$ error of 0.4-4.3%, compared with 13.4-61.3% for token-proportional allocation. Under continuous batching with 8-128 requests, the corresponding errors are 0.5-6.4% and 20.6-71.7%.
Performance.comment: 13 pages, 11 figures

Performance.title: Exploiting What NVIDIA Profilers Hide: Fast and Accurate Analytical GPU Performance Modeling
Performance.summary: GPUs have become essential to many fields, including AI and scientific computing. As GPUs grow more complex, the design space of their hardware configurations becomes increasingly large, yet cycle-level simulators remain too slow to explore it. Analytical models make this exploration much faster. However, existing GPU analytical models fall short of accurately predicting performance across hardware configurations, because they re-estimate or scale every stall of a warp on the target configuration. We observe that fixed-latency stalls stay the same across configurations, whereas queueing stalls vary with the pressure on each hardware unit. Based on this observation, we propose ForeSight, a queueing analytical model that reuses the fixed-latency stalls measured on GPU hardware and recomputes the queueing stalls of each hardware unit from its pressure. To provide ForeSight with the counter values of each hardware unit, we build UnitSight, a profiler that recovers these values, which NVIDIA's official profilers hide by aggregating across units. Our evaluation on hardware configurations of nine NVIDIA GPUs shows that ForeSight predicts kernel execution time with a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 8.3%, compared with 14.1% for the best baseline. ForeSight also predicts the end-to-end execution time of LLM inference on vLLM with a MAPE of 2.0%. It runs 49x faster than the cycle-level simulator Accel-Sim and faster than interval-based models such as GCoM. With the aid of ForeSight, we explore configurations derived from the H20 GPU for LLM inference and find one with 1.78x its performance/cost.
Performance.comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 2 tables

Performance.title: OSCAR: Offline Spectral Covariance-Aware Rotation for 2-bit KV Cache Quantization
Performance.summary:
INT2 KV-cache quantization is attractive for long-context LLM serving, yet making it both accurate and practical remains challenging. Data-oblivious rotations such as Hadamard transforms flatten channel outliers, but still degrade sharply at INT2 because they ignore how downstream attention queries the cache. We propose OSCAR, an ultra-low-bit KV-cache quantization method that estimates attention-aware covariance targets offline and uses them to derive fixed per-layer rotations and clipping thresholds. By aligning the quantization basis with the second-moment structures consumed by attention, OSCAR preserves attention fidelity at 2-bit precision. Beyond theoretical analysis under a frozen-error surrogate, we build a serving-ready OSCAR system with fused Triton write and decode kernels that preserve paged KV-cache layouts and prefix caching, integrating into modern serving engines such as SGLang and vLLM.
  We evaluate OSCAR on reasoning and coding benchmarks with generation traces of up to 32K tokens across five tasks. On Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 and Qwen3-8B, OSCAR narrows the BF16 accuracy gap to 3.78 and 1.21 points, respectively, where Hadamard-only INT2 collapses, and matches BF16 within run-to-run variance on Qwen3-32B and GLM-4.7 (358B parameters). On RULER-NIAH up to 128K tokens, OSCAR substantially outperforms QuaRot-style INT2 across context lengths. System-wise, OSCAR compresses KV-cache memory by nearly $8\times$, boosts multi-request throughput by up to $7.8\times$ at large batch sizes within the same memory budget, and accelerates batch-size-1 decoding by up to $3.1\times$ over BF16 by cutting KV memory traffic.
Performance.comment: 46 pages, 10 figures. v2 adds matched-baseline comparisons, residual diagnostics, and expanded long-context analysis

Performance.title: UniPipe: Unified Inference Serving and Fine-Tuning for Deadline-Constrained DNN Surrogate Workflows
Performance.summary: DNN surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate scientific workflows that must process high-rate sensor streams in near real time, exemplified by Ptychographic imaging at next-generation X-ray light sources. Such surrogates deliver 100-1000x higher throughput than iterative solvers, enabling faster steering of experiments. To preserve surrogate accuracy during an experiment, as the input distribution evolves, state-of-the-art deployments freeze the pretrained surrogate or run a separate CUDA context that fine-tunes concurrently with serving. However, multi-context concurrency causes significant contention on the GPU, inflating both the mean and the variance of inference latency, triggering deadline misses in workflows where sensor data has to be processed within a hard per-unit deadline. To address this challenge, we propose UniPipe, a single-context system that unifies inference serving and fine-tuning of a DNN surrogate on a single edge GPU. UniPipe is driven by three key insights: both serving and fine-tuning require a forward pass and can be fused into one; the per-sample latency of modern GPUs is non-linear in batch size; and the workload is repetitive across intervals, enabling offline scheduling. Specifically, UniPipe fuses training and inference data in a single forward pass with a selective backward pass on the training subset, and uses a polynomial-time scheduler that exploits the latency curve to compute the batch composition. We evaluate UniPipe on a real-world Ptychographic reconstruction workflow with sensor rates up to 5000 patterns/sec.; UniPipe lowers reconstruction MSE by up to 30% and inference MSE by up to 50% over a pretrained baseline, and reduces the deadline-miss rate by 13%-22% over a multi-context baseline. UniPipe's unified deployment reduces the latency spread from 106% to 57% of the mean, and increases total throughput compared to multi-context baseline.

Performance.title: Reconstructing Fine-grained Memory Reuse Structure in GPU Kernels
Performance.summary: Optimizing GPU data movement requires knowing which instructions access the same data and across which execution scopes reuse occurs. Existing profilers can attribute memory behavior to individual instructions but do not expose the reuse relations among them, while aliasing, dynamic indexing, and runtime parameters prevent static analysis from establishing these relations in general. Cycle-level simulation can reconstruct such relations, but at costs prohibitive for production workloads. We introduce two abstractions for representing this structure: Topological Distance, which labels each dynamic memory access with the smallest execution scope (thread, warp, block, or grid) containing its most recent reuse, and PCDepGraph, which organizes these labels into a PC-level graph of the kernel's memory reuse structure. Defined over logical execution scopes rather than transient hardware state, the representation remains stable across runs and GPU targets while directly indicating the sharing scope that candidate optimization mechanisms must cover. Our tool, cuVein, reconstructs PCDepGraph directly from optimized binaries, without sampling, at generally under 10x overhead. Across HPC and AI workloads on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and H100, optimizations guided by PCDepGraph eliminate up to 90.18% of memory instructions and yield up to 2.84x kernel speedup; reuse-scope distributions remain consistent across platforms, supporting that the representation captures program structure rather than transient hardware behavior.

Performance.title: HistogramTools for Efficient Data Analysis and Distribution Representation in Large Data Sets
Performance.summary: Histograms provide a powerful means of summarizing large data sets by representing their distribution in a compact, binned form. The HistogramTools R package enhances R built-in histogram functionality, offering advanced methods for manipulating and analyzing histograms, especially in large-scale data environments. Key features include the ability to serialize histograms using Protocol Buffers for distributed computing tasks, tools for merging and modifying histograms, and techniques for measuring and visualizing information loss in histogram representations. The package is particularly suited for environments utilizing MapReduce, where efficient storage and data sharing are critical. This paper presents various methods of histogram bin manipulation, distance measures, quantile approximation, and error estimation in cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) derived from histograms. Visualization techniques and efficient storage representations are also discussed alongside applications for large data processing and distributed computing tasks.

Hardware Architecture.title: SkipLane: Write-Once, Conflict-Free Accumulation for Zero-Skipping CNN Engines on FPGAs
Hardware Architecture.summary: Skipping zero activations saves multiplications in CNN accelerators, but it complicates accumulation: the products in a compressed input window belong to different output columns and must be merged. In our earlier engine, this merging was done by read-modify-write (RMW) of a row buffer, which made sparse inputs slower than dense ones even at 87% sparsity. Existing designs either merge kernel rows through RMW or reduce bank conflicts with extra hardware, without eliminating them. SkipLane makes the entire accumulation path write-once. Each kernel row is processed in its own lane, which holds partial sums in three registers and retires up to three finished columns per cycle into memory banks that cannot conflict. Lanes and input channels are summed only at readout, so no partial sum is ever read back. Multipliers left idle by zero weights compute a second filter in the same pass. In RTL simulation, the engine stays within 0.5% of its frontend bound up to 70% sparsity and is 1.10-1.26$\times$ faster than an SCNN-style scatter accumulator with 18 banks and ideal RMW at 50-80% sparsity. Six engines meet 140 MHz on a PYNQ-Z2 using 21.1k LUTs and run LeNet-5 bit-exact on the board. For conv1, the engine needs 1.94$\times$ fewer cycles than a dense engine (1.26$\times$ faster end to end); for conv2, whose rows are only 13 pixels wide, it reaches 0.87$\times$ the dense speed.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 5 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables

Hardware Architecture.title: TAPCO-G: LLM-Guided Design-Adaptive Timing and Power Co-Optimization with Graph-Based Physical Priors
Hardware Architecture.summary: Post-placement timing and power co-optimization is critical to meeting setup timing targets and reducing power within placement constraints. A cell replacement can improve timing along one path while increasing power or reducing slack on others. Conventional optimizers follow fixed rules for scheduling and accepting repairs, limiting their ability to address design-specific bottlenecks. A large language model (LLM) can propose changes to these rules, but on its own it cannot reliably estimate how a cell replacement affects endpoint slack and power. TAPCO-G combines LLM-guided optimizer adaptation with graph-based physical priors to evaluate candidate cell replacements. The outer loop tunes tool settings using physical-design feedback and revises executable repair policies when tuning stalls. The inner loop anchors delay estimates to static timing analysis snapshots, accounts for upstream driver-load changes, and propagates delay shifts to timing endpoints. It combines these estimates with coarse-to-fine power screening to prioritize candidates for physical trials. TAPCO-G produced placement-legal, logic-equivalent implementations and outscored CERBERUS on all eight ASAP7 benchmarks from the MLCAD 2026 Contest, with a mean quality score gain of 5.516 points, and scored 21.648 points higher than TAPCO on average. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed co-optimization framework.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 27 pages

Hardware Architecture.title: SFU-Sim: Bit-Exact Reverse Engineering of NVIDIA MUFU and Validation of PTX Paths
Hardware Architecture.summary: Reproducing the numerical behavior of a GPU requires predicting the exact output of special function instructions. Vendor documents give only the function semantics and error bounds. These do not fix the output bit pattern. We present SFU-Sim, which builds bit-exact models of NVIDIA multi-function unit (MUFU) instructions by black-box reverse engineering on real GPUs. We first model a single bare MUFU instruction. We then add the surrounding operations found in the disassembly to model full PTX paths. The model covers 12 common MUFU forms and two BF16 forms on the tested Blackwell GPU. Using SIN/COS as a complete case study, we show how we analyze the PTX-to-SASS compilation path and recover the segment structure, the equivalent coefficient tables, and the finite-width arithmetic. On NVIDIA GPUs of three architectures (Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Blackwell), we exhaustively compare every tested PTX path over its specified input domain. FP16 and FP32 paths cover all $2^{16}$ and $2^{32}$ input encodings, respectively. The model output matches the hardware bit for bit, with zero mismatches. SFU-Sim computes each output directly from its input. It needs neither a lookup table of all inputs nor access to a physical GPU. It can serve as a bit-exact special function component for instruction simulators. It can also serve as an arithmetic reference for hardware design and functional verification that target the same numerical behavior. SFU-Sim and its validation programs are open source at https://github.com/hzX40000000/SFU-Sim

Hardware Architecture.title: Uncovering the Memory Hierarchy of Modern NVIDIA GPUs for Accurate Simulation
Hardware Architecture.summary: Emerging artificial intelligence workloads, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), place unprecedented demands on GPU memory systems. Consequently, architectural innovations increasingly target the memory system to alleviate these bottlenecks. However, existing works still rely on outdated memory hierarchy models that fail to capture the complexities of modern hardware. This fidelity gap leads to inaccurate characterization and could misguide optimization strategies. To bridge this gap, we present GemAtlas, the first systematic reverse engineering of the memory hierarchy in modern NVIDIA GPUs. By developing fine-grained SASS-level benchmarking, we expose critical, previously undocumented micro-architectural details across different cache levels, including cache set associativity, slice-routing and set-indexing hash functions, replacement policies, coherence behavior, and interconnect topologies. We integrate these discovered micro-architecture details into the state-of-the-art GPU simulation framework. The final results demonstrate that GemAtlas reduces the mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) from 31.69% to 22.24% on average across four GPUs. Specifically, GemAtlas reduces the MAPE from 34.04% to 23.98% for real-world LLM operators.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 14 pages, 8 figures, 6 tables

Hardware Architecture.title: fRAC: Remote Accelerator Calls on Hostless FPGAs
Hardware Architecture.summary: Hardware accelerators are essential for meeting microsecond-scale demands in distributed applications, but invoking them over the network remains bottlenecked by host software. Host-mediated paths (RPC, RDMA) still rely on the CPU to reassemble requests and launch accelerators, which dominates end-to-end latency, while packet-level offload on SmartNICs lacks any notion of a complete request. We introduce the Remote Accelerator Call (RAC) paradigm, in which transport ingestion, request reassembly, dispatch, and accelerator invocation are handled entirely in hardware. We build fRAC, a hostless prototype that implements this network-to-accelerator interface as a lightweight shim on an FPGA hosting multiple virtualized accelerators, reconfigurable at runtime in a few milliseconds. Serverless functions backed by fine-grained accelerators are a natural fit, since host-mediated invocation overhead can match or exceed their short execution times. fRAC achieves under 7.8us end-to-end latency while sustaining application throughput of up to 90 Gbps. Compared to highly optimized DPDK-based CPU and DPU baselines, it achieves at least 80% lower latency under saturation, while consuming 85% less power.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted at ACM SIGOPS Annual Technical Conference (ATC) 2026 Previously titled: OffRAC: Offloading Through Remote Accelerator Calls 17 pages

Hardware Architecture.title: Toward Autonomous RTL and Synthesis Optimization: Benchmarking and Self-Improving Agents
Hardware Architecture.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents are creating new opportunities for hardware design optimization. This paper examines three connected directions toward autonomous RTL and synthesis optimization: (1) Realistic benchmarking. We discuss reference-based and open-ended RTL optimization benchmarks that evaluate optimization opportunities under realistic EDA workflows. (2) Tool-grounded RTL optimization. We present Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting, and implementation-level evaluation, while continuously improving through reusable optimization skills. Evaluated on 20 real-world RTL designs, Dr.~RTL achieves average WNS/TNS improvements of 21\%/17\% with a 6\% area reduction over commercial synthesis. (3) Design-specific synthesis optimization. We explore agent-driven synthesis script tuning and the discovery of executable synthesis algorithms across intermediate representations, technology-independent optimization, and technology mapping. Finally, we envision AI-native design automation that jointly explores architectural, RTL, and EDA algorithm design spaces, guided by verification constraints and implementation feedback.
Hardware Architecture.comment: ASP-DAC'27 Invited Paper

Hardware Architecture.title: Agentic AI Meets Formal Verification in the Era of Agentic Hardware Development
Hardware Architecture.summary: As AI agents become increasingly capable of generating and optimizing hardware circuits, ensuring the correctness of AI-generated designs becomes more important. Meanwhile, advances in AI lower the barriers to developing and applying formal methods, creating new opportunities to automate and improve hardware verification. This invited paper presents an overview of the methodologies and applications of hardware formal methods in the AI era. First, we examine how agentic AI advances hardware formal methods across three levels: specification, proof construction, and reasoning engines. Second, we discuss how formal methods support reliable AI-driven hardware development through RTL generation, debugging, and correctness-preserving optimization. We review representative research alongside our recent contributions, highlighting key technical advances and insights from experimental results. Finally, we discuss future research opportunities toward proof-native hardware development, where formal reasoning could become an integral part of autonomous hardware design.
Hardware Architecture.comment: ASP-DAC'27 Invited Paper

Hardware Architecture.title: Tri-Stack-PIM: A Heterogeneous Multi-Die 3D-Integrated Processing-in-Memory Architecture for Efficient LLM Inference
Hardware Architecture.summary: Large language model (LLM) inference during autoregressive decoding is fundamentally memory-bandwidth-bound. Existing three-dimensional (3D) stacked processing-in-memory (PIM) architectures alleviate the off-chip bandwidth wall, yet remain constrained by several limitations: physical layer (PHY), controllers, and direct memory access (DMA) engines compete with arithmetic units for advanced-node base-die area; hybrid-bonding keep-out zones fragment the base-die floorplan and impede physical design; compute tiles built in a dynamic random access memory (DRAM) process are restricted to low logic density, capping achievable throughput; and nonlinear operations offloaded to the host reintroduce a communication bottleneck. We present Tri-Stack-PIM, a heterogeneous three-die architecture that resolves these tensions by dedicating a top DRAM die to storage, a middle buffer die on a mature process node to PHYs, DMA engines, and near-memory compute units, and a bottom base die on an advanced node exclusively to single-instruction-multiple-data (SIMD) multiply-accumulate (MAC) arrays. We further introduce a Unified Buffer-Aware Ready-based (UBAR) hardware out-of-order micro-operation scheduler that enforces cross-die dependency correctness at runtime while maximizing issue-slot utilization through a multi-term priority function, recovering up to 90% of the cycles that an in-order policy would forfeit. A joint architecture-dataflow co-exploration identifies Pareto-optimal configurations that reduce the energy-delay product (EDP) by 33-66x over naive parameter selection. Evaluated across multi-head, grouped-query, and multi-query attention (MHA, GQA, MQA) mechanisms with batch sizes 1-32, Tri-Stack-PIM achieves geometric-mean speedups of 4.95x, 2.57x, and 1.68x across all three attention mechanisms and batch sizes over a graphics processing unit (GPU) baseline, AttAcc, and H2-LLM, respectively.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 11 pages, 9 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: Machine-learning decoders for fusion-based quantum computing in real time
Hardware Architecture.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires decoders that combine accuracy, throughput, low latency, and scalability to large numbers of physical qubits. In photonic fusion-based architectures, erasures from photon loss and probabilistic fusion measurements are a dominant error mechanism, motivating decoders that remain accurate at high erasure rates. We introduce PRISM, a transformer-based machine-learning decoder designed to exploit the known locations of erasures in protocols subject to both Pauli and erasure errors. We benchmark PRISM across a wide range of fault-tolerant protocols based on surface codes, color codes, and quantum low-density parity-check codes, with distances up to 24. Across these benchmarks, PRISM matches the logical error rates of integer-programming-based decoders while being significantly faster, including at error rates up to 50% of threshold. We further optimize the decoder and its real-time hardware implementation to reduce latency while maintaining accuracy. Our optimized implementation on an AMD VP1902 FPGA can decode logical blocks of distance 8 in both space and time, demonstrating a latency of 6.59 microseconds and an amortized decoding time of 1.56 microseconds per logical block is possible. These results show that machine-learning decoding can provide accurate, low-latency inference for erasure-dominated fault-tolerant quantum architectures.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 22+21 pages, 20 figures, 4 tables, comments welcome

Hardware Architecture.title: CACHEFORGE: LLM-Guided End-to-End Generative Cache Replacement Policy for Performance and Hardware Efficiency
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Modern cache replacement designs saturate because they operate within fixed representational structures, hand-crafted and heuristic based feature-engineered predictors, or offline imitation models that cannot generate new decision logic on their own. At the same time, replacement is shaped by the causal interaction of prefetching, thrashing, spatial locality, and access-type behavior, producing an enormous design space that is difficult to traverse manually. Prior approaches typically rely on heuristics, parameter tuning, or imitation of an offline optimal policy, capturing correlations rather than synthesizing new mechanisms. As a result, their performance gains often plateau and they overfit under dynamic workload conditions.
  CACHEFORGE is the first framework to evolve cache-replacement policies end-to-end by embedding a large language model inside a governed hardware-aware loop. In each iteration, the LLM proposes new C++ replacement logic, the policy is evaluated under a trace-based CRC-2 ChampSim simulator, and the framework enforces feasibility through reward shaping, structural checks, dynamic mutation, temperature scheduling, and cross-policy crossover. This closed-loop generation-evolution loop specifically designed for cache replacement policy enables the discovery of compact policies that satisfy hardware constraints while exploring algorithmic transformations beyond fixed predictor structures.
  Across SPEC CPU2006, CACHEFORGE outperforms all CRC-2 baselines. It improves the total hit rate by 27.36%, 19.69%, 13.72%, 13.15%, 11.83%, and 5.73% over MPPPB, ReD, Hawk-eye, SHiP++, LIME, and LRU, respectively. On memory-intensive workloads, it increases IPC by 10.15%, 7.89%, 6.34%, 3.64%, 3.12%, and 2.71% over LRU, MPPPB, LIME, ReD, SHiP++, and Hawkeye.

Hardware Architecture.title: PENSA: A Spatial Accelerator for BitNet b1.58 Inference on an HBM-equipped AMD Alveo FPGA
Hardware Architecture.summary: Ternary large language models (tLLMs) replace general multiplication in dominant linear layers with sign-controlled accumulation, shifting hardware bottlenecks toward packed-weight delivery, reduction, and operator occupancy. PENSA is an end-to-end FPGA accelerator for the BitNet b1.58 2B4T model on an AMD Alveo U50. Two row-partitioned ternary matrix engines consume packed TQ1_0 weights from eight independent high-bandwidth memory (HBM) pseudo-channels, each processing 1,280 ternary weights per cycle through sign selection and integer reduction. The sequencer, attention, and vocabulary-projection units remain resident on the FPGA, while two-stream interleaved scheduling overlaps sequences across the persistent pipeline to form the Penta-Unit. At 104.1~MHz, PENSA achieves 58.09 tok/s at context 128 and 24.60 tok/s at context 2048, corresponding to 2.14-3.14$\times$ the throughput of a same-model Xeon E-2356G baseline. The resulting system demonstrates end-to-end FPGA execution of 2B-scale BitNet topology without modifying its model structure.

Hardware Architecture.title: HAWK: Heterogeneity-Aware KV Cache Transfer for Efficient GPU-NPU Phase-Disaggregated LLM Inference
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Large language model (LLM) inference exhibits distinct computational characteristics across its two phases: prefill is compute-intensive, whereas decode is more memory-bound. As a result, AI accelerators achieve varying levels of efficiency across the two phases. GPUs are well suited to prefill, but are often underutilized during decode. By contrast, NPUs can utilize their compute resources more effectively during decode. Motivated by this observation, we explore a heterogeneous architecture that integrates GPUs and NPUs, mapping prefill to GPUs and decode to NPUs to achieve high performance and efficiency. However, realizing such heterogeneous integration is challenging because LLM phase disaggregation requires KV cache transfer from prefill to decode (that is, from GPUs to NPUs), which is complicated by differences in inter-device communication mechanisms and KV cache tensor layouts.
  To address this, we propose HAWK, a transfer mechanism that enables rapid KV cache transfer across heterogeneous devices. HAWK establishes a remote direct memory access (RDMA) path for direct cross-device transfers while handling inter-device tensor layout discrepancies as part of the transfer process. In particular, HAWK allocates tensor-layout-aware RDMA buffers on the NPU side to match the target tensor layout. Leveraging these buffers, HAWK orchestrates data transfer from a conventional contiguous GPU RDMA buffer to the corresponding NPU buffers, allowing transferred tensors to be consumed directly without additional data rearrangement while maintaining transfer efficiency. We implement and evaluate HAWK on a system built with commercially available GPUs and NPUs, demonstrating performance within 7.88% of a GPU-only system under the same SLO constraints while achieving up to 1.26$\times$ higher power efficiency and 1.72$\times$ higher cost efficiency.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 15 pages, 14 figures, 9 tables

Hardware Architecture.title: SlipStream: Enabling HBF for GPU Systems by Mitigating the Latency and SRAM Overheads
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Large language model (LLM) inference demands ever more memory capacity for larger models and batch sizes. High-Bandwidth Flash (HBF) replaces the DRAM dies of HBM with NAND flash and provides up to 16x the capacity at comparable read bandwidth. However, HBF can incur a read latency of nearly 20$μ$s, 20x that of HBM, so on-demand HBF accesses slow inference by up to 12.8x. Conventional cache-line prefetchers require 20x more in-flight tracking state to cover this latency. Tensor-streaming designs, such as H3, follow virtual-address order as opposed to kernel-demand order, and therefore need hundreds of megabytes of buffering.
  We propose SlipStream, a software-hardware co-designed prefetcher that turns prefetching into a demand-paced producer-consumer pipeline. In software, SlipStream profiles the repeatable weight-page demand order of data-independent LLM kernels and inserts a staging warp that replays this order with non-blocking STAGE instructions. In hardware, the staging warp acts as the producer and the work warps as consumers. Our key insight is to retire each STAGE tracking entry only when demand first accesses the page, as opposed to when the page returns from HBF. Demand thus paces staging and bounds how far staging leads consumption. SlipStream tracks 4 KB pages instead of cache lines and allocates buffer slots only when pages return, which decouples the buffer size from outstanding traffic. Across seven dense models spanning 16-800 GB, SlipStream with a 40 MB staging buffer achieves 92.4% of the performance of an ideal HBF with HBM-like latency. H3 achieves only 43.1%, even with a 320 MB buffer. The buffer sizing of SlipStream is independent of HBF latency and workload. SlipStream with 16 MB buffer, 20x smaller than that of H3, performs within 4% of SlipStream-40MB. SlipStream also supports Mixture-of-Experts models and reaches 91.2% of ideal performance (40 MB buffer).
Hardware Architecture.comment: To appear in 2027 IEEE International Symposium on High-Performance Computer Architecture (HPCA)

Hardware Architecture.title: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
Hardware Architecture.summary: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.

Cryptography and Security.title: Analyzing Linear Layers in Related-Differential Cryptanalysis
Cryptography and Security.summary: In AES-like ciphers, diffusion layers are commonly instantiated using MDS matrices, since their optimal branch number yields strong diffusion guarantees and underpins classical resistance arguments against differential and linear cryptanalysis. However, Daemen and Rijmen (2009) showed that linear layers may still exhibit related-differential structure beyond what the MDS criterion captures, and Bardeh and Rijmen (2022) demonstrated that this phenomenon can be exploited in attacks on reduced-round AES. In this work, we systematically investigate the conditions under which linear layers avoid or exhibit these differentials, identifying matrix classes for which such structure is unavoidable. We first prove that every non-MDS matrix admits a nontrivial pair of related differentials, showing that the MDS property is necessary for avoiding them. We then establish that every odd-order symmetric MDS matrix admits related differentials, which rules out broad families of Cauchy-based constructions. We also substantially strengthen the circulant case by proving that related differentials are unavoidable for every circulant matrix of order $n$ with $n \not\equiv \pm 2 \pmod{12}$. Finally, we revisit the characterization of $3 \times 3$ MDS matrices over $\mathbb{F}_{2^m}$ for the absence of related differentials, and derive an explicit necessary and sufficient criterion in terms of $15$ polynomial constraints.

Cryptography and Security.title: How Well Do SAST Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using OCPP Implementations
Cryptography and Security.summary: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates globally, securing electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) software becomes increasingly critical. The Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP), widely adopted for EVCS management, places significant responsibility on developers to securely implement specifications that are subject to multiple interpretations. The variety of OCPP implementations across different programming languages provides a unique opportunity to evaluate security tooling in a real-world, multi-language context where implementation variability may introduce vulnerabilities. This study provides the first empirical evaluation of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool performance across multiple programming languages using OCPP implementations as a real-world test corpus. We applied both comprehensive multi-language tools (SonarQube and Semgrep) and language-specific analyzers to twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations--each written in a distinct programming language--to examine how detection patterns vary across language ecosystems. Total issues ranged from just two in Rust to 1,689 in Java. Mature programming languages like Java yielded substantially more findings than newer languages like Rust, likely because established languages have more developed SAST tool ecosystems rather than inherently worse code quality. These results suggest that developers should consider available SAST tooling when selecting implementation languages for security critical systems.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 6 pages, 2 tables, Author-accepted manuscript. Published at IEEE CSR 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: SVP Is NP-Hard for Some Rank-2 Cyclotomic Modules
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Let $q$ be an odd prime. Let $ζ_q$ be a primitive $q$th root of unity, and put $K=\mathbb{Q}(ζ_q)$, with ring of integers $\mathcal{O}_K=\mathbb{Z}[ζ_q]$. As $q$ ranges over odd primes, we prove that the decision version of the Shortest Vector Problem ($\mathsf{SVP}$) in the canonical $\ell_2$-norm is $\mathsf{NP}$-complete on full-rank free submodules of $\mathcal{O}_K^2$ by giving a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from Exact Cover by 3-Sets (X3C). The module rank is fixed at two. The main obstacle is closure under the action of $\mathcal{O}_K$. A module containing a nonzero vector also contains every scalar multiple of that vector by a nonzero element of $\mathcal{O}_K$, and some of these multiples may be shorter.
  Three ideas overcome this obstacle. First, we map the Bennett--Peikert Reed--Solomon lattice to a principal cyclotomic ideal and use Wan's point-count estimates to prove that a coset of this ideal contains many binary coefficient representatives. Second, we construct a checker whose canonical squared norm encodes the X3C equations, with a controlled nonnegative error term. Third, the checker and a second module coordinate combine with a separation bound for ideal cosets to rule out short vectors in NO instances. Each constructed instance consists of an odd prime $q$, two integral generators whose $2\times2$ generator matrix has nonzero determinant, and an integer squared threshold. The construction also gives $\mathsf{NP}$-hardness of search-$\mathsf{SVP}$ under deterministic polynomial-time Turing reductions with at most one oracle call.

Cryptography and Security.title: MammothDP: Private Boosted Decision Trees Ready for Trusted Hardware and Leakage-free Hyperparameters
Cryptography and Security.summary: Data spaces like the European Health Data Space (EHDS) require the protection of sensitive data in studies during the data's processing and the study's release alike. In this work, we investigate how to implement this mandate using established trusted execution environments (TEEs) and timing side-channel hardening to protect the processing even under a compromised server, and the state-of-the-art differential privacy (DP) notion to protect the release of studies on tabular data. This combined setup could seem to complete the picture, but in fact raises unexpected security challenges that we mitigate by introducing MammothDP: a significant milestone towards a holistic machine learning system based on the recent gradient boosted decision tree learner S-BDT that is provably DP if used within a privacy filter, timing side-channel hardened, and deployed on a TEE. To achieve a strong privacy-utility tradeoff, we introduce two novel components: an early stopping criterion that adaptively selects the number of trees without any privacy overhead, and an improved rollback protection that is no longer vulnerable under timing side-channel attacks.

Cryptography and Security.title: NICE: A Framework for Declarative and Machine-Checkable Vulnerability Reproduction
Cryptography and Security.summary: Reproducing software vulnerabilities is fundamental to security researchers, open-source maintainers, and educators. Yet, vulnerabilities are often hard to reproduce, and even when they can be reproduced once, recreating a software environment where the vulnerability can be exploited becomes harder and harder over time. We present NICE, the NIx CvE reproduction framework, which uses declarative recipes to build and automatically validate vulnerable environments. In NICE, a reproduced CVE comprises one or more NixOS virtual machine configurations, a scripted exploitation scenario, and machine-checkable assertions that provide factual evidence of exploitation. This design facilitates sharing, validation, review, and long-term reproducibility. Building on NICE, we construct a public archive of 56 reproduced vulnerabilities spanning multiple CWE categories, attack vectors, and target types (user-space, system software, kernel, and graphical applications), combining manually authored recipes with recipes produced by an LLM-based automated pipeline and merged after human review. We evaluate the feasibility of the automated pipeline on 110 real-world CVEs, achieving fully automated reproduction in 54.5% of the cases, at an average cost of $0.73 per CVE. The evaluation demonstrates that NICE provides a practical target for LLM-assisted recipe generation, while also identifying where human refinement or additional automation remains necessary.

Cryptography and Security.title: Location Matters: Sparse Latent-Variance Attacks for Face Privacy against Diffusion Personalization
Cryptography and Security.summary: Text-to-image diffusion models can learn and reproduce an individual's identity from only a few reference photos, creating risks of unauthorized and misleading content generation. Proactive defenses address this risk by adding adversarial perturbations to facial images before release, thereby disrupting identity acquisition during downstream personalization. However, existing methods typically rely on dense $L_\infty$-bounded perturbations, whose accumulated distortions can become visible around facial structures. Recent methods improve protected-image quality, but often at the cost of reduced protection effectiveness. In this paper, we propose Sparse Encoder Attack on Latent Variance (SEAL), a sparse adversarial protection framework that modifies only 5% of the spatial locations in a facial image. SEAL combines a differentiable top-k masking scheme that jointly optimizes perturbation locations and values with a variance-oriented objective over the frozen VAE encoder's latent distribution to disrupt identity-consistent representations. A saliency-guided dispersion penalty further discourages perturbation concentration in perceptually salient facial regions. Experiments on CelebA-HQ and VGGFace2 show that SEAL achieves the best protected-image quality among the compared methods, exceeding 41 dB PSNR with 0.97 SSIM and at most 0.07 LPIPS, while reducing identity similarity to at most 0.15 after diffusion personalization. These results demonstrate that sparse location optimization enables strong identity protection while preserving high visual quality. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Lvxan/SEAL

Cryptography and Security.title: Model-Based Authoring of SOC Simulation Exercises for Cybersecurity Education
Cryptography and Security.summary: Cybersecurity training and classroom exercises with a virtual Security Operations Center (SOC) combine alerts, evidence, timeline entries, learner tasks, and assessment items that must remain consistent across an evolving incident. This paper presents a model-based authoring method in which a technical and educational specification is used to construct an incident exercise model and a large language model (LLM) generates selected scenario text based on that model. The incident exercise model combines an incident model of events, objects, and evidence with an exercise orchestration model of SOC alerts, timeline entries, learner tasks, and assessment items. The method is implemented in a Virtual SOC prototype and evaluated using a phishing-to-ransomware reference exercise. Its incident exercise model contains eight incident events, eight incident objects, six evidence items, seven alerts in five batches, 13 timeline entries including 12 learner tasks, and five representative assessment items. GLM-5.3-generated alert descriptions are inserted and a separate validator checks references, ordering, evidence links, assessment completeness, and selected fixed fields. Validation is demonstrated with reference data, resulting in true-negative outcomes for valid data and true-positive outcomes for deliberately placed inconsistencies. The resulting exercise package is executable within the Virtual SOC learner environment. Overall, the evaluation indicates consistency across the involved model elements and establishes the feasibility of the model-based and generative approach.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Presented at 2026 6th Asia Education Technology Symposium (AETS 2026), November 2026. Accepted for publication in the conference proceedings. Official publication forthcoming

Cryptography and Security.title: Design and Evaluation of Secure Distributed Chaotic Image Encryption on ESP32-S3
Cryptography and Security.summary: The limited computational resources of Internet of Things (IoT) devices present challenges for secure image processing. This paper presents a distributed chaotic image encryption system using independent Wi-Fi-connected ESP32-S3 microcontrollers. A master-worker architecture distributes image blocks through master-coordinated chaotic sequence management, maintaining one logically continuous chaotic sequence by assigning block-specific starting states independently of worker assignments. The implemented system uses reversible chaotic substitution (SUBSTITUTE), while Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)-signed discovery messages and Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 with mutual authentication secure device communication. Experimental evaluation using one, two, and four workers demonstrates a reduction in execution time from 43.215 to 15.878 seconds, achieving a speed-up of 2.72 times. The encrypted image achieves a Shannon entropy of 7.999940 bits/byte and near-zero adjacent-pixel correlation. Exact image recovery is verified through matching Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit (SHA-256) hashes and a Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) value of 1.0. Additional experiments demonstrate successful encryption and decryption using different worker counts and block sizes, automatic task reassignment following worker failure, and rejection of a mismatched private key during TLS authentication. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of secure, flexible, and distributed chaotic image processing across independent resource-constrained IoT devices.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 12 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables. Corrected spelling of an author's name; research content unchanged

Cryptography and Security.title: Known By Their Actions: Fingerprinting LLM Browser Agents via UI Traces
Cryptography and Security.summary: As LLM-based agents increasingly browse the web on users' behalf, a natural question arises: can websites passively identify which underlying model powers an agent? Doing so would represent a significant security risk, enabling targeted attacks tailored to known model vulnerabilities. Across 14 frontier LLMs and four web environments spanning information retrieval and shopping tasks, we show that an agent's actions and interaction timings, captured via a passive JavaScript tracker, are sufficient to identify the underlying model with up to 96\% F1 within a fixed harness. Although fingerprints are harness-specific, with cross-harness transfer falling to near chance, pooling traces across harnesses recovers model identification at 0.74 to 0.81 Macro-F1. We further show that strong classifiers can be trained from roughly one third of the available traces, and that identification improves steadily as more events are observed. Injecting randomised timing delays between actions substantially degrades classifier performance, but does not provide robust protection: a classifier retrained on delayed traces largely recovers performance. We release our code and a labelled corpus of agent traces at https://github.com/KabakaWilliam/known_actions.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: An Empirical Study on CVE-based Vulnerabilities Propagation from one System to another System (IntraProject vs InterProject)
Cryptography and Security.summary: Vulnerabilities in applications, including browsers, media players, online services and document readers, etc. are often exploited and cause a serious damage. The vulnerabilities could exist in your system maybe because of some coding errors, design oversights, outdated software, AI generated codes or maybe transferred from another system during development (e.g., code clones). The propagation of software vulnerabilities is a critical concern in cybersecurity. This study examines the root cause problem of vulnerabilities propagation with experiments. We analyzed the propagation of CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) based vulnerabilities within and between different software projects (IntraProject vs. InterProject). We performed several experiments on CVE based vulnerability dataset (retrieved from NVD source) by using our vulnerability detection tool (SQVDT). In the results, we discovered similar patterns of vulnerable code in several very famous recently used software, including latest version of Linux, Android operating systems, and in thousands of open source projects available on GitHub. We found several very high severity level (CVSS) vulnerabilities that propagated from one system to another system, just because of copy/paste (reuse) the code. Furthermore, we performed an empirical evaluation and verification of these vulnerable patterns that propagated to other systems by also considering the frequency of their propagation. Finlay, we recommended the impact of these vulnerabilities propagation on the interconnected systems.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 17 Pages, 14 Figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent.
  To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 61 pages, 13 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: GARD: Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense against Backdoors in Multimodal Contrastive Learning Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Multimodal contrastive learning models such as CLIP are vulnerable to backdoor attacks with diverse trigger structures, ranging from localized patches to globally distributed perturbations, with recent attacks increasingly optimizing these triggers in the representation space. Existing post-hoc defenses based on clean fine-tuning may leave backdoors active, while trigger-inversion methods depend on accurately estimating the attack target and trigger. We observe that backdoored encoders exhibit structure-dependent representation sensitivity: global perturbations preferentially expose distributed backdoors, whereas local patch perturbations are more effective for localized backdoors. Based on this observation, we propose Gradient-Guided Adversarial Representation Defense (GARD), a target- and trigger-agnostic post-hoc defense. GARD optimizes complementary global and local adversarial probes to maximally displace clean-image representations, and then realigns the perturbed representations with detached clean anchors while preserving image-text alignment. The resulting model requires no additional computation at inference time. Across six visual backdoor attacks and two CLIP visual backbones, GARD reduces the attack success rate below 1% in all 12 evaluated attack-backbone combinations while maintaining competitive clean accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of adversarial representation probing for repairing backdoored multimodal contrastive encoders.

Cryptography and Security.title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: We present Sable, an argument system and single-GPU prover for the statement that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. Sable fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step, in which every rounding, normalization, softmax and sampling decision is determined by its inputs, and proves it with a constraint system whose relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime. The proof batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits to every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees and a mixed-length BaseFold opening. The prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU. On one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU, Sable proves all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5 s for 4,096 tokens and 398 s for 16,384 tokens, and covers Qwen3-32B and the mixture-of-experts Qwen3-30B-A3B (4,096 tokens in 121.8 and 84.7 s). A proof costs 41 to 50 times the serving time, or 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request at public GPU prices, and 40 to 64 times less time per parameter and token than zkLLM. On WikiText-2, F_O's greedy token matches the BF16 model's at 86.3% of positions; on Qwen3, F_O is within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K. A verifier with a compiled core checks a proof on one CPU core in 19 to 56 s. In the random-oracle model, the interactive proof has round-by-round soundness error 2^-103. The proof is not zero-knowledge, so the system targets open-weight models. Code: https://github.com/moonmath-ai/Sable

Cryptography and Security.title: Rotated Robustness: A Training-Free Defense against Bit-Flip Attacks on Large Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Bit-flip corruption of quantized weights poses a serious reliability threat to Large Language Models (LLMs), as even a small number of weight faults can trigger catastrophic model degradation. We show that such failures can be strongly amplified when corrupted weights are coupled to high-sensitivity activation channels. Based on this observation, we propose Rotated Robustness (RoR), a training-free sensitivity-aware hierarchical rotation that applies matched orthogonal transformations to activations and weights, redistributing sensitive channel contributions across feature dimensions while preserving the underlying linear mapping in exact arithmetic.
  Across eight evaluated LLMs, RoR matches or exceeds all compared methods in the number of cumulative PBS flips sustained before PPL exceeds 100 within the 100-flip evaluation horizon. Under BER-based random bit-flip injection, no RoR failures are observed in the evaluated 1,000-trial experiments for the tested models. Under defense-aware SPoF reconstruction, RoR increases the cost of reproducing specified one-bit catastrophic failures to thousands of deployed INT8 bit changes. RoR also preserves downstream-task utility under PBS perturbations. On NVIDIA H200 at batch size 8, RoR incurs 0.097\%--0.584\% persistent storage overhead, 5.2\%--14.1\% Prefill overhead, and 0.5\%--9.8\% Decode overhead across four representative models. These results show that sensitivity-aware hierarchical rotation provides a practical approach to improving the bit-flip robustness of quantized LLM Linear weights.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 15 pages, 8 figures. Accepted by TIFS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: What a CAGE 4 Score Measures: An Audit of a Learned Cyber-Defense Benchmark, Its Reference Defenders, and the Tables Built on Them
Cryptography and Security.summary: CAGE Challenge 4 is the benchmark on which learned multi-agent cyber defenders are compared. We reproduce its two reference defenders, KEEP and H-MARL Expert, in a pinned container and show that three things read from it measure less than they are taken to measure. First, the simulator silently discards any action asserted for an agent whose previous action is still running, and charges one point for a discarded Restore as for one that runs. The documented observation does not expose the busy flag. Both reference defenders read it in their own wrappers, and switching that check off at evaluation costs KEEP's released policy 99.58 points per episode and H-MARL's 145.98, in both cases the charge for Restores sent to busy agents, with H-MARL's executed actions unchanged step for step. On a supervisory harness, holding interventions until the agent is idle is worth 25.3 and 27.6 points per episode at the published setting. In training, the check decides how a busy step enters the trajectory. Trained without it, KEEP leads at a hundred updates in all four paired seeds and trails from two hundred on in all four. Continued to two thousand updates on three seeds, the repaired recipe ends inside the released interval on one seed and short on two, by 27 and 125 points, a spread across training seeds far wider than the released reproduction interval. Second, the evaluation seeds the environment but not the policy, so a reported mean is one draw, and 88.9% of per-episode outcome variance is the policy's own sampling draw. Third, recovery precision depends on the truth it is scored against. Across five published comparison tables, none states the artifact, sampling, criterion and adversary that would make its numbers comparable. We release the instrument, our patches to both defenders, the traces and checkpoints behind every number, and a five-item disclosure checklist.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 47 pages. Code at https://github.com/jrice-ai/cage (tag arxiv-v1), data at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23681828

Cryptography and Security.title: Isolation Is Not Confidentiality: Security Boundaries of Geometric Access Control in RAG
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly rely on vector databases containing documents governed by different access-control policies. Recent search-preserving geometric approaches enforce such access control by structuring the embedding space so that transformed embeddings, which we call protected representations, remain retrievable without exposing information across policy boundaries.
  We provide a unified security analysis of this paradigm, covering policy isolation, representation confidentiality, query forgery resistance, and policy-membership hiding. We consider both a curious cloud service provider observing the protected representations stored in the vector database and a curious user holding aligned pairs of original embeddings and protected representations. Evaluating the available implementations of the works proposing these geometric transformation mechanisms across three encoders, we find that geometric transformations preserve retrieval utility and provide strong policy isolation, but do not provide the other security properties. A curious user can recover the original embeddings from a few hundred pairs and forge policy-compatible queries at a higher cost that grows with encoder dimension for secret per-policy transformations. Moreover, policy-dependent geometry can leak policy membership even when unauthorized retrieval is prevented. These results show that policy isolation, confidentiality, forgery resistance, and membership hiding are distinct security objectives.

Cryptography and Security.title: Nash Incentive-compatible Online Mechanism Learning via Weakly Differentially Private Online Learning
Cryptography and Security.summary: We study a multi-round mechanism design problem, where we interact with a set of agents over a sequence of rounds. We wish to design an incentive-compatible (IC) online learning scheme to maximize an application-specific objective within a given class of mechanisms, without prior knowledge of the agents' type distributions. Even if each mechanism in this class is IC in a single round, if an algorithm naively chooses from this class on each round, the entire learning process may not be IC against non-myopic buyers who appear over multiple rounds. On each round, our method randomly chooses between the recommendation of a weakly differentially private online learning algorithm (e.g., Hedge), and a commitment mechanism which penalizes non-truthful behavior. Our method is IC and achieves $O(T^{\frac{1+h}{2}})$ regret for the application-specific objective in an adversarial setting, where $h$ quantifies the long-sightedness of the agents. When compared to prior work, our approach is conceptually simpler,it applies to general mechanism design problems (beyond auctions), and its regret scales gracefully with the size of the mechanism class.
Cryptography and Security.comment: ICML 2024, 19 pages. v3 adds a lower bound on the regret and corrects minor errors in the published version

Cryptography and Security.title: Pulse or Provenance? What rPPG-Based Deepfake Detectors Learn
Cryptography and Security.summary: Remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) has been proposed as a physiological cue for deepfake detection, based on the premise that synthesized faces lack a genuine cardiac signal. We examine what rPPG-style detectors learn on Celeb-DF++ (22 forgery methods) and FaceForensics++ (FF++), using one identically sampled window per real and fake video. On talking-face forgeries, simple chrominance traces reach an AUC of 0.998, exceeding a dedicated rPPG extractor (0.87). Controlled experiments indicate that this signal is not physiological in origin. On fully synthesized forgeries, it is equally discriminative when extracted from background regions or from full frames without face detection, and it is concentrated above the 0.7 to 4 Hz heart-rate band. It is largely removed by shuffling frame order but persists after normalizing resolution, frame rate and encoding, and an independent reimplementation reproduces these findings. Removing high-frequency content makes most synthesized videos appear real, adding it makes real videos appear fake, and injecting a synthetic pulse has little effect. In controlled self-reenactment experiments with two generators, animating a face from a single frame introduces the same high-frequency signal, whereas reconstructing each frame from its own source does not. Face-based chrominance detectors trained on Celeb-DF++ classify over 99% of real FF++ videos as fake, indicating that they largely encode video source rather than manipulation, and a CLIP-based detector exhibits the same behavior. A frozen CLIP backbone matches or exceeds fusions of CLIP with rPPG and frequency features. Finally, we show that the official Celeb-DF and Celeb-DF++ splits share identities and source-video content between training and test, and that custom protocols reusing test videos and identities in training inflate weaker detectors by up to 0.30 AUC.

Cryptography and Security.title: Gradient Inversion through Linear and Affine Subspace Constraints
Cryptography and Security.summary: Federated learning enables multiple clients to collaboratively train a machine-learning model without directly sharing their local datasets. However, as prior works have shown, the gradients exchanged during training may reveal sensitive information about client data. Most existing attacks usually optimize dummy inputs to match the true client gradients (Gradient Inversion Attacks), while some attempt to reconstruct them based on the observation that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer are a linear combination of its inputs. In this work, we extend this observation by showing that aggregate gradients from an FC layer with the correct scaling are actually an affine combination of its inputs. We evaluate a gradient inversion attack that leverages either known linear-subspace information or its affine-subspace counterpart at each FC layer to improve reconstruction accuracy. Our results show that subspace-based methods can substantially improve reconstruction quality over the chosen baselines in certain settings. We further demonstrate that moderate overestimation of the batch size can generally improve or preserve reconstruction quality, even when the true batch size is unknown. We additionally examine reconstruction under gradient perturbations introduced by a differential privacy (DP) mechanism, providing insight into the effectiveness of the considered formulations under noisy conditions.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 26 pages, 10 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Comparing WeChat and Telegram MiniApp Security Architectures: Toward Cross-Platform Analysis
Cryptography and Security.summary: MiniApps are increasingly central to super-app ecosystems, yet architectural differences complicate the transfer of security analysis techniques across platforms. Existing WeChat analyzers rely on packaged applications and platform-specific APIs, limiting their direct applicability to Telegram's web-based MiniApps. We present a qualitative comparison of WeChat Mini Programs and Telegram MiniApps, grounded in official documentation, prior research, and manual analysis of a specific Telegram Android source revision. Using a shared taxonomy of security controls, assets, and threat sources, we examine execution environments, communication paths, and trust boundaries. WeChat provides a dedicated MiniApp runtime; Telegram combines web execution with host controls. Both retain developer responsibilities for backend authentication and resource authorization. Two worked examples derive requirements for cross-platform analysis: distinguishing credential roles and validation boundaries, and associating host capabilities with concrete execution contexts and permission handlers. These findings inform future automated analysis without ranking the ecosystems by security or claiming validated vulnerability detection.

Cryptography and Security.title: From Attack Surface to Defense Architecture: Compositional Security for Agentic Coding Harnesses
Cryptography and Security.summary:
AI coding harnesses couple language models to shells, filesystems, and network sockets, turning the harness into an automated Living-off-the-Land (LotL) platform: once an adversary injects instructions into retrieved content, dual-use binaries such as bash, curl, and find become the payload. We argue that security in agentic systems is a structural property of the cognitive architecture and permission composition rather than an emergent property of individual models. Static regex blacklists miss structural evasions, whereas LLM-as-a-Judge guardrails incur high latency while over-blocking benign work.
  We present ActiveSecHarness, a neurosymbolic reference-monitor architecture built around Separation of Intelligence and Authority. It combines (1) Macaroon-inspired HMAC capability tokens across four Trust and Authority Rings, (2) a 2D product taint lattice $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{trust}} \times \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{sens}}$ and a workspace provenance ledger that prevents secret laundering across disk, (3) deterministic Ring-0 OS/tool guards, and (4) bytecode certificates, split-horizon audit logs, self-healing security test synthesis, and an adaptive UserWikiManager.
  Across $N=252$ fixtures ($120$ attack, $120$ benign, $12$ kill chains), a live local LLM judge (qwen3:4b) refuses $98.3\%$ of benign work at $142.3\,\mathrm{ms}$ latency, whereas Ring 0 achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ in $12.7\,μ\mathrm{s}$ ($11{,}200\times$ faster). In a multi-step trajectory ablation, an oracle Conseca-style stateless policy misses $4/12$ kill chains ($\mathrm{ABR}=0.667$) and coarse Boolean taint blocks $83.3\%$ of benign workflows, while our 2D product lattice achieves $\mathrm{ABR}=1.000$ and $\mathrm{FPR}=0.000$ at $\approx 20\,μ\mathrm{s}$ per step.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 21 pages, 3 figuers, 1 sublement

Cryptography and Security.title: Data4Cyber: Labeled Cyber-Physical Datasets for Distribution-Grid Management Systems Under Representative OT Attacks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Cyberattacks against power systems increasingly exploit industrial communication and control dependencies arising from distributed energy resources (DER), remote management, and market-based incentives. Progress on intrusion detection is constrained by a lack of public datasets that align operational technology (OT) network telemetry with physical measurements and control context. Data4Cyber is a labeled cyber-physical dataset recorded in a laboratory distribution management system (DMS) for self-consumption optimization with photovoltaic generation, battery storage, controllable loads, and substation metering. It captures synchronized process measurements, controller context, price incentives, and packet captures (Modbus/TCP and MQTT) across one benign baseline and six attack scenarios spanning protocol-semantic Modbus manipulation, man-in-the-middle (MitM) false-data injection, and MQTT price manipulation. Its fixed 1 s time base, phase-resolved labels, and state-oriented representation support temporally blocked stateful-detector evaluation. Baseline results show that high recall alone is insufficient: several detectors achieve sensitivity through alarm saturation. Context-driven attacks require process-aware interpretation rather than single-channel thresholding.

Cryptography and Security.title: Domain-Invariant and Language-Model-Assisted Acoustic Side-Channel Attacks on Keyboards
Cryptography and Security.summary: Acoustic side-channel attacks (ASCA) recover typed text from the sound of keystrokes, using only a commodity microphone and no access to the victim's device. Prior work establishes that such attacks succeed under idealized laboratory conditions - a single keyboard, a fixed microphone, a quiet room, and training and testing on the same device but leaves open the question that matters for security: whether keystroke inference survives the open world of unseen keyboards, diverse users, noisy environments, and compressed transmission channels. The answer developed here is that it does, provided the acoustic model is made explicitly domain-invariant and its noisy predictions are corrected by a language model.

Cryptography and Security.title: BadMoE: Backdooring Mixture-of-Experts LLMs via Routing-Aware Triggers and Task-Underutilized Experts
Cryptography and Security.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures are rapidly becoming the standard for building scalable and efficient large language models (LLMs), thanks to their routing mechanism that activates only a subset of experts for each input. However, the modular structure and sparse activation of experts also introduce new security risks, as manipulating a small portion of experts may influence the behavior. In this work, we study a white-box, task-specific model-supply-chain setting and propose BadMoE, a routing-aware backdoor attack against MoE LLMs. We motivate BadMoE through a routing-aware decomposition of the MoE-layer output, which separates the contributions of the selected target experts from those of the remaining experts.
