This analysis highlights two measurable factors underlying the attack: the routing mass assigned to the target experts and their relative contribution to the layer output. Guided by this insight, BadMoE selects task-underutilized experts and utilizes routing-aware triggers to activate them, enabling reliable activation of task-specific, predefined backdoor behaviors. Specifically, BadMoE involves three steps: 1) identifying experts with low usage on a target-task calibration set, 2) optimizing a routing-aware trigger toward these experts, and 3) associating the selected-expert activations with attacker-specified behavior. We evaluate BadMoE on Mixtral, OLMoE, and Deepseek across sentiment, topic, and emotion classification, sentiment steering, and targeted refusal.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 16pages, accepted to IEEE TIFS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: On Private Knowledge Retrieval and Private Inference for secure multi-agent systems
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Multi-agent systems provide a convenient framework for the massive deployment of agents based on Large Language Models (LLMs). It provides a sound framework where agents can interact with existing software to perform actions in an autonomous way. Agentic AI is the new term to denote these AI-based autonomous systems.
  In real multi-agent systems, agents need to deal with malicious agents some of which can exploit security vulnerabilities to do harm. A memory poisoning attack is an example of exploiting a vulnerability to modify agents knowledge and, thus, affect its behavior. In an agent, there are different types of memory systems (semantic, episodic, and short-term) which have their own characteristics and for which different memory poisoning attacks may be developed.
  In this paper we focus on semantic memory, we discuss its attack, and mitigation strategies. We introduce private knowledge retrieval and private inference. We propose a signature system in the knowledge base to prevent from undesired manipulation. This should avoid memory poisoning attacks by introducing security by design in the construction of the semantic memory. In our architecture, an agent contains a local Prolog-like inference system (i.e., using Horn clauses to represent knowledge) which accesses an external knowledge base to get the required knowledge. This externally signed knowledge base is accessed privately. We provide different implementations in Python using different privacy levels including k-anonymity and information-theoretical privacy (IT-PIR).

Cryptography and Security.title: BypassGym: A Benchmark for Evaluating AI Agents' Endpoint Defense Evasion Capabilities
Cryptography and Security.summary: Artificial intelligence agents increasingly automate cybersecurity tasks, including offensive operations. Frequent attacks across the web make endpoint detection and response (EDR) a critical defense, but whether AI agents can evade it remains unclear. Benchmarks evaluate the offensive capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents in areas such as penetration testing and vulnerability discovery. One important capability that these benchmarks do not address is defense evasion, specifically whether an agent can develop a program that executes a payload without being blocked or terminated by a deployed EDR. We introduce BypassGym, to our knowledge the first benchmark to systematically evaluate this capability on real endpoints. Given command-and-control (C2) shellcode, an agent must generate and compile a loader that executes the payload without being blocked or terminated. A supplementary evasion knowledge skill provides domain knowledge and supports comparisons with and without this input. BypassGym is built on Proxmox VE(PVE), so the evaluation environment runs real Windows systems and EDR products inside virtual machines and returns structured detection feedback to the agent. We evaluate 5 lightweight model backends against 6 EDR products and 3 payloads, and find that even these simple models generate successful submissions, with DeepSeek-V4.1 Flash reaching 17/18 successful runs and Bitdefender allowing only 5 of 15 runs to pass. These results provide a systematic measurement of current AI agents' endpoint defense evasion capabilities and identify areas for defenders to investigate.

Cryptography and Security.title: Specification-based Security Evaluation of Real-World Agents Tool-Calling under Long-Horizon Context Tasks
Cryptography and Security.summary: As large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed in long-horizon unattended scenarios, security evaluation of them before deployment becomes increasingly essential and challenging. Existing evaluation methods mainly follow the paradigms of LLM-as-a-Judge or Agent-as-a-Judge. However, such judges are themselves often vulnerable to hallucination and can even be affected by perturbations. Furthermore, because capturing full environment states at every step is often prohibitively expensive in open-ended environments, existing evaluations typically rely on textual logs and the final environment state. As a result, they may miss transient violations that are overwritten before the trajectory ends or never reflected in textual logs. We present RAS-Eval, a specification-based security evaluation framework for LLM agents. RAS-Eval uniformly expresses utility and security objectives as Linear Temporal Logic (LTL) specifications over tool-call trajectories and dynamic environment observations, and verifies them with an off-the-shelf model checker. This design addresses both limitations above. First, unlike LLM-as-a-Judge and Agent-as-a-Judge, RAS-Eval derives deterministic verdicts from formally defined properties, eliminating evaluator-side uncertainty and remaining reliable even for long-horizon trajectories. Second, RAS-Eval observes exactly the states on which the verdict depends, making it affordable to monitor the environment throughout execution and detect transient violations that leave little trace in the logs or final environment state. Moreover, we design a multi-agent-based dataset construction pipeline. Using it, we construct a benchmark (https://github.com/lanzer-tree/RAS-Eval) of 200 normal tasks and 800 attack tasks spanning four attack surfaces: indirect prompt injection, tool poisoning, skill code injection, and tool code injection.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 22 pages, 5 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: MOAI: Module-Optimizing Architecture for non-interactive secure transformer Inference
Cryptography and Security.summary: Privacy concerns have been raised in Large Language Models (LLM) inference when models are deployed in Cloud Service Providers (CSP). Homomorphic encryption (HE) offers a promising solution by enabling secure inference directly over encrypted inputs. However, the high computational overhead of HE remains a major bottleneck. To address this challenge, we propose MOAI, an efficient HE-based, non-interactive framework for secure transformer inference. MOAI gains significant efficiency improvement from: (1) a novel evaluation flow that combines column and diagonal packing with consistent strategies across all layers, eliminating expensive format conversions. (2) rotation-free algorithms for Softmax and LayerNorm that significantly reduce the number of costly HE rotations, removing 2,448 HE rotations in BERT-base inference. (3) Column packing removes rotations in plaintext-ciphertext matrix multiplications and interleaved batching further reduces the rotations in ciphertext-ciphertext matrix multiplications. MOAI uses at least 1.7x fewer HE rotations compared to the state-of-the-art works across all matrix multiplications of BERT-base. As a result, we achieve a $52.8 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to the state-of-the-art HE-based non-interactive secure transformer inference, THOR (Moon et al., CCS 25). We then apply MOAI on the Powerformer's framework and achieve a $55.7 \%$ reduction in evaluation time compared to Powerformer (Park et al., ACL 25), which approximates Softmax and LayerNorm with simpler functions in transformer and proposes HE-based non-interactive transformer inference. We report an amortized time of 2.36 minutes per input on a single GPU environment. We show the extendibility by applying MOAI in LLaMA-3-8B. Our implementation is publicly available as open source.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Published elsewhere. Minor revision. ICLR 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Auditing Cross-Lingual Fairness in Language Model Watermarking
Cryptography and Security.summary: Watermarking schemes for large language model output are evaluated almost exclusively on English text using each scheme's detection threshold and a narrow set of quality measurements. Multilingual deployment exposes evaluation-design choices that are inconsequential on English but determine conclusions cross-lingually. We propose an evaluation framework with four components: detection thresholds calibrated empirically per deployment context, a threshold-independent companion measurement that distinguishes calibration failures from detection failures, three disjoint quality measurement paradigms (distributional, paired-semantic, and reference-perplexity), and a generalized-entropy decomposition of cross-language disparity over a typological family partition. Applied to six watermarking schemes, three open-weight generators, eleven languages spanning four scripts and eight typological families, and both base and instruction-tuned regimes, the framework reveals failure modes that single-language, single-paradigm evaluation cannot surface. Against a shape-matched null, detection disparity is predominantly between-family on the typological partition, indicating that detection gaps are structural to language properties rather than idiosyncratic to particular languages; quality disparity is large but not reliably family-structured.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Evaluations & Datasets Track

Cryptography and Security.title: POEM: Output-Relative Block-Sparse Attention for Long-Context Prefilling
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

Cryptography and Security.title: TERM: Target-Free Jailbreak Defense via Entropy-Guided Residual Modulation
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong capabilities across diverse applications, making both safety and utility essential for reliable deployment. Jailbreak attacks use diverse forms of adversarial prompting to bypass alignment safeguards and induce LLMs to generate harmful responses. Some representation-based defenses regulate internal activations using predefined steering directions or learned safety regions. However, adapting intervention to each input without a predefined representational target while limiting over-refusal remains a challenge. In this paper, we propose Target-free Entropy-guided Residual Modulation (TERM), an inference-time defense that uses prompt-calibrated attention entropy deviations to guide adaptive modulation of the model's own residual updates. Attention patterns vary across prompts and decoding steps, making raw entropy values difficult to interpret as a consistent signal for intervention. We therefore calibrate attention entropy against each prompt's own prefill baseline to establish an input-specific reference for reducing unnecessary intervention on benign requests. Adaptive scale normalization and temporal accumulation then account for differences in deviation scale and persistence to determine intervention strength. The resulting signal controls bounded scaling of the model's own residual updates, without relying on a predefined safety direction. We compare our method with seven defenses on seven jailbreak attacks and two over-refusal benchmarks across Llama, Qwen, and Gemma models, including Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B. Results show our method improves jailbreak robustness while maintaining low over-refusal on benign safety-sensitive requests with modest inference overhead.

Cryptography and Security.title: RoCoMark: Robust Code Watermarking Against LLM-Based Functionality-Preserving Rewriting Attacks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) present significant challenges to source tracing of generated code, as LLM rewriting can substantially alter the syntactic and structural characteristics of watermarked code. However, existing watermarking methods often suffer severe performance degradation under LLM-based functionality-preserving rewriting attacks. We attribute this vulnerability not merely to the intensity of rewriting, but to a fundamental distribution mismatch between the perturbations encountered during watermark training and the global, non-deterministic rewriting behaviors induced by LLMs. In order to deal with this challenge, we propose RoCoMark, a Robust Code waterMarking framework that explicitly learns and adapts to LLM rewriting behaviors. RoCoMark is a multi-round minimax game between the watermark embedder and LLM rewriter. In each round, the embedder first learns threat profiling from LLM-rewritten code by optimizing the watermark encoder through contrastive learning and knowledge distillation while mitigating catastrophic representation drift. Then the embedder improves strategies by optimizing the watermark encoder and extractor simultaneously. Finally, an adaptive attack-evolution mechanism based on Reflexion and short- and long-term memory pools is applied, enabling continuous interaction between the watermark embedder and evolving rewriting strategies. This iterative attacker-defender process progressively improves the robustness of the watermark against diverse and previously unseen LLM rewriting behaviors. Extensive experiments on four typical benchmarks, under attacks generated by five LLMs, show the effectiveness of RoCoMark. RoCoMark achieves an average detection AUROC of 74.2% and a Rewrite BitACC of 75.3%, while maintaining a code functionality pass rate above 99.7%.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 17 pages (minor update)

Cryptography and Security.title: MIRAGE: Misleading Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Black-box and Query-agnostic Poisoning Attacks
Cryptography and Security.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems enhance LLMs with external knowledge but introduce a critical attack surface: corpus poisoning. While recent studies have demonstrated the potential of such attacks, they typically rely on impractical assumptions, such as white-box access or known user queries, thereby underestimating the difficulty of real-world exploitation. In this paper, we bridge this gap by proposing MIRAGE, a novel multi-stage poisoning pipeline designed for strict black-box and query-agnostic environments. Operating on surrogate model feedback, MIRAGE functions as an automated optimization framework that integrates three key mechanisms: it utilizes persona-driven query synthesis to approximate latent user search distributions, employs semantic anchoring to imperceptibly embed these intents for high retrieval visibility, and leverages an adversarial variant of Test-Time Preference Optimization (TPO) to maximize persuasion. To rigorously evaluate this threat, we construct a new benchmark derived from three long-form, domain-specific datasets. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MIRAGE significantly outperforms existing baselines in both attack efficacy and stealthiness, exhibiting remarkable transferability across diverse retriever-LLM configurations and highlighting the urgent need for robust defense strategies.

Cryptography and Security.title: TGCM: Topic-Guided Consistency Modeling for One-Step Disentanglement of Interleaved APT Technique Sequences
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Multiple Advanced Persistent Threat (APT) campaigns may execute concurrently, producing audit logs whose events are interleaved without explicit campaign boundaries. We formulate this setting as Unknown-K Interleaved Sequence Demixing (UKISD): recovering coherent campaign episodes when the number of concurrent campaigns is unknown. Each episode is represented as a sequence of MITRE ATT&CK technique occurrences, and demixing is cast as occurrence-level assignment with sequence reconstruction. Existing methods often assume single-campaign observations or rely on local heuristics, limiting robustness to severe interleaving, repeated techniques, abstraction noise, and unknown mixture cardinality.
  We propose Topic-Guided Consistency Modeling (TGCM), a consistency-inspired one-step framework for UKISD. TGCM maps an interleaved technique sequence to campaign episodes, jointly performing occurrence assignment and sequence reconstruction in one forward pass. It combines topic guidance from ATT&CK narratives with an embedding-space self-consistency objective to improve semantic coherence and retain efficient inference.
  We evaluate TGCM on synthetic mixtures, mixed benchmarks, DARPA engagement traces, and CAPTure, an end-to-end benchmark containing 200 scenarios, 855 million audit events, and 25 ATT&CK-aligned attack profiles in single-host and multi-host settings. TGCM improves occurrence-level assignment under heavy interleaving, repeated technique reuse, symbolic extraction errors, and budgeted unknown-K inference. It also generalizes to unseen benchmarks without retraining and remains effective with practical ATT&CK extraction pipelines. These results establish TGCM as a practical post-abstraction framework for reasoning about concurrent APT campaigns. Code and artifacts are available at https://irish-kw.github.io/TGCM_Website/.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 14 pages, Due to arXiv's abstract length limit, the web version of the abstract has been shortened while preserving the paper's original scope, claims, and results. The implementation and experimental artifacts are publicly available at https://irish-kw.github.io/TGCM_Website/

Cryptography and Security.title: Data-Efficient Unlearning-Based Backdoor Detection in Federated Learning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Detecting backdoor attacks in federated learning (FL) is challenging because malicious clients can manipulate the global model while preserving main-task performance. Static model-update statistics may therefore fail to clearly distinguish malicious from benign clients. Unlearning-based detectors instead probe client models through loss ascent on clean server data, but detection performance degrades with scarce proxy data. We propose Screening via Unlearning Response Analysis (SURA), a data-efficient detector. SURA reuses the same small clean proxy across multiple train-mode loss-ascent steps, strengthening client responses without additional clean data. For federated vision models with batch normalization (BN), repeated probing also changes BN running statistics and can confound endpoint measurements. SURA addresses this by restoring the shared pre-probe BN state only at readout while preserving the parameter changes induced by probing. This separates repeated probing from response measurement and removes BN drift and the interaction between parameter and BN-state changes from the readout. Across six backdoor attacks, SURA uses only 10 clean server images, outperforms methods under the same data budget, and approaches the robustness obtained with much larger proxy sets.

Cryptography and Security.title: Differential Privacy for Euclidean Jordan Algebra with Applications to Private Symmetric Cone Programming
Cryptography and Security.summary: In this paper, we study differentially private mechanisms for functions whose outputs lie in a Euclidean Jordan algebra. Euclidean Jordan algebras capture many important mathematical structures and form the foundation of linear programming, second-order cone programming, and semidefinite programming. Our main contribution is a generic Gaussian mechanism for such functions, with sensitivity measured in $\ell_2$, $\ell_1$, and $\ell_\infty$ norms. Notably, this framework includes the important case where the function outputs are symmetric matrices, and sensitivity is measured in the Frobenius, nuclear, or spectral norm. We further derive private algorithms for solving symmetric cone programs under various settings, using a combination of the multiplicative weights update method and our generic Gaussian mechanism. As an application, we present differentially private algorithms for semidefinite programming, resolving a major open question posed by [Hsu, Roth, Roughgarden, and Ullman, ICALP 2014].
Cryptography and Security.comment: NeurIPS 2025. This version corrects the private covering SDP and symmetric cone programming theorems of Section 5 by taking OPT as a public input and give $(ε, δ)$-privacy

Cryptography and Security.title: SnapAudit: Active Auditing of Differentially Private In-Context Learning via Snapshot-Based Simulation
Cryptography and Security.summary: In-context learning (ICL) enables LLMs to adapt to tasks using demonstrations that may contain sensitive data. Differentially private (DP) ICL mechanisms mitigate this risk by adding noise during aggregation. However, verifying their claimed privacy bounds through repeated end-to-end membership-inference attacks is costly and yields unstable estimates. We propose SnapAudit, an active auditing framework that decomposes a DP-ICL pipeline into a deterministic clean-inference stage and a stochastic DP-noise stage, and audits the full pipeline by combining a small snapshot of the former with bootstrap simulation of the latter. Because clean LLM outputs are near-deterministic at low temperature, tens of thousands of clean LLM calls suffice to approximate the snapshot distribution; SnapAudit then bootstraps hundreds of thousands of noisy trials at negligible additional cost, controlling finite-sample uncertainty via an empirical Bernstein correction. For embedding-based mechanisms, a multi-sweep search constructs maximally separable audit signals. Compared with passive auditing, SnapAudit yields tighter, more stable privacy estimates that closely match theoretical guarantees. Across privacy budgets, SnapAudit reuses snapshots across noise configurations, whereas passive auditing requires fresh end-to-end trials. Across four DP-ICL pipelines and five privacy budgets, this reduces total wall-clock auditing time by $4.3$--$5.5\times$. SnapAudit also uncovers two flaws in existing DP-ICL designs: (i) classical Gaussian noise calibrations underestimate leakage at large privacy budgets, allowing empirical leakage to exceed the theoretical bound; (ii) an embedding-aggregation mechanism's sensitivity analysis is incorrect when the number of partitions equals one, leading to undersized noise and a privacy violation.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Mitigating Private Data Leakage in LLMs with Whiteout
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Modern large language models (LLMs) are trained on massive, largely unfiltered datasets, including content scraped from nearly every accessible website and user inputs. As a result, LLMs often memorize and reproduce personally sensitive information (PSI) such as birth dates, phone numbers, and home addresses. This leads to significant privacy risks, particularly for high-profile individuals such as executives, politicians, and judges. Existing mitigations largely rely on machine unlearning. However, these methods often remove more information than needed, degrade model utility and safety, and are highly vulnerable to attacks.
  This paper presents Whiteout, a practical tool that, upon requests by individuals, prevents LLMs from regurgitating their genuine PSIs, by overwriting them using precise and carefully designed obfuscation samples. We evaluate Whiteout on modern LLMs of varying sizes and makers, including a widely-used OpenAI model. Results show that Whiteout effectively prevents disclosure of the targeted PSIs, has negligible impact on model utility and safety, and outperforms existing alternatives. We also test Whiteout against a wide range of countermeasures, from black-box attacks like jailbreaking to white-box adaptive attacks like relearning and quantization. Finally, we conclude with a discussion on the security and ethical implications of Whiteout.
Cryptography and Security.comment: v2: minor typos and formatting corrections

Cryptography and Security.title: 5G CATS: 5G-Based Cryptographic Authorization Against Trafficking of Semiconductor Devices
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Enforcing export controls on AI accelerators requires verifying where a chip operates after deployment. Round-trip time measurements can bound a chip's distance from a trusted landmark, but any jitter in honest replies forces the verifier to loosen its timeout, giving an attacker slack to relay traffic over fiber from a restricted region. Prior approaches either cross the untrusted host stack or rely on noisy power-line channels that inflate this slack.
  We present 5G CATS, a location certification system that pairs a co-packaged 5G radio, cryptographic engine, and hardware interlock on the GPU package with 5G Ultra-Reliable Low-Latency Communication (URLLC) base stations. Terminating the radio link inside the package removes the host software, PCIe fabric, and baseboard management controller from the verification path. We map an authenticated challenge-response protocol onto 5G's slot structure, replace permanent key erasure with short-lived execution leases, and specify a cross-check of the chip's reported serving cell against the carrier's own attachment records. In ns-3 and 5G-LENA simulations of an unloaded cell, our URLLC-based radio profile narrows the 99.9th percentile round-trip spread to 2.60 ms, more than ten times narrower than default 5G. A tracer rejects every round of a fiber relay from 300 km, against 2,000 km for default 5G. Against a 3,000 km attacker, a tracer stays safe at up to 1,410 km from the chip, against at most 619 km for PowerCATS's published model, while default 5G is never safe.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Stinging the Swarm: Extracting Attacker Intelligence from a Twin-Controller OT Honeypot
Cryptography and Security.summary: Autonomous language-model agents can drive industrial controllers over fieldbus protocols, probing a plant at machine speed and in coordinated swarms. We present Talos, an inline gate that judges every agent request to a controller in milliseconds and routes agents it flags as hostile to a device-faithful decoy -- a mirror twin of the real plant -- where their attack continues harmlessly and is read for intelligence. We evaluate the full pipeline (detect -> quarantine -> mirror -> extract) against 2,400 autonomous attacker agents, 600 in each of four tiers that escalate the attacker's effort to stay hidden, from no concealment to an explicit non-disclosure rule and a trained cover story. No write reached the real plant in any tier: the gate denies the damage path and a device-level envelope check backstops it, while unmapped registers are denied without exception and the gate still permits safe-direction stop commands. Decisions are model-driven in every tier with no inference timeouts, closing a common objection to small on-device judges. Beyond blocking, the pipeline reads the attacker. We find a behavioral structure along two axes -- how persistently an agent attacks and how much it discloses -- and show that the system has a capture channel for three of the four resulting regions: hardened, silent attackers escalate most and are read on the mirror; compliant, talkative attackers volunteer their identity to a diagnostic form before they are ever quarantined; only the paranoid, low-yield region resists both. Attacker identity fields are self-authored cover stories, but involuntary tells -- the self-reported toolchain fingerprint and the attacker's own list of targeted registers -- accumulate across the swarm into a high-confidence profile drawn from agents under explicit orders to stay silent. The gate, mirror, and harness are released under Apache 2.0 with a synthetic device family.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 11 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Integrated Identity Protection for Semantic Communications in Embodied IoT Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary: Embodied Internet of Things (IoT) systems are promoting the adoption of task-oriented semantic communication (SemCom), in which the trustworthy task decisions increasingly require both semantic reliability and source legitimacy. However, existing trustworthy SemCom designs mainly focus on semantic content recovery and protection, with limited attention to source identity protection. Motivated by this limitation, this paper establishes a new information exploitation perspective for integrated SemCom-identity protection that leverages task-level error tolerance to coordinate semantic information and source identity information carried by the same waveform. We first examine these two information resources and then analyze their integration feasibility at the observation, processing, and decision levels. To exploit these resources for different identity protection objectives, we further develop a dual-branch identity protection mechanism with two operating modes. In the authentication mode, semantic recovery and physical-layer source verification are performed in parallel using the same received observation. In the concealment mode, identity exposure is suppressed while semantic reconstruction quality is maintained to support anonymous transmission. Finally, two representative case studies on active source impersonation and passive identity inference are presented to evaluate the proposed framework.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 5 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: What Does an RF Fingerprint Identify? A Cross-Corpus Evaluation of Hardware-Family-Associated and Unit-Level Signal
Cryptography and Security.summary: RF fingerprinting benchmarks report how well a classifier separates transmitters, not whether that separability reflects the individual unit or its hardware family. We compare a benchmark's real hardware grouping with size-matched random groupings of the same devices, using calibrated, unclipped variational lower bounds under label-blind, device-level cross-fitting on devices never seen in training. On WiSig (OFDM Wi-Fi), the generation grouping exceeded all 999 matched random groupings (permutation p = 0.001, the resolution floor), although no grouping attained a positive certified bound, and the direction survives removing channel equalization. A preregistered replication on a LoRa corpus (chirp spread spectrum, three hardware models), with a front-end frozen on synthetic data, again exceeded all 999 (p = 0.001), and two sensitivity analyses judged by a reversal rule fixed in advance did not reverse the direction. This is a directional replication only: the excess magnitude reflects a miscalibrated null, the chain-rule decomposition leaves a residual of +0.296 bits, and capture order is undocumented. In a same-model corpus of 122 ESP32 radios, a temperature-calibrated held-out bound of +3.338 bits (label entropy 6.931 bits) indicates substantial device-specific identity, not separable from per-device capture-session effects; relying on the calibrated bound was decided after the uncalibrated bound changed sign. On synthetic transmitters a high-capacity convolutional decoder reaches 98.5% of a known 6-bit ceiling, and the audit protocol leaves chain-rule residuals of +0.072 bits (synthetic, fixed physical features) and +0.060 bits (WiSig, audit features). Two further corpora were excluded by preregistered ingest gates. Across WiSig and LoRa, hardware-family groupings consistently produced stronger identity-associated signal than size-matched random groupings.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 20 pages, 4 tables, no figures

Cryptography and Security.title: OverServe: Resource Amplification Attacks on SaaS Agents via Tool--Prompt Co-Design
Cryptography and Security.summary: Advances in large language models (LLMs) are enabling software-as-a-service (SaaS) providers to automate longer business workflows with agents. In subscription-based SaaS deployments, model and tool calls consume provider resources without additional customer payments. Because the agent autonomously decides when to stop, a malicious tenant can send a prompt to the agent, exploiting its completion decisions to extend execution and waste provider resources. In this paper, we present OverServe, a multi-agent framework for constructing such attacks against SaaS agents. OverServe co-designs Model Context Protocol (MCP) status tools and completion-confirmation prompts for the attacker. Each tool call returns accurate status and terminates normally, yet the agent may repeatedly check an unfinished condition to satisfy the prompt. This consumes the SaaS provider's resources even after the original business task is completed. OverServe constructs service-specific tool--prompt pairs and uses separate tool and prompt reviews to guide candidate pair selection. Tested tool specifications trigger no alerts in the evaluated MCP scanners. We evaluate Qwen, Nemotron, DeepSeek, and Sonnet on selected tasks from nine benchmarks. All OverServe runs pass the original task checks. OverServe can reach a maximal amplification of API requests by $93.88\times$ while preserving the original task goal and collateral checks.

Cryptography and Security.title: AI Sandboxes: A Threat Model, Taxonomy, and Measurement Framework
Cryptography and Security.summary: AI sandboxes produce evidence about systems that may act through software tools, networked devices, or physical actuators. The interpretation of that evidence depends on the boundary of the experiment. We define a sandbox apparatus, distinguish five overlapping archetypes, and specify fifteen claim-relative measurement dimensions. A weakest-link licensing rule caps a deployment claim at its weakest necessary evidence dimension. We connect this rule to a threat model covering both outward harm and corruption of the evaluation apparatus, then apply it to four worked examples spanning driving, industrial control, tool-using agents, and vision-language-action manipulation. We also map the required artifacts to standards and regulatory instruments. The framework identifies which claims a bounded experiment supports, which failures its controls contain, and which assumptions require further validation before deployment.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 42 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Security and Privacy Prompts in the Wild: What Users Ask LLMs and How LLMs Respond
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to answer users' information needs: users ask LLMs about the weather, pose educational questions, and consult them for legal assistance. One particularly understudied area is digital security and privacy (S&P), where users may seek LLMs' help on how to secure their online accounts or protect their computers from cyber attacks. To the best of our knowledge, no prior study has collected or analyzed the S&P questions users ask LLMs; prior research on LLM response quality relied on expert-authored S&P misconceptions or FAQs rather than user queries. Drawing from WildChat, a dataset of 3.2M user-LLM conversations collected in the wild, our study identifies 14,727 S&P prompts and categorizes them into nine categories covering a wide range of S&P topics. We sampled 450 S&P prompts, and performed a thematic analysis to characterize the S&P questions users ask LLMs. Separate from the thematic analysis, we curated 270 advice-seeking S&P prompts, where users ask for recommendations, guidance, or specific S&P information. We measured LLM response quality and consistency when posing each prompt to the LLMs 10 times. We found that commercial LLMs outperform open-weight models (GPT 5.5 provided "good enough" responses on 98% of prompts; Llama 4 on 47%). However, among prompts that received high-quality responses on average, commercial models sometimes produce semantically inconsistent responses across runs (some are contradictory, and others are different in specificity), thereby risking confusing or misleading users.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Published as a main conference paper at EMNLP 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: CellularS2-Bench: A Staged, Evidence-Grounded Benchmark for Cellular Network Security Reasoning
Cryptography and Security.summary: Cellular networks are critical infrastructure supporting billions of worldwide users and safety- and mission-critical services. Vulnerabilities in cellular networks can therefore cause service disruption, privacy breaches, and broad societal harm, motivating growing efforts to analyze 3GPP specifications that define required device and operator behavior. However, existing benchmarks for this domain share three systematic deficiencies: they rely on LLM-generated entries without expert verification, they do not require faithful interpretation of normative language, reasoning across cross-referenced clauses, and verifiable conclusions grounded in multimodal evidence such as tables and figures, and they do not evaluate security reasoning over end-to-end protocol behavior. To address these gaps, we present CellularS2-Bench, a staged benchmark. CellularS2-Bench covers core control-plane specifications, processing over 1,866 paragraphs, 22,033 sentences, 424 figures, and 248 tables. It comprises 13,851 questions and instances across three progressive stages, of which 10,269 (74.14%) are newly constructed from 3GPP specifications and 43 real-world vulnerabilities. Beyond newly constructed tasks, CellularS2-Bench integrates and corrects 3,582 (25.86%) instances from 7 prior datasets to broaden task coverage. To establish a reproducible baseline on CellularS2-Bench, we introduce CellularS2-ARI, a unified Adapt-Retrieve-Integrate framework for systematic understanding and specification-driven security analysis of 3GPP specifications. Together, they establish an accessible and reproducible foundation for quantifying progress in specification understanding and security reasoning in cellular network security.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted to the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026), Evaluations and Datasets Track

Cryptography and Security.title: Robust & Scalable Website Fingerprinting via Minimal DRAM Traffic
Cryptography and Security.summary: Website fingerprinting attacks infer websites visited by users and threaten their privacy. These attacks are classified as on-path, which monitor network traffic, and co-located, which exploit shared system resources. Existing co-located attacks, such as sweep-counting and loop-counting, achieve over 90% accuracy but suffer significant performance degradation on many-core systems. Loop-counting accuracy drops from 93% on 8 cores to 50% on 24 cores, while sweep-counting accuracy decreases from 84% to 45% across multiple Core Complex Dies (CCDs). To address these limitations, we propose memory-chasing, a scalable website fingerprinting attack that exploits DRAM traffic interference through pointer-chasing traversals with minimal interference. By counting DRAM accesses over fixed intervals, the attack generates distinctive traces for website classification. Evaluated on the top 50 websites, memory-chasing achieves 96% accuracy on a 24-core system, 86% across multiple CCDs, 80% across multiple sockets, and 97% in an open-world setting. Extensive evaluation across hardware configurations, browsers, operating systems, isolation mechanisms, system noise, and countermeasures demonstrates its robustness and scalability.

Cryptography and Security.title: Incrementally Verifiable Oracle Aided Computation
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Incrementally verifiable computation (IVC) allows a prover to maintain a short proof that can be efficiently updated after each computation step, without retaining or recomputing the preceding execution. Standard IVC schemes do not directly address a crucial feature of AI tasks: their dependence on external information and expertise.
  We construct IVC schemes for oracle-aided computations under the LWE assumption by first constructing SNARGs, and then extending them to IVC. We consider the following two settings, where below, k is the security parameter, n is the input length, and T, S, and Q are the time, space, and oracle-query bounds.
  1. Robust computations: For bounded-space computations, including non-deterministic computations, in which every accepting purported execution on a false input contains at least an eps-fraction of incorrect oracle answers, we construct privately verifiable SNARGs and IVC. Public parameters, private verification keys, and proofs have length poly(k ,S, log T,1/eps), and verification uses O(k/eps) oracle calls. We complement this result with a lower bound ruling out (deterministic) publicly verifiable SNARGs and IVCs with public parameters of length o(n), and o(Q) verifier oracle queries.
  2. Signed oracles: For oracles that digitally sign their query-answer pairs, we construct publicly verifiable SNARGs and IVC without a robustness assumption, and with oracle-free setup and verification. Public parameters and proofs have length poly(k,S,log T). For deterministic computations with oracle query and answer lengths poly(k,log T), we remove the dependence on S, obtaining public parameter and proof lengths poly(k,log T).
  All our constructions have adaptive completeness and soundness.

Cryptography and Security.title: Adversarial Risk in the Generative AI Era Necessitates Dropping the Small Epsilon Ball
Cryptography and Security.summary: Adversarial Machine Learning research is currently centered on the search for the epsilon-ball: minimal perturbations designed to fool models while remaining imperceptible to humans. We argue that this fixation on $\ell_p$ norms is a metrological trap that communicates a distorted perception of risk to defenders, one that is unaligned with real-world system vulnerabilities. This paradigm misleads defenders into optimizing for narrow, mathematical robustness at the expense of systemic security, while simultaneously incentivizing attackers to exploit non-overlapping alternative adversarial pathways. Ultimately, we argue that the dominance of the $\ell_p$ ball does not just fail to reduce harm---it may actively facilitate it by communicating a false sense of security against the wrong threats.
Cryptography and Security.comment: neurips 2026, 10 pages, position paper on adversarial risk, certified robustness

Cryptography and Security.title: When Evaluators of AI Agents Disagree: An Empirical Study of Native Scoring, LLM Judges, and Commit-Boundary Checks on tau2-bench
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Agentic workflows, in which a large language model (LLM) calls tools to read and write data, are evaluated in two ways. Benchmarks compare the final state against a gold answer. Deployed services have none; an LLM judge reads the transcript and decides. Practice treats the two as interchangeable. This paper measures whether they are.
  We ran 2,160 episodes in tau2-bench's airline and retail domains and recorded every database write. We scored each episode four ways: native scoring against gold state, an LLM judge, that judge given the policy document, and the boundary evaluator, a minimal rule-based check of whether a write was expected against whether one occurred in the trace. Two annotators independently labeled 120 episodes for task correctness, policy compliance, and commitment correctness.
  The judge repeated its verdict 98.2% of the time but agreed with native scoring on 56.2%. In 11 episodes the agent executed a forbidden write. The judge passed 10 to 11, with or without the policy or transcript. A stronger judge still passed 6. The boundary evaluator, with no model call, caught all 11; no judge significantly exceeded it on human labels. Forbidden writes occurred in 11.1% of episodes without gates. Verification, correction, and safe-termination gates did not reduce them significantly. The traces show a candidate cause: the gates' evidence digest dropped the order status and customer authentication, so valid requests were rejected. The choice of evaluator decides the conclusion; the minimal check exposes failures the judges miss. Traces, code, prompts, and labels are released.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 38 pages, 3 figures, 11 tables. Submitted to Empirical Software Engineering. Replication package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23683806. Supplementary material (Online Resource 1) is included as an ancillary file

Programming Languages.title: Performance Portability Explained: Insights from accelerating ICON microphysics
Programming Languages.summary:
Scientific computing is under increasing pressure to adapt to HPC hardware that is shaped by AI workloads. In these modern ecosystems, extracting reasonable performance without investing major engineering effort is a central issue for domain scientists. Correctness constraints and intricate reference implementations represent further impediments to development. Instead of using a double-precision implementation as a reference, considering the underlying scientific problem directly opens more opportunities for performance improvements when updating and rewriting applications.
  We take seven different portability frameworks---covering pragma-based, DSL, and data-centric approaches---and evaluate them on a microphysics kernel of the ICON climate model. Our performance benchmarks show that each different HPC system benefits from a different combination of optimizations, so we develop the measure of framework expressivity to gauge how easily each framework can customize portable implementations in this way.

Programming Languages.title: CFGKAT: A Complete Calculus for Non-Local Control Flow
Programming Languages.summary: CFGKAT is an extension of guarded Kleene Algebra with Tests (GKAT) that adds non-local control flow (e.g., break, goto) while maintaining an efficient decision procedure. An axiomatization of equivalence for CFGKAT presents unique barriers created by the presence of non-local control flow and contextual semantics of goto which compromises compositional reasoning. In this paper, we overcome these barriers and present a sound and complete axiomatization of program equivalence in CFGKAT. We verify the loop case of the Erosa-Hendren goto elimination algorithm, a difficult syntactic metatheorem which requires reasoning about fixpoints, control-flow contexts, and mutable state. We mechanize the metatheory and case study in Rocq.

Programming Languages.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
Programming Languages.summary:
Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent.
  To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.
Programming Languages.comment: 61 pages, 13 figures

Programming Languages.title: RECURSUM: Automated Code Generation for Recurrence Relations Exceeds Expert Optimization via LayeredCodegen
Programming Languages.summary:
Automated code generation can systematically exceed expert hand-optimization for recurrence relations--computational primitives ubiquitous in orthogonal polynomials, special functions, numerical integration, and molecular integral evaluation. We present RECURSUM, a Python DSL generating optimized C++ for arbitrary recurrence relations via three backends--template metaprogramming, a novel LayeredCodegen backend, and runtime loop-based evaluation--specifying recurrences in 10--30 lines of Python that generate 650+ lines of production C++.
  LayeredCodegen achieves 9.8$\times$ speedup over expert hand-written code and 1.9$\times$ over template metaprogramming for McMurchie-Davidson Hermite coefficients, through zero-copy output parameters, guaranteed inlining, and exact-sized stack buffers. A DAG-topological generalization of this architecture--built to express the four-center electron-repulsion integral that LayeredCodegen's tower model cannot--beats libint2, a mature, two-decade-refined production library, on 12 of 14 Cartesian integral classes, with $\sim$2$\times$ faster contracted Coulomb/exchange (J/K) matrix construction (alkanes and 3-D DNA fragments alike) and 1.1--2.7$\times$ faster one-electron integrals, completing the full Hartree-Fock integral set from one DAG framework.
  We validate 24 recurrence types spanning pure mathematics, numerical analysis, and quantum chemistry; production benchmarks confirm these speedups propagate to complete algorithms, matching expert baselines within 3.3\%. By eliminating the dual expertise barrier of domain knowledge and C++ metaprogramming, RECURSUM establishes systematic code generation--not hand-tuning--as the performance ceiling for recurrence algorithms.
Programming Languages.comment: 84 pages, 9 figures

Programming Languages.title: For Generalised Algebraic Theories, Two Sorts Are Enough
Programming Languages.summary: Generalised algebraic theories (GATs) allow multiple sorts indexed over each other. Categories have two sorts, objects and morphisms, and the latter are double-indexed over the former. Martin-Löf type theory has four sorts: contexts, substitutions, types and terms. For example, types are indexed over contexts, and terms are indexed over both contexts and types. In this paper we show that any GAT can be reduced to a GAT involving only two sorts: a first one without dependencies, and another one indexed over the former. We show that a model of the reduced GAT is equivalently given by a pair consisting of a model of the original GAT, which we call the core model, and a "cartesian" morphism from the family of sets induced by this core model. In a type-theoretic metatheory, the initial model of a GAT is called a quotient inductive-inductive type (QIIT). The above characterisation justifies soundness of the reduction, in the sense that the QIIT of the original GAT can be simulated from the QIIT of the reduced GAT, by taking its core model. A particular case of our reduction is the well-known method of reducing mutual inductive types to a single indexed family. Other instances of this reduction can be found in the literature to simulate sophisticated QIITs in Cubical Agda. Indeed, the reduced GAT is simpler than the original GAT in the following aspects: it does not have sort equalities; it does not have interleaved sorts and operations; if the original GAT did not have interleaved sorts and operations, then the reduced GAT won't have operations interleaved between different sorts. Our approach is semantic in that it does not rely on a syntactic description of GATs, but instead, on Uemura's bi-initial characterisation of the category of (finite) GATs in the 2-category of finitely complete categories with a chosen exponentiable morphism.

Programming Languages.title: Retargetable Compilation for Tensor Kernels via a Unified Layout Abstraction
Programming Languages.summary:
Modern hardware accelerators achieve high performance through specialized instructions coupled with tightly managed memory hierarchies. These instructions impose strict layout requirements on their operands: where tensor fragments reside, how they are organized, and how parallel units access them. Such instruction-visible layout is critical to kernel performance, as it determines whether instructions execute correctly and how much data movement they incur. However, existing compilers either scatter layout requirements across handwritten programs and local scheduling rules, or provide layout representations and conversions specific to a single class of targets. Both approaches expose the same abstraction gap: the absence of a unified model for instruction layout requirements across backends.
  This paper presents Arknife, a retargetable compiler that treats instruction-visible layout as first-class instruction semantics. Its central idea is a constraint-based layout algebra: tensor layouts map logical axes to hardware axes spanning parallel levels and memory spaces. Instruction operands declare layout requirements, and target-provided repairs resolve conflicts. Layouts are then solved globally across the program. ISA-specific layout facts are supplied by target-side instruction descriptions rather than hardcoded in the compiler. Retargeting reuses the layout algebra and solver while defining the new target's instructions and their operand requirements. We evaluate Arknife across x86 CPU, Hexagon NPU, and NVIDIA A100 GPU. Arknife matches cuBLAS on A100, and on x86 and Hexagon outperforms vendor-optimized libraries by $2.17\times$ and $3.78\times$ and the retargetable compiler MISAAL by $5.08\times$ and $4.53\times$, respectively.

Programming Languages.title: Gödel's Incompleteness Theorems in Grounded Arithmetic
Programming Languages.summary: Reflective Grounded Arithmetic (RGA) is a paracomplete arithmetic in which every term is a program and truth is grounded evaluation. RGA discharges a hypothesis only when it proves the hypothesis decided. This paper shows, in a machine-checked Isabelle/HOL development, how Gödel's incompleteness theorems hold for RGA and for systems built on it. RGA's implication is material and RGA has the disjunction property, so the implications the textbook proof of the second theorem uses fail while its entailments and rules hold: Gödel's proof survives as entailments. RGA does not prove its consistency sentence Con, and RGA derives its own second theorem as the entailment $\mathit{Con}\vdash\neg\mathit{Pr}(\ulcorner\mathit{Con}\urcorner)$ and as one sentence quantified over proofs. The second theorem is then proved once, for every Gödel extension of RGA: an entailment relation on RGA's language, closed under RGA's rules, with a checker that meets three structural conditions, NEC, D3 and EXPL as proof transformers, D1 as closed acceptance, and consistency. D2 is not among the conditions. RGA with its checker is one instance. Inductive Grounded Arithmetic (IGA), RGA with ground induction, is another, its checker adding one rule detector, and IGA does not derive its consistency sentence for it. Adoption, a reflection rule whose premise is a derived warrant that the checker accepts computed proofs of every instance of a universal, gives consistent extensions RGA$^+$ and IGA$^+$. RGA$^+$ derives RGA's consistency sentence and IGA$^+$ derives RGA's and IGA's, so each strictly extends its base, and IGA$^+$ both. The second theorem holds at every adopted notation claim, and adopting Turing's code for that claim's checker derives its consistency sentence, so no claim certifies itself. Whether IGA alone derives RGA's consistency sentence is open, and the paper names what two routes to an answer need.
Programming Languages.comment: 103 pages; splits the Goedel incompleteness material out of Internal Reasoning companion paper 2608.16140, which is getting a corresponding major update

Programming Languages.title: Curriculum proof repair with learned counterexamples
Programming Languages.summary: Language models (LMs) have substantially lowered the barrier to applying formal verification for building reliable and secure software. Existing approaches commonly follow the verifier-in-the-loop paradigm, but the verifier often provides only coarse, binary pass/fail feedback, which offers little actionable signal on how the proof should be repaired. Recent work shows that counterexamples provide more actionable feedback by grounding proof failures in concrete program states, but generating useful ones at inference time requires costly iterative refinement. We present TopoVerus, an LM-based framework for Verus proof repair that internalizes counterexample-guided diagnosis as a model capability, producing useful counterexamples in a single pass. Our key insight is to train counterexample generation not as a standalone validation task, but as a data-driven diagnostic objective: a counterexample is useful when conditioning on it helps the model produce a safe, verifier-passing proof. Given a failed Verus proof and verifier error, TopoVerus generates a structured source-level counterexample, repair rationale, and repaired proof in one trajectory, optimized with reinforcement learning from Verus feedback and a proof-code safety gate. To guide the order of invariant repairs, TopoVerus introduces a curriculum with a topological graph reward based on invariant dependencies derived from inductiveness tests, which encourages counterexample generation to follow the same topological order. Across seven Verus benchmarks with 471 problems, TopoVerus achieves 61.6%/72.2% weighted-average Safe-Pass@1/Safe-Pass@3, outperforming the strongest baseline, Claude Sonnet 4.5, by 5.7/6.3 points. We also show that TopoVerus's learned counterexamples can directly augment the reasoning of existing LM-based proof repair approaches, improving their success rate by 64.3% compared to chain-of-thought diagnostics.
Programming Languages.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 28 pages

Programming Languages.title: Context Types: Bunched Modalities for Unifying Safety and Reachability
Programming Languages.summary: Most type systems are designed to verify safety properties: the judgement $e : τ$ holds if $e$ may evaluate to any value contained in the denotation of $τ$, but nothing more. More recent type systems have considered the complementary class of reachability properties: in these systems, the typing judgment holds if $e$ must be able to evaluate to every value denoted by $τ$, and possibly more. This paper introduces a refinement type system for higher-order functional programs where types can capture both safety and reachability properties. Simultaneously supporting both is challenging because each imposes different constraints on how variable bindings in a typing context are interpreted. We address this challenge by treating typing contexts as a kind of resource that mediates which capabilities are available when typing a program. We formalize this notion by developing a resource algebra of contextual capabilities and a bunched modal context logic over this algebra. We then interpret our type system in this logic, establishing soundness with respect to a denotational semantics that unifies safety and reachability guarantees within a single typing judgement.

Programming Languages.title: Fibered Separation Logic: Weakest Preconditions, Universal Constructions, and Local Independence
Programming Languages.summary:
This paper introduces a categorical framework for models of higher-order separation logic including the weakest precondition modality. Weakest preconditions are interpreted by strong monads on a category fibered over a model of Moggi's computational lambda calculus. The fibered categories in question are termed bunched fibrations and shown to be equivalent to BI hyperdoctrines.
  Well-known heuristic techniques for obtaining weakest preconditions are shown to be expressible in categorical terms and are proved sound. The ``baking in the frame rule'' trick is shown to satisfy a universal property. Constructions are given for extending a program logic with cost credits. Our largest case study is parametrized by a category having local independent product (LIP) structure, a notion due to Simpson that axiomatizes name generation, randomness, and local state. From an LIP category, we construct an allocation monad, a bunched fibration, and a monad lifting. We instantiate our construction to obtain a novel probabilistic separation logic for measure-theoretic probability that both simplifies and clarifies prior work.
Programming Languages.comment: 41 pages, 5 figures

Programming Languages.title: Model Checking Probabilistic Multiparty Session Types
Programming Languages.summary: Distributed systems increasingly rely on randomisation; yet, verification techniques for such systems remain separate from the programming abstractions used to build them. This paper proposes the first probabilistic extension of general multiparty session types - typing sessions bottom-up, with no global specification - deriving quantitative properties of a multiparty session from its session types alone. Our types combine probabilistic choice with nondeterministic choice that abstracts data-dependent control, and allow separated choices, where each branch of a selection or branching may involve a different participant - a combination beyond previous probabilistic multiparty session type systems. To achieve this, we develop a novel probabilistic subtyping relation and merge operator, using which we prove type soundness and session fidelity. The semantics of typing contexts separates nondeterministic resolution, probabilistic choice, and synchronisation, so that every typing context induces a finite Markov decision process. On it, we derive sound lower bounds, holding under every fair adversarial scheduler, on the probability that a session is deadlock-free and live - the first behavioural property guarantees, partial or otherwise, for a probabilistic session calculus. To connect session types with probabilistic model checking, we introduce the first translation from session types into the PRISM modelling language, and prove it sound and complete with respect to our operational semantics. We implement the framework in the toolchain Prose, which translates probabilistic multiparty session typing contexts into PRISM and checks safety, deadlock-freedom, and liveness.
Programming Languages.comment: 108 pages, full version of "Model Checking Probabilistic Multiparty Session Types" appearing at POPL 2027

Programming Languages.title: Reconstructing Fine-grained Memory Reuse Structure in GPU Kernels
Programming Languages.summary: Optimizing GPU data movement requires knowing which instructions access the same data and across which execution scopes reuse occurs. Existing profilers can attribute memory behavior to individual instructions but do not expose the reuse relations among them, while aliasing, dynamic indexing, and runtime parameters prevent static analysis from establishing these relations in general. Cycle-level simulation can reconstruct such relations, but at costs prohibitive for production workloads. We introduce two abstractions for representing this structure: Topological Distance, which labels each dynamic memory access with the smallest execution scope (thread, warp, block, or grid) containing its most recent reuse, and PCDepGraph, which organizes these labels into a PC-level graph of the kernel's memory reuse structure. Defined over logical execution scopes rather than transient hardware state, the representation remains stable across runs and GPU targets while directly indicating the sharing scope that candidate optimization mechanisms must cover. Our tool, cuVein, reconstructs PCDepGraph directly from optimized binaries, without sampling, at generally under 10x overhead. Across HPC and AI workloads on NVIDIA RTX 4090 and H100, optimizations guided by PCDepGraph eliminate up to 90.18% of memory instructions and yield up to 2.84x kernel speedup; reuse-scope distributions remain consistent across platforms, supporting that the representation captures program structure rather than transient hardware behavior.

Software Engineering.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted to KDD 2026, Jeju, Korea. 9 pages, 3 figures

Software Engineering.title: Operational limits of reference renewal for retained quantum-service results
Software Engineering.summary: We implement reference renewal to reconsider retained physical quantum-service results under a prespecified protocol. Twelve transitions retained six results each; ten completed renewal, eight met the prespecified endpoint, and five succeeded using retained results alone. The exact one-sided p=0.0546875 does not establish the recovery hypothesis. Incomplete references, binding failures and sequential waits expose operational limits. Offline reconstruction recovers decisions from preserved counts. Retrospective binding-plus-oracle checking accepts all 60 usable-transition results without renewal. With the exact oracle also supplying calibration scores, the study does not demonstrate incremental numerical-correctness utility of renewal.
Software Engineering.comment: 23 pages, 3 figures. Supplementary material (14 pages; ESM_1.pdf) is available as an ancillary file. Submitted to Quantum Information Processing, Quantum Software Engineering collection. Numerical artifact (ESM_2.zip) and reproducibility archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24108573

Software Engineering.title: Reliable and explainable analysis of AVS/RS by Statistical Model Checking and Process Mining
Software Engineering.summary: Automated Vehicle Storage and Retrieval Systems (AVS/RS) are increasingly adopted to boost warehouse throughput while containing operational costs. We present an integrated analysis framework that couples discrete-event simulation with Statistical Model Checking (SMC) and Process Mining (PM) to quantify and explain AVS/RS performance. SMC, implemented through the MultiVeStA tool, delivers statistically reliable estimates of key indicators, such as cycle times, throughput, and storage utilization, across alternative stocking and picking policies with user-specified confidence levels. MultiVeStA orchestrates multiple independent simulations in a black-box manner, enabling automated verification. PM ingests the resulting event logs to uncover the behavioral patterns and bottlenecks that drive those indicators, closing the interpretability gap typical of simulation studies. We instantiate the framework on a new open-source AVS/RS simulator configured according to recent industrial guidelines and evaluate multiple control strategies. Results show that the joint use of SMC and PM enables both predictive what-if analyses and post-hoc diagnostics, providing the first combined SMC+PM assessment of AVS/RS operations and a reusable toolchain for automated warehousing research.
Software Engineering.comment: 40 pages, 12 figures. Original manuscript submitted before peer review. A revised version has been accepted for publication in Expert Systems with Applications

Software Engineering.title: How Well Do SAST Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using OCPP Implementations
Software Engineering.summary: As electric vehicle (EV) adoption accelerates globally, securing electric vehicle charging station (EVCS) software becomes increasingly critical. The Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP), widely adopted for EVCS management, places significant responsibility on developers to securely implement specifications that are subject to multiple interpretations. The variety of OCPP implementations across different programming languages provides a unique opportunity to evaluate security tooling in a real-world, multi-language context where implementation variability may introduce vulnerabilities. This study provides the first empirical evaluation of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) tool performance across multiple programming languages using OCPP implementations as a real-world test corpus. We applied both comprehensive multi-language tools (SonarQube and Semgrep) and language-specific analyzers to twelve OCPP 1.6 implementations--each written in a distinct programming language--to examine how detection patterns vary across language ecosystems. Total issues ranged from just two in Rust to 1,689 in Java. Mature programming languages like Java yielded substantially more findings than newer languages like Rust, likely because established languages have more developed SAST tool ecosystems rather than inherently worse code quality. These results suggest that developers should consider available SAST tooling when selecting implementation languages for security critical systems.
Software Engineering.comment: 6 pages, 2 tables, Author-accepted manuscript. Published at IEEE CSR 2026

Software Engineering.title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
Software Engineering.summary: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

Software Engineering.title: Measuring Tabular Data Formats Cold: A Replicated Cold-Cache Benchmark of Serialization, Scan, and Index Performance on Real Datasets
Software Engineering.summary: Choosing a file format for tabular data is a routine engineering decision, yet published comparisons often time reads served from the operating-system page cache, use one session, or rely on a single synthetic dataset. This article benchmarks fifteen format and access-path configurations (CSV, JSON Lines, Pickle, Feather, Parquet, ORC, DuckDB, and SQLite, with several access paths) on two real public datasets, New York City taxi trips and United States airline on-time records, at 50,000 to 3 million rows. Every measurement uses an explicitly cold cache, randomized execution order, and three independent sessions (with restarts on the laptop), and is analyzed with bootstrap intervals and Holm-adjusted permutation tests. Parquet answered a filtered aggregation 2.6 to 11 times faster than CSV, while JSON Lines was 10 to 27 times slower. A secondary index made SQLite queries 2.6 to 4.8 times slower on randomly ordered data and helped only on data sorted by the filtered column, at low selectivity. A row filter inside the Parquet reader was significantly faster than a projected scan on flight data from one million rows and on both datasets at three million, and row-group skipping needs several row groups, which the default writer produced only at 3 million rows. A 4 GB Linux host ran out of memory on configurations that a 24 GB laptop completed and reversed some orderings, such as Pickle versus Parquet. Code, derived data, and raw timings are released.
Software Engineering.comment: Submitted to IEEE Open Journal of the Computer Society

Software Engineering.title: Writing Bug Reports for Software Repair Agents: What Information Matters Most?
Software Engineering.summary: Software development is increasingly moving toward agentic-first workflows. This includes AI agents responsible for generating initial fixes for submitted issue reports. In this setting, issue reports are no longer merely documentation for human maintainers; they become the primary task specification for the agent. However, little is known about how such reports should be written to maximize the agent's chances of producing a correct fix. We study what makes a bug report agent-ready. Starting from the SWE-Bench Verified benchmark (i.e. a collection of 500 real repository issues with human-written gold patches and test suites for evaluating generated fixes) we manually classify each issue by change type (e.g. bug fix vs refactoring) and annotate each sentence with its information type, such as observed behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps, localization cues, and suggested fixes. We focus on the 441 issues representing bug reports, and we run on them mini-swe-agent using three LLM backbones (i.e. GPT-5-mini, MiniMax M2.5, and Gemini 3 Flash). We then fit a binomial regression model to estimate the incremental association between each information type and agent success, controlling for confounding factors. Our results suggest that agentic-first reports benefit most from information that narrows the agent's search and repair space. Suggested fixes, expressed either in code or natural language, show the strongest positive associations with pass probability, while localization cues show positive but non-significant associations. An ablation study removing selected information types confirms that agents benefit less from information traditionally useful to humans, such as reproduction steps, and more from sentences that expose a repair direction.

Software Engineering.title: An Empirical Study on CVE-based Vulnerabilities Propagation from one System to another System (IntraProject vs InterProject)
Software Engineering.summary: Vulnerabilities in applications, including browsers, media players, online services and document readers, etc. are often exploited and cause a serious damage. The vulnerabilities could exist in your system maybe because of some coding errors, design oversights, outdated software, AI generated codes or maybe transferred from another system during development (e.g., code clones). The propagation of software vulnerabilities is a critical concern in cybersecurity. This study examines the root cause problem of vulnerabilities propagation with experiments. We analyzed the propagation of CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) based vulnerabilities within and between different software projects (IntraProject vs. InterProject). We performed several experiments on CVE based vulnerability dataset (retrieved from NVD source) by using our vulnerability detection tool (SQVDT). In the results, we discovered similar patterns of vulnerable code in several very famous recently used software, including latest version of Linux, Android operating systems, and in thousands of open source projects available on GitHub. We found several very high severity level (CVSS) vulnerabilities that propagated from one system to another system, just because of copy/paste (reuse) the code.
