Leveraging UAV flexibility, our framework decouples key distribution from encrypted computation, enabling secure encrypted weighted aggregation (EWA), encrypted matrix multiplication (EMM), and encrypted decision tree (EDT) inference. Experimental results show that our framework outperforms existing schemes: for EDT, it supports floating-point operations and achieves better time efficiency than Brakerski-Fan-Vercauteren (BFV); for EMM, it demonstrates superior time and space efficiency compared to Brakerski-Gentry-Vaikuntanathan (BGV) and Somewhat Homo- morphic Encryption (SHE); while for EWA, it ensures high numerical precision and robustness across varying data length.

Cryptography and Security.title: Harness Matters: Measuring and Dissecting Security Resilience in Web Agents
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Web agents extend LLMs from text generation to real-world web interaction by relying on execution harnesses that interpret user goals, perceive webpages, plan actions, and ground model decisions into browser operations. While prior work has recognized that agent security depends on more than the backend model alone, how harness design quantitatively shapes web-agent security remains insufficiently measured.
  To systematically study web-agent harness security, we first characterize web-agent harnesses as a four-stage execution workflow covering goal interpretation, webpage perception, reasoning and planning, and action execution. Based on this abstraction, we build WebTrap Farm, a systematic and extensible evaluation framework covering three representative attack categories: malicious user prompts, malicious prompt injection, and deceptive web design. To avoid conflating security with task capability, we use paired usability calibration tasks to separate genuine defensive behavior from capability limitations.
  Our evaluation shows that existing web-agent harnesses remain vulnerable to typical attacks, with some unsafe behaviors occurring even without explicit attack content, revealing harness-intrinsic security failures (RQ1). Statistical analysis further shows that both harness and backend model significantly affect security outcomes, indicating that deployed-agent security is jointly shaped by the harness and backend model (RQ2). Finally, we localize where defensive behavior emerges across workflow stages and identify more secure design mechanisms, providing actionable guidance for building more robust web agents (RQ3). These findings highlight the web-agent harness as an important security boundary and motivate moving beyond model-centric defenses toward harness-level security design.

Cryptography and Security.title: Spectral Unlearning: Transformer Structure-Preserving Updates for Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Machine unlearning in large language models (LLMs) aims to remove specific learned knowledge, capabilities, or behaviors while preserving model utility. Existing methods have mostly focused on the design of unlearning objectives, while largely overlooking the intrinsic matrix structure of transformer weights. In particular, standard optimizers operate on independent scalar coordinates, thereby ignoring this matrix structure. We propose spectral unlearning, an update framework that combines standard unlearning objectives with matrix-structured optimization. We show that the spectral update corresponds to the steepest-descent direction for transformers composed of linear layers with normalized inputs and outputs. Our approach is applied on top of existing unlearning methods and evaluated across complementary axes of memorization, privacy, and utility, summarized via their harmonic mean. Spectral unlearning consistently outperforms a broad range of baselines and closes most of the gap to a retain-trained reference. Code is available at https://github.com/unlearn-ml/spectral-unlearning/.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Scaling Adaptive Prompt Injection Attacks with Agent Swarms
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Prompt injections have emerged as one of the top security risks faced by AI agents today. Early work in prompt injection attacks looked at simple tool-call agents and static attack payloads, and were saturated since mid-2025. As of Fall 2026, human red-teaming may be nearing saturation, especially on the Gemini family of models. In this work, we argue that despite this apparent plateau, prompt injection attacks are still possible and continued effort into prompt injection defense is needed.
  We design a new synthetic evaluation dataset which uses random non-malicious actions as adversarial goals. Such dataset design helps us to evaluate prompt injection robustness as a model ability to respect instruction hierarchy, and disentangle this ability from model knowledge of security practices. We show that an agentic attacker of increased capabilities can reliably trick model to follow instructions in tool output in our evaluation, even for models previously considered robust on public prompt injection benchmarks such as GraySwan Arena. This shows that current frontier defenses may require proactive, automated red-teaming to remain resilient to increasingly capable adversaries.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: Enforcing Demographic Coherence: A Harms Aware Framework for Reasoning about Private Data Release
Cryptography and Security.summary:
The technical literature about data privacy largely consists of two complementary approaches: formal definitions of conditions sufficient for privacy preservation and attacks that demonstrate privacy breaches. Differential privacy is an accepted standard in the former sphere. However, differential privacy's powerful adversarial model and worst-case guarantees may make it too stringent in some situations, especially when achieving it comes at a significant cost to data utility. Meanwhile, privacy attacks aim to expose real and worrying privacy risks associated with existing data release processes but often face criticism for being unrealistic. Moreover, the literature on attacks generally does not identify what properties are necessary to defend against them.
  We address the gap between these approaches by introducing demographic coherence, a condition inspired by privacy attacks that we argue is necessary for data privacy. This condition captures privacy violations arising from inferences about individuals that are incoherent with respect to the demographic patterns in the data. Our framework focuses on confidence rated predictors, which can in turn be distilled from almost any data-informed process. Thus, we capture privacy threats that exist even when no attack is explicitly being carried out. Our framework not only provides a condition with respect to which data release algorithms can be analysed but suggests natural experimental evaluation methodologies that could be used to build practical intuition and make tangible assessment of risks. Finally, we argue that demographic coherence is weaker than differential privacy: we prove that every differentially private data release is also demographically coherent, and that there are demographically coherent algorithms which are not differentially private.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 56 pages. ITCS 2027 version

Cryptography and Security.title: Doubly-Efficient Private Information Retrieval from Modular Forms
Cryptography and Security.summary:
We present new information-theoretic protocols for $s$-server, doubly-efficient private information retrieval (PIR) in sublinear server time and one extra bit of space on the servers, for every constant $s \geq 2$. On an $n$-bit database, each of the $s$ PIR servers first builds and stores a preprocessing data structure consisting of $n+1$ bits (which is unique to each server, and after which the server may discard the original database). Then, each server answers a PIR query in time $T_s(n)$, by reading at most $T_s$ bits of its data structure and sending them to the user.
  In the two server setting ($s=2$), our PIR protocols achieve $T_2 = n^{0.82}$, matching the server time of the state-of-the-art schemes of Henzinger and Ragavan (EUROCRYPT 2026) while shrinking their storage from $O(n\sqrt{\log n})$ to $n+1$ bits. With $s \geq 3$ servers, our PIR protocols retain the $n+1$ bits of storage and additionally improve on the server time of all prior information-theoretic $s$-server schemes with $n^{1+o(1)}$ storage: for example, achieving $T_3 = n^{0.74}$ and $T_{10} = n^{0.61}$ (previously $n^{0.79}$ and $n^{0.75}$). Asymptotically, as the server count $s$ grows, we shrink the number of servers required to achieve a given server-work exponent from $s^{3.9}$ to $s$.
  Our results draw inspiration from matching-vector techniques (Efremenko, STOC 2009), which we generalize to handle degree-two computations in the exponent. Using this generalization, we build doubly-efficient PIR from the new intermediate abstraction of Fourier-sparse cone-delta functions. Then, we construct such Fourier-sparse cone-delta functions via a connection to modular forms and complex analysis: if a Fourier-sparse cone-delta function does not exist, then there exists a modular form which has too many roots, contradicting the valence formula.

Cryptography and Security.title: VeilTune: Secure Fine-Tuning of Private LoRA Adapters on Public Pretrained Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Fine-tuning public pretrained language models with lightweight adapters such as LoRA has become the mainstream way to adapt them to downstream tasks. A service provider often trains its adapter on a data owner's samples, so two assets need protection: the data owner's samples and the provider's adapter. Existing secure fine-tuning protocols protect the samples but reveal to the data owner intermediate results of every training step, such as the hidden representations or logits of its inputs. We show that a single step suffices to copy the adapter: from the hidden representations of one mini-batch of 32 samples, the data owner fits an adapter that agrees with the provider's on 99.2% of test inputs, and logits alone yield about 94%. Protecting both assets therefore requires that no value that depends on the adapter be revealed throughout training. We present VeilTune, to the best of our knowledge the first protocol that fine-tunes a pretrained language model with backpropagation entirely in secure multi-party computation (MPC). VeilTune computes only what the loss depends on, replaces generic MPC operators with training-aware nonlinear operators that stay accurate on the values that training produces, and obliviously skips the steps corrupted by truncation failures. On four few-shot tasks with RoBERTa-large, VeilTune nearly matches plaintext training and is 5.3 points more accurate on average than SecP-Tuning, the state-of-the-art secure fine-tuning protocol. On SST-2, it achieves a 3.5x end-to-end speedup and a 3.6x reduction in communication over SecP-Tuning, and 26x and 17x over full fine-tuning in MPC.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 13 pages, 7 tables

Cryptography and Security.title: Ultrasound-Assisted Biometric Watermarking Against Face Video Deepfakes
Cryptography and Security.summary: Currently, artificial intelligence-generated content (AIGC) poses a severe threat to facial video deepfakes, and many AIGC companies employ video watermarking to mitigate unauthorized fake video usage, but its effectiveness is limited due to watermark tampering and private-model forgery. Additionally, some schemes actively add watermarks to user videos. However, current approaches focus primarily on the quality of watermark embedding in offline scenarios, and no existing work offers a solution for protecting human facial videos in real-time online applications. To fill this gap, we propose, to the best of our knowledge, a novel biometric video watermarking method, UltraGuard, for the first time. It uses the smartphone's built-in speaker and microphone to emit ultrasonic signals and capture biometric features, which are then fused with spatio-temporal dynamic features derived from the video content. The fused features are encoded as watermarks and embedded into videos in real time, enabling dynamic, content-aware watermarking throughout transmission and propagation. Extensive experimental validation demonstrates that UltraGuard can effectively defend against malicious attacks such as forgery and editing, both at the source and during propagation, proving the system's efficacy. In the future, it can be deployed on users' mobile devices to provide real-time protection for users' facial videos, thereby preventing security and privacy breaches caused by various malicious attacks.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Submitted to Proceedings of the ACM on Interactive, Mobile, Wearable and Ubiquitous Technologies (IMWUT)

Cryptography and Security.title: Advantage Distillation in Paired-State Quantum Key Distribution
Cryptography and Security.summary: We investigate advantage distillation for paired-state Loop-Back quantum key distribution, with a fixed optical station serving a lightweight portable terminal. Alice prepares two polarization-encoded pulses, Bob selects and applies a polarization filter to each pulse, and Alice infers his selections from the returned detection pattern. The proposed advantage-distillation step selects consistent blocks of three two-bit records using two independent public parity checks on a minimal connected graph. The closing edge of a parity polygon is shown to be redundant: any spanning tree of the same vertices has the same acceptance set. We derive exact acceptance probabilities, residual-error laws, and retention rates. Under independent bit errors, the three-record filter reduces the leading error term from e to e^2, while its cost in discarded records and public information is accounted for explicitly. A modular security theorem bounds the additional guessing advantage available to an adversary after syndrome disclosure and block acceptance, including arbitrary quantum side information. We also evaluate a specified single-photon passive-tap optical channel, obtaining a positive conditional entropy bound and exact accepted-block security quantities. This parity-based advantage-distillation step detects discrepancies by postselection; it does not correct individual errors and is intended to precede conventional reconciliation. The architecture suggests two further directions: hybrid filtering and reconciliation, and key establishment between portable users accessing a shared quantum station.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 27 pages, 9 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: ShadowBench-MCP: Measuring Shadow Invocations in MCP-Style Tool Routing
Cryptography and Security.summary: LLM agents increasingly act as routers for tools, APIs, and software-supply-chain workflows, making an execution path - rather than generated text alone - a security-relevant model output. We study shadow invocation: a task-preserving request variant that causes an LLM router to select a riskier execution path, potentially skipping validation, provenance, staging, redaction, or audit controls even though the request does not ask for a malicious action. We introduce ShadowBench-MCP, a benchmark and metric suite that separates task preservation (TPSS), operational pressure (OPSS), and route-geometric drift (RGAS), and combines them in the pre-execution SODS score. In a focused policy-ablation study using a Groq-hosted qwen/qwen3-32b router, 120 routing decisions yield 96 original-versus-variant comparisons across six security-sensitive workflows. Efficiency-first routing produces a 29.2% shadow-invocation rate and 26.7% safety-tool skip rate. Policy-aware routing reduces these to 4.2% and 1.7%, respectively, corresponding to an 85.7% relative reduction in shadow invocations. Pre-execution signals distinguish shadow routes with ROC AUC up to 0.94. These results are early, single-router evidence of a policy-dependent routing-layer security effect, not a claim of universal vulnerability.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Presented at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 2026)

Programming Languages.title: Discovering formally verified quantum programs with AI
Programming Languages.summary: The timeline by which quantum computers can solve breakthrough problems in science depends on improved quantum algorithms as much as on better hardware. Such algorithmic advances are typically achieved through many years of expert human collaboration. In mathematics and computer science, large language models have accelerated progress through automated discovery loops. However, quantum algorithms can only be evaluated by classical computers on restricted or small instances. Here we demonstrate automated discovery of quantum programs beyond these regimes including order-of-magnitude improvements on scientific applications. To achieve this, we build a quantum program library in the Lean theorem prover in which Gemini 4 agents synthesize novel programs against formal problem specifications and verify their correctness and cost. Agent teams collaborate, sharing results and knowledge through wikis and discussing ideas at organized conferences. Our results improve on prior baselines for parallel search (up to 2.55x), quantum arithmetic (290x), and simulations relevant to fusion, photochemistry and drug-metabolism by 11x, 8x and 2.5x respectively. Combining human and artificial intelligence at scale, under the rigor of mathematical proof, lets researchers design algorithms that today's classical and quantum computers cannot test, shortening the path to practical quantum computation.

Programming Languages.title: Validating direct solvers for Newton's gravitational N-body problem, and the systematic comparison between IEEE floating point and Posits
Programming Languages.summary: We present a systematic comparison between arbitrary precise arithmetic and integration, IEEE-754 compliant floating point arithmetic (fp16, bfp16, fp32, double precision fp64, and quadruple precision fp128), and two implementations of Posits (type III unum) for solving Newton's chaotic N-body problem. Each implementation is benchmarked with arbitrary precise calculations to objectively evaluate their performance in precision as well as speed. We rely on hardware and compiler implementations for fp64, and software implementations for arbitrary-precision arithmetic and Posits. Half precision arithmetic (fp16, bfp16, and Posits$<16,1>$) are insufficiently precise for solving Newton's equations of motion. Single precision (fp32, and Posits$<32,2>$) could be used for statistical ensemble calculations, but lead to relatively large errors in any individual strong encounter. All 64-bit implementations fp64 as well as Posits (Posits$<64,3>$) experience difficulty in our tests. One of the implementations of Posits (Universal) gives precision comparable to fp64 but is slow (by at least an orders of magnitude compared to fp64 after correcting for the more efficient hardware support for the latter). The other (CPPPosits) has a speed comparable to fp64 but has systematically larger errors (by about an order of magnitude compared to fp64 with excesses exceeding two orders of magnitude). As a consequence, this implementation leads to a systematic drift in the result space and has difficulty resolving close encounters. Posits and fp64 have difficulty when integrating a dynamical system in a moving reference frame; testing Galileo invariancy. In their current implementation, Posits do not seem to be the ideal alternative for fp64 when integrating chaotic or stiff ordinary differential equations, such as Newton's equations of motion.
Programming Languages.comment: submitted to Computer Physics Communication (processed referees comments)

Programming Languages.title: The Left Ripple of Byte-Pair Encoding: Certified Lookbehind for Every Dictionary
Programming Languages.summary: Berglund and van der Merwe formalized byte-pair encoding and bounded how far an appended string can change a tokenization, leaving the converse open: how far can a string prepended on the left change it, which dictionaries make that ripple infinite, and can it be computed efficiently when finite? We answer all three for every dictionary. The origin radius, how far a prepend can change covering spans, is decided with radius certificates by a product of two runs of the automaton that guesses the final tokens, in time polynomial in the dictionary written out, and it is infinite exactly when one periodic word has two canonical tilings with no common boundary. Under their ordering condition it is infinite exactly when some rule (t, t) finds its two copies adjacent at its own stage, and such a rule makes any dictionary infinite. A finite radius makes every window of a width read off the radii have a cut, and the radius is finite exactly when such cuts are dense. The token machine completes for every dictionary, and the tokenization is subsequential, extending what Berglund, Martens and van der Merwe proved for proper ones under one pass per rule. A streaming tokenizer emits after every symbol exactly the tokens that no continuation changes, in polynomial time, answering a question of Dalirrooyfard and Ye. Boundedness of the label measure, the edit distance of the token sequences, is decided for every dictionary in polynomial time as well, and under the ordering condition the largest distance one edit causes over dictionaries of m rules lies asymptotically between m^2/10 and m^2/2. GPT-2's merge table carries 244 effective self-pairs, so its origin radius is infinite from the forty-second merge on, and that of cl100k, o200k and Llama 3 from their first. Every measured number is its program's output, and what is not executed is named.
Programming Languages.comment: 87 pages, 13 tables. Artifact: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23988871 . The programs and their outputs are in the artifact, with a verifier that reruns every program and holds each reported number to the output line it rests on. Companion to arXiv:2608.03473, arXiv:2608.09761, arXiv:2609.10600, arXiv:2610.08854 and arXiv:2610.30168

Programming Languages.title: A Hoare Logic for Continuous-Time Stochastic Processes
Programming Languages.summary:
Programming language researchers have developed a wide array of tools to reason about probabilistic programs, but it remains unclear how to apply these proof techniques to continuous-time stochastic processes. To bridge this gap, we propose a verification method for properties of continuous-time stochastic processes by reasoning about them as standard programs.
  To demonstrate our approach, we define a continuous semantics for a probabilistic imperative language $\mathrm{pWhile}^{\mathrm{dt}}$ by taking the Kuratowski limit of the standard semantics, which collects limit points of the standard program semantics as the time-step approaches zero. Then, we present a Hoare-style logic that uses loop invariants and decreasing functions to verify properties of continuous programs. To establish soundness, we identify a broad class of assertions that are preserved from the standard semantics to the continuous semantics. To demonstrate our approach, we verify properties of ten continuous-time stochastic processes modeled in $\mathrm{pWhile}^{\mathrm{dt}}$, including variants of Brownian motion and a stochastic hybrid system.

Programming Languages.title: Ceci n'est pas une pipe: A semantics of justified reliance for AI systems
Programming Languages.summary: An AI agent may keep a successful check in context after an edit has invalidated its evidence. We give a semantics for specifying when a system may rely on a message and act on it. Reliability checks an asserted claim against accepted domain knowledge, sources, and messages in the selected context. Justified reliance additionally checks current evidence, authority, and the proposed world change. Relational component semantics and event traces represent nondeterministic outputs, iteration, and external changes. We characterise when merging claims preserves derivable conclusion classes, then construct the coarsest permitted quotient whose rules preserve the exact statuses of designated concrete claims. Construction is polynomial for unary rules; deciding even one permitted merge is coNP-complete for acyclic binary rules. This applies completeness and strong-preservation methods to the execution of quotiented rules. We also relate transition safeguards to runtime enforcement. Relative to a supplied set of possible worlds, a sound guard accepts an observation only when every matching world passes the checks. Exact acceptance requires observations that distinguish opposite-decision worlds; choosing sufficient services is NP-complete on explicit finite tables. A complete finite passport-renewal instance, Lean theorem encodings, Z3 instance checks, and an OCaml harness exercise the semantics. Domain knowledge, interpretation, source licenses, and policy remain application inputs.

Programming Languages.title: ANCORA: Learning to Question via Manifold-Anchored Self-Play for Verifiable Reasoning
Programming Languages.summary: We propose a paradigm shift toward open-ended curriculum self-play: rather than learning to answer on a fixed prompt set, a unified policy learns to question: generating verifiable problems, solving them, and turning verifier feedback into self-improvement. We introduce ANCORA, in which the policy alternates between a Proposer that synthesizes novel specifications and a Solver that produces verified solutions, anchored by three mechanisms: a two-level group-relative update coupling Proposer advantages across specifications with Solver advantages across solution attempts; iterative self-distilled SFT projecting the base model onto its valid-output manifold before RL; and a UCB-guided Curriculum DAG whose policy-induced problem set can provably expand under self-composition. Without these stabilizers, sparse verifier feedback drives Proposer collapse even under MLRL-aligned rewards; with them, ANCORA bootstraps a verifiable curriculum from curated seeds. Instantiated in Verus, ANCORA lifts Dafny2Verus pass@1 from a 26.6% SFT baseline to 81.5% in test-time training (TTT, 0-shot), outperforming PSV self-play (1-shot) by 15.8 points; in a transfer setting, training from Dafny2Verus seeds yields 36.2% and 17.2% pass@1 on MBPP and HumanEval.
Programming Languages.comment: v3: Added a prompt-matched comparison with PSV, data-provenance audits, and a limitations section; corrected transcription errors in pass@5/10 values of Table 3; updated abstract; reformatted for journal submission

Programming Languages.title: Statically Verifying Well-Definedness of Separately Compiled Attribute Grammars
Programming Languages.summary: The development of programming languages involves complex theoretical and practical challenges, particularly when addressing modularity and reusability through language extensions. While language workbenches aim to enable modular development under the constraints of the language extension problem, one critical constraint--separate compilation--is often relaxed due to its complexity. However, this relaxation undermines artifact reusability and integration with common dependency systems. A key difficulty under separate compilation arises from managing attribute grammars, as extensions may introduce new attributes that invalidate previously generated abstract syntax tree structures. Existing approaches, such as the use of dynamic maps in the Neverlang workbench, favor flexibility at the cost of compile-time correctness, leading to potential runtime errors due to undefined attributes. This work addresses this issue by introducing nlgcheck, a theoretically sound static analysis tool based on data-flow analysis for the Neverlang language workbench, which detects potential runtime errors--such as undefined attribute accesses--when separately compiled language components are composed, before the resulting language is ever run, thus preserving separate compilation while maintaining strong static correctness guarantees. Experimental evaluation using mutation testing on Neverlang-based projects demonstrates that nlgcheck effectively enhances robustness without sacrificing modularity or flexibility and with a level of performance that does not impede its adoption in daily development activities.
Programming Languages.comment: 56 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables, 5 Listing

Programming Languages.title: Beating Rytter's Bound: All-Pairs CFL Reachability in $O(n^3(\log\log n)^2/(\log n)^2)$ Time
Programming Languages.summary:
Context-free reachability and 2NPDA recognition are fundamental problems in program analysis and language theory. Despite years of effort, the best algorithms for these problems run in time $O(n^3/\log n)$ on a word RAM model; they are based on an observation of Rytter in 1985 for 2NPDA which was adapted for CFL reachability by Chaudhuri in 2008. No better algorithm has been designed since.
  We give the first improvement to Rytter's algorithm. For both all-pairs context-free reachability and 2NPDA recognition, we show a deterministic algorithm running in $O(n^3(\log\log n)^2/(\log n)^2)$ time and $O(n^{2+ε})$ words of space for every fixed $0<ε<1$ on a word RAM. Our improvement is based on a new data structure that reports set differences using batched maintenance of exact intersection counts, allowing saturation to skip regions that contain no new reachability information.
Programming Languages.comment: 25 pages

Programming Languages.title: EcoSearch: A Constant-Delay Best-First Search Algorithm for Program Synthesis
Programming Languages.summary: Many approaches to program synthesis perform a combinatorial search within a large space of programs to find one that satisfies a given specification. To tame the search space blowup, previous works introduced probabilistic and neural approaches to guide this combinatorial search by inducing heuristic cost functions. Best-first search algorithms ensure to search in the exact order induced by the cost function, significantly reducing the portion of the program space to be explored. A key limitation of existing best-first search algorithms is that they slow down over time: the delay between outputting successive programs grows with the number of programs already generated. We ask whether best-first search algorithms with constant delay exist. We design Eco Search, a new best-first bottom-up search algorithm. It combines the cost tuple representation of Bee Search with the per non-terminal data structures of Heap Search, thanks to a new frugal expansion strategy, and it uses bucket queues instead of priority queues, which is possible because the costs stored in each queue always lie in a window of constant width. We prove that Eco Search is the first constant-delay best-first search algorithm for pre-generation cost functions. Experimentally, we evaluate Eco Search on two classic program-synthesis benchmarks (DeepCoder and FlashFill) and observe that Eco Search solves 12% to 70% more tasks than its predecessors, and reaches the number of tasks they solve 1.6 to 3.2 times faster. This shows that constant delay can be achieved for best-first search in program synthesis, and that it makes a difference in practice.
Programming Languages.comment: 36 pages. Journal version of the AAAI 2025 paper "Eco Search: A No-Delay Best-First Search Algorithm for Program Synthesis" (doi:10.1609/aaai.v39i18.34139)

Programming Languages.title: Beyond atol and rtol: Sound Test Oracles for Low-Precision GPU Kernels
Programming Languages.summary:
Low-precision GPU kernels are commonly tested against a reference using hand-picked absolute and relative tolerances. Legitimate numerical error varies with the input, format and precision plan, so a fixed tolerance trades false alarms for missed faults. We present numoracle, which derives per-element acceptance regions from precision-annotated reference programs. Its calculus tracks shared rounding errors, provenance-ordered products, block-scaled quantizers and calibrated math-library errors. A rounding-interval check detects faulty stores that symmetric bounds can admit. Soundness is conditional on explicit rounding, hardware, domain and implementation assumptions; a fixed-input mode removes the zero-mean rounding assumption.
  We evaluate 13 Triton operators from Liger-Kernel, Unsloth and vLLM on two GPU generations. The main campaigns produce no false alarm on 33,960 correct-kernel and behavior-preserving-variant runs per GPU. Under input shift, the GPU campaigns record no false alarm while tuned tolerances flag up to 30% of correct runs; final-version reference checks identify inputs without complete finite-range certificates. On the RTX PRO 6000, numoracle kills 116 of 124 effective mutants, versus 59-83 for four fixed baselines. Among 400 tuned tolerance configurations, requiring at most 1% false alarms in every evaluated Liger input group permits at most 31 of 53 main-mutant kills, versus numoracle's 50. Historical replays expose accuracy faults in eight change pairs without rejecting their matched corrected controls; a ninth change concerns rounding parity.
Programming Languages.comment: 37 pages, 5 figures

Programming Languages.title: How Far Must a Test Explore? Certifying Composable Read-Write Interfaces from Their Own Random Edits
Programming Languages.summary:
Random tests of stateful code check laws, like reading back a written value, at states that random writes reach. The laws hold at every state exactly when the code behaves like a record with hidden data, so a pass is taken as evidence. This can fail: the laws can hold at every sample while the code is far from any record. The laws are local, but behaving like a record is global. Self-testing and stability theorems bridge this gap when the query distribution is controlled by the tester or preserved by the tested maps, but here it is generated by the tested writes, which need not be invertible.
  We ask how far a test must explore. An interface has $m$ binary variables, each with a read and two writes; in a record, reads return their bits and writes set only their bits. Samples are the ends of geometric runs of mean $\ell$ of uniformly random writes from a start distribution; a tester adds its own write chains of depth $d$. The distance is the least, over records with hidden data, of the largest probability that a read or write differs from it at a sample.
  From one start state, law checks at $O(m^2\log m/ε)$ samples certify, at fixed confidence, any threshold $ε$ after geometric runs of every positive mean, while runs of fixed positive length can pass at distance $1/2$. For the worst start distribution, take $ε=m^{-β}$ with fixed $0<β\le1$. For $d\le cm$ with fixed $c<1/2$, a polynomial budget of samples and writes exists exactly when $\ell=Ω(m)$, where law checks suffice. With no runs, the least depth for this budget is $(1/2+o(1))m$. Counting samples alone, in the worst case at $ε=1/(32m)$ and $d\le m/16$, the critical mean for a polynomial budget is $Θ(m\log(m/d)/\log m)$, by exhaustive search. So one start state needs only law checks, and the worst case at these thresholds needs exploration linear in $m$ if writes are counted.

Programming Languages.title: TauLang: A Language and Compiler for Space-Time Programming on Statically Scheduled Accelerators
Programming Languages.summary: Statically scheduled accelerators such as Groq's Tensor Streaming Processor (TSP) achieve low-latency large language model inference by stripping dynamic synchronization hardware from the chip. With no caches, arbiters, or hardware schedulers, the compiler must fix the exact slice and issue cycle of every operation, so when an operation runs is a condition for correctness. Existing kernel languages cannot target such machines because they rely on hardware to resolve cycle timing and instead encode schedules implicitly in code structure. We present TauLang, a kernel language and compiler that makes time a first-class citizen of the program. The programmer schedules operations, loops, and composed kernels with parameterized explicit times, so exploring schedules means changing parameter values rather than rewriting code. TauLang validates explicit times algebraically in TauIR, its timed intermediate representation. It then solves tensor placement and cycle scheduling jointly in an integer linear program, using explicit times to group connected operations into timing clusters that prune the search space. On a cycleaccurate model of a TSP-like machine, joint search achieves a $1.40\times$ latency speedup across ten kernels over a space-first flow. A few explicit time pins keep latency within one cycle of the untimed schedules and scale joint search to 1,636 GEMM blocks, whereas untimed search finds no schedule at 32.

Programming Languages.title: A Compiler for Fault Tolerant Quantum Computing
Programming Languages.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) needs compiler intermediate representations (IRs) that preserve error-correcting-code choices, syndrome information, and non-Clifford resource requirements through analysis, simulation, and hardware lowering. We report practical experience building FTQC, an open-source Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR) dialect that makes logical qubits, syndromes, magic states, and Pauli frames typed static single assignment (SSA) values. Its error-correction-aware type system, two-level lowering design, and IR-resident resource analysis provide one inspectable pipeline to Open Quantum Assembly Language~3 (OpenQASM~3), the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR), Stim, and IQM hardware. Case studies across three code families show that typed metadata makes code-specific decisions verifiable and retargetable: on the 20-qubit Pathfinder at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, decoding reduced logical readout error by 3.3 times. They also expose hidden architectural costs: for a three-qubit Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT-3), a magic-state factory requires five times the peak qubits of the encoded circuit. These experiences demonstrate a practical foundation for developing and evaluating fault-tolerant compiler transformations across software and hardware targets.

Software Engineering.title: DEPUTYBENCH: Evaluating Contextual Safety in Enterprise Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Enterprise agents must determine whether ordinary requests are permitted by organizational records and policies while continuing legitimate work. We introduce DEPUTYBENCH, an executable benchmark with 79 base items, 375 instances, paired permission contexts, and graded evidence requirements. Across 12 models, revised audits give 88.0% pooled safety and 79.1% paired success. A controlled study of 28 derived tasks and six models tests authorization-fact flips, evidence masking, and irrelevant rewrites. Outcomes track backend permissions, yet restricted execution is more frequent with missing evidence than explicit non-permission: 10.3% versus 3.5% on 27 matched tasks, a 6.8-percentage-point difference (95% interval: 1.9-13.0; secondary analysis). A post-hoc analysis locates 61 of 100 masked-condition executions in four privacy tasks requiring complete cumulative counts or person-specific consent. The difference persists when the most error-prone model or the largest contributing task is excluded, but is much smaller outside those four tasks. Thus high safety with available evidence does not establish reliable stopping when permission cannot be verified. Mean paired success is equivalent within a prespecified five-point margin under irrelevant rewrites, while strong-model safety remains near ceiling. Scorer validation improves from 178 to 266 correctly scored cases out of 284 held-out counterexamples. Two security experts manually verified task ground truth over a two-week period; stage labels remain LLM-generated. The concentration analysis describes task structure and audited outcomes, not an identified internal mechanism.

Software Engineering.title: PegasusAI Studio: Legible Cyberinfrastructure and Accountable AI Agents for Scientific Workflows
Software Engineering.summary: AI coding agents can now construct scientific workflows, but operating them on shared cyberinfrastructure (CI) raises problems that code generation does not solve. Agents need current knowledge of the workflow system and its execution sites and access to the runtime state of distributed executions, while facilities need to attribute every agent action to a user and bound it by that user's privileges. We present PegasusAI Studio, an AI-assisted science gateway built on the Pegasus and HTCondor stack. Studio makes CI legible to agents by projecting one facility-curated knowledge base into the native configuration of several coding agents, by introspecting workflow interfaces and execution sites, and by grounding diagnosis in workflow and scheduler telemetry. Agent actions operate within a trust envelope that combines federated authentication, per-user execution environments and scheduler credentials, provider-neutral model access, observability, and approval controls for state-changing actions. The same application runs as a JupyterHub-based gateway on a research cloud and as an Open OnDemand application on HPC systems. We evaluate Studio through case studies of legacy CASA weather workflow modernization, a gravitational-wave reanalysis, an EEG analysis built with an open-weight model, and an Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) M87 image reconstruction that recovered from two failed runs to a zero-failure execution. The evaluation establishes that these mechanisms operate as designed.

Software Engineering.title: Project Progress Desk: Know Where All Your Claude Code and Codex Projects Stand at a Glance
Software Engineering.summary: Codex and Claude Code let developers work on many projects in parallel, but keeping track of them still means switching between chats, terminal sessions and providers. We present Project Progress Desk, a local desktop interface that brings overall progress, blockers and pending decisions into one view. Users can see which projects need attention, inspect what remains, and compare earlier approaches before choosing how to continue. Agent receipts link reported outcomes to each project's weighted acceptance checklist; the overview distinguishes receipt-supported progress from dated estimates. We describe daily use across 36 projects, including a choice between two implementations based on their recorded outcomes. At the demo, attendees will explore 30 simulated projects, trace completed work to overall progress, and watch a coding agent's new result update the overview.
Software Engineering.comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to IUI 2027 Demos

Software Engineering.title: Using Proof Dependencies to Manage Verification Projects
Software Engineering.summary:
Verification technology now scales to sizable projects, but techniques for managing such projects fall short. There are no effective ways to assess the progress made so far and to determine which verification tasks to perform next. A key issue is that the successful run of a verification tool provides little indication about what has actually been achieved. The guarantees provided depend on the specifications of the verified code as well as any unverified assumptions made in the proofs, e.g., about the behavior of unverified libraries. Manual inspection of specifications and assumptions to determine progress is error-prone and prohibitively expensive.
  In this paper, we present automated techniques to assess and guide verification projects. All of these techniques employ an automatic proof dependency analysis that computes, for each proof obligation in a project, the specifications, statements, and assumptions that are needed to prove it. We show that this analysis enables effective proof audits by determining all assumptions a proof depends on. We also use it to determine which statements in a program are constrained by the provided specifications, which indicates how strong a specification is. Based on these two insights, we propose a novel progress metric for verification projects and show how to use it to guide verification projects to maximize progress.
  We implement our approach in the symbolic execution backend of Viper and lift it to the Go verifier Gobra. Our evaluation on real-world benchmarks, including a verified Internet router, shows that the dependency analysis is sound and sufficiently precise, that our progress metric accurately reflects the state of a verification project over time, and that our guidance outperforms standard bottom-up and top-down verification strategies.

Software Engineering.title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
Software Engineering.summary: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Grok 4.6 (32-34%). No task is fully solved by every model, and on 80 tasks no model earns full credit on all five runs. Scores span 35 points. Depending on the model, agents take a median of 33 to 166 steps per run, with little relation to score. We release 24 tasks with their environments, graders and results, and hold out 76 to limit contamination.

Software Engineering.title: Characterising divergence between heuristic and language-model ratings of mobile user interface quality
Software Engineering.summary: Automated assessment of mobile user interface quality is attractive because manual review does not scale, and large language models are increasingly proposed for the task. Whether their ratings correspond to those produced by established rule-based heuristics has not been characterised at scale. We construct a 15,000-screen corpus from the RICO dataset using six documented filters, score every screen with a literature-grounded heuristic scorer, and collect ratings from three open-weight language models across two input representations, yielding 270,000 ratings. We report linearly weighted Cohen's kappa with bootstrap confidence intervals, offset-corrected kappa, intraclass correlation, and Bland-Altman limits of agreement, together with a chance baseline for the tolerance-band agreement rule. Agreement between the two rating sources is consistently weak: raw kappa falls below 0.15 in seventeen of eighteen model-representation-dimension cells. However, fifteen of eighteen cells are statistically distinguishable from zero, and correcting for a constant offset raises five cells above 0.15, so the divergence is better described as a combination of systematic bias and weak covariation than as absence of relationship. Model ratings track structural properties of the interface, but substantially less strongly than the heuristic does, and more strongly from an untruncated structural element list than from a screenshot. We further show that dimensions elicited in a single generated response are correlated by construction, reaching rho = 0.97 in one condition, which constrains what such designs can measure. We report these results as a characterisation of divergence between two automated raters rather than as evidence that either is correct, and we set out the validation a stronger claim would require.
Software Engineering.comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 12 tables (incl. appendix). Data and code in ancillary files. An earlier abstract was presented at EFAST 2026 under the title "Seeing Without Understanding: Large Language Model Evaluation of Mobile User Interface Quality, Failure Taxonomy, and Architectural Explanation"

Software Engineering.title: FlowPlan: Reducing the Token Cost of Coding Agents with Abstraction-Guided Planning and Verification
Software Engineering.summary:
LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code can resolve real-world repository issues, but their iterative interaction loop can be expensive. Existing approaches reduce this cost primarily by limiting, compressing, or selectively avoiding information and actions within the repair process. We investigate a complementary question: Can an agent reason about a repair at an abstract program level, rather than repeatedly operating over raw source code, to reduce both the exploration needed to identify a repair and the repeated checking needed to verify it afterward?
  We present FlowPlan, an abstraction-guided repair approach that structures localization, planning, and verification around per-function control-flow or data-flow graphs. The agent first localizes the candidate fault location on the program abstraction and expresses the intended repair as explicit graph deltas before modifying the concrete source. After the edit, FlowPlan reconstructs the same abstraction and compares the observed structural change with the planned one. Then, a verification checks the complete repair before termination.
  Across all six benchmark-model settings, FlowPlan does not significantly change resolution rate relative to the vanilla agent while reducing token consumption in every setting, significantly in five of six settings. With Claude Haiku 4.5, it uses only 0.46-0.47x the baseline tokens on SWE-bench Pro, 0.32-0.35x on SWE-bench Verified, and 0.68-0.74x on SecBench; with Sonnet 5, it uses 0.72-0.76x, 0.73-0.74x, and 0.92-0.94x, respectively. Overall, FlowPlan achieves the largest token reduction among the compared methods in three of the six settings and ties the strongest compared method in a fourth. Trajectory analysis shows that FlowPlan saves tokens by replacing much of the costly post-edit re-reading and testing with explicit verification and reducing per-call context.

Software Engineering.title: Deletion Sensitivity Is a Property of the Model: A Three-Condition Measurement across Seven Open Reasoning Models
Software Engineering.summary: Reasoning models write a reasoning trace at every turn of a multi-turn tool session, and later turns read this history. Across 94k ShareGPT conversations, 73 percent of user interactions span multiple turns. Upstream providers bind each trace to its issuer, so a request forwarded across issuers arrives with its history deleted, and the task cost of this stripping remains unmeasured. To the best of our knowledge, this paper presents the first direct, blind, multi-seed measurement of full reasoning-history deletion in multi-turn tool calling, through three rendering conditions, seven open-weight reasoning models, three seeds, 794 tasks, and the official checker. The same deletion spans -4.4 to +51.3 points with both ends excluding zero, and for the one model re-dosed from 0 to 100 percent deletion, the reading varies by at most 1.5 points. Deletion sensitivity is a model-level property. The reading follows the model itself and stays constant across deployments, and a retrained or re-released model is a new model that a two-cell screen, one retention run and one deletion run, re-reads for the cost of two runs. Deletion sensitivity is thus a measurable property of the model, and the reading must enter routing and aggregation as prior information rather than persist as an invisible default cost.

Software Engineering.title: AgentScript-Eval: Benchmarking LLMs and Agents for Code Generation in an Enterprise DSL
Software Engineering.summary: Domain-specific languages (DSLs) are widely used in enterprise software, giving a compact interface to complex tasks, from data access to infrastructure automation. Platforms increasingly extend them to agents, where a developer declares the topics, permitted actions, and guardrails of an agent rather than writing general-purpose code. Large language models (LLMs) write general-purpose code well, but that ability has been measured almost entirely on languages abundant in public pretraining data, and enterprise DSLs are neither abundant nor public. We introduce AgentScript-Eval, an execution-graded benchmark of 100 real tasks for AgentScript, the declarative DSL that Salesforce uses in Agentforce to build conversational agents. Tasks span authoring an agent from a specification, debugging a broken definition, and optimizing a working one. Evaluating five models zero-shot, we find that the regime is hard: the best model reaches only 25.0% pass@3, and every model scores 0% on authoring from scratch. We further find that model scale and price are weak predictors of success -- a 31B open-weight model attains the highest compilation rate of any model tested (48.0%) and matches the strongest frontier model on partial-credit accuracy at the lowest token cost. Adding an agentic compile-and-edit loop is the single largest lever, roughly doubling partial-credit accuracy. Beyond that gain, the wording of domain guidance matters more than its packaging. The same skill pack scores 28% as plain documentation but only 14% as a live plugin. Rewriting one skill inside that plugin then raises it to 37%, our best result, with catalog and tooling untouched. Larger models did not reliably outperform smaller ones; what mattered was the harness surrounding the model and the guidance supplied to it.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted to 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: 2nd Workshop on Agentic AI Benchmarks and Applications for Enterprise Tasks (AABA4ET), NeurIPS 2026

Software Engineering.title: MiniZoo: An Evolving Dataset of Mini Apps for the Research Community
Software Engineering.summary: Mini apps run within host applications (apps) such as WeChat, Alipay, Baidu, and Telegram, providing services without requiring users to install separate native apps. Their growing ecosystem has attracted research on software quality, security, and privacy, creating a need for reusable datasets. However, building and maintaining such datasets is challenging, requiring platform-specific collection infrastructure and mechanisms to handle incomplete packages, changing availability, and heterogeneous metadata. A shared, continuously maintained collection is still lacking, therefore motivating the development of a common research resource, whose value has been demonstrated by the experience of AndroZoo in the Android ecosystem. In this paper, we present MiniZoo, an evolving corpus of mini apps and associated metadata. The initial release comprises 16,273 mini-app packages, with multiple versions of the same mini apps. The dataset is managed and distributed through AndroZoo under its existing access conditions. To facilitate its reuse, we describe the collection process, data organization, provenance, and limitations, and explain how researchers can select and access the data. MiniZoo is designed to grow continuously through the addition of newly discovered mini apps, the inclusion of further host ecosystems, and the collection of successive versions of previously collected apps. This ongoing expansion will enable both comparisons across ecosystems and longitudinal studies of how mini apps evolve over time.

Software Engineering.title: WorkflowArena: Benchmarking Executable Workflow Orchestration in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems
Software Engineering.summary: Large language model agents are increasingly deployed as multi-agent systems rather than as a standalone model operating within a single context. Recent agent harnesses allow the model to instantiate worker agents and to author the executable workflow that coordinates them, shifting the design of system structure from developers to the model at run time. The quality of this organization therefore constitutes a distinct capability, yet existing benchmarks either measure end-to-end task completion or evaluate coordination under structures specified in advance. We formalize this capability as workflow orchestration and introduce WorkflowArena, a benchmark of 145 long-horizon tasks spanning 8 professional domains, from software engineering and formal mathematics to legal analysis and 3D production. Each task specifies an initial workspace and an integrated deliverable composed of interdependent components, which is assessed by a hidden verifier. Agents determine autonomously whether and how to delegate, and all delegation is recorded, enabling joint evaluation of deliverable quality and the organization of the underlying work. Experiments with nine models show that no single configuration performs best across all domains and that systems exhibit distinct delegation strategies: at high effort, Claude models in Claude Code invoke workflows less frequently but with larger worker groups, whereas GPT models in Codex delegate more frequently in smaller units. When the executing model is held fixed on a challenging subset of tasks, workflows authored by Claude Opus 5.5 substantially improve weaker executors, indicating that workflow organization is itself a measurable determinant of task performance.

Software Engineering.title: Cataloguing Hugging Face Models to Software Engineering Activities: Automation and Findings
Software Engineering.summary: Context: Open-source Pre-Trained Models (PTMs) provide extensive resources for various Machine Learning (ML) tasks, yet these resources lack a classification tailored to Software Engineering (SE). Objective: To address this gap, we derive a taxonomy encompassing 146 SE tasks and apply an SE-oriented classification to PTMs in a popular open-source ML repository, Hugging Face (HF). Method: Our repository mining study followed a five-phase pipeline: (i) identification of SE tasks from the literature; (ii) collection of PTM data from the HF API, including model card descriptions and metadata, and the abstracts of the associated arXiv papers; (iii) text processing to ensure consistency; (iv) a two-phase validation of SE relevance, involving humans and LLM assistance, supported by five pilot studies with human annotators and a generalization test; and (v) data analysis. This process yielded a curated catalogue of 5,027 SE PTMs. Results: We find that most SE PTMs target code generation and coding, emphasizing implementation over early or late development stages. In terms of ML tasks, text generation dominates within SE PTMs. Notably, the number of SE PTMs has increased markedly since 2023 Q2, while benchmarking remains limited: only 5.55\% of all SE PTMs in our catalogue provide evaluation results. Conclusions: Our catalogue reveals documentation and transparency gaps, highlights SE activity imbalances, and supports automated SE scenarios, such as the selection of suitable PTMs.

Software Engineering.title: Coding Agents in KVM: Practical Containment and User Control with Limited Resources
Software Engineering.summary: Coding agents often need broad authority for productive development work, but granting that authority can expose users' data and infrastructure. Off-the-shelf cloud workspaces can help contain agent activity, but reliance on provider-specific platforms can lead to vendor lock-in and reduced user control. Researchers and engineers must therefore balance agent autonomy, enforced containment, and user control within available financial, computational, and human resources. We analyze these trade-offs and present KVM-Agent, an open-source implementation that automates most setup and provisioning steps. It gives agents broad authority inside replaceable Ubuntu VMs while keeping host administration outside those VMs and supporting multiple coding-agent applications, model services, and remote job delegation. The approach retains familiar workflows and user choice at the cost of VM resources, maintenance, and residual risks from secrets accessible inside the VMs and permitted network access.

Software Engineering.title: Inference Validation for Regulated AI: Building a Decision Pipeline on NVIDIA AIPerf
Software Engineering.summary: Deploying large language models in regulated industries requires more than picking the fastest inference engine: it requires evidence that a configuration meets contractual and legal obligations before it serves a single customer request. We describe Runway, an internal validation harness built at MasterControl that builds a governed decision pipeline around NVIDIA AIPerf. The key insight is separating concerns: AIPerf provides the trusted measurement, while Runway provides the experiment design that comes before it and the compliance, cost, and audit decisions that come after. We describe the architecture and the storage model that makes caching and audit one mechanism. We report three findings from Runway sweeps: TensorRT-LLM and vLLM rankings invert with concurrency; a newer, pricier GPU instance can be the cheaper one per request; and speculative decoding behaves differently across engines under load, so engine configuration can outweigh engine choice.

Software Engineering.title: The Range Shrinks, the Threat Remains: Re-evaluating LLM Package Hallucinations on the 2026 Frontier-Model Cohort
Software Engineering.summary: Package hallucinations, LLM-generated references to packages that do not exist, enable slopsquatting: an attacker registers the hallucinated name. We replicate Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security '25) on five 2026 frontier models over 199,840 Python and JavaScript generations. This version reports a preregistered live revalidation that replaces the static package lists of earlier versions with two independent checks against the live PyPI and npm registries. Hallucination rates are 3.6-5.0% of package mentions (2.2-3.4% of generations): the 2026 frontier sits at the level of 2024's commercial models, and the open-weight gap seen in 2024 has disappeared. Python exceeds JavaScript for every model. The set of names hallucinated by all five models shrinks from the 127 reported earlier to 104; 26 earlier entries were correct import statements whose module name differs from the package name. Using the accidental six-month public exposure of our own list as a natural experiment, we find no detectable effect of publication: about 1% of hallucinated names were registered within six months, at the same rate for published and unpublished names, and the 95% interval excludes increases above 2.5 percentage points. Still, at least 23 package names that the models suggest had previously hosted malware later removed by the registries, and one hallucinated name was registered with malware after our runs.
Software Engineering.comment: 18 pages, 3 figures. v4: preregistered live revalidation against PyPI and npm; numbers revised (Sec. 7); new analysis of registrations of hallucinated names (Sec. 8). Supersedes v1-v3 and the SCORED '26 version. Replicates Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security 2025). Code: https://github.com/churik5/slopsquatting-replication-2026 Artifact: https://github.com/churik5/slopsquatting-revalidation-2026

Software Engineering.title: Will AI mess my RTL? A snapshot-based approach to verifying AI-written RTL
Software Engineering.summary: With the growing interest in using AI (Artificial Intelligence) for RTL (Register-Transfer Level) hardware development, robust and comprehensive verification has become more important than ever. As Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly assist in creating and modifying RTL designs, ensuring that these changes preserve existing functionality is paramount for building trust in AI-driven workflows. We present SVApshot, a fully automated framework that leverages LLMs to generate and systematically attempt to correct SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) for RTL modules, completely removing the human from the generation loop. SVApshot introduces a novel snapshot methodology that captures the current functionality of a design as a comprehensive set of formal assertions, creating a regression suite for validating future changes--whether made by humans or AI. The framework features automated duplicate detection, assertion set expansion, and iterative repair of failing assertions using LLM-guided debugging with formal verification feedback. Our experimental evaluation across diverse RTL modules demonstrates high coverage for complex modules, with successful detection of both manually-injected and AI-introduced bugs. Additionally, this framework opens the door for automatic generation of formal testbenches to benchmark LLMs for hardware design, moving beyond binary pass/fail metrics towards nuanced assertion-based scoring.

Software Engineering.title: WasmLens: Automatic Glass-Box Instrumentation for Composed WebAssembly Applications
Software Engineering.summary: The WebAssembly Component Model enables language-independent composition of independently developed components, but complicates observability. Existing tracing support flattens execution hierarchy by attributing every span created inside a composition to a single host-level parent context, so execution across component boundaries cannot be reconstructed. The problem is amplified because components are typically deployed as black boxes whose internals cannot be modified or inspected by the system integrator. To address these limitations, we propose a revised wasi:otel/tracing design in which the runtime maintains a per-component span stack, restoring parent-child relationships across component boundaries without changing component interfaces or source code. This change has since been adopted upstream. Building on this design, we present WasmLens, an automatic instrumentation tool that derives instrumentation points from a composition graph and injects tracing middleware into already composed binaries, yielding end-to-end traces for black-box compositions with no developer configuration. This automatic instrumentation raises mean request latency from $238$ $μ$s to $454$ $μ$s across six component boundaries. Raising the expected number of boundary crossings from 6 to 11 further increases latency to $514$ $μ$s, an incremental cost of $12$ $μ$s per crossing, of which $10.4$ $μ$s is attributable to instrumentation. These results show that instrumentation overhead is additive in composition depth rather than proportional to baseline execution time.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted article in WebAssembly, Cloud and Edge: Shaping the Future of Computing (WACE '26)

Software Engineering.title: A local language model layered with rule-based and neural detectors for clinical text de-identification: an open-source toolkit and evaluation
Software Engineering.summary:
Objectives: To measure whether a locally hosted large language model (LLM), stacked with deterministic and clinical named-entity recognition (NER) detectors, finds more protected health information (PHI) than open tools, and at what precision.
  Materials and Methods: DeidSharp, an open-source .NET toolkit, combines the findings of pluggable detectors (patterns, a clinical NER model, a local 26B mixture-of-experts LLM) and fails closed on any detector error. Configurations fixed on tuning halves were compared, under a prespecified protocol, with deid, Philter, the Stanford/Penn de-identifier, OpenAI Privacy Filter and GLiNER on reporting halves of PhysioNet's nursing notes (889 spans) and semi-synthetic MIMIC-IV-Note discharge summaries (29,023 spans), and on synthetic ASQ-PHI queries, with paired patient-level bootstrap intervals.
  Results: In the nursing notes, against Stanford/Penn, the recall-first stack found 98.9% of PHI (+2.8, 95% CI 1.4 to 4.4) at 9.3 points lower precision; the precision-first stack, without NER, found 96.5%, matching Stanford/Penn, at 19.6 points higher precision (83.2%). In the discharge summaries, both stacks led Stanford/Penn by more than 20 points (recall-first 95.3%, +21.5, 20.5 to 22.4), almost entirely on generated untyped names; on typed labels all three exceeded 99%. All four prespecified comparisons held. No configuration beat deid significantly on its home corpus; Philter found more discharge-summary spans than the recall-first stack at 23 points lower precision.
  Discussion: The LLM was the main detector and NER added place names; asked to verify its own findings, the LLM discarded a quarter of true PHI.
  Conclusion: A local LLM layered with deterministic detectors offers recall-first and precision-first operating points without sending text off-site.
Software Engineering.comment: 17 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables; supplementary material as ancillary file. Code: https://github.com/valburkin/DeidSharp

Software Engineering.title: Surrendering and Reclaiming Judgment: How Software Engineering Students Experience AI Reliance
Software Engineering.summary: Software architecture is one of the skills novice developers must master to succeed in industry, and as AI disrupts software development, it is also transforming how students learn architecture. Existing work on how students and novices work with AI has mostly focused on small programming exercises or on students' perceptions of AI, so little is known about how students experience AI as they learn software architecture in larger team projects. We report on an exploratory case study of 43 senior software engineering students who used AI throughout a semester-long, team-based software architecture project. We combined surveys with focus groups and analyzed the focus group transcripts and the open survey responses through Braun and Clarke's reflexive thematic analysis. We constructed two themes. The first, Surrendering Judgment to AI, traces how participants' reliance on AI deepened as they used it to architect and implement their systems, until they surrendered their judgment and became stuck in a codebase they had created but could not understand, which made them rely on AI even more. Participants described feeling ashamed, frustrated, and emotionally disconnected from their work, a toll that, in our reading, left them with even less reason to break their reliance. The second, Applying Human Judgment, centers on participants who kept or reclaimed their judgment: the knowledge and experience it rested on, and the strategies they used to apply it. Participants' accounts suggest that relaxed deadlines and a lecture and lab on working with AI gave them room to acquire knowledge and reclaim judgment. Given the expectations placed on junior developers and the widespread adoption of AI, we believe these first-hand accounts can help software engineering education and industry adopt AI in ways that preserve novice developers' judgment, ownership, and motivation.

Software Engineering.title: Reducing Cold-Start Latency on the WebAssembly Edge via Locality and Network-Aware Scheduling
Software Engineering.summary: Edge computing places computation closer to users and data sources, but introduces heterogeneous hardware, limited resources, and variable network conditions. WebAssembly (Wasm) is increasingly considered for these environments because modules are compact, portable, and quick to start. However, cold-start latency remains a challenge: when a worker node does not yet hold the required artifact, it must fetch it before execution, adding transfer overhead that directly increases the end-to-end (E2E) latency, especially for large artifacts or slow network links. At the same time, the geographical distance between the requester and the assigned worker independently contributes to latency through network routing overhead. Together, artifact locality and network proximity do not always point to the same placement decision, and naive scheduling strategies fail to account for either. This work extends a Wasm-native edge orchestrator with state-aware scheduling strategies that jointly optimize for both objectives. Evaluation on a Raspberry Pi testbed with emulated regional network latency shows that a hybrid scheduler combining cache-state and network-proximity signals reduces mean E2E latency by up to 40.8% compared to a default round-robin baseline. Artifact locality-aware placement is most effective when artifacts are large or repeatedly requested, while network-aware placement dominates when artifacts are small and routing latency has a larger relative effect, but combining both objectives consistently yields the lowest E2E latency across diverse edge workloads.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted article in WebAssembly, Cloud and Edge: Shaping the Future of Computing (WACE '26)

Software Engineering.title: Rethinking the Value of Agent-Generated Tests for LLM-Based Software Engineering Agents
Software Engineering.summary: Large Language Model (LLM) code agents increasingly resolve repository-level issues by iteratively editing code, invoking tools, and validating candidate patches. In these workflows, agents often write tests on the fly, but the value of this behavior remains unclear. This raises a central question: how does agent-written testing relate to task outcomes and resource use during repository-level issue resolution? To better understand the role of agent-written tests, we analyze 5,000 recorded agent runs produced by six strong LLMs on SWE-bench Verified using the lightweight mini-SWE-agent scaffold. Our results show that test writing is common for most models. GPT-5.2 is an exception: it rarely writes new test files while achieving a resolution rate close to the top-ranked model. Test-writing frequency varies widely across models. Within a given model, it differs less between resolved and unresolved tasks. When tests are written, their files contain substantially more statements that print runtime values than assertions that check conditions. We then compare baseline prompts with revised prompts that encourage or discourage writing new test files for four models. Agents start or stop writing test files as requested on 36.8%-93.2% of tasks. Resolved-task totals differ by 0-13 out of 500 per model, with no statistically significant difference, while API calls or token use differ substantially for three models. Similar resolution totals can therefore hide substantial differences in how agents test and how many resources they use.

Software Engineering.title: Beyond the Document: Compiled Context and Governed Agents for Any Work Product
Software Engineering.summary: A document preserves the visible result of professional work but often discards the research, calculations, assumptions, evidence, and authorization boundaries behind it. We study a different unit of delivery: a Portable Agent Format (PAF) package that carries a work product together with compiled context, evidence, provenance, and rules for subsequent interaction. To test whether this context remains useful beyond the process that produced it, we evaluate four new packages, created after the hosted and offline readers were fixed: an investment proposal, fund research, financial-statement analysis, and an engineering incident review. Two packages were produced by specialized agents and two through a general-purpose assistant's packaging skill. Across 400 frozen questions and 12,000 evaluated responses, a hosted governed reader succeeds on 96% of questions versus 86% with instructions plus raw-file retrieval (Holm-adjusted p < 10^-7). On the 260 answerable questions per condition, success is 94% versus 79%; the gap varies by package. Source-material chat and instructions alone reach 48% and 74% overall. A separate 0.8-billion-parameter offline reader succeeds on 69% overall, but 54% on answerable questions. Its -1 response rate is 2.9%, combining materially wrong and unauthorized answers, versus 56% with the source and instructions alone. Ablations suggest advantages for the integrated selector and package-adapted writer, without isolating representation from training effects. The same run exposes a failure: offline retrieval resolves none of the 40 historical-record questions in one financial-data package. These findings support treating compiled knowledge as part of the delivered work product, while leaving independent standards interoperability and end-to-end governance conformance unproven.
Software Engineering.comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, 4-package held-out evaluation; 12,000 evaluated responses

Software Engineering.title: Update from Hell: Can Coding Agents Survive Hidden Breakage in Dependency Upgrades?
Software Engineering.summary:
Modern software systems rely heavily on third-party dependencies, but upgrading those dependencies remains a costly maintenance activity. Dependency upgrades do not always preserve the function signatures, type systems, APIs, or runtime semantics assumed by existing code. Consequently, developers often need to perform source code adaptations to accommodate dependency-induced changes. However, such code-level changes are often not explicitly communicated to project maintainers, posing a significant challenge to software reliability.
  Meanwhile, coding agents have emerged as a new form of software development tool and are increasingly adopted by developers due to their automation capabilities. In this paper, we introduce DEPBENCH, a benchmark consisting of 203 real-world dependency-upgrade tasks across five package ecosystems spanning five language communities, each involving hidden code-level changes that require source code adaptation. We evaluate mainstream coding agents on DEPBENCH. The best completed configuration solves only 104/203 tasks (51.2%), with substantial variation across agent harnesses, models, and ecosystems, highlighting an important gap between current agent capabilities and real-world software maintenance needs.

Software Engineering.title: The Gene Is Not the Gate: Conceptualizing the Semantic Genome of Quantum Software
Software Engineering.summary:
Quantum software spans applications, program representations, compilers, runtimes, and hardware-facing control. Existing abstractions describe these artifacts and layers, but they do not capture the semantic responsibilities that must remain valid as a computation is transformed across the stack. This limits systematic reasoning about cross-layer correctness, evolution, and reuse.
  We present QGenome, a semantic foundation for quantum software genomics. We define a quantum software gene as a typed, reusable responsibility characterized by an explicit contract, execution context, concrete expressions, and supporting evidence.
