Furthermore, the generalizability of the method is assessed under multi-step adversarial attacks, adversarial attacks in black-box scenarios, and within the non-spiking domain.

Cryptography and Security.title: Provenance Verification of AI-Generated Images via a Perceptual Hash Registry Using Merkle Patricia Trie and BK-Tree
Cryptography and Security.summary: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has made the generation of synthetic images widely accessible, increasing concerns related to misinformation, digital forgery, and content authenticity on large-scale online platforms. This paper proposes a registry-based framework for verifying AI-generated images through a registry-based provenance mechanism. Each AI-generated image is assigned a digital fingerprint that preserves similarity using perceptual hashing and is registered at creation time by participating generation platforms. The Merkle Patricia Trie, provides prefix-based organization and cryptographic integrity of the registry structure, while Burkhard-Keller tree enable similarity search based on Hamming distance. Verification is performed when images are re-uploaded to digital platforms such as social media services, enabling identification of previously registered AI-generated images even after benign transformations or partial modifications. The proposed system does not aim to universally detect all synthetic images, but instead focuses on verifying the provenance of AI-generated content that has been registered at creation time. By design, this approach complements existing watermarking and learning-based detection methods, providing a platform-agnostic, tamper-evident mechanism for scalable content provenance and verification at the point of large scale online distribution.

Cryptography and Security.title: Beyond Tokens: NumAnchor for Address-Grounded Numeric Operand Representation in Assembly Language Models
Cryptography and Security.summary: Assembly language models (ALMs) are becoming important for automated binary analysis, yet their token-level interfaces often obscure numeric-like operands. In two corpora, such operands account for 45.7% and 40.9% of operand occurrences and may denote branch targets, global data, stack slots, constants, or unresolved pointer-derived values. Existing normalization strategies often lose their identities and structural relationships. We present NumAnchor, an input-boundary adapter that represents recoverable numeric-like operands as typed, canonicalized program entities. NumAnchor encodes code, data, and stack context in compact structural side descriptors, preserving entity identity and locality without increasing the host sequence length. These descriptors are fused into input embeddings before the first Transformer layer, while the host architecture, pretraining objectives, and downstream protocols remain unchanged. Probing frozen instruction-level embeddings yields 98.7% hierarchical-location accuracy and AUROC scores of 0.932 and 0.907 for jump and call target alignment, respectively, showing that the encoded structural information remains recoverable. Across multiple ALM families, NumAnchor achieves relative improvements of up to 35.0% in Recall@1 and 31.7% in MRR on 10k-candidate function retrieval, and improves execution-aware type recovery by up to 5.2 F1 points. Ablations show complementary gains from code, data, and stack descriptors with modest overhead.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted by ICSE 2027

Cryptography and Security.title: OpenMarkX: An Extensible Platform for Watermarking Open-Source Model and Agent Outputs
Cryptography and Security.summary: We introduce OpenMarkX, an extensible platform for watermarking open-source model and agent outputs under standard inference. It takes models, compatible methods, private keys, and evaluation settings, and produces watermarked weights, detection results, and quality and robustness reports. Its 16 text-watermark configurations are complemented by agent, vision-language, image, and physics-field workflows. Our proposed method, OpenMark, addresses learnability and robustness through joint model--policy learning and perturbation-aware training. On several open-source LLMs, OpenMark achieves 0.92 TPR at 1% FPR while reducing perplexity by 20.5% on average relative to the strongest prior method, and remains more detectable after such modifications, e.g., retaining 0.57 TPR at 5% FPR after 0.5-ratio model merging, compared with at most 0.34 for prior methods.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Agents of Chaos: A Systematization of Knowledge (SoK) on Malicious Attacks on Agentic AI Systems
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Agentic AI systems extend large language models with tools, memory, retrieval, browser or computer-use interfaces, code execution, external services, and multi-agent coordination. Although these capabilities enable agents to act beyond text generation and perform tasks, they also create attack paths through which adversaries can exploit untrusted content, deceptive metadata, poisoned state, compromised skills, mutable dependencies, or malicious code. Such attacks can manipulate planning and tool use, corrupt memory, abuse code-execution environments, and trigger harmful downstream effects.
  In this paper, we present a systematic review of malicious attacks targeting agentic AI systems. We screened 186 candidate sources and retained 98. Following independent coding and resolver adjudication, we identified 284 atomic attacks, 452 atomic safeguards, and 660 explicit attack--safeguard relationships. We organize attacks into eight causal-mechanism classes while retaining insertion points, activation conditions, abused capabilities, objectives, impacts, persistence, and evidence as orthogonal dimensions.
  Our analysis shows that tool, MCP, and action-layer attacks account for the largest share of atomic attacks, while the prompt-injection and action-hijacking class has the broadest paper coverage. We identify distinct class-specific activation patterns and separation between insertion and later activation. Safeguard coverage remains uneven: only 278 of 660 relationships are directly assessed, and strong coverage is uncommon. These findings support lifecycle-aware threat modeling, agent evaluation, tool governance, and defense-in-depth security for agentic AI systems.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Agentic AI in Offensive and Defensive Cyber Operations (AIDC 2026), co-located with ACSAC 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: The Devil Wears Markdown: Detecting Malicious Intent Hidden in AI Agent Skill Instructions through Hybrid Static, Dynamic, and Agentic Analysis
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Agentic AI ecosystems increasingly rely on reusable agent skills that combine executable code, natural-language instructions, configuration artifacts, and external tool integrations. These hybrid artifacts create software supply-chain risks because malicious intent may be distributed across instructions, code, metadata, and runtime behavior, making isolated alerts difficult to interpret.
  We evaluate three open-source scanners on a held-out test set of 140 skills comprising 80 malicious and 60 benign samples, including Cisco Skill Scanner with and without its optional LLM analyzer. The default Cisco configuration achieves a recall of 0.91 with 33 false positives among the 60 benign skills, while the LLM-enabled configuration using Qwen3:8B achieves a recall of 0.85 with 40 false positives.
  We then present a framework that combines static findings, safety-constrained sandbox evidence, and LLM-based reasoning to assess malicious intent. The framework tracks the origins of findings and relates evidence across analysis layers. In a within-system evidence-source ablation using the same reasoning backend, adding dynamic evidence to skill-content reasoning increases F1 from 0.70 to 0.85. Combining static and dynamic evidence further increases F1 to 0.89, with five false positives among 60 benign skills. Dynamic evidence provides the largest observed improvement.
  The Full Pipeline detects 68 of 80 malicious skills, achieving 0.88 accuracy, 0.93 precision, and 0.85 recall. It matches the observed recall of Cisco Skill Scanner with LLM while reducing false positives from 40 to five. This system-level comparison does not isolate model or architecture effects.
Cryptography and Security.comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Agentic AI in Offensive and Defensive Cyber Operations (AIDC 2026), co-located with ACSAC 2026

Cryptography and Security.title: Token Inflation: How Dishonest Providers Can Overcharge for Large Language Model Usage
Cryptography and Security.summary: Per-token billing is now the standard pricing model for commercial large language models (LLMs), so the honesty of reported token counts directly affects what users pay. We show that this kind of billing is hard to audit by design: providers hide the model, the tokenizer, and the execution to protect their IP, mitigate jailbreaks, and preserve user privacy, which means an auditor can only inspect proofs the provider supplies. The audit therefore reduces to a consistency check on the provider's own reports. We call this a trust paradox: every audit must trust some artifact, but current frameworks trust exactly the ones a provider has the strongest reason to manipulate. We study three recent token auditing frameworks and show that a provider with ordinary commercial capabilities can systematically inflate billed token counts. In the most permissive setting, hidden reasoning usage can be inflated by 1,469% on average without detection. At current frontier reasoning prices, that turns a \$100 honest bill into roughly a \$1,569 bill on the same query. Even when the user can see the full reasoning string, tokenization ambiguity alone still allows 50.85% over-reporting below the detection threshold. These results suggest the problem is not in any specific auditor but in any audit whose evidence comes from the audited party. Restoring honest billing will require verification that ties reported token counts to evidence the provider does not control, such as trusted execution attestation, cryptographic proofs of inference, or third-party re-execution.

Cryptography and Security.title: SIExBench: A Benchmark for Automated Repair of Sensitive Information Exposure
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Modern software systems routinely process credentials, personal records, and other sensitive information. A sensitive information exposure (SIEx) defect makes such information accessible to an unauthorized actor and can cause serious and often irreversible disclosure. However, prior research has focused largely on detecting such exposures rather than repairing the underlying defects, and existing repository-level issue-resolution benchmarks do not specifically target this defect class. We present SIExBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark dedicated to automated repair of SIEx defects. SIExBench contains 161 execution-verified instances from 64 widely used Python and Java repositories, each with an issue report, buggy repository snapshot, developer patch, executable exposure and regression tests, and defect characterization.
  We evaluate six repair systems with three LLMs, yielding 18 configurations, and systematically analyze their overall effectiveness, performance across defect characteristics, and failure mechanisms. The strongest configuration resolves only 39.1% of the instances, while 40.4% remain unresolved by all 18 configurations. More importantly, 62.1% of unsuccessful attempts produce a valid patch that still leaves sensitive information exposed, making incomplete exposure removal a central challenge. Systems often generate plausible patches and modify relevant code without fully eliminating the exposure, indicating that effective repair must ensure that all relevant paths to sensitive-information exposure are closed. Overall, SIExBench provides a foundation for systematically evaluating and advancing automated repair of sensitive information exposure defects.

Cryptography and Security.title: New Classes of CCZ-Inequivalent APN Functions with Boomerang Uniformity One in Odd Characteristic: Differential and Boomerang Spectra
Cryptography and Security.summary: Let $q=p^n>3$ be an odd prime power and let $g:\F_q\to\F_q$ be an even perfect nonlinear (PN) function with $g(0)=0$. We construct almost perfect nonlinear (APN) functions $G_{λ,M}(x)=g(x)+M(x)+λ(x^{q-1}-1)$, where $λ\in\F_q^*$, $-λ\notin g(\F_q)$, and $M$ is an $\F_p$-linearized permutation polynomial. These one-point modifications of $g+M$ have boomerang uniformity one, the smallest possible value for APN functions in odd characteristic. We give complete differential and boomerang spectrum formulas and obtain closed-form evaluations for selected constructions based on Coulter--Matthews monomials and Dembowski--Ostrom polynomials. For $q>7$, comparison of differential spectra establishes CCZ-inequivalence to all APN monomial families listed in the paper and every APN binomial in the original Ness--Helleseth family or its extension by Zeng et al. We characterize CCZ-equivalence within our construction, showing that any two linearly inequivalent even PN functions over the same field yield CCZ-inequivalent APN functions. We obtain three pairwise CCZ-inequivalent APN functions with boomerang uniformity one over $\F_{p^{15\ell}}$ for every $\ell\ge1$, six over $\F_{p^{120r}}$ for every $r\ge1$, and unbounded numbers of such classes in characteristic three. We further prove that CCZ-equivalence and EA-equivalence coincide for functions at Hamming distance at most $m$ from a PN function, provided that $m(m+1)<q-q/p$. We also show that all our APN functions have the maximal possible algebraic degree $n(p-1)$. Finally, we exhibit both CCZ-equivalent and CCZ-inequivalent APN pairs with boomerang uniformity one at Hamming distance one.

Cryptography and Security.title: Mirage: Provable Defense Against LLM KV Cache Timing Side Channels with Topology-Aware Isolation
Cryptography and Security.summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as shared multi-tenant services, relying on advanced optimizations like KV cache and prefix sharing to improve throughput and reduce latency. However, these optimizations introduce a critical vulnerability: attackers can exploit time-to-first-token (TTFT) variations between KV cache hits and misses to infer sensitive prompt tokens via prefix-matching side-channel attacks. Existing defenses indiscriminately restrict cross-tenant cache sharing, which incurs prohibitive performance overhead and negates the fundamental efficiency benefits of the KV cache.
  We propose Mirage, a topology-aware emission obfuscation framework that provably bounds timing leakage without sacrificing the performance gains of cache sharing. Instead of stalling the GPU or forcing redundant recomputations, Mirage delays token emission at the gateway so the attacker observes a natural cache miss distribution, while the GPU seamlessly continues serving other requests at full speed. Mirage uses a Privacy Odometer that persistently tracks the topological novelty of prefix fan-out expansions to distinguish aggressive probing from benign traffic. Once a prefix exceeds a safety threshold, Mirage engages a two-phase policy that uses a dynamic estimator to pad the TTFT to a calibrated cache-miss baseline. On a 500-sample public corpus across three models, Mirage suppresses the timing side-channel to near the random-guessing floor, while maintaining a significantly lower TTFT than defense baselines. We further show that Mirage withstands a strong adaptive adversary and the same principle carries over to semantic caching layers.

Cryptography and Security.title: CyberBinGym: Can AI Agents Turn Binary Patches into Real Exploits?
Cryptography and Security.summary: Security fixes usually reach users as compiled updates, but deployment delays leave unpatched systems exposed. During this window, comparing patched and unpatched binaries can reveal how to exploit a vulnerability, turning a defensive update into actionable information for attackers. Existing benchmarks do not measure this capability: they expose source code, rely on human-crafted challenges, or evaluate binary comprehension without requiring exploitation. We introduce CyberBinGym, a benchmark containing 100 tasks derived from real vulnerabilities in 53 widely used projects, spanning six vulnerability families and three levels of analysis complexity. Agents receive stripped vulnerable and patched binaries without source code or vulnerability information, and must combine static and dynamic analysis to recover and exploit the vulnerability. Evaluation separately measures vulnerability recovery through differential crash testing and end-to-end exploitation through flag retrieval, with trajectory audits to reject reward hacking. The strongest evaluated agent recovers the target vulnerability in 88% of tasks and exploits it in 20%. Providing the patched binary raises its exploit rate from 10% to 25% on a matched 20-task subset; with standard binary hardening enabled, it still exploits two of its 20 previously successful tasks. These results demonstrate that current agents can turn released binary patches into working exploits in a controlled setting, although exploitation remains unreliable. These capabilities lower the barriers to targeting unpatched software and compress defenders' effective response window, increasing the urgency of timely patch deployment.

Cryptography and Security.title: Towards Lightweight IoT Intrusion Detection: Feature Optimization and Explainable Machine Learning for Resource-Constrained Environment
Cryptography and Security.summary: Machine learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) can improve IoT security but often rely on large feature sets that increase computational overhead and limit deployment on resource-constrained devices. This paper presents a resource-efficient and explainable feature optimization framework for lightweight IoT intrusion detection using the CICIoT2023 dataset. A Random Forest model was used to rank feature importance and identify compact feature subsets. Experimental results show that a three-feature model achieved an MCC of 0.9622 while reducing the feature space by 92.1%, whereas a six feature model achieved an MCC of 0.9675 with an 84.2% reduction. Furthermore, a fifteen-feature model achieved an MCC of 0.9744, preserving 99.97% of the performance of the full 38-feature baseline model while reducing the feature space by 60.5%. SHAP-based explainability analysis validated the selected features and provided interpretable insights into model decisions. The results demonstrate that lightweight, explainable, and high-performance IoT intrusion detection can be achieved using only a small subset of carefully selected features, significantly reducing resource requirements with minimal loss of detection effectiveness.

Cryptography and Security.title: f-Differential Privacy Filters: Validity and Approximate Solutions
Cryptography and Security.summary: Accounting for privacy loss under fully adaptive composition---where mechanism choice and privacy parameters may depend on the history of prior outputs---is a central challenge in differential privacy (DP). Here, privacy filters are stopping rules ensuring a prescribed global budget is not exceeded. A leading candidate for optimal filter design is $f$-DP, which characterizes the full extent of adversarial hypothesis testing and recovers $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP through piece-wise linear trade-off functions, while enabling tight $(\varepsilon,δ)$-DP accounting in standard compositions via tensor products. Yet whether such filters can be correctly defined under $f$-DP remains unclear. We show that the natural $f$-DP filter---tracking path-wise accumulating tensor products and stopping when the prescribed curve is crossed---is fundamentally invalid, precluding the direct use of standard efficient numerical Fast-Fourier-Transform accounting in the fully adaptive setting. We characterize this failure, establishing necessary and sufficient conditions for the natural filter's validity. Furthermore, we prove a fully adaptive central limit theorem for $f$-DP, establishing Gaussian convergence of cumulative privacy losses under full adaptivity. As a demonstration, we construct a closed-form approximate GDP filter for subsampled Gaussian mechanisms that provably outperforms RDP-based accounting in asymptotic regimes ($q\ll 1$ and $q\approx 1$) without tracking the full trade-off function, demonstrating that the slack in RDP is not intrinsic to adaptive composition---though CLT-based approximations are known to be optimistic at realistic subsampling rates, a limitation that remains an open challenge.
Cryptography and Security.comment: NeurIPS 2026. 54 pages, 12 figures

Cryptography and Security.title: A Case Study of a Phishing Cluster Targeting German Universities
Cryptography and Security.summary: In light of recent ransomware attacks, this study analyzes and measures the impact of cyberattacks against academic institutions in German-speaking areas. First, we provide an overview of 25 confirmed cyberattacks against universities in German-speaking areas between February 2022 and February 2023. In this time frame, we find that 5% of all German universities have experienced a confirmed cyberattack with a measurable impact. Second, we document victimology and Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTP) of a phishing activity cluster spanning more than three years and showing a particular focus on universities in German-speaking areas. Of the 93 targeted universities, 58 (62%) are German, representing a significant fraction with approximately 14% of the total number of universities (423) in Germany. A notable technique is that the phishing emails are sent via university infrastructure, using valid, compromised credentials of university-associated personnel and involving university Virtual Private Network (VPN) tunnels.

Cryptography and Security.title: Audit Before You Merge: Provenance, Probing, and Continual LoRA Composition
Cryptography and Security.summary: Post-hoc merging of public LoRA adapters is an attractive gradient-free path to continual adaptation, but reliable measurement of catastrophic forgetting in this setting depends on infrastructure that prior work has not addressed. We treat each adapter merge as a sequential task in a continual-learning setting, with the instruction-tuned base model's capabilities as Task 0, and study forgetting on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Public adapter hubs contain modules that fail basic provenance checks: silent base-version mismatches and near-zero delta norms whose inclusion inflates measured interference by ~10pp. We propose a two-check audit (base-model match, non-trivial delta norm) and a leakage-free probing protocol as preconditions for any forgetting study in this setting. On an audited 4-adapter set, naive merging causes -10.5pp on GSM8K and -18.3pp on HumanEval, while Task Arithmetic at lambda=0.5 sits within a standard error of the unmerged baseline. A coordinate search including negative coefficients identifies the math adapter as probe-optimal at lambda=-0.5, outside the reach of positive-only mergers, suggesting forgetting has structure that negation-aware merging may exploit. The same protocol replicates on Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3, where 2 of 4 candidate adapters fail the audit and the audited merge reproduces the same merge-method ranking on GSM8K, supporting that our findings are not Llama-specific.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 17 tables. ICML 2026 Workshop on Continual Adaptation at Scale (CATS). Code: https://github.com/LennyAharon/audit_continual_learning

Cryptography and Security.title: Practical Adversarial Attacks on Stochastic Bandits via Fake Data Injection
Cryptography and Security.summary: Adversarial attacks on stochastic bandits have traditionally relied on some unrealistic assumptions, such as per-round reward manipulation and unbounded perturbations, limiting their relevance to real-world systems. We propose a more practical threat model, Fake Data Injection, which reflects realistic adversarial constraints: the attacker can inject only a limited number of bounded fake feedback samples into the learner's history, simulating legitimate interactions. We design effective attack strategies under this model, explicitly addressing both magnitude constraints (on reward values) and temporal constraints (on when and how often data can be injected). Our theoretical analysis shows that these attacks can mislead a class of bandit algorithms into selecting a target arm in nearly all rounds while incurring only sublinear attack cost. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets validate the effectiveness of our strategies, revealing vulnerabilities in stochastic bandit algorithms under practical adversarial scenarios.

Cryptography and Security.title: CAROUSEL: GPU-Accelerated Private Vector Search via Homomorphic Sketching
Cryptography and Security.summary: Vector search on untrusted infrastructure exposes the \emph{query embedding}, a faithful summary of the user's intent. Fully homomorphic encryption can hide the query, but existing approaches still require a full scan followed by ranking of encrypted scores. Scalable private systems avoid encrypted ranking by either sending scores from a single cluster to the client or moving the search to the client, which must first stream the entire vector index for preprocessing. We present \textsc{Carousel}, which instead scores the full corpus under encryption and compresses the results for client-side ranking. The server scores every vector under encryption, raises the scores to a power that preserves their order by magnitude while suppressing all but a handful, and compresses the resulting sparse vector into a logarithmic number of ciphertexts using homomorphic additions alone. Because every vector is scored, \textsc{Carousel} incurs no recall loss from discarding candidates. Since clients hold no database-dependent state, insertions and deletions take effect immediately at the cost of a single vector write. \textsc{Carousel} searches $1$ billion vectors of BIGANN SIFT1B across multiple GPUs and achieves recall@100 of $0.9715$. At $100$ million SIFT vectors, it achieves recall@100 of $0.9845$ with a query latency of $3.735$ seconds on a single GPU.

Cryptography and Security.title: From Tool Connection to Execution Control: Benchmarking Security Invariants in MCP-Style Agent Runtimes
Cryptography and Security.summary: Tool-connected agents need execution-time invariants that hold even when a model follows an adversarial instruction. We formulate eight execution-layer invariants (I1-I8) covering structured authority, canonical resource resolution, principal and delegation binding, handle lifecycle, explicit source-to-target transfer, request-correlated denial evidence, and single-use approval state. To test whether these protections require a centralized runtime or follow from the invariants themselves, we compare HCP, an in-memory runtime with managed handles and tasks, against an independent gateway/server ACL (B3) enforcing the same I1-I8 contract over identical grants and labels. Both block 18 modeled violations and complete 25 workflows, while 16 source-code ablations pinpoint the checks responsible. Outside our scripted corpus, we test three boundaries. First, on 24 held-out AgentDojo tasks with live models, DeepSeek reaches attacker goals in 4 direct sessions while both controllers deny every attacker call; however, strict reference-derived grants also deny 40 non-attacker calls, and first-divergence replay under an approve-all control reaches 4 new attacker goals. Second, across 132 conditions on unmodified ChainCaps and Playwright MCP servers, per-call grants block ungranted writes but cannot stop a secret passed as an ordinary argument to an authorized sink; session source budgets block that copy but refuse unrelated actions; and explicit handle pipes or sealed reads block handle-mediated exfiltration while preserving unrelated workflows. Third, on a matched MCP backend, HCP adds 0.13 ms per workflow outside MCP calls while retaining 7.7 MB of state over one thousand workflows versus 0.7 MB for B3. Identical decisions across HCP and B3 show that enforcing explicit I1-I8 invariants at controlled entrances secures tool execution across centralized and gateway designs.
Cryptography and Security.comment: v2: Expanded evaluation with an independent gateway baseline, live-model AgentDojo experiments, and tests on third-party MCP servers. Includes supplementary appendices and machine-readable results

Cryptography and Security.title: An Agentic Multi-Agent Framework for System Log Anomaly Detection
Cryptography and Security.summary: As enterprise systems grow in scale and complexity, manual log analysis and conventional SIEM tools struggle to keep pace with the volume and diversity of incidents. To address this challenge, this paper proposed a multi-agent AI framework supporting in analyzing the system log to trace the attack forensic in the system more effectively and efficiently. The framework is designed using n8n platform and Gemini large language model. The framework consists of 7 AI agent layers. Each agent work on a specific task. When the task is done, the agent will forward the result to the output-associated agent of the next layer. The multi agent model improves the analysis velocity, so it is able to support numerous log analysis requirement at the same time. We deployed 16 test cases to test operation of the multi agent workflow, and evaluate the accuracy per test case and the operative performance. The result findings are very promising.
Cryptography and Security.comment: 14th International Conference on Multidisciplinary Research (ICMR 2026), ISBN 978-974-474-120-2, Thaksin University Publisher, Bangkok, Thailand, pp. 63-80, 2026 (Published)

Cryptography and Security.title: On Relative Greedy Weights
Cryptography and Security.summary: Relative greedy weights were introduced by Li and Liu in [19] as a measure of information leakage in coordinated two-party wire-tap channels of type II when the adversary follows a greedy strategy. Their definition can be viewed as a relative version of the CEZ greedy weights, which are only locally greedy. In this paper, we revisit the concept of greediness and relative greediness introducing new measures, and we discuss other perhaps more relevant applications of relative greedy weights than the coordinated two-party wire-tap channel of type II. We pay special attention to bottom-up greedy weights, which correspond to an adversary with an ultimate greedy approach, and we present families of nested codes for which such weights are larger than the relative CEZ greedy weights.

Cryptography and Security.title: When Experience Becomes a Backdoor: Poisoning Self-Evolving LLM Agents via Failure-Aware Task Optimization
Cryptography and Security.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly improve themselves through self-evolution, distilling execution experience into persistent, reusable skills. However, this persistence creates a new attack surface: malicious rules implanted into skills can compromise subsequent agent behavior. Existing skill backdoor attacks typically assume direct manipulation of the victim's skills, which is impractical when skills are constructed internally by a trusted evolver. In this paper, we study a novel problem of task-level backdoor attacks, where the attacker can only inject poisoned evolution tasks, inducing the agent to implant backdoors into its own skills. Since the attacker controls neither skill induction nor downstream execution, a natural approach is to iteratively optimize poisoned tasks based on attack success. However, our preliminary analysis reveals two key challenges: (i) failures at different stages of skill evolution and downstream execution can produce indistinguishable outcomes, providing little guidance for targeted poisoned-task updates; and (ii) unsuccessful updates may undermine earlier progress, while simply discarding them may lead to repeated ineffective updates. To address these challenges, we propose BadEvolve, a failure-aware task-poisoning framework against self-evolving LLM agents. BadEvolve diagnoses attack failures across four stages, i.e., Induction, Activation, Following, and Effect, and directs updates toward the failing stage. It further employs rollback to preserve earlier progress and failure memory to avoid repeating ineffective updates. Extensive experiments across diverse self-evolution frameworks, benchmarks, and backbone LLMs demonstrate the effectiveness of BadEvolve. Our code is available at https://github.com/ventr1c/BadEvolve.

Programming Languages.title: A Calculus for Units of Measure with Conversion
Programming Languages.summary:
Programs that compute with physical quantities often need to convert between units of measurement, and as the Mars Climate Orbiter showed, these conversions can be a rich source of errors. Meanwhile, typed unit calculi, our most rigorous formalisms for checking physical units in a program, have excluded unit conversions. Through this exclusion, they have established a powerful property: well-typed programs are invariant under rescaling (no program can depend on how big a meter is). But losing the ability to convert between units is a significant cost. In contrast, practical languages provide conversion but no invariance theorem. We present $Λ_S$, a typed lambda calculus with conversion, quantification over units and dimensions, and vectors and linear maps with per-component units, and we determine exactly how much invariance survives conversion. For terms without unit constants we prove two abstraction theorems: (i) a convert-free term is invariant under every rescaling; (ii) a term with conversions is invariant under every rescaling that scales all units of one dimension by the same factor. The condition in (ii) cannot be weakened: under any other rescaling, some conversion of a nonzero value is not invariant.
  For first-order programs, a verified decision procedure returns one of three verdicts: it certifies that no error in the declared conversion factors can change the program's answer, names the accumulated ratio through which such an error would scale it, or declines. A verified checker decides whether unit declarations are consistent and determine every conversion factor, and extracts each factor exactly. We also prove adequacy, erasure, and the $n$-variable Pi theorem of dimensional analysis with conversion. Every theorem is mechanized in Lean 4, and the evaluator compiles to a native binary.
Programming Languages.comment: 24 pages, 5 figures. Lean 4 mechanization: https://github.com/ericeallen/lambda-s

Programming Languages.title: Representing Tensors as Compositions for Efficient Computation on Sparse and Structured Data
Programming Languages.summary: We propose a new mathematical formalism in which all kinds of tensors and of operations on those tensors are represented as simple function compositions. Tensors are functions from indices to values. An element-wise operation (e.g. an activation function) is a composition with a function applied to values; re-indexing (e.g. reshape, transposition) is a composition with a function applied to indices; and a reduction is a composition with both an index function, mapping each index to several indices, and a reduction operation (e.g. product, sum, max). Combined with tensor stacking, these compositions can represent most interesting kinds of tensors (e.g. dense, jagged, all kinds of sparsity patterns, matrix factorizations), as well as lazy versions of almost every operation available in modern tensor computation frameworks, including einsums between tensors of any kind. Identities between compositions can then be used to rewrite such expressions into equivalent ones, without evaluating them. For instance, the product of two sparse matrices can be rewritten so that only products between non-zero values are computed, turning a sparse problem into a dense one. Using this algebra as the intermediate representation of a tensor computation engine would shift the focus from defining operations on tensors (e.g. einsum between sparse tensors) to defining an algebra on index functions. This should reduce the codebase complexity from $\mathcal{O}(mn^2)$, with $m$ the number of binary operations between tensors and $n$ the number of tensor types, to $\mathcal{O}(m + k^2)$, with $k$ the number of types of index functions. A draft implementation of a tensor computation framework based on this algebra is publicly available.
Programming Languages.comment: 15 pages, 6 figures

Programming Languages.title: Lipschitz-Based Robustness Certification Under Floating-Point Execution
Programming Languages.summary:
Lipschitz-based certification checks a neural network's robustness with a small numerical computation: milliseconds per input, and small enough to be formally verified. Its soundness is proved for execution in real arithmetic, whereas deployed networks execute in floating point, so rounding must be accounted for in the network and in the certifier itself.
  We show that the conservatism of Lipschitz-based certification does not absorb the rounding in the network's execution: we exhibit counterexamples to a formally verified real-arithmetic certifier that computes in exact arithmetic, and show that an adversary who controls the weights can make it issue false certificates for ordinary test images at standard perturbation bounds. We present the first Lipschitz-based certification method that is both efficient and sound with respect to floating-point execution. It keeps the real-arithmetic network's Lipschitz constant and bounds separately how far the floating-point outputs can depart from the real-arithmetic ones, through a compositional theory of the deviation that also rules out overflow; pre-deployment measurements of a high-precision execution tighten the bound. Its spectral norms come from a float64 Gram iteration proved never to under-estimate the true norm.
  We mechanise the theory in Rocq and implement it in a certifier, evaluated on dense image, tabular and many-class classifiers. It rejects every certificate a counterexample refutes and certifies entire test sets at milliseconds per instance on a CPU, losing relatively few real-arithmetic certificates, many of which the measurement reclaims. At float32, ERAN's GPUPoly, to our knowledge the only other public floating-point-sound verifier for networks of our size, loses most of its certificates on most of our models to its own rounding accounting; ours does not, and is more than an order of magnitude faster.
Programming Languages.comment: Includes supplemental appendices

Programming Languages.title: Language-Based Agent Control
Programming Languages.summary: This paper introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a new programming model for agentic applications that brings techniques from programming languages and language-based security to the problem of agent control. In conventional programming, combinations of static typing and runtime enforcement have long been used to guarantee that well-typed programs satisfy user-specified policies, including policies for access control, information flow, data provenance, and more. The key idea behind LBAC is to extend these guarantees to agentic applications by requiring agents to generate programs that are themselves well-typed in the context of the surrounding scaffolding code. Unsafe programs are rejected by the typechecker before execution, allowing policies to apply uniformly across the entire application, including both agent-generated behavior and developer-written scaffolding. At the same time, LBAC preserves substantial expressiveness: agents may perform arbitrary side-effect-free computation and recursively invoke subagents, which retain full tool access subject to the same--or potentially more restrictive--policies. We demonstrate LBAC with three case studies: I/O sandboxing via filesystem capabilities, data provenance, and information-flow control.

Programming Languages.title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing
Programming Languages.summary:
Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand.
  We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave. They build on three tools that we contribute: (a) ffibox, Rust primitives for C/Rust interop that mirror Box, Arc, and Vec for C objects without ever forming a reference to memory that C may alias; (b) Wavefront, a neuro-symbolic static analyzer that orders a target's items by their dependencies, including those that casts and type-erased pointers hide; and (c) ffimap, a rustc-based analysis that maps the unsafe surface of bindings.
  On libgit2 and ffmpeg, with one developer in the loop, Crustify generated safe bindings for 41.9% and 42.8% of their public APIs in about 51.9 and 58.9 hours. On the interface consumers are expected to use, only 1.6% and 0.4% of the bindings' public functions are unsafe, and only 0.1% and 0.6% have a raw pointer in their signature. Their tests cover 98.92% and 99.07% of the Rust code and 45.95% and 67.20% of libgit2 and of ffmpeg's libavutil, and the reviewers fixed 8 and 13 defects that caused UB reachable from Rust. To our knowledge, this is the first work to automate the generation of safe Rust bindings for C libraries.

Software Engineering.title: LibEvoBench: Probing Temporal Knowledge Stratification in Code Generation Models
Software Engineering.summary: Large software projects often depend on older versions of libraries, even as APIs continue to evolve across releases. This creates a challenge for LLMs: they must maintain knowledge of multiple API versions, not merely the latest or most common one. However, current LLMs are trained on temporally mixed corpora and lack explicit mechanisms for such version-specific reasoning, leading to anachronistic errors - calling APIs as they exist in a different library version. To systematically evaluate this phenomenon, we introduce LibEvoBench, a multi-task benchmark spanning multiple versions of widely used Python libraries, along with a new metric, the Software Evolution Understanding Score (SEUS), to measure models' consistency when working with evolving APIs. Our results show that state-of-the-art models are largely version-oblivious: performance degrades for evolving APIs, while for stable APIs it remains the same across versions. Moreover, simply specifying the target version provides no benefit, while relevant documentation significantly boosts models' accuracy. These findings highlight a systematic limitation of current training paradigms and motivate new approaches for temporally grounded knowledge in code generation.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations and Datasets Track

Software Engineering.title: DM-Call: Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling with Cumulative Verification Feedback
Software Engineering.summary: Reliable function calling requires Large Language Models (LLMs) to select appropriate functions and generate arguments consistent with user intent. However, syntactically valid calls may still be semantically incorrect due to inappropriate function selection or mismatched arguments. In this paper, we propose Decision-Model-Guided Function Calling (DM-Call), a framework that combines local schema validation with separate decision-model verification of function selection and argument correctness. For rejected candidates, DM-Call accumulates verification probabilities, binary judgments, and schema errors across attempts. A hybrid feedback representation further combines numerical probabilities with verbal correctness labels to guide iterative refinement without executing external tools. Extensive evaluation across BFCL and API-Bank (first-call) demonstrates DM-Call boosts function-calling accuracy versus direct generation, at modest additional cost.

Software Engineering.title: PQC-Corpus: A Dataset of Linked Development Histories for Post-Quantum Cryptography
Software Engineering.summary: As post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standards evolve, developers must adapt implementations, tests, and protocols. Studying this work requires connecting code changes to problem reports and developer reviews. We present PQC-Corpus, a dataset of linked development histories from 179 public GitHub repositories, spanning cryptographic libraries and general-purpose projects. It connects issues and closing pull requests to commits and full patches, with comments and reviews. We combine Git histories with GitHub threads, reconstruct 23 pull-request commit lists truncated at 250 entries, and check file integrity, schemas, and links. Two annotators independently assessed sampled commits and issues ($κ=0.86$ and $0.93$), labeling about seven in ten commits and two in three issues PQC-related within these samples. We provide full and filtered views with removal ledgers, and quantify how filtering reduces links from issues to commits. A patch-free view supports inspection before downloading patches, while traversal scripts follow issues to code changes. We make the dataset and collector publicly available for studies of specification changes, hybrid interoperability, cryptographic review, and migration assistance.

Software Engineering.title: VeriContest: A Competitive-Programming Benchmark for Verifiable Code Generation
Software Engineering.summary: Large language models can generate useful code from natural language, but their outputs come without correctness guarantees. Verifiable code generation offers a path beyond testing by requiring models to produce not only executable code, but also formal specifications and machine-checkable proofs. Progress in this direction, however, is difficult to measure: existing benchmarks are often small, cover only part of the pipeline, lack ground-truth proofs or rigorous specification validation, or target verification settings far from mainstream software development. We present VeriContest, a benchmark of 1,006 competitive-programming problems from LeetCode and Codeforces for verifiable code generation in Rust with Verus. Each problem includes a natural language description, expert-validated formal specifications, judge-accepted Rust code, Verus-checked proofs, and positive and negative test suites. VeriContest is constructed through a three-phase pipeline that scales from manually verified seed problems to semi-automated expansion with human-in-the-loop review. To strengthen benchmark quality, we also use testing to validate postcondition completeness. VeriContest supports both isolated and compositional evaluation of specification, code, and proof generation, and end-to-end verified program synthesis. Evaluating ten state-of-the-art models reveals a sharp gap between ordinary coding and verifiable code generation: the strongest model reaches 97.51% on natural-language-to-code generation, but only 57.16% on specification generation, 13.82% on proof generation, and 6.76% end-to-end. These results identify proof and specification generation as the central bottlenecks for current models and establish VeriContest as a rigorous platform for evaluating and training future systems that generate code with machine-checkable correctness.

Software Engineering.title: Hybrid Source Code Change Impact Analysis
Software Engineering.summary: Change impact analysis (CIA) helps developers identify code entities impacted by their initial changes. While several approaches for CIA were proposed, they still struggle with either low precision or low recall, thereby increasing manual effort for developers to verify the results. Furthermore, limitations in the used datasets and experimental setups can bias the results reported by many CIA approaches. In this paper, we first address the dataset limitations by manually labeling 1,931 changed code entities stemming from 263 commits of 22 open-source Java projects. Next, we introduce two variants of katIA, our code change impact analysis approach that combines static impact analysis with the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). The first variant uses a single prompt (katIA-SP) for refining an initial static impact set while the second variant uses three specialized agents (katIA-MA). The evaluation with our curated dataset shows that katIA-SP with Gemini 2.5 Flash achieved an F1-score of 22.4% when matching impacted entities by their fully qualified names (FQN) and 27.0% when matching them by their class and entity names (CE). The latter shows an improvement of 2.0 percentage points over the state-of-the-art. This score is further improved by katIA-MA which, using Gemini 2.5 Flash, yields an FQN-matching F1-score of 29.1% and a CE-matching F1-score of 33.3%. While these improvements come at the cost of increased median generation time from 0.570 s to 11.214 s and median token usage from 1,235 to 6,462 tokens, the improved performance justifies the additional cost. The comparison of three LLMs using katIA-SP finds that Gemini 2.5 Flash is the most consistent model. These results indicate that combining static impact analysis with LLM-based refinement, particularly with the multi-agent variant, can improve code change impact analysis.

Software Engineering.title: Designing LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems for Software Engineering Tasks: Quality Attributes, Design Patterns and Rationale
Software Engineering.summary: As the complexity of Software Engineering (SE) tasks continues to escalate, Multi-Agent Systems (MASs) have emerged as a focal point of research and practice due to their autonomy and scalability. Furthermore, through leveraging the reasoning and planning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), the application of LLM-based MASs in the field of SE is garnering increasing attention. However, there is no dedicated study that systematically explores the design of LLM-based MASs, including the Quality Attributes (QAs) on which designers mainly focus, the design patterns used by designers, and the rationale guiding the design of LLM-based MASs for SE tasks. To this end, we conducted a study to identify the QAs that LLM-based MASs for SE tasks focus on, the design patterns used in the MASs, and the design rationale for the MASs. We collected 106 papers on LLM-based MASs for SE tasks as the source. Our study shows that: (1) Code Generation is the most common SE task solved by LLM-based MASs among ten identified SE tasks, (2) Functional Suitability is the QA on which designers of LLM-based MASs pay the most attention, (3) Role-Based Cooperation is the design pattern most frequently employed among 16 patterns used to construct LLM-based MASs, and (4) Improving the Quality of Generated Code is the most common rationale behind the design of LLM-based MASs. Building on the study results, we presented the implications for the design of LLM-based MASs to support SE tasks.
Software Engineering.comment: 42 pages, 3 images, 12 tables, Manuscript submitted to a Journal (2026)

Software Engineering.title: Patch correctness in automated program repair: A five-dimensional evidence framework and cross-benchmark audit from classical repair to coding agents
Software Engineering.summary: Tests guide automated program repair and determine which candidate patches are reported as successful. Repository-level coding agents extend this feedback loop by generating tests and revising code after observing execution results. This technical report introduces a five-dimensional evidence profile and reporting protocol to audit how test observations support patch-correctness claims across classical repair systems and coding agents. We assemble an audit dataset of 39 benchmark and evaluation artifacts: 32 primary empirical studies, one institutional technical audit, and six prior taxonomic baselines. We code the 33 primary contributions along five dimensions: test provenance and exposure, behavioral scope, oracle basis and dependence, execution integrity, and label adjudication. The central distinction separates checks visible during repair search from evidence reserved for final assessment. Four worked comparative audits show how changed candidate populations, oracle rules, or execution budgets alter reported detection rates. Additional tests can expose missed faults while rejecting valid alternatives or reducing correct-repair yield under a fixed budget. Repository-level audits separate issue reproduction from candidate-patch discrimination and distinguish automated discrepancy detection from requirements-based adjudication. An evidence matrix links each coded decision to supporting passages and records shared benchmark ancestry. We specify a reporting protocol for repair benchmarks and maintenance pipelines that retains uncertain judgments and records validation cost alongside fault detection and valid-patch retention.
Software Engineering.comment: Technical report. 24 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Dataset and evidence matrix available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23639376

Software Engineering.title: SIExBench: A Benchmark for Automated Repair of Sensitive Information Exposure
Software Engineering.summary:
Modern software systems routinely process credentials, personal records, and other sensitive information. A sensitive information exposure (SIEx) defect makes such information accessible to an unauthorized actor and can cause serious and often irreversible disclosure. However, prior research has focused largely on detecting such exposures rather than repairing the underlying defects, and existing repository-level issue-resolution benchmarks do not specifically target this defect class. We present SIExBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark dedicated to automated repair of SIEx defects. SIExBench contains 161 execution-verified instances from 64 widely used Python and Java repositories, each with an issue report, buggy repository snapshot, developer patch, executable exposure and regression tests, and defect characterization.
  We evaluate six repair systems with three LLMs, yielding 18 configurations, and systematically analyze their overall effectiveness, performance across defect characteristics, and failure mechanisms. The strongest configuration resolves only 39.1% of the instances, while 40.4% remain unresolved by all 18 configurations. More importantly, 62.1% of unsuccessful attempts produce a valid patch that still leaves sensitive information exposed, making incomplete exposure removal a central challenge. Systems often generate plausible patches and modify relevant code without fully eliminating the exposure, indicating that effective repair must ensure that all relevant paths to sensitive-information exposure are closed. Overall, SIExBench provides a foundation for systematically evaluating and advancing automated repair of sensitive information exposure defects.

Software Engineering.title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
Software Engineering.summary: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.
Software Engineering.comment: NeurIPS 2026, Track on Evaluations and Datasets. 41 pages, 10 figures, 24 tables. Benchmark: https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench. Website: https://distdebug.com

Software Engineering.title: Porting Declarative UI to HarmonyOS: A Heuristic-guided Approach for lightweight LLMs
Software Engineering.summary:
As an emerging operating system, HarmonyOS has a significant demand for software migration, where the User Interface (UI) translation accounts for a critical link. However, recent UI development has shifted to declarative paradigms, e.g., Kotlin Jetpack Compose (KJC) for Android, SwiftUI for iOS, and ArkUI for HarmonyOS, making prior translation approaches inapplicable because they target either backend logic or legacy imperative UIs. Thus, related research is limited.
  To systematically evaluate KJC/SwiftUI-to-ArkUI migration, we build a parallel benchmark of 100 KJC and 100 SwiftUI files across eight scenarios, plus 52 real-world UI pages from nine open-source apps. Evaluating nine direct-translation setups (including diverse LLMs and agents), we find Compilation Success Rate (CSR) spans 0.00%-35.00%; common strategies (reference screenshots and compiler-guided repair) lift capable setups to 94.00%-99.00% CSR but fail on lightweight LLMs. By manually analyzing a 3,102-sample subset, deriving a regular-expression pattern for each failure family, and applying these patterns to generalize the resulting taxonomy to the full 29,593-sample set, we find residual errors rooted in (1) broken structure, (2) nonexistent APIs, and (3) missing resources (e.g., colors, strings, and icons).
  Accordingly, we propose ArkTrans, a declarative UI translation framework that maps these roots to deterministic structure supply, ArkUI knowledge and resource reference injection via a demonstration example, and iterative repair targeting residual errors, via four steps: Metadata Extraction, Skeleton Construction, LLM-driven Translation, and Compiler-Guided Iterative Repair. With Qwen3.6-27B, ArkTrans raises CSR from 0.00% to 70.00% on KJC and 64.00% on SwiftUI, achieving strong visual fidelity, and attains 65.63%/80.00% CSR on real-world pages, far outperforming the best common strategy at lower token cost.

Software Engineering.title: Spaghetti Architect: A Controlled Code Benchmark Generator, and What Its Own Comments Do to Model Scores
Software Engineering.summary: Code corpora mined from the wild cannot change one thing at a time: a program's behaviour, messiness and size vary together, and nothing marks the correct answer. We present Spaghetti Architect, a generator that turns a small JSON description of a program into deliberately messy programs in five languages. It compiles and runs every program, checks the output against a reference computed from the description, and labels each program by problem size and by messiness. This control lets us change one property at a time and still know the correct answer. The generator writes comments into its own output, so we first re-render identical code without them. Removing the comments lowers the refactoring score of all four models we tested, and lowers the weakest model's about ten times as much as the strongest model's; a pre-registered replication confirms the difference at a smaller magnitude. The comments also hide an effect: messiness leaves scores flat while they are present and lowers them on both tasks once they are gone. We therefore recommend evaluating on the comment-free rendering. Changing only problem size drives direct-answer aggregation accuracy to zero for every model, and changing only literal values moves scores by less than 0.012. The generator, the dataset and the evaluation records are open source.

Software Engineering.title: Motivators and Demotivators of Integrating Large Language Models in Software Engineering Education: An Exploratory Familiarity Allocation Framework
Software Engineering.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly influencing software engineering practice and education, yet little research has examined their systematic integration using stakeholder evidence and quantitative decision-support models. This study presents an exploratory familiarity-allocation framework for analyzing motivating and demotivating factors in LLM integration in software engineering education. Building on our earlier literature-based taxonomy, we evaluated 19 factors (nine motivators and ten demotivators) through a survey of 126 stakeholders from multiple countries. Naive Bayes and Logistic Regression were used to examine associations between factor ratings and high self-reported LLM familiarity. Both models reached an accuracy of 0.461, below the majority-class baseline, so their probabilities were used as exploratory relative scoring functions rather than individual-level predictions. These estimates were fed into a Genetic Algorithm with a defined allocation score to support Global Factor Allocation (GC), Local Factor Allocation (LC), and category-level Delta-Fitness analyses. The most highly rated motivators were Programming Assistance and Debugging Support, Personalized and Adaptive Learning, and AI as a Learning Partner. The most highly rated demotivators were Plagiarism and Intellectual Property Concerns, Over-Reliance on AI in Learning, and Reduced Critical Thinking and Problem-Solving. Under the fitted models and allocation assumptions, GC assigned higher levels to integrity- and governance-related factors, while LC revealed further pedagogical and risk-related patterns within categories. These configurations are exploratory scenarios, not validated implementation priorities or evidence of educational effectiveness, and classroom and institutional validation is needed before the framework can guide practice.

Software Engineering.title: Safe by Accident: Crash-Testing LLM-Written Code
Software Engineering.summary: Evaluations of LLM-written code run it once, in one environment, and credit the code with whatever passes. We show that this credit can belong to the environment. We crashed LLM-written backend code just before each database, file and email call, re-ran it as an operator would, and judged the result under two transaction modes of Python's sqlite3: the default, in which the library quietly opens a transaction, and autocommit, in which it does not. Across 9,100 solutions from ten models on 24 backend tasks, more than half (54%) of the database code that survives every crash in the default mode is left half-updated in autocommit mode. This holds for every model, and it hides in ordinary code, including with conn: blocks that look like transactions but open none. Telling the model that its connection is in autocommit mode does not change what the local code models write, while the API models' unsafe share falls by 30 points. Asking for crash safety helps every model, and strong models repair nearly all unsafe code, but often write safe code only when asked. Thus, much of the crash safety that LLM-written database code appears to have is borrowed from the library rather than designed into it, and a second test under a less forgiving configuration reveals the difference.

Software Engineering.title: What extraction cannot slim, and whether function injection can: a pre-registered study of 580 Java repositories
Software Engineering.summary: A method of 26 code lines or more reads as a Long Method, and Extract Method is the usual fix. Some long methods have no single-exit fix: a return cannot leave an extracted piece, a piece hands back one value, and some methods are knotted so that every cut is blocked. Function injection, as the OfficeFloor framework does it, cuts differently: each piece becomes a function the framework injects and sequences, an early return ends a function, and a function hands on several values. The framework's author pre-registered a test of whether it takes apart what extraction cannot. A stratified random sample of 580 open-source Java repositories, each pinned before AI coding assistants were in general use, was scanned by released tools whose cost models were fixed before the sample was drawn: 3,026,902 methods, 168,466 of them long. Single-exit extraction cannot slim 22.8% of the long methods. The registered hypothesis, that at least a quarter of those stuck methods are ones only function injection takes apart, is refuted: 22.2% (95% CI 20.3 to 24.3). Nearly half of the stuck methods are early-return methods the plan counts as conventionally fixable, and the split takes three in four of those apart as they stand. Where extraction would do, the split chooses injection and costs less for 29.0% against extraction wrapped as one function and 17.2% against plain extraction, almost always as a straight sequence of functions. An exploratory reading of the quarter of the stuck methods that neither takes apart finds a third of it tables and literals, long for their data rather than their logic, and most of the rest blocked by a jump inside a loop, by a nested statement too large to cut, or by values too many for any cut. Three registered studies are proposed: the classes as rules in the tools, a refinement per class, and the same measures on code written with AI assistants.
Software Engineering.comment: 19 pages, 1 figure, 10 tables. Pre-registered; every number regenerated by script. Replication package in the ancillary files and at https://github.com/officefloor/long-method-slim-study

Software Engineering.title: Mismeasuring the Life of a Line of Code: Lessons Learned the Hard Way
Software Engineering.summary: Studies of how long lines of code live, including lines written by AI agents, rest on choices that look technical: when a line counts as gone, what to do with lines still alive, whether to pool projects, and how to evaluate a model. We studied 32.5 million line births in 120 TypeScript repositories and got several of these choices wrong at first. For ten of them, we compare the result as we first computed it, or as commonly done, with the result after correction. All ten change conclusions, or would have. Six were our own mistakes. Counting moved and rewritten lines as dead shortens a line's median life from 3.0 years to 1.3. Counting any change as a death hides an outcome that can be predicted: within-project concordance falls from 0.71 to 0.56. Regressing observed lifetimes discards three quarters of the lines. Keeping rewritten lines at risk makes protective effects grow with age. Lines are born and removed together, so treating them as independent misleads twice: nine of fifteen effects look significant only under that assumption, and a split by file makes a barely predictable outcome look good (within-project concordance 0.71 instead of 0.61). After the corrections, removal depends on a line's age and project, but our models could barely rank it within a project. Local revision they could rank (0.71). Obvious cases aside, the top 1% of a project's new lines are revised at 2.3 times the base rate. Each pitfall leaves a symptom; we give a checklist.
Software Engineering.comment: 12 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Corrects results of arXiv:2606.04993

Software Engineering.title: DDBench: A Benchmark for Agentic Debugging on Distributed Systems
Software Engineering.summary: LLM-based coding agents have advanced rapidly on single-process SWE tasks, with frontier models now clustering in the high-70s on SWE-bench Verified. Distributed-system debugging, however, remains an under-explored regime: bugs span processes, nodes, and protocol interactions, with root causes rarely recoverable from source alone and brute-force exploration intractable across non-deterministic interleavings. This leaves two gaps in LLM and agent evaluation: no code-repair benchmark targets distributed-system bugs, and no controlled study isolates how much externally provided debugging context changes agent success on them. We introduce DDBench, a code-repair benchmark of 60 historical bugs mined from 13 open-source distributed systems, partitioned into three reasoning-scope tiers. DDBench evaluates every case under two matched conditions: a symptom-only condition where the agent receives only the bug symptom and repository, and a context-augmented condition where it additionally receives bounded debugging context (logs, traces, runtime state, and targeted code-investigation notes), isolating the effect of debugging context from model capability. The evaluation of 10 LLMs on DDBench reveals several findings. First, distributed debugging exercises a reasoning dimension that single-process benchmarks do not surface: models' pass rates span 45 pp, and pairwise bootstrap separates 6 of 15 top-tier model pairs at p < 0.05 on DDBench's hardest case-set. Second, bounded debugging context lifts aggregate pass rate by +19.0 pp, and the lift is asymmetric: weaker models gain more in pass rate, while stronger models gain more in efficiency. Third, debugging context requires careful curation, as even faithful debugging context can anchor a strong model on the wrong layer of the system when its observation sits far from the fault.
Software Engineering.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages for the main body (7 figures, 3 tables), 23 pages for the appendix

Software Engineering.title: Toward an Evidence-Based Template for Agent Instruction Files: An Empirical Study of Adoption, Consistency, and Maintenance
Software Engineering.summary: AI coding agents rely on repository-level instruction files to understand project conventions, development workflows, and constraints. However, different agents support different instruction formats, and limited empirical evidence exists about how these files are adopted, what information they contain, whether coexisting formats provide consistent guidance, and how they are maintained. We conduct an empirical study of 3,387 instruction files from 1,000 GitHub repositories across four formats: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, GitHub Copilot instructions, and Cursor rules. We find that 42.2% of instruction-bearing repositories in the higher-popularity cohort maintain multiple formats. Among 386 manually examined pairs of corresponding sections, 16.1% provide divergent guidance. Our maintenance analysis further shows that 40.4% of the analyzed files have only one recorded modification event and that maintenance patterns differ across formats. Based on category prevalence and category addition ratios (CAR), we derive an evidence-based template containing ten Required, four Gap, and two Recommended categories. In an exploratory generation experiment, explicit template guidance increases structural category coverage from 18.7% to 82.8%. We further introduce AGIT-Instruct, a benchmark for evaluating instruction-file generation through structural coverage and content alignment. Across four generation configurations, retrieval-augmented generation achieves the highest full-file ROUGE-1 F1 of 0.459. A manual assessment of 278 generated category instances finds that 19.4% fully preserve and 61.2% partially preserve developer-written intent. Our findings provide empirical guidance for organizing and maintaining agent instruction

Software Engineering.title: SpreadsheetBench 2: Evaluating Agents on End-to-End Business Spreadsheet Workflows
Software Engineering.summary: Spreadsheets are widely used for business analysis, financial modeling, reporting, and decision-making. However, most existing spreadsheet benchmarks evaluate isolated operations such as single-formula generation or local cell edits, and therefore fail to capture end-to-end workflows in realistic business settings. We introduce \textsc{SpreadsheetBench 2}, a workflow-level benchmark for spreadsheet agents that covers three task categories: generation, debugging, and visualization. The benchmark is constructed from authentic business data, including financial reports and corporate filings, and is annotated and validated by domain experts. The benchmark contains 321 tasks; each instance averages 11.8 worksheets and requires 593.5 cell modifications, reflecting large multi-sheet workbooks with cross-sheet dependencies. We evaluate eight frontier large language models under a unified multi-turn agent scaffold, and additionally include several LLM-based spreadsheet products as complementary baselines. Results show that current systems remain far from reliable on real-world workflows: the best model achieves 34.89\% overall task accuracy, and debugging accuracy is as low as 12.00\%. Trajectory analysis and a failure taxonomy further indicate that insufficient spreadsheet inspection and incorrect target-cell selection are the dominant bottlenecks. Together, these findings position \textsc{SpreadsheetBench 2} as a challenging testbed for advancing reliable spreadsheet automation. Project page: https://spreadsheetbench.github.io/

Software Engineering.title: CRANE: Constrained Reasoning Injection for Code Agents via Nullspace Editing
Software Engineering.summary: Code agents must both reason over long-horizon repository state and obey strict tool-use protocols. In paired Instruct/Thinking checkpoints, these capabilities are complementary but misaligned. The Instruct model is concise and tool-disciplined, whereas the Thinking model offers stronger planning and recovery behavior but often over-deliberates and degrades agent performance. We present CRANE (Constrained Reasoning Injection for Code Agents via Nullspace Editing), a training-free parameter-editing method that treats the Thinking-Instruct delta as a directional pool of candidate reasoning edits for the Instruct backbone. CRANE combines magnitude thresholding to denoise the delta, a Conservative Taylor Gate to retain edits that are jointly beneficial for reasoning transfer and tool-use preservation, and Graduated Sigmoidal Projection to suppress format-critical update directions. By merging paired Instruct and Thinking checkpoints, CRANE delivers strong gains over either individual model while preserving Instruct-level efficiency: on Roo-Eval it achieves pass1 of 66.2% (+19.5%) for Qwen3-30B-A3B and 81.5% (+8.7%) for Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B; on SWE-bench-Verified it resolves up to 14 additional instances at both scales (122/500 and 180/500); and on Terminal-Bench v2 it improves pass1/pass5 by up to 2.3%/7.8%, reaching 7.6%/17.9% and 14.8%/30.3%, respectively, consistently outperforming alternative merging strategies across all three benchmarks.

Software Engineering.title: CWE-bench: Refocusing Agentic Security from Exploitation to Defense
Software Engineering.summary: Cybersecurity evaluations of AI agents have focused largely on offense, yet a working exploit does not show that an agent can make software safe. An attacker needs to exploit only one vulnerability; a defender must find and fix all of them. We introduce CWE-bench, a benchmark of 250 repository audit-and-repair tasks spanning 185 CWE types and eight languages, grouped into ten weakness classes. We release 100 tasks publicly and keep 150 held out. Agents are given a repository to audit and a description of its threat model, but are not told the weakness, where it occurs, or how many vulnerable sites there are. Each patch must block the exploit while preserving original functionality, as checked by a deterministic programmatic verifier. Verifiers were curated with panels of agentic judges and reviewed by hand, so that they reject incomplete repairs without penalizing correct ones. The best agent reaches 67% pass@1 and 79% pass@4. We further conduct analyses showing that (i) agents with similar pass@1 differ widely in retry gains and cost, and (ii) no single agent is best across languages or weakness classes. As the offensive capabilities of agents improve, CWE-bench provides a broad and rigorous measure of whether their defensive capabilities keep pace.

Software Engineering.title: SkillOps: Managing LLM Agent Skill Libraries as Self-Maintaining Software Ecosystems
Software Engineering.summary: Large language model agents increasingly rely on skill libraries for multi-step tasks, yet these libraries can accumulate persistent defects as skills are added, reused, patched, and linked to changing dependencies. We call this failure mode skill technical debt: library-level defects that may not break a single skill locally but can harm future retrieval, composition, and execution. Existing skill-based agents mainly focus on task-time retrieval, planning, and repair, while library-time maintenance remains underexplored. We propose SkillOps, a method-agnostic plug-in framework for maintaining skill libraries. SkillOps represents each skill as a typed Skill Contract (P, O, A, V, F), organizes skills with a Hierarchical Skill Ecosystem Graph, and diagnoses library health across utility, compatibility, risk, and validation dimensions. Given a raw skill library, SkillOps produces a maintained library that can be used by existing retrieval or planning agents without changing their internal code. On ALFWorld, SkillOps achieves 79.5 percent task success as a standalone agent, outperforming the strongest baseline by 8.8 percentage points with no additional task-time large language model calls. As a plug-in layer, it improves retrieval-heavy baselines by 0.68 to 2.90 percentage points. The current rule-based maintenance implementation uses nearly zero library-time large language model calls or tokens, showing that skill-library maintenance can be added as a low-overhead architectural layer.

Software Engineering.title: Crustify: Repository-Level Generation of Safe Rust Bindings with LLM Agents and Coverage-Guided Testing
Software Engineering.summary:
Wrapping C code in a safe Rust interface lets Rust applications use it without writing unsafe code, until the code itself is migrated to Rust. Such bindings are tedious and error-prone to write, however: their internals use unsafe code that the Rust compiler does not check, so a single mistake can introduce undefined behavior (UB), and they have so far been written mostly by hand.
  We present Crustify, an agentic co-translator that generates safe Rust bindings for repository-level C libraries. Crustify schedules a target's types and symbols into dependency-ordered waves of independent batches that agents bind concurrently. Its agents derive the ownership and lifecycle contract of every pointer and type they wrap, check each binding with coverage-guided equivalence and UB tests under sanitizers and Miri, and review every wave.
